artigo.texto: BYD Atto 3 Gets New Atlantis Gray Colour Option in India BYD has replaced Surf Blue with Atlantis Gray on the Atto 3, which continues to offer two battery options, up to 521km of claimed range, and the same equipment list. BYD has introduced a new colour option for the Atto 3 electric SUV in India, with Atlantis Gray replacing the previously available Surf Blue. The change is limited to the exterior colour palette, with no reported updates to the SUV's features, battery packs, or performance. The Atto 3 continues to be offered in multiple variants. Also Read: BYD Denza India Entry Confirmed; Here's What to Expect BYD Atto 3: What's Changed? With Surf Blue discontinued, the BYD Atto 3 is now available in four colours: Atlantis Gray, Cosmos Black, Ski White and Harbour Grey. The SUV retains its existing design, including full-LED lighting, chrome and black exterior elements, a panoramic sunroof and either 17-inch or 18-inch wheels, depending on the variant. BYD Atto 3: Battery The electric SUV is available with 49.92kWh and 60.48kWh battery packs. Both use an electric motor that develops 201bhp and 300Nm of torque. The smaller battery offers an ARAI-certified range of 468km, while the larger unit has a claimed range of 521km. BYD claims a 0-100km/h acceleration time of 7.3 seconds. For charging, the smaller battery supports DC fast charging at up to 70kW, while the larger pack supports up to 80kW. The cabin features a 12.8-inch rotating touchscreen, wireless smartphone connectivity, wireless charging and a six-speaker audio system. Other equipment includes a powered tailgate, a 360-degree camera, an NFC key card, tyre pressure monitoring and auto-hold. The front seats are electrically adjustable, with six-way adjustment for the driver and four-way adjustment for the front passenger. Safety equipment comprises seven airbags, Level 2 advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and disc brakes on all four wheels, with ventilated discs at the front. The BYD Atto 3 is priced from Rs 24.99 lakh to Rs 34.49 lakh (ex-showroom), depending on the variant. The new colour has not brought a price increase, and the SUV's existing specifications remain unchanged.

artigo.texto: BYD India Introduces Limited-Edition Sealion 7 Premium with New Interior The BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition continues to deliver 308.4 bhp and a claimed 567km NEDC range, alongside a 15.6-inch touchscreen and 11 airbags. BYD India has launched the Sealion 7 Festive Edition at Rs 50.60 lakh (ex-showroom), adding a new interior colour combination to its electric SUV range for the festive season. The limited-edition model is based on the Sealion 7 Premium and will be available in only 150 units. Its main change is the Tan and Black cabin, which distinguishes it from the standard version. The new edition retains the Premium variant’s battery, performance figures, equipment, and safety features, meaning the update focuses on the cabin rather than mechanical changes. Also Read: BYD Denza India Entry Confirmed; Here's What to Expect BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition: What's New? Apart from the Tan and Black interior, the rest of the cabin equipment remains unchanged, including quilted Nappa leather seats, a 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen, a panoramic glass roof with an electric sunshade, and a head-up display. BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition: Battery, Range and Performance The BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition uses the same 82.56kWh Blade Battery as the Premium variant. The battery incorporates BYD's Cell-to-Body (CTB) technology, which integrates the battery structure with the vehicle's body, while Intelligent Torque Adaptation Control (iTAC) manages torque distribution. The electric SUV produces 308.4bhp and 380Nm of torque. BYD claims a 0-100km/h acceleration time of 6.7 seconds and a range of 567km under the NEDC test cycle. BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition: Safety and Features Safety equipment includes 11 airbags, and the Sealion 7 has received a five-star safety rating from Euro NCAP. The SUV also offers a range of technology and comfort features, including the rotating infotainment display and head-up display. artigo.texto: Reeleito, Lula quer IA brasileira; promete incentivar data centers e acelerar regulação das big techs O discurso do presidente reeleito, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, logo depois dos resultados teve boa parte dedicada à economia digital. Em seu primeiro discurso após ser reeleito com 51,79% dos votos no domingo (25), Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) tratou como prioridade no seu quarto mandato a regulação das big techs e o fomento de uma inteligência artificial que fale português. Ao falar sobre as big techs, Lula afirmou ter vencido a “intromissão das plataformas digitais” e disse que vai trabalhar pela regulação das big techs. “Não é possível que a gente não tenha consciência que o crime no mundo digital tem que ser tratado igual o crime na vida real. Nós não podemos ter empresas monstruosas de grandes, ganhando milhões e bilhões, não pagando nenhum imposto pra esse país e tentando direcionar o resultado eleitoral desse país.”, disse. O projeto de regulamentação das Big Techs está no Congresso Nacional e travou por conta das eleições. Ao longo das últimas semanas, a campanha do petista acusou a Meta, empresa que controla o Instagram, Facebook e WhatsApp, de tentar interferir no processo eleitoral brasileiro em benefício da candidatura de Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula falou que vai incentivar os data centers e é bom lembrar que a regulamentação do Redata, programa de benefícios está no Poder Executivo para ser regulamentado. “Quero investir em economia digital, economia verde e economia criativa”, sinalizou. Lula também falou sobre Inteligência Artificial. No seu discurso, o presidente reeleito sustentou que vai reforçar o ensino de matemática e engenharia nas escolas. “Iremos ensinar mais matemática, mais engenharia, porque eu não quero ficar dependendo de inteligência artificial chinesa ou americana, eu quero criar uma brasileira. Nós temos que aproveitar o potencial energético de um país que talvez seja o que tem a maior capacidade de energia renovável, pra trazer pra cá os data centers necessários para acumular também os nossos dados pro Brasil”, afirmou. “Nós queremos fazer desse país um país que pare de ser um país em via de desenvolvimento e se transforme num país desenvolvido. Nós vamos exercitar o potencial criativo desse povo. Deixar de ser um país periférico. Nós queremos ser um país central nas decisões políticas, econômicas e na decisão pela paz”, disse Lula.

artigo.texto: Data Centers Bring Boom Times, But Will Gains Last? Data center projects can bring major capital investment to smaller markets, but lasting economic returns depend on realistic job expectations and protection against public cost exposure. Data center expansion is giving smaller US communities access to major investment opportunities, but it is also testing their ability to support power-intensive developments and secure lasting economic benefits. For local leaders, the calculation extends beyond the size of a construction budget or a headline investment announcement. Utility capacity, workforce availability, water resources, and the allocation of infrastructure costs can determine whether a project strengthens the local economy or leaves residents carrying expenses that outlast the initial building boom. A report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility and Heartland Forward examines these investment-readiness challenges across smaller communities. While the analysis addresses economic development broadly, it emphasizes the infrastructure and institutional capacity required to absorb major investment. “One of the central findings of our research is that attracting investment and generating lasting economic value are not necessarily the same thing,” Dominic Williams, a report author and senior expert at consulting firm McKinsey, told Data Center Knowledge. Looking Past the Headline Investment The report focuses on micropolitan communities with urban cores of 10,000 to 49,999 residents. Its framework assesses economic conditions, community assets and systems, and coordination among economic development institutions. Williams said smaller communities often have fewer institutions and less redundancy, making infrastructure or workforce gaps particularly consequential when a large project arrives. “Local leaders should take a comprehensive view of the costs and benefits associated with any potential investment, rather than focusing exclusively on the headline capital expenditure or the number of jobs announced,” he said. For data center proposals, that means distinguishing construction activity from ongoing employment and considering whether incentives or public infrastructure spending would produce greater benefits elsewhere. “A large construction project may generate substantial near-term activity but relatively fewer permanent positions once operational,” Williams said. Power Availability Pushes Development into Smaller Markets Developers’ search for sites they can bring online is widening the geography of data center investment, according to Sean Farney, vice president of data center strategy at commercial real estate services firm JLL. “With time-to-revenue driving site selection, the gulf between small and large cities vis-à-vis new development has shrunk considerably,” he told Data Center Knowledge. Power constraints, community opposition, and market saturation have pushed developers toward alternative locations. Farney pointed to activity in Abilene, Texas, Fort Wayne, Indiana, and Wisconsin’s Lake Michigan corridor. He argued that communities should account for spending generated by ongoing operations alongside construction and direct employment. Facilities require mechanical, electrical, and plumbing maintenance, as well as security, cleaning, and other services throughout their operating lives. “The spend just starts with construction,” Farney said. For local businesses, the opportunity includes securing recurring service contracts. Farney also identified spending on hotels, restaurants, and housing, as well as tax revenue and infrastructure improvements, as components of the economic benefits communities should evaluate. Measuring What Actually Stays Local Those opportunities require scrutiny of which benefits will remain in the community, Ruthbea Yesner, group vice president for worldwide public sector at analyst firm IDC, told Data Center Knowledge. “The deciding factors are power, broadband, and water, not land or tax appetite,” she said. Communities risk overextending themselves when they accept projects before utilities commit to supply and distribution upgrades required to support them. Water availability and workforce capacity also need to be assessed before development proceeds. Yesner cautioned against treating construction employment as a permanent expansion of the local jobs base. Workers may need to relocate to find comparable employment after a facility is completed, while direct operating teams can be relatively small. “My opinion is that small cities often undervalue what they are offering and potentially overvalue what they are receiving,” she said. Yesner recommended that communities enter negotiations with specific infrastructure priorities in mind. Local leaders should examine opportunities for electrical contractors, HVAC providers, fiber businesses, and other suppliers, while avoiding the assumption that broader industry-wide employment effects will necessarily materialize locally. Locking in Benefits Beyond the Build Yesner advised communities to use written infrastructure commitments, public reporting on resource consumption, and protections against stalled projects. Potential safeguards include incentive clawbacks, cost-overrun sharing arrangements, and bonds covering decommissioning and site restoration. Williams similarly recommended linking incentives to verified investment milestones and establishing developers’ responsibilities for infrastructure upgrades. “Communities should also consider how infrastructure investments can serve broader local needs rather than being designed exclusively around a single development,” Williams added. Workforce partnerships can extend the benefits. artigo.texto: The Power Challenge Behind Hyperscale AI Expansion The number of new AI data center projects being announced continues to far outpace the number delayed by local opposition. The power grid is straining under the ambitions of hyperscale AI data center developers. Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Google have increased their data center investment roughly tenfold over the past eight years, according to Industrial Info Resources (IIR). Up from a combined $64 billion in 2018, their announced spending is expected to exceed $700 billion this year. “Twelve straight months of new project announcements with spending running consistently elevated indicates a structural, multiyear theme of digital infrastructure buildout that is set to continue for the foreseeable future,” said Shane Mullins, an analyst with IIR at the Data Center World Power event in September 2026. Community Opposition Grows, but Project Momentum Holds The rapid expansion of data center development, fueled in large part by AI demand, has whipped up a growing wave of community resistance. According to IIR, more than 500 data center moratoria are on record across 42 states. New Jersey and Michigan lead with 41 and 36, respectively. New York has enacted a statewide ban on new data centers larger than 50 MW, at least temporarily, while Texas has paused new grid interconnections as it works through about 200 GW of requests. “$130 billion in projects were rejected in Q1 of 2026 alone, more than the total rejected for the whole of 2025,” Mullins said. “The number of opposition groups has more than doubled over the past year.” Even so, resistance has slowed only a fraction of the broader AI infrastructure buildout. Capital continues to pour into the sector. IIR data show at least $400 billion per month in newly announced data center projects globally since April 2026, with May exceeding $650 billion. That has pushed cumulative capex beyond $7 trillion. In the US and Canada alone, that pipeline amounts to roughly $4.75 trillion and more than 4,250 planned or in-progress data center projects. Texas accounts for nearly $1.25 trillion of that total. Altogether, more than 400 GW of new data center load is in planning, and almost 100 US sites are being designed for at least 1 GW. Where Will the Power Come From? The scale of the challenge is already visible. The US now has 53 GW of operational data center load, up from 23 GW in 2023. Another 42 GW has been approved or is under construction. That could push data center electricity demand from 35 GW in 2024 to 125 GW by 2030. Grid planners have struggled to keep up. In 2022, US planners projected that the country would need 24 GW of additional electricity demand within a decade. By 2025, that forecast has climbed nearly sevenfold, to 166 GW. As a result, hyperscalers and other developers are increasingly being pushed to build, own, or co-develop power generation. Gas turbines remain the preferred option for projects that need to scale beyond 1 GW. But turbine manufacturers are facing capacity constraints of their own. GE Vernova, Mitsubishi Power, and Siemens Energy are sold out of larger turbines through 2029, with some orders now stretching into 2031. All three are expanding production, while other suppliers are offering fuel cells, reciprocating gas engines, and jet engines as faster alternatives. “If you need more than 300 MW and the utility queue says 2034, building or contracting for your own gas plant is the fastest and most certain path to power,” Mullins said. Natural Gas Reemerges in the AI Power Mix AI data center growth has reshaped the North American power market. In 2022, wind and especially solar were ascendant, and some analysts predicted the end of gas turbine sales in North America. Solar project announcements continue to rise, but so does interest in natural gas generation and battery energy storage systems (BESS). IIR estimates that $228 billion in new natural gas power plant projects are currently in play. Hyperscalers and AI data center developers are, in practice, largely power-source agnostic. Most organizations want clean energy, but the need for reliable power now is taking precedence. That has contributed to renewed investment in coal plants scheduled for retirement, as operators seek to keep them running for a few more years. Older natural gas plants are also being upgraded to increase output. “Natural gas is filling the AI data center demand gap, with 347 grassroots, expansion, and conversion projects,” said IIR analyst Britt Burt. “Gas is the fastest, most reliable path to new dispatchable capacity.” According to IIR, the North American power industry could attract more than $1.5 trillion in investment across nearly 7,000 planned projects. But the story is not only about gas. Nuclear energy now accounts for 111 projects worth $311.4 billion, including 61 small modular reactors (SMRs) as well as several nuclear plant restarts. Meanwhile, renewables continue to expand. One of the fastest-growing combinations is solar paired with BESS, which extends solar’s usefulness beyond sunset and improves dispatchability. IIR counts 701 BESS projects worth almost $200 billion. Wind development has slowed, and offshore wind may continue to fade in the US, but onshore wind remains active. Speed to Power Is Reshaping Energy Strategy The same set of constraints is shaping every energy source: interconnection delays, labor and equipment shortages, grid congestion, limited transmission capacity, and increasing community opposition. In that environment, data center developers are pursuing whatever path offers the fastest, most reliable route to power at the required scale. “AI and data center buildout, reshored manufacturing, and an aging generation fleet are driving electricity demand growth not seen in a generation,” Burt said. “This is one of the broadest capital cycles the US and Canadian power sectors have seen in decades.”

Mais uma semana que começa com a nossa lista de indicações, para te ajudar a escolher o que jogar nos próximos dias. O destaque dessa vez é Battlefield 6, game mais recente da famosa franquia FPS da Electronic Arts que está de graça para assinantes do serviço Xbox Game Pass Ultimate.
Outro destaque é Days Gone Remastered. A versão remasterizada do game de mundo aberto, onde é preciso sobreviver a um apocalipse zumbi, está em promoção na PlayStation Store. Confira a lista completa de indicações de jogos da semana!
PlayStation 4 - Horizon Forbidden West
Horizon Forbidden West é o segundo game da franquia de mundo aberto desenvolvido pela Guerrilla Games. A história acompanha mais uma vez Aloy, uma caçadora que viaja para o Oeste Proibido para investigar uma praga que ameaça a vida na Terra. Durante a jornada, o jogador encontra novas tribos, explora ruínas antigas e enfrenta diferentes tipos de máquinas em um ecossistema diversificado.
O título está disponível de graça para os assinantes dos planos PS Plus Extra e Deluxe. Esta é uma excelente oportunidade para os membros do serviço aproveitarem a sequência direta da franquia sem custo adicional no PS4.
PlayStation 5 - Days Gone Remastered
Days Gone Remastered é um título de ação e sobrevivência em mundo aberto focado na exploração com veículos e combate contra zumbis. Nele, você controla Deacon St. John, um caçador de recompensas que viaja de moto por uma versão pós-apocalíptica do estado de Oregon, nos Estados Unidos. A principal mecânica envolve o gerenciamento de recursos, a manutenção da motocicleta e o confronto direto contra hordas de infectados.
Na PlayStation Store, o jogo está em promoção por R$ 99,80, o que representa um desconto de 60% em relação ao seu valor original. A versão remasterizada para PS5 traz melhorias na parte visual e no desempenho.
Xbox One - Fallout 4
Fallout 4 é o capítulo mais recente da franquia de RPG de ação desenvolvido pela Bethesda. A história começa após um evento nuclear, onde o protagonista acorda de um congelamento criogênico no Refúgio 111 e sai em busca do seu filho desaparecido na região de Boston. O jogo oferece sistemas de construção de bases, modificação de equipamentos e interação direta com diferentes facções que disputam o controle do território.
O título pode ser adquirido na loja oficial do Xbox por R$ 24,98, um desconto de cerca de 75%. O momento perfeito para conferir um dos títulos mais aclamados da série, pagando muito pouco por isso.
Xbox Series S / X - Battlefield 6
Battlefield 6 é o novo game da série de tiro em primeira pessoa focado em combates multijogador em larga escala. A experiência coloca os jogadores em mapas gigantes, com suporte a veículos terrestres e aéreos, além de apresentar estruturas destrutíveis que mudam a dinâmica das partidas em tempo real. O título inclui uma campanha principal e diversos modos de jogo online.

On Tuesday morning, Zsolt Tárkányi, a member of the National Assembly from TISZA, published seven pages of documents on social media regarding the agreement signed for the Chinese battery factory in Debrecen (eastern Hungary), Világgazdaság reported.
The tone of the post suggests that this politician strongly disapproves of what the Orbán government promised the world’s largest battery manufacturer to persuade it to build its next plant in Hungary. However, upon reviewing the letter of intent, no glaringly unusual promises can be found in it; rather, it can be concluded that the previous FIDESZ-KDNP-led cabinet sought to make a good offer to the Chinese side.
This is, of course, no coincidence, since when this agreement was reached, CATL was considering a massive investment
totaling 7.3 billion euros to build a battery manufacturing plant with an annual capacity of 100 GWh.
The Hungarian government, for its part, expressed its intention to support the implementation of the planned investment in Hungary at the priority site in Debrecen that CATL was considering. This is because the Chinese side had previously considered Hungary as a potential investment location after deciding to expand its manufacturing presence outside of China.
The fact that CATL ultimately chose Debrecen was by no means a foregone conclusion, as several European countries—including Western ones—were competing for the project.
In other words, the Orbán government’s proposal deserves to be evaluated from this perspective: it fought hard to win the Chinese company’s favor in a highly competitive situation, securing a commitment to invest more than 2,600 billion forints here.
Hungary may have caught the attention of the Chinese because, by that time, it had already become one of the most attractive destinations for direct foreign investment (FDI) by major battery manufacturers. According to the Orbán government’s view, the related large-scale investment projects contribute significantly to the country’s economic development.
In addition, they have a substantial impact on long-term employment, technology transfer, and cluster effects, as well as stimulating industrial and technological development.
It is a fact that, thanks to FDI, Hungary’s innovation performance has improved rapidly and significantly in recent years. Zsolt Tárkányi, however, focuses not on this but on the fact that the Chinese investment was granted VIP status. In reality, though, this simply refers to a completely standard category.
The point is that with the establishment of the Debrecen Southern Industrial Park in 2015, Debrecen committed itself to attracting future industrial investments to boost economic growth in the region and in Hungary.

artigo.texto: O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) destacou o potencial brasileiro de energia renovável para atrair data centers ao país em seu primeiro discurso após a vitória nas eleições presidenciais, na noite de domingo, 25 de outubro. Reeleito para um novo mandato de quatro anos, Lula também defendeu o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial nacional e a destinação de parte da capacidade dos centros de processamento de dados para atender à demanda brasileira. “Temos que aproveitar o potencial energético de um país que talvez seja o que tenha mais capacidade de energia renovável”, afirmou o presidente, ao defender a instalação de data centers no Brasil. >> Relembre os planos de Lula para o setor energético Lula disse ainda que as empresas terão de reservar parte dessas estruturas para informações brasileiras. A declaração ocorreu durante um trecho do discurso dedicado à educação e ao desenvolvimento tecnológico. “Eu não quero ficar dependendo da inteligência artificial chinesa ou americana, eu quero criar uma brasileira”, afirmou. O presidente também defendeu investimentos na economia digital, na economia verde e na economia criativa, ao apresentar prioridades para o próximo mandato. Redata foi citado A atração de data centers faz parte da política do governo federal. Em setembro, Lula sancionou a Lei 15.504/2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), com incentivos fiscais para a instalação, modernização e ampliação dessas estruturas no país. O programa prevê a suspensão de tributos federais na aquisição de equipamentos e componentes utilizados nos empreendimentos, incluindo PIS/Cofins, Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI) e Imposto de Importação, observadas as condições previstas na legislação. Para acessar os benefícios, as empresas deverão atender à totalidade de sua demanda de energia elétrica por meio de contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução a partir de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A legislação também estabelece critérios de sustentabilidade e eficiência no consumo de água. Outra contrapartida prevista no Redata é a disponibilização ao mercado interno de pelo menos 10% dos serviços de processamento, armazenagem e tratamento de dados instalados com os incentivos. A capacidade poderá ser comercializada no Brasil ou cedida a instituições científicas e tecnológicas e ao poder público. A lei permite substituir essa obrigação por um investimento adicional equivalente a 10% do valor dos equipamentos adquiridos com o benefício fiscal em projetos de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. Independentemente dessa alternativa, as empresas deverão destinar 2% do valor das aquisições incentivadas a projetos de pesquisa e desenvolvimento tecnológico no país. Os compromissos de atendimento ao mercado interno e de investimentos em pesquisa poderão ser reduzidos em 20% para empreendimentos instalados nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste.

artigo.texto: O presidente reeleito do Brasil ,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, afirmou em seu primeiro discurso de vitória que as plataformas de redes sociais precisam ser reguladas. Em São Paulo nesta noite de domingo, 25, Lula afirmou que as eleições sofreram intervenção externa por meio dessas plataformas. Importante lembrar, o imbróglio entre a campanha do presidente e a Meta teve vários embates entre o primeiro e o segundo turno, desde a redução de alcance dos posts e a facilidade de criação de materiais de campanha com o Meta AI do concorrente, senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ). Essa diferença resultou em mais de uma reunião do TSE com a big tech pedindo paridade de armas no pleito. Com isso, Lula defendeu neste domingo: “Nós não podemos ter empresas monstruosas de grande, ganhando milhões e bilhões, não pagando nenhum imposto para esse país e tentando direcionar o resultado eleitoral”. Também afirmou que “os crimes no ambiente virtual devem ser tratados da mesma forma” do que os crimes no mundo físico. Às 23h37 com 100% das urnas apuradas, Lula estava com 51,79% e 64,2 milhões de votos. Por sua vez, o senador Bolsonaro obteve 48,21% com 59,8 milhões de votos. Ou seja, uma diferença de 4,4 milhões de votos, segundo dados confirmados pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). IA e Data Centers O presidente reeleito para o ciclo 2027-2030 ainda afirmou que vai incenticar a educação e o ensino voltado à engenharia para desenvolver a inteligência artificial brasileira. Em suas palavras, Lula disse que deseja criar uma IA brasileira, pois não quer depender de uma tecnologia chinesa ou norte-americana. Também propôs aproveitar a matriz energética renovável do Brasil para atrair data centers: “Nós temos que aproveitar o potencial energético de um país que talvez seja o que tenha mais capacidade de energia renovável para trazer para cá os data centers”, disse, ao defender a chegada dos centro de dados para garantir a soberania de dados nacional. “E essa gente vai ter que deixar uma parte do data center para as informações brasileiras. Nós queremos um país que pare de ser ‘em desenvolvimento’ para ser desenvolvido, como diz o Rafael (Fonteles, governador do Piauí), com muito investimento na economia digital, na economia verde e na economia ativa”, completou. Lula afirmou ainda que pretende estreitar a relação com o povo brasileiro por meio do digital e do mobile. Reforçou que agora está com um celular e que a comunicação digital vai ganhar um espaço muito grande, algo impulsionando pelo canal de WhatsApp Exército de Lula, que chegou a 10 milhões de usuários na sexta-feira, 23. O canal passou a ser o segundo maior do país, segundo levantamento feito pelo Mobile Time. Os dois temas foram reforçados em um segundo discurso aos eleitores na Avenida Paulista, em frente ao MASP, às 00h30 da segunda-feira, 26. Imagem principal: presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva discursa após vitória nas eleições 2026, no hotel Intercontinental. (crédito: Paulo Pinto/Agencia Brasil)

artigo.texto: Standing at the site of a future microgrid for Project Jupiter in Santa Teresa, Mahesh Thiagarajan, executive vice president and head of Oracle Cloud Infustructure, leads a tour of the data center site earlier this month. An environmental advocacy group’s attempt to halt progress on approval for a Southern New Mexico data center’s state air quality permit hit a roadblock Monday. Hearing officer James O. Browning, who was appointed in recent weeks to preside over the permit decision, refused Monday to dismiss Project Jupiter’s air quality permit application as “administratively incomplete,” despite a request from Santa Fe-based New Energy Economy. The permit is the main regulatory hurdle for the massive and controversial data center’s power source. As a result, buildings at the site remain without power as proceedings inch along. Browning’s decision follows the disclosure of emails from the Environment Department to Project Jupiter attorneys this month noting new modeling requested by agency staff showed higher concentrations of pollutants than emissions modeling the developers submitted earlier this year. In the wake of the Environment Department’s questions about emissions estimates, Oracle and Yucca Growth Infrastructure, the company developing the microgrid, announced additional changes to their design Oct. 14, which they said would cut emissions by about 35%. “This is a radical redesign of a complex fuel cell installation that the parties had already been struggling to understand before YGI purported to revise its application,” Christopher Dodd, counsel for New Energy Economy, said during Monday’s four-hour hearing, calling the application a “moving target” that presents a “direct affront to due process.” In the new design, Bloom Energy — the company behind the fuel cells that has faced scrutiny and investor lawsuits — says they will now only use 1,600 megawatts of what will amount to 2,462 allocated megawatts. Lindsay Leveen, a chemical engineer based in Northern California and longtime Bloom critic, questioned in an interview why the company would need 862 “redundant” megawatts. “There’s no way to account for the gap except for some crookery or some scheme,” said Leveen, who has called for an investigation into what he sees as an effort to shift fuel cell maintenance costs onto taxpayers. The Environment Department’s own counsel seemed to break with the data center’s developers in a Friday filing, writing that “material revisions at this late stage” meant the application was “not ready for primetime.” Nevertheless, Kelsea Sona, counsel for the department, said Monday they did not support dismissing the application. But she did not have an estimate for how long the department’s analysis of the modeling would take. The state Environment Department’s deadline to make a decision on the permit is currently set for Nov. 23, but it might be pushed to Dec. 18 to account for the 25-day state Supreme Court-mandated pause on proceedings. A public hearing — originally scheduled for September — will now start Dec. 7 in Sunland Park. While Browning said it was “premature” to change the schedule Monday, he added it might need to be revisited later as the department reviews the application — or if they do not get back to him on how long the technical review will take. “YGI cannot have it both ways: fundamentally redesign its facility while demanding that NMED, the public, and opposing parties rush to accommodate its corporate deadline,” New Energy Economy Executive Director Mariel Nanasi said in a statement. “Public health and due process must come before Project Jupiter’s timetable.” Fraudulent public comments Maslyn Locke, a staff attorney for the New Mexico Environmental Law Center, said Monday the revised application merits a new public comment period. But Jennifer Bradfute, counsel for Yucca Growth Infrastructure, argued meaningful public input had been established through “numerous public comments.” However, thousands of comments on the air quality permit application have been deemed fraudulent amid an ongoing New Mexico Department of Justice investigation. In an Oct. 14 letter to Environment Secretary James Kenney, Attorney General Raúl Torrez wrote a “substantial share” of the comments were “not sent by members of the public acting on their own.” He said about 60% of the comments, roughly 10,000 to 10,600, used the same pro-Jupiter form letter and came from about 9,000 email addresses. Filings will not be restricted On the other hand, developers argued the recent design shift claiming to decrease emissions by 35% did not constitute a significant change, and therefore did not warrant delaying the Dec. 7 hearing. Jennifer Biever, counsel for Yucca Growth Infrastructure, said during Monday’s hearing reducing emissions would improve air quality, rather than “impermissibly impact it.” “The purpose of the deadline was ultimately to protect the applicants so that these types of permit hearings don’t end up lasting for years,” Biever added. Amid a deluge of recent filings in the case, the state Environment Department asked Monday for them to be limited in some way. Browning said he would not impose restrictions on the number of filings parties submit, or how frequently they can submit them as “a courthouse always has to be open.” Julia Gentin is a reporter for The Las Cruces New Mexican, The Santa Fe New Mexican and Searchlight New Mexico through a partnership with Report for America, a national service program that places journalists into local newsrooms.

artigo.texto: India’s electric-vehicle battery manufacturing industry is growing with investments from Tata Group’s Agratas, Ola Electric and Amara Raja Energy & Mobility. These industries span from Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Telangana to Karnataka and Maharashtra, where manufacturers are set to build large-scale lithium-ion gigafactories and battery-pack assembly units to expand India’s EV supply chain, as well as create opportunities for industrial development, logistics and real estate growth. Gujarat India registered around 23 lakh electric-vehicle (EV) sales in 2025, up nearly 16% year-on-year, with electric vehicles accounting for around 8% of new vehicle registrations. Rising adoption is driving investment in domestic battery manufacturing, with Gujarat emerging as a major hub for large-scale production. The state’s key projects include Agratas in Sanand, set to develop a battery-cell facility with a planned first-phase capacity of 20 GWh annually and production slated for 2027. Reliance New Energy’s Jamnagar battery gigafactory will see first operations in 2026, with an initial capacity of 40 GWh annually, scalable to 100 GWh. Meanwhile, Toshiba, Denso and Suzuki’s TDSG venture adds to Gujarat’s lithium-ion battery manufacturing ecosystem. TDSG has already produced battery packs for more than one million vehicles, with an annual production capacity of 18 million battery cells, with a further expansion of 12 million cells planned. Its batteries serve hybrid vehicles, while Agratas and Reliance will pursue larger-scale battery-cell production and energy storage. Tamil Nadu Tamil Nadu is a major EV manufacturing hub with established automotive supply chains, as well as the electric two-wheeler industry. India recorded 24.52 lakh EV sales in FY2026, up 24.6% year-on-year, including 14.01 lakh electric two-wheelers. In Krishnagiri, Ola Electric’s Futurefactory spans around 417 acres, with annual vehicle production capacity of up to 10 lakh units, while its battery gigafactory has a targeted capacity of 20 GWh. The company had established 1 GWh of installed cell-manufacturing capacity under the government’s PLI scheme as of December 2025. In Hosur, Ather Energy operate electric two-wheeler and battery-pack manufacturing facilities and together they support demand for battery suppliers, component manufacturers, logistics facilities and industrial land across the Krishnagiri–Hosur belt. Telangana Telangana is strengthening its position in India’s EV battery supply chain, with investments in lithium-ion cell manufacturing, battery packs, and energy storage. At Divitipally in Mahabubnagar district, Amara Raja Energy & Mobility is developing its Giga Corridor across around 262 acres, with a planned investment of ₹9,500 crore and long-term capacity of 16 GWh for battery cells. The company inaugurated a 60 MWh Customer Qualification Plant in July 2026, backed by an investment of ₹500 crore, to validate lithium-ion cells before commercial-scale production. Its first major cell-manufacturing phase is targeting 2 GWh of capacity in 2027, while the wider project also includes battery-pack assembly and energy-storage solutions. The project is expected to enhance the Mahabubnagar–Hyderabad industrial belt, by attracting battery component suppliers, engineering operations and logistics infrastructure as India’s EV market expands. Karnataka Karnataka is strengthening its position in India’s battery industry, with lithium-ion cell manufacturing and battery technology development. Exide Energy Solutions, a wholly owned subsidiary of Exide Industries, commissioned Phase I of its Devanahalli, Bengaluru, facility in Sept 2026, with a capacity of 6 GWh annually. The company plans to expand the facility to 12 GWh across two phases, backed by a cumulative investment of ₹5,202 crore in the subsidiary as of March 2026. Bengaluru also has a substantial battery-pack assembly ecosystem, with more than 28 recorded operations cited in industry directories. As India’s lithium-ion battery demand grows from an estimated 20 GWh to 140-150 GWh by 2030, domestic cell production could help reduce import dependence and attract further investment in battery components, engineering and industrial infrastructure. Maharashtra Maharashtra is a major market for electric vehicles, with 2.79 lakh EVs sold in FY2026, including 34,139 electric passenger vehicles, a 100% year-on-year increase in the latter category. In Pune’s Chakan industrial belt, Mahindra & Mahindra has allocated ₹4,500 crore towards its EV manufacturing and battery assembly operations, as part of its wider ₹16,000-crore investment plan for FY2022-FY2027. Its dedicated EV facility occupies around 88,000 sq m, within the larger Chakan manufacturing hub spanning 657 acres, and has an initial annual production target of 90,000 electric SUVs, scalable to 1.2 lakh units. Hindalco invested ₹500 crore in a five-acre Chakan facility to manufacture aluminium battery enclosures, with an initial capacity of 80,000 units annually and plans to double it to 1.6 lakh. These investments reinforce Pune’s role in EV assembly, battery integration and component manufacturing, supporting demand for industrial space and logistics infrastructure. NCR The National Capital Region (NCR), particularly Gurugram and Noida, is developing a supporting ecosystem for India’s EV battery industry, with a focus on battery recycling, critical mineral recovery and battery solutions. BatX Energies, headquartered in Gurugram, operate a battery recycling facility at Sikandrabad in Uttar Pradesh with processing capacity up to 5,100 tonnes annually. Its technology recovers lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese from used lithium-ion batteries, with reported recovery rates of 97-99%. Meanwhile, Attero, based in Noida, is among the country’s established e-waste and lithium-ion battery recycling companies, while other firms in the region are involved in battery-pack manufacturing and energy-storage solutions. artigo.texto: A SpaceX, do bilionário Elon Musk, firmou um compromisso de financiamento de cerca de US$ 40 bilhões com uma entidade administrada pela Apollo Global Management para adquirir equipamentos destinados a centros de dados. Segundo documento enviado nesta segunda-feira, 26, à Securities and Exchanges Commission (SEC, a CVM dos EUA), a operação prevê o arrendamento de unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs) e equipamentos relacionados. O compromisso vinculante foi assinado em 24 de outubro e estabelece que a entidade ligada à Apollo comprará os equipamentos e os alugará à SpaceX, que realizará pagamentos trimestrais ao longo de aproximadamente cinco anos. Os equipamentos serão entregues em lotes, com contratos individuais de arrendamento previstos para começar no primeiro semestre de 2027. Cada contrato terá duração de cinco anos a cinco anos e três meses. Segundo a companhia, os pagamentos trimestrais serão feitos antecipadamente e incluirão, em geral, um vigésimo do custo financiado de cada lote, além de juros calculados a uma taxa anual fixa sobre o saldo devedor e despesas adicionais. A taxa de juros ainda será definida. A SpaceX estima que os pagamentos de principal totalizem aproximadamente US$ 40 bilhões durante a vigência dos contratos, sem incluir juros e outros custos. A empresa espera concluir a formalização do acordo antes do fim de 2026, mediante o cumprimento de determinadas condições.

artigo.texto: By Emma Renly For Columbia Gorge News In the original version of this story, which ran Oct. 21, Klickitat County Commissioner Ron Ihrig was misquoted. Commissioner Todd Andrews asked his fellow seatmates to consider a moratorium on data centers — not Ihrig. The original story also didn’t report on the most recent draft data center ordinance. We regret the errors, and have opted to rerun the entire story to correct the public record on this important topic. Online versions have been similarly corrected. KLICKITAT CO. — Near the end of a two-hour public comment period on Oct. 13, Klickitat County Commissioner Todd Andrews again asked his fellow commissioners, Ron Ihrig and Lori Zoller, whether they would consider a moratorium on data centers. “I feel as helpless as some of you guys. I’m one vote,” Andrews said to the audience. To the commissioners, he asked, “Would either of you guys entertain a motion to do a moratorium?” One audience member could be heard saying, “Finally!” Neither Ihrig nor Zoller did, however, during another morning workshop session on the financially lucrative but resource-intensive facilities. The exchange took place before a packed audience with standing room only, with at least 50 individuals joining from Zoom. Every public comment, save one, asked the board of commissioners to implement a temporary pause on data center applications in Klickitat County while an ordinance and potential interim zoning rule were finalized. So far, no developers have submitted building permits to the planning department. Andrews had previously brought a draft moratorium ordinance to the Aug. 11 meeting, which also did not move forward, though it wasn’t on the agenda. “I need to talk to legal counsel about it,” Zoller replied. “There are some caveats that go with that.” She stated concerns about possible legal repercussions for the county that would be costly. However, there are no accounts of a data center developer suing a Washington or Oregon county because it enacted a data center moratorium. At the time of the meeting, six known data centers countywide were in various stages of planning, as previously reported by Columbia Gorge News. But now there is a seventh. On Sept. 28, Klickitat Public Utility District (KPUD) submitted another energy access request to Bonneville Power Administration for a data center from Clenera Tech Center Holdings. It would be for 300 megawatts and use the Energizer substation, with diesel generators providing backup power. Clenera, a renewable energy company, did not respond to comment on the data center’s location, what energy sources will be used and whether water sources have been confirmed. A moratorium would not affect whether developers can submit a power access request to KPUD and Bonneville, and Zoller has noted that obtaining transmission capacity can take anywhere from six to twelve years. Public responds “I’m not seeing a timeline emerge from this process, which is very concerning,” said Snowden resident Jenn Sharp, noting that nearly six weeks have passed since commissioners hosted a Sept. 3 workshop on data centers without approving an ordinance. Sharp began an online petition in early Sept. asking for a data center moratorium in Klickitat County, which had 1,024 signatures as of Oct. 12. She submitted the petition to the commissioners the afternoon before the meeting. “We’re going to continue to collect signatures. We’re not done,” Sharp added. Other residents felt similarly. “We have seen eminent domain [used] to expand energy infrastructure to power data centers,” said Lyle resident Pam Springer. “They threaten tribal sovereign rights. The county and state have ignored the needs and rights of Indigenous residents who were promised control and a say in how their remaining lands are used.” Mike Todd, a Goldendale resident, said, “Behind me you have a slice of Americana. You have a group of people who all we’re trying to do is be good citizens.” Enacting a moratorium is a no-brainer, regardless of the income it could bring to the county, said Todd, who formerly worked as a career firefighter at the City of Seattle and now volunteers locally. “I would love to see the fire service here with better resources, but not at this cost,” he said. “This is not the way to do it.” The public comment period followed a discussion about the current data center ordinance draft that Klickitat County’s Planning Department brought to the commissioners. Under the most recent language, data centers would only be allowed conditionally in general industrial and industrial park zones, and nowhere else. Three possible outcomes, no approval At the meeting, three potential avenues for data centers were discussed: a moratorium, an ordinance and an interim zoning rule. None were passed, and none would permanently stop a data center from developing. For the ordinance, commissioners were concerned that if data centers were allowed conditionally, those conditions needed to be explicit. Additional questions arose about whether developers could side-step local ordinance policy in favor of state laws, using the Carriger Solar Project as an example. Gov. Bob Ferguson approved the facility in December 2025. Currently, Klickitat County follows a 2023 code interpretation on data center policy — allowing them outright on land zoned as industrial park, which eliminates public input except during the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA) review. “Conditional use allows that second stage of public input, not just on SEPA, but on the actual development and its potential impacts on the neighbors,” said Scott Edelman, community development director. “As conditional use would imply, you put conditions on it that would mitigate those impacts.” The first ordinance draft was completed Sept. 22, followed by a second on Oct. 1 and a third on Oct. 13. artigo.texto: By Emma Foehringer Merchant In September, Gov. Gavin Newsom unveiled what is likely one of the last large climate announcements of his tenure: California will move forward with linking its decade-old carbon market with a newly formed market in Washington state, aiming to merge it with the market California already shares with Quebec. Newsom said California was “choosing certainty, partnership, and clean energy” amid a stream of federal climate policy rollbacks. But the announcement didn’t distract environmental advocates from the sting of a challenging year back home for the so-called “cap-and-invest” program. As Newsom leaves his post, many policy and climate experts say the adjustments to the program put California’s climate goals further out of reach. The program provides billions of dollars in funding for climate and other programs. Yet with little talk of climate policy in the governor’s race, Californians are largely left guessing about how Steve Hilton or Xavier Becerra would handle the program or California’s broader climate ambitions. The Becerra campaign did not respond to multiple emailed requests for comment. Hilton told CalMatters he would move to suspend the carbon market — which he called “a disaster of a program” — entirely. Twenty years ago, lawmakers made California the first state to mandate broad cuts in greenhouse gas emissions with AB 32, the landmark carbon emissions reduction law, which authorized the subsequent creation of a market. The law requires the program to be as cost-effective as possible while maximizing benefits to the state’s economy. Whoever wins in November can appoint a handful of new members to the California Air Resources Board, which has to finish writing the linkage rules and will propose the budget that leans on carbon market revenue. The next governor will also help decide how aggressively California leads on climate, after a year of mixed signals about where the program is headed. “It’s really set up the politics of these issues to get worse and not better over time, and that is the problem that is being tossed like a live grenade into the lap of the next governor,” said Danny Cullenward, an economist who sits on an advisory committee focused on the carbon market. A question of climate leadership In May, a process to reauthorize the keystone climate program ended with a controversial agreement that the Legislative Analyst’s Office projects will roughly halve annual auction revenue, offering about $2 billion less in funding for priority environmental programs while opening a separate pool of free permits for polluters that pledge to invest in decarbonization, valued at as much as $4 billion. Oil companies fought the initial cap-and-invest reauthorization proposal, arguing it would encourage companies to leave the state or further increase fuel prices. The California Air Resources Board, which manages the program, said the increased allowances it eventually approved were meant to balance affordability and economic uncertainty alongside emissions targets. In an email, a board spokesperson said the new incentives would not have any impact on the market’s auction revenue. (The Western States Petroleum Association, which represents refiners in the state, declined an interview for this story.) The concern comes as California prepares to elect its next governor and nears its own 2030 target to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 40% below 1990 levels, on its way to zeroing out emissions by 2045. “This is not a question anymore of whether or not we’ll reach the target. This is a guarantee that we won’t,” said Katie Valenzuela, a consultant for Communities for a Better Environment who previously co-chaired an environmental justice committee that advised regulators on the state’s program. State officials have long framed cap-and-invest as a backstop, keeping the state on track for its climate targets by ratcheting down the emissions limit even if other programs fall short. Advocates worry the changes will have a chilling effect rather than signal the market’s long-term strength, just as California loses ground to federal rollbacks. “It is going to become very difficult for us to say we are a climate leader when we are visibly missing our targets,” Cullenward said. Others remain more optimistic. Cap-and-invest is one tool in California’s toolbox, even if this year dulled it. Meredith Fowlie, an economist at the University of California, Berkeley, said the program is not optimal but has done the basics of its job: sending a price signal to drive down emissions while raising revenues for important programs. Linking with Washington’s market will strengthen California’s program overall, air board Chair Lauren Sanchez wrote to Newsom in September. In addition to creating a larger market with more credits available to industries in both states, the link is expected to raise carbon credit prices in California, where recent auctions have yielded prices at state minimums. A connected market could also lower prices in Washington, making the state’s more stringent program less lucrative. Low prices reduce the program’s revenues and starve polluting industries’ incentive to invest in lowering emissions. Regulators have not yet established a rulemaking timeline for the linkage process, a spokesperson for the board told CalMatters, but the board expects the joint market to begin operating next year. Chloe Ames, policy adviser at NextGen Policy, an organization founded by former gubernatorial candidate Tom Steyer, called linkage a strong step forward. The group is disappointed by the other changes made to cap-and-invest this year, she said, and will keep urging the legislature to adjust the industry incentives and California’s next governor to take climate seriously. “It’s been more challenging for us to say that we’re a climate leader, and that’s why we need to step up,” Ames said. “In this work, what are you going to do other than to be hopeful?” Kicking the can Since th

artigo.texto: Muitos analistas do setor — eu incluso — acreditavam que um salto expressivo na autonomia dos iPhones seria inviável sem a migração para baterias com tecnologia de silício-carbono. Contudo, a Apple provou o contrário na linha iPhone 18 Pro. A grande responsável por essa evolução não é uma bateria fisicamente gigante, mas sim a eficiência extrema da arquitetura de 2 nanômetros do novo processador A20 Pro. O segredo por trás do salto de autonomia está na litografia de 2 nm do chip, que exige significativamente menos energia para executar as mesmas tarefas da geração passada. Na prática, o iPhone 18 Pro menor consegue entregar quase a mesma autonomia do antigo iPhone 17 Pro Max, ficando atrás por uma diferença de apenas alguns minutos em testes comparativos. O rendimento do modelo Pro menor impressiona tanto em testes de estresse quanto na rotina comum do usuário: - Uso pesado: alcança mais de 9 horas e 20 minutos de tela ligada, mesmo em dias intensos que incluem mais de 3 horas de jogos pesados na rede 5G; - Uso moderado: chega ao fim da noite com cerca de 40% de carga restante, dispensando recargas intermediárias ao longo do dia. O iPhone 18 Pro Max consegue superar os rivais Android? No iPhone 18 Pro Max, o impacto do novo processador é ainda mais evidente. Mesmo contando com uma bateria de aproximadamente 5.500 mAh (nos mercados em que o aparelho vem sem bandeja para SIM de operadora), o dispositivo consegue empatar ou até superar ligeiramente concorrentes do ecossistema Android equipados com baterias brutas de mais de 7.000 mAh. Essa vantagem atual deve-se à implementação bem-sucedida da Apple da litografia de 2 nm no mercado consumidor. A grande dúvida é se essa liderança em autonomia se manterá quando os primeiros smartphones Android com chips equiparáveis começarem a ser lançados — como é o caso da nova geração Qualcomm Snapdragon. Caso tenha outras dúvidas sobre o aparelho, confira nosso review completo do iPhone 18 Pro. Enquanto isso, queremos saber: você acredita que a eficiência energética do processador é mais importante do que colocar uma bateria fisicamente gigante dentro do celular? Signed during a leadership summit in Seoul, South Korea, the agreement aims to support Energix’s expanding storage portfolio and strengthen long-term supply certainty. The partnership includes potential deployment of U.S.-manufactured, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC)-compliant battery systems for American projects. Building on their existing collaboration in Poland, both companies plan to extend cooperation across additional projects and markets. artigo.texto: Table of Contents Japanese billionaire Masayoshi Son is planning to invest $50 billion in artificial intelligence and data centers in Malaysia, in what could become one of the largest technology commitments in Southeast Asia. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim disclosed the plan on Saturday in Melaka, Bloomberg reported. Anwar said the SoftBank Group founder had already identified sites for the investment in Kuching, the capital of Sarawak state, and in Peninsular Malaysia. The two men discussed the plan during a video call last week. Anwar said Son’s focus would be on three areas. “In what areas? AI, new technology and data centers,” Anwar said. The $50 billion figure is equal to about 204.3 billion ringgit. Details on how the money will be deployed, when construction will start and how the project will be financed have not been announced. SoftBank had not commented publicly on the plan. Anwar said the investment could create jobs for Malaysians, especially young people and university graduates. He said the country must build skills in AI, digitalization and semiconductors, and train its workforce so it can move into higher-value technology work. He also said Malaysia must maintain political stability and a supportive investment climate to keep the confidence of international investors. The plan would add to a wave of data center spending in Malaysia, which has become a regional hub for the computing capacity that AI systems need. Alibaba Cloud opened two data centers in the southern state of Johor in June, bringing its total in the country to five. Sarawak has also drawn interest from SoftBank before. Earlier this month, SoftBank, ride-hailing company Grab and Sarawak state energy company PETROS were reported to be exploring AI infrastructure development in the state. The Malaysian proposal is the latest in a string of large bets by Son on AI. This month alone, he has sought $100 billion from Gulf investors for AI expansion and eyed a $30 billion takeover of Allied Universal. SoftBank is also involved in a $500 billion data center project in Ohio, which Bloomberg describes as among the largest in the world, and is pursuing a project in France that could cost up to $84 billion. Son founded SoftBank in 1981 and built it into one of the world’s biggest technology investors. His AI push has been heavily funded with borrowed money, including an $11.87 billion loan tied to his OpenAI bet, and his AI-related debt has kept growing. So far, the plan rests on Anwar’s account of his call with Son. Investors will be watching for confirmation from SoftBank and for details on timing, partners and funding. artigo.texto: Springfield City Council hears from the public on its proposed administrative delay extension and definitions of data centers SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (KY3) - In June, the Springfield City Council passed an administrative delay on the development of data centers; that delay is up on Nov. 17. On Monday night, council heard from the public about a proposal to push this delay back again to February. Citizens also addressed the council on its proposal to add definitions related to data centers into the city code. The first hearing on the city’s proposal to add definitions related to data centers, defining them and breaking them up into three groups: accessory, micro, and large load. “To be an Accessory Data Center: it has to be inside the principal building; it can’t be more than 20% of the principal building’s gross floor area; it needs to serve only the owner or the tenants, so it has to be used on site; and its maximum power demand has to be less than one megawatt,” said Justin Crighton, the City of Springfield’s Assistant Director of Planning and Development. “If it does not meet all four of those criteria, then the next test is size and power. So a data center is considered a Large Load Data Center if it meets either of these two thresholds: if it’s five megawatts or more in maximum power demand, or it’s more than 10,000 square feet. If it’s under both thresholds, then it’s a Micro Data Center.” Ten Springfield residents signed up to speak on this proposal. Cameron Rose, who works for a local internet provider, spoke to the council, saying the definitions are too broad and could have a negative effect on their business. “They would prevent us from setting up a fiber hut, which is just a small building that is usually about 8 by 10 that we use to provide service to other businesses or to residents,” said Rose. “Because the Accessory Data Center definition says that you cannot provide services to anyone other than tenants or the occupant of the building.” The second public hearing regards an extension of the city’s existing administrative delay on data centers. Springfield resident Ren Bortosky is in favor of the extension and said ideally, the moratorium would be indefinite, citing environmental concerns as the most prominent issue regarding data centers. “We need to put limitations in place either on how many data centers we’re building, which would ideally be zero, or at least on how much energy they’re allowed to use,” said Bortosky. “Because every megawatt of energy is more emissions that really don’t need to be put into the atmosphere.” Council will vote on both issues at the Nov. 16 meeting. artigo.texto: The increasingly contentious national debate over data centers moved into Mesa two weeks ago as Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes told a town hall that their explosive growth threatens to leave communities with higher utility bills, a range of health and environmental problems and inadequate government oversight. Addressing over 250 people at a Mesa community center Oct. 14, Mayes questioned whether Arizona has done enough to protect residents as developers rush to build the enormous facilities needed to support artificial intelligence, cloud computing and other digital services. The setting was particularly appropriate. Mesa has become a major data center hub, with over 7.5 million square feet of existing and proposed facilities. Yet roughly three-quarters of those attending the meeting had traveled from Ahwatukee, where residents have organized against a 1-million-square-foot facility currently being constructed amid neighborhoods with thousands of homes. And for Pinal County, her message is hardly irrelevant, according to a website that tracks 5,098 existing and projected data centers across the country. According to dcmap.us, seven data centers are being planned so far in Pinal County with a combined need for 1.5MW of electricity – enough to power 1.1 million to 1.5 million homes. But one center that alone needed 1MW of electricity to operate won’t be coming to Pinal, after the Pinal County Board of Supervisors in August denied rezoning for Vermaland’s 3,000-acre data center near Eloy. Those still on the books, according to dcmap.us, include Edgecorp’s 720MW campus in Florence, LPI Company’s 400MW campus in Casa Grande and Ryan Companies’ 400 MW data center in Eloy. Four others are planned in Pinal County, although dcmap.us had no information on them, including a 96-acre center at Felix and East Judd roads in San Tan Valley, a second in Florence and Casa Grande and another in Maricopa. According to Mayes, those projects represent a sliver of what has made the Phoenix Metro area “the second largest U.S. data center hub.” Telling the audience, “My office has identified more than 180 operating or planned data centers across Arizona,” the attorney general said 110 already are operating. Mayes, a Democrat seeking reelection, has called for a moratorium on data center construction “to get our house in order to determine the principles that should guide this build-up, if it happens, and to decide what’s needed to protect our communities in Arizona. “This issue is too important to let data center developers themselves decide what is right for our state and our communities,” Mayes told the audience. The Legislature and Gov. Katie Hobbs agreed in June to impose a three-year moratorium starting July 1 on millions of dollars in tax incentives that data centers have been getting from the state. Mayes said that’s not enough because data center growth in Arizona poses especially dire circumstances amid the state’s unfolding water crisis. “If all planned data centers in the Phoenix area are built,” she said, “stress on our local water supplies will increase by 32%. That would occur at the same time that Arizona loses 30% of our Colorado River water supplies.” She also asserted that data centers’ demand for electricity would drive up customers’ utility bills. Just hours before her town hall, Chris Bauer, vice president and treasurer for Pinnacle West Capital Corporation and its primary subsidiary, Arizona Public Service Company (APS), told the audience at the East Valley Partnership’s Statespersons’ Luncheon his company intends to “make growth pay for growth.” The attorney general currently is suing APS’ proposed 14% rate hike. Mayes also cited noise and even temperature impacts of data centers. She said data centers “regularly generate 94 decibels of noise.” Mesa’s noise ordinance has a 24-hour average sound limit of 60 decibels for residential zones and 65 for commercial zones. She also cited a recent Arizona State University study that says data centers can add 4 degrees to a neighborhood’s temperature downwind from a facility. Mayes outlined a series of demands she wants Arizona to develop for data centers, starting with transparency. She said some data center companies have required municipalities to enter nondisclosure agreements “which limit the ability of local governments … to discuss the project with their constituents.” She said she is currently suing unidentified municipalities over such agreements. She also said data centers should be forbidden from creating nuisances, that natural resources must be protected, that developers be required to pay fully for their power, and that the facilities “must give back.” “In Arizona, it is a tradition that any large development project gives back to the community it inevitably impacts, whether this is through taxes, fees, assessments, or even water storage credits,” she said. “We must ensure that communities that host data centers and that choose to host data centers indeed all Arizonans benefit from their development.” Mayes conceded her office is studying a major issue that has developed when municipalities in Arizona try to deny a data center from being built. Proposition 207, passed by an overwhelming majority of voters in 2006, requires any government level in Arizona to compensate a property owner if zoning or other restrictions lower the fair market value of the property. Earlier this year, Phoenix City Council reversed a denial of a permit for a data center after the property owner filed a claim for over $50 million. “We’re hearing a lot about Prop 207 from cities,” Mayes told the audience – well, mainly from the city of Phoenix, and we are analyzing that issue. So I’m not going to opine yet on Prop 207. artigo.texto: CATL's Profit Engine Sputters Just as Its Swap Network Takes Shape Published on 10/26/2026 at 20:20 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL closed a strategic cooperation agreement with Shaanxi Transportation Holding Group on Wednesday, covering the electrification of commercial vehicles, battery-swap infrastructure for heavy trucks, and energy storage with related services. The timing is pointed: the world's largest battery maker is signing new deals at a brisk clip while its core earnings power is under its sharpest pressure in nearly two years. Third-quarter figures released on October 20 landed well short of expectations. Revenue climbed 58.58% year on year to 165.22 billion yuan, yet net profit advanced just 14.54% to 21.25 billion yuan — far below the LSEG SmartEstimate consensus, which had pencilled in growth above 40%. Gross margin slid to 20.69%, down 5.1 percentage points from a year earlier and the weakest reading since the fourth quarter of 2022. Sequentially, net profit fell 5.77%. The stock tells its own story. At 238.00 CNY, the shares sit just above their 52-week low of 216.51 CNY and a long way from the 52-week high of 468.75 CNY. Investors now face a straightforward question: is this a temporary dip, or the start of structurally lower profitability? Tax Changes and Contract Mix Weigh on Margins Pricing pressure is only part of the explanation. Since September 1, 2026, China has levied a 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries, scheduled to double to 4% on September 1, 2027. Lower export tax rebates and the delivery of thinner-margin long-term contracts in the energy storage segment have added to the drag. Whether management can offset this headwind through scale effects and technical differentiation will decide the story from here. Pull it off, and the business model stays intact. Fail, and the de-rating has further to run. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Buybacks and a Widening Global Footprint Supporting the bull case is an undisputed lead abroad. Between January and August 2026, CATL lifted its global share of battery installations to 39.4%, up from 37.7% a year earlier. Stationary energy storage already accounts for roughly a quarter of global revenue and is projected to reach about half of total sales by 2030. The company is also pushing into new applications. It unveiled the Tianxing II battery line for commercial vehicles, which it says enables a pack swap in under five minutes. On October 19, CATL, Shidai Dianfu and Huawei-affiliated Yinwang signed an agreement reportedly linking Huawei's intelligent driving systems with CATL's swap ecosystem. A week earlier, CATL had presented the Tianxing II platform alongside an upgraded swapping solution. Management is putting money behind the vision. The truck-swap network in China is targeted at 900 stations by the end of 2026, 2,000 by 2027, and 10,000 over the longer term, according to Reuters. On the storage side, CATL and the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) published the "Storage+" report on October 16, jointly promoting a global energy storage initiative. Shareholder returns are part of the picture too. By the end of September, CATL had repurchased a cumulative 10,945,162 A-shares — 0.2482% of total A-share capital — for 3.303 billion RMB excluding fees, a figure booked in the quarterly report. The Home Front Is Where the Ground Is Shifting The bear case rests on structural share losses in China, the company's home market. Between January and September 2026, CATL's domestic share of traction batteries fell sharply from 49.8% to 40.9%. Rival BYD was the main beneficiary, expanding from 17.4% to 21.1% over the same period. Compounding the problem, automakers are working to loosen their dependence on the market leader. Li Auto is pursuing a dual-sourcing strategy, investing in competitors such as Sunwoda and planning its own battery capacity for the second half of 2026. XPeng is pressing ahead with in-house battery production from 2026. If that diversification continues while the Chinese consumption tax rises to 4% in September 2027, CATL's shipment volumes and pricing power come under pressure from two directions at once. What to Watch in the Coming Quarters Defending the margin line in the core business is the decisive variable. So long as gross margin holds around the current 20% level and international leadership remains intact, the depressed share price leaves room for a fundamental bottoming-out. Should profitability slip below that range in coming reporting periods, the valuation discount to historical averages is likely to entrench. The first concrete test comes at the end of 2026, when the 900-truck-station target in China falls due. How that build-out is executed will offer the first real read on whether CATL's new business lines beyond cell manufacturing can carry their weight. artigo.texto: NVIDIA's DSX POD Pushes AI Factory Construction Toward the Assembly Line Key Highlights - NVIDIA's DSX POD reference design aims to industrialize AI factory construction, integrating Vera Rubin computing, networking, power and liquid cooling into factory-built modular containers designed for deployment at prepared sites in as little as 14 days. - A growing partner ecosystem is bringing scale to the modular AI infrastructure movement, with Armada and Johnson Controls targeting 500 MW of distributed capacity in 2027, alongside manufacturing initiatives from Crusoe, Schneider Electric and major OEMs. - Prefabrication is demonstrating measurable installation advantages. A Schneider Electric–Compass Datacenters study found an 80% reduction in onsite installation time for prefabricated white-space modules, while Vertiv models nearly 30% greater first-year cumulative AI token output through accelerated deployment. - DSX POD extends NVIDIA's broader DSX AI Factory architecture into physical manufacturing, building on the company's 2026 initiatives in infrastructure simulation, power optimization and behind-the-meter energy integration. - Power availability and supply chain constraints remain the ultimate tests. NVIDIA's 14-day deployment vision depends on prepared sites, reliable component supplies and energy infrastructure that can take years to deliver, raising questions about how quickly industrialized AI factories can scale. NVIDIA is making a new push to change how AI data centers are built, introducing a factory-integrated infrastructure model intended to move much of the complex work of assembling, connecting and validating high-density computing systems away from construction sites and into manufacturing facilities. Unveiled October 21 at GTC Berlin, the company's new DSX POD reference design is designed around the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and packages computing, networking, rack-level power and liquid cooling inside standardized modular containers. Rather than bringing those systems together through successive stages of onsite installation, participating manufacturers would complete integration, cabling, piping and functional testing before shipment. NVIDIA claims the approach could reduce deployment time at a suitably prepared site from six months to as little as 14 days, allowing operators to begin generating production AI tokens and earning revenue substantially sooner. A global partner ecosystem is preparing to deliver the systems beginning in early 2027. "An AI factory creates value when it starts producing tokens — not when construction is complete," said NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The announcement arrives as operators face mounting pressure to bring increasingly power-dense AI infrastructure online while managing skilled labor shortages, long construction schedules and rapidly changing hardware requirements. But the larger development is not simply NVIDIA's two-week deployment target. Separate announcements from its infrastructure partners reveal an increasingly substantial industrial base taking shape around standardized, factory-manufactured AI capacity. From Crusoe's new modular manufacturing facility in Colorado to Schneider Electric's expanding prefabrication capacity, Armada's proposed 500 MW sovereign AI infrastructure program and Vertiv's work on a 41 MW deployment in Norway, the common objective is to make AI infrastructure delivery more repeatable, predictable and less dependent on assembling every system from scratch in the field. Modular construction has been one of the defining trends of the AI data center buildout, as developers look for ways to accelerate deployment while managing increasingly complex, power-dense infrastructure. What makes NVIDIA's DSX POD announcement potentially consequential is the scale of the proposed standardization. The ambition is no longer simply to manufacture electrical rooms, cooling systems or other infrastructure components offsite, but to deliver the AI factory itself as a repeatable, factory-integrated product. The emerging model does not eliminate the need for conventional data center development. It does, however, propose a significant reorganization of where—and when—the most intricate infrastructure integration work gets done. NVIDIA outlines how its DSX platform integrates computing, power, cooling and infrastructure simulation, with DSX POD extending the architecture into factory-built, containerized AI factories. (Source: NVIDIA) From the DSX AI Factory Blueprint to DSX POD The underlying engineering proposition is straightforward: as AI computing becomes more complex, particularly with the adoption of rack-scale liquid-cooled architectures, traditional methods of assembling and integrating equipment onsite introduce scheduling risks that become increasingly consequential. Electrical infrastructure, cooling distribution, networking, racks and compute hardware must operate as an integrated system. Delays or design changes in one discipline can affect multiple others. DSX POD is intended to address that coordination problem by establishing a repeatable, validated architecture that manufacturers can assemble and test in controlled environments while site preparation proceeds separately. Importantly, DSX POD is distinct from NVIDIA's broader Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory reference design, introduced in March. That design provides a facility-wide architectural framework encompassing compute, networking, storage, electrical distribution, cooling, controls and the engineering systems required to operate an AI factory. The larger DSX platform also incorporates simulation, infrastructure orchestration and software for optimizing computing output within available power budgets. NVIDIA's recently introduced DSX Ready qualification program extends that standardization effort to battery energy storage and liquid-cooling equipment, establishing technical requirements for the infrastructure supporting AI computing.
