artigo.texto: - The second-generation Seal 07 grows to 5,080 mm in length and will feature the DiSus-M intelligent magnetorheological body control system. - Reservation holders will receive priority production and delivery, with deposits fully refundable before orders are locked in. BYD (HKEX: 1211) has opened reservations for the second-generation Seal 07, a larger electric sedan equipped with its second-generation Blade Battery and flash charging technology. Zhang Zhuo, general manager of BYD's Ocean lineup sales division, announced the opening of reservations on Weibo on Monday, without disclosing pre-sales prices — a practice known as blind reservations. An official poster shows that reservation holders will receive priority production and delivery, with deposits fully refundable before orders are locked in. The reservations serve only as expressions of purchase intent, allowing customers to change colors and configurations after the launch. BYD is also offering exclusive gifts to customers who place reservations and take delivery. The move follows a series of previews. Zhang first unveiled the exterior on September 28 and shared cabin details on October 23. The second-generation Seal 07 will feature the second-generation Blade Battery and flash charging, with BYD promoting its charging capability as "ready in 5 minutes, full in 9 minutes." The car will also feature the DiSus-M intelligent magnetorheological body control system, front double-wishbone and reinforced rear 5-link suspension, and BYD's Smart Ecosystem 2.0. The second-generation Seal 07 adopts the Ocean Aesthetics 2.0 design language, with styling consistent with the Seal 08. It offers 6 exterior colors and 3 interior color schemes. The car measures 5,080 mm in length, 1,960 mm in width and 1,495 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 2,960 mm. It is 85 mm longer than the Seal 07 EV launched in March, with a 60 mm longer wheelbase. The cabin features front zero-gravity seats with massage, ventilation and heating functions, along with a 20-speaker Devialet audio system. BYD lists trunk and front-trunk capacities of 618 liters and 160 liters, respectively. The vehicle shown is equipped with roof-mounted LiDAR, though BYD has yet to detail its driver-assistance capabilities or how equipment will vary across trims. Earlier filings with China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) showed that the second-generation Seal 07's battery-electric version offers peak motor outputs of 245 kW (329 hp) and 300 kW, both above the 240 kW of the model launched in March. Alongside the battery-electric model shown in the poster, the filings included a plug-in hybrid retaining the Seal 07 DM-i name, with a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine and a 160 kW electric motor. The plug-in hybrid has a 38.029-kWh battery and a WLTC electric range of 245 km (152 miles). The latest official poster did not specify reservation arrangements for that version. For reference, the Seal 07 EV launched on March 5 was offered in 2 variants priced at 169,900 yuan ($25,300) and 189,900 yuan. The redesign comes as the Seal lineup faces sales pressure. Data compiled by CnEVPost shows that the series sold 46,718 vehicles in September, down 9.04% year-on-year and 1.57% from August. In the first 9 months of the year, Seal-series sales totaled 304,723 vehicles, down 14.11% year-on-year. The lineup includes the Seal 07 and several other battery-electric and plug-in hybrid models. ($1 = 6.7162 yuan)

artigo.texto: BAIC Group and CATL signed an expanded battery-swapping agreement on October 22, 2026, to connect compatible models from multiple BAIC brands to CATL’s Choco-Swap network. The partners’ reported ambition is a mature Chinese ecosystem serving vehicles at the million-vehicle scale, with BAIC dealerships helping support station locations. How the agreement is meant to work CnEVPost reported, citing a BAIC statement, that the cooperation covers vehicle and battery development, swap-station network construction, battery-energy services and new business models. BAIC is to connect compatible vehicles from several of its brands to Choco-Swap. Its dealership network is to help identify station sites, and the companies are exploring joint development and operation of stations with dealers. The partners also aim to consolidate swap assets under specialized management and promote unified standards and interoperable networks. For drivers, compatibility depends on the vehicle and battery system: a CATL-supplied battery alone does not establish that a vehicle can use a CATL swap station. A million-vehicle ambition, alongside CATL’s existing network The million-vehicle figure describes the scale of the partners’ ambition, not a dated deployment target. CATL’s network was reported at 2,520 battery-swap stations across 200 Chinese cities as of September 29, 2026, before the agreement was signed. Battery swapping replaces a depleted pack with a charged one at a station. The agreement sets out cooperation on vehicles, stations and related services, while its stated goal describes the scale the partners hope the Chinese ecosystem will reach. BAIC and CATL had already worked on swap-compatible vehicles The October agreement builds on earlier BAIC-CATL cooperation signed in June 2024, which covered swap-compatible vehicles, battery-block development and battery-data management, according to CnEVPost. CnEVPost reported that the Arcfox Beta S3 swap version, using CATL’s Choco-SEB system, launched on May 22, 2026. A swap version of the Arcfox Beta T1 appeared in an August 2026 filing with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

artigo.texto: Segundo o TecMundo, no primeiro discurso após ser reeleito, Lula (PT) sinalizou que pretende usar a capacidade de geração renovável do Brasil como atrativo para empresas de computação e criar uma inteligência artificial nacional. Ele venceu Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno, com 51,74% dos votos válidos, ante 48,26% do adversário, conforme os números do TSE divulgados no domingo (25). O novo mandato começa em janeiro de 2027. A proposta, de acordo com o plano de governo disponível no TSE, inclui investimentos em infraestrutura digital, formação de profissionais e reforço da indústria tecnológica local. Para os centros de dados, o documento prevê contrapartidas: parte da capacidade computacional deve ficar à disposição do mercado brasileiro. Também menciona exigências socioambientais, como eficiência no consumo de energia, avanço para fontes renováveis e análise dos efeitos sobre recursos hídricos, rede elétrica e moradores das áreas vizinhas. Na área de inteligência artificial, Lula quer ampliar o ensino de matemática e engenharia para diminuir a dependência de soluções dos Estados Unidos e da China. O plano cita sistemas de linguagem natural voltados ao português e a outros idiomas, uma base nacional de dados destinada a treinar e testar esses sistemas, além de apoio a pesquisas públicas e a fabricantes nacionais de equipamentos e programas de computação de alto desempenho. Agronegócio, saúde e serviços financeiros aparecem como setores de aplicação. O documento também prevê conectar instituições de ensino, laboratórios e companhias. Ele também retomou a defesa de regras para as grandes plataformas digitais e relacionou o tema à atuação dessas empresas no processo eleitoral. No discurso, associou a necessidade de regulação à influência das plataformas no pleito e disse que delitos no ambiente digital devem receber tratamento equivalente ao de crimes cometidos fora da internet.

artigo.texto: BOTETOURT CO., Va. – Mike Herwald gives a tour of the Munters plant located in the Botetourt Center at Greenfield. He points to the massive space filled with workers and equipment. “We’re receiving raw metal. We’re bending it, forming it, painting it, welding it. It all happens within this factory,” Herwald said. Mike Herwald knows data center cooling inside and out. He is the North American Sales Manager in Data Center Technologies at Munters, one of the top suppliers of data center cooling systems in the world. At their plant in Daleville, which hopes to soon employ 1,000 workers, they make cooling systems from the ground up. “Data centers are a big part of our business,” Herwald said. And for good reason. With the advent of AI and other chip technologies, Data Centers are popping up everywhere. According to Cleanview, there are nearly 1,400 data centers in the U.S. with more than 2,800 planned. The site says there are 359 in Virginia with 459 in planning. “At its core, data centers produce a lot of heat,” explained Virginia Tech researcher Eric Sjostedt, who is searching for ways to make data centers less impactful to the communities where they are located. It’s getting rid of that heat that uses so much water, he explained. “When people say data centers use a lot of water, it’s all attributed to the cooling system,” Sjostedt said. When stacks of servers do their work – called “compute” they heat up. If they get too hot, they fail. Boiled down: conventional data center cooling uses large amounts of water evaporation to cool the systems. This is called evaporative technology. A 100-megawatt or medium-sized data center can use more than 2 million gallons of water per day. Eventually, for instance, in Google’s project in Daleville, it could go as high as 8 million. With drought conditions at Carvins Cove, one of the proposed water sources this year, dissenters claim that’s too much water. One of the reasons Munters is pivoting away from evaporative technologies. “When I look at our entire portfolio of equipment we’re building today, almost all of it is what’s called a waterless cooling technology. So, it’s not using evaporative technology to cool the data center,” Herwald said. Herwald showed us the massive systems Munters is now building. Unfortunately, there’s a catch – waterless systems present a different problem. “But I want to make this point really clear that the water question, if we’re only looking at the data center, is the wrong focus point,” Sjostedt said. If Data Centers move to waterless technology, they will require more energy – more electricity. “We can make all of our data centers air-cooled, so they don’t use a drop of water on the facility. We can absolutely do that. That’s an option. They’re gonna require more electricity to do so,” Sjostedt said. Sjostedt says it’s like kicking the can down the road. If the data center uses more energy, it may save water, but there are environmental impacts when the power is created. A problem Munters is trying to meet head-on with evolving technologies. “So you have to analyze the impact to the environment. Where is the electricity coming from? How am I being most responsible to the community? Either I’m going to consume water or I’m going to consume electricity. It’s one or the other,” Herwald said. That begs the question protestors have been asking all along. Do we need data centers? “Well, that’s a problem, right? Because our call right now is hosted by a data center. The texts that I’m getting right now are from a data center. My bank account is hosted by a data center,” replied Sjostedt. “Can our infrastructure sustain this given the change of climate and going up in our power generation and what’s needed for our society to keep on going? That’s the tough nut that I’m trying to figure out. And I don’t have an answer to it, but I know that problem exists,” he said. Both men interviewed for this story said data centers must be built in a place where either water or electricity is available, along with a population that requires connectivity to computing. Where those lines meet is where data centers will be built.

artigo.texto: - CATL confirms Firefly uses its Qilin Battery, with the 60-kWh version offering a CLTC range of 560 km. - The original 42-kWh battery is supplied by Sunwoda and offers a CLTC range of 420 km. Nio Inc's (NYSE: NIO) Firefly brand uses CATL's (HKEX: 3750) Qilin Battery in its newly launched 60-kWh pack, adding a longer-range option for the small electric vehicle. CATL said on Weibo on Saturday that Firefly uses its Qilin Battery, delivering a CLTC range of 560 km (348 miles). Firefly officially launched the larger-capacity battery a day earlier. Firefly's original 42-kWh standard-range battery is supplied by Sunwoda (SZSE: 300207) and uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, offering a CLTC range of 420 km. Sunwoda is among China's major second-tier battery makers and is also a major partner of Li Auto (NASDAQ: LI). Firefly's new 60-kWh battery uses nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) cells, increasing range by 140 km, or about 33%. Battery dimensions and vehicle curb weight remain unchanged, according to Firefly. Qilin is a battery product line CATL introduced in 2022, with its third generation unveiled in April this year. The Weibo post did not specify which generation Firefly uses or its charging rate. For owners, however, these details may matter less, as Firefly vehicles, like other models from Nio Inc, can replenish their batteries through a 3-minute battery swap. For new buyers, Firefly EV equipped with the 60-kWh battery starts at 136,800 yuan ($20,360), including the battery. Under the BaaS (battery as a service) subscription plan, the car starts at 79,800 yuan, with a monthly battery rental fee of 599 yuan. The new battery is also available to existing owners. Under Firefly's announced plan, customers who purchased their vehicles with the battery included can apply for a permanent upgrade once at least 1 year has passed since their purchase invoice date. The upgrade costs 17,000 yuan. Existing BaaS users pay a permanent upgrade service fee of 3,000 yuan, with monthly battery rent rising to 599 yuan from 399 yuan for the 42-kWh version. Firefly said the 2 battery capacities use compatible standardized module designs, with identical casing dimensions, mounting points and locking mechanisms. This allows existing vehicles to receive the upgrade through battery swapping without replacing the car. The brand first gained access to Nio's fifth-generation battery swap stations on August 7. Previously, Firefly's shorter body and wheelbase prevented it from using Nio's fourth-generation stations. The use of Qilin batteries in Firefly extends Nio's cooperation with CATL. In January, the companies announced a 5-year agreement to deepen their strategic partnership, focusing on areas including joint development of long-life batteries and battery swap compatibility technologies. Firefly's first model, which shares the brand's name, launched in China in April 2025, targeting the small electric vehicle market and competing with brands including Mini and Smart. The brand announced on October 16 that cumulative deliveries had reached 90,000 vehicles. Firefly delivered a record 7,327 vehicles in September, bringing its total for the first 9 months of this year to 48,122, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. ($1 = 6.7180 yuan)

artigo.texto: Novas regulamentações para o registro de contas de crédito de carbono. O governo emitiu o Decreto nº 396/2026/ND-CP, que estipula claramente a autoridade, os procedimentos e os prazos para a concessão de contas de registro de créditos de carbono no Sistema Nacional de Registro. Em nome do Governo, o Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Ho Quoc Dung assinou o Decreto nº 396/2026/ND-CP, que altera e complementa diversos artigos do Decreto nº 06/2022/ND-CP, que regulamenta a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e a proteção da camada de ozono, o qual foi alterado e complementado pelos Decretos nº 119/2025/ND-CP, nº 83/2026/ND-CP e nº 112/2026/ND-CP. O Decreto 396/2026/ND-CP altera e complementa o inciso 2º do artigo 18º, relativo ao cadastro de contas no Sistema Nacional de Cadastro de Cotas de Emissão de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Créditos de Carbono, especificando o órgão responsável pela concessão de contas no Sistema Nacional de Cadastro para cada grupo de entidades. Especificamente, o Decreto estipula que, para as instalações que recebem cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa, para as agências e organizações participantes em programas e projetos registrados de acordo com os mecanismos especificados nos itens a e b da Cláusula 1, Artigo 20a deste Decreto, e para as agências e organizações participantes em projetos de carbono florestal com áreas florestais dentro dos limites administrativos de duas ou mais unidades administrativas de nível provincial , o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente concederá contas no Sistema Nacional de Registro e enviará informações para a instalação, agência ou organização. Você também pode gostar Para as agências e organizações que participam de projetos registrados no âmbito do mecanismo de troca e compensação de créditos de carbono, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que receber o pedido de registro do projeto concederá uma conta no Sistema Nacional de Registro e enviará as informações à organização após a aprovação do registro do projeto. Para as agências e organizações participantes em programas e projetos registrados de acordo com o mecanismo especificado no ponto c, cláusula 1, do artigo 20a deste Decreto, a agência ou organização deverá apresentar o dossiê de registro da conta em uma das seguintes formas: diretamente ou via correio ao Centro de Serviços da Administração Pública Provincial, no caso de um projeto registrado em uma unidade administrativa de nível provincial, ou ao Centro de Serviços da Administração Pública Provincial de uma das áreas de implementação do projeto, no caso de um projeto registrado em duas ou mais unidades administrativas de nível provincial, ou online no Portal Nacional de Serviços Públicos ou no Aplicativo Nacional de Identificação. No prazo de 5 dias úteis a partir da data de recebimento do dossiê de inscrição, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que o recebeu deverá conceder uma conta no Sistema Nacional de Registro e enviar as informações à agência ou organização; em caso de recusa da concessão da conta, os motivos deverão ser claramente indicados. A identificação e autenticação de organizações e indivíduos no acesso e utilização do Sistema Nacional de Registro são realizadas em conformidade com a lei sobre identificação e autenticação eletrônicas. Você também pode gostar O Decreto 396/2026/ND-CP acrescenta a Cláusula 10 após a Cláusula 9 do Artigo 20. Especificamente, os procedimentos para registro, ajuste e cancelamento de registro de projetos de carbono florestal; concessão de créditos de carbono florestal no âmbito do mecanismo; e troca e compensação de créditos de carbono nacionais serão aplicados de acordo com as normas do Decreto Governamental nº 180/2026/ND-CP, de 21 de maio de 2026, sobre serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono em florestas. O Decreto 396/2026/ND-CP também altera e substitui alguns formulários do Anexo V e revoga a Cláusula 3 do Artigo 20a, juntamente com alguns formulários antigos. Os pedidos recebidos pelos ministérios competentes antes de 1º de agosto de 2026 continuarão a ser processados de acordo com os regulamentos vigentes na data de recebimento e não precisam ser reenviados. O Decreto entra em vigor em 12 de dezembro de 2026.

artigo.texto: Nano One Materials Corp. has provided an update on its strategic collaboration with Sumitomo Metal Mining Co. Ltd (SMM), highlighting continued progress in validating its One-Pot process for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials. The partnership, supported through Natural Resources Canada (NRCan)-funded programmes, focuses on developing cost-effective LFP production technology as demand for lithium battery energy storage continues to grow. Since SMM’s strategic investment in Nano One in 2023, the companies have worked together on technical development and commercial opportunities for the One-Pot process. Positive results from validation work SMM has continued evaluating the technology through economic modelling, product testing and supplying One-Pot LFP samples to its customers. Feedback on the samples has been positive, while SMM’s economic assessment continues to indicate potential for a cost-effective manufacturing solution. Based on the modelling, Nano One estimates that conversion costs could be reduced by up to US$1 million annually for every 1,000 tonnes of production capacity. SMM is continuing to develop its existing LFP production capabilities and solid-phase processes, while assessing the One-Pot technology as an additional route to competitive supply. Munekazu Kawata, Managing Executive Officer and General Manager of SMM’s Battery Materials Division, said the process offered potential benefits from both production and commercial perspectives, with customer feedback supporting its ongoing evaluation. Progress towards commercial supply Nano One’s latest One-Pot LFP material has achieved a pressed density suitable for assessment by high-performance battery cell manufacturers, and samples are ready for customer evaluation. Discussions are underway with SMM’s existing cell manufacturing and automotive customers. Product qualification remains a multi-stage process that must be completed before commercial offtake can proceed. Denis Geoffroy, Chief Operating Officer of Nano One, said the positive customer response could strengthen the technology’s appeal to prospective customers, licensees and joint venture partners. Plans for Canadian production The companies are continuing to explore a large-scale LFP production facility in Canada. Progress towards the project remains subject to securing customer offtake agreements, financing and government funding. SMM has contributed technical expertise, testing and validation through NRCan initiatives, including a C$9.3 million Energy Innovation Program award and a C$3 million LFP supply chain initiative. artigo.texto: What’s It Like Inside a Data Center? Northern Virginia is laden with structures that house data for Fortune 500 companies. I went inside just one of those monstrosities that bothers its neighbors. What’s It Like Inside a Data Center? Northern Virginia is laden with structures that house data for Fortune 500 companies. I went inside just one of those monstrosities that bothers its neighbors. The sun was beating down as I made my way through a quiet community in Ashburn, Virginia. The roads were wide and lined with cars; there was a nice central playground with no one playing in it; the houses seemed monstrously large; and there were ample trees dotting the clean-cut lawns of the neighborhood. In so many ways, it felt like your typical US suburb, until you looked past the thick wall of trees that defined its boundaries. The white walls of a large facility peeked out from above the deep green foliage. It ran on in the distance, the large houses making it impossible to see its full extent. Towering above it a little farther away were the high-voltage transmission lines that fed it with electricity. The trees acted like a shield, allowing those who lived in the community not to think about what stood on their doorstep and the growing demands that came from the surrounding industrial expansion. I’m talking, of course, about hyperscale data centers. No location on the entire planet has more data centers than Virginia. The state holds more than 13 percent of global hyperscale capacity—double that of Beijing, which comes in second. There were nearly 600 data centers within the state’s boundaries in 2025, about 150 of which were hyperscale—the monstrously large variety that have become much more common since the advent of generative AI—and most of them were clustered in an area in the north of the state around Ashburn, which has since been dubbed “Data Center Alley.” Data centers are unavoidable in Northern Virginia. When I sat on a bench next to a neighborhood lake, a hyperscale data center owned by Microsoft stared back at me from the opposite bank. As I drove through industrial parks, they were dotted throughout. When I pulled into a shopping area to grab a bite to eat, facilities that powered Amazon Web Services loomed behind the strip mall. I could even feel their influence in the street names: Cloud Plaza, Performance Circle, and, worst of all, Growth Mindset Lane. We can thank Microsoft for that one. In short, they were everywhere when I visited in 2025, and following them wherever they set down were the high-voltage power lines needed to keep them running. Data centers were remaking the fabric of a whole region; there seemed to be no end in sight for their expansion. They had become a major industry, and neither worries over local resource demands nor growing concern from residents seemed able to stop the ambitions of some of the most powerful companies on the planet. It’s hard to generalize about the data centers themselves. They come in many shapes and sizes, operate at various scales—from rooms in a nondescript building to entire parks of warehouse-sized facilities crammed with thousands of servers apiece—and seem to be getting bigger with every passing year. Some of them exist to serve the companies operating them; others exist as places where many different groups can rent space for servers of their own. Certain facilities are cooled with air-conditioning, while others depend more on water-based cooling, and even the way those systems are implemented can differ. I guess what I’m trying to say is that one description of a data center will never cover the gamut: There is some standardization, but there is also a lot of room for operators to put their own stamp on how their facility or network of locations is going to work. The interiors of some Google data centers have clusters of brightly colored tubes running throughout them—echoing the primary colors present in the company’s branding—while the average Microsoft or Amazon facility might appear more utilitarian. Digital Realty is one of the largest data-center operators in the world. The company has two major lines of business: It builds entire facilities that then get leased to other companies, including the major cloud providers, but it also offers colocation services. Those are facilities where Digital Realty runs the data center, renting space in racks to other companies that they can then fill with their own servers. I stopped to walk the length of one of its facilities in Northern Virginia. The simplest way to describe it is to say that it looks like a massive box. The company’s logo was visible near the upper portion of the building, and it had some different shades of gray and blue across its exterior. The data center seemed quiet that weekend afternoon, though even on a weekday there weren’t likely to be many people there. Data centers don’t need many employees to keep them clean, secure, and running; the bulk of the jobs they provide are created in the construction phase and mostly disappear once that’s over. The parking lot at the front of the building was surrounded by a large black fence that went around the entire property. I wasn’t trying to get in, but I did wonder if there was a security officer behind a desk somewhere inside the building peering at me through the video feed of one of the facility’s many security cameras. Data centers are notoriously well-guarded, to keep their data safe and to assuage the worries of their clients. There wasn’t much to see as I walked along the fence, the spikes at the top of each pole warning me not to try anything rash. It took nearly five minutes to walk from one end of the building to the other, and this wasn’t even one of the bigger ones I’d seen that day. At the far end, a little beyond the fence, I walked onto a wooden platform where I could make out a serene pond obscured by tall trees and plants. The chirps and trills of birds and insects were just barely audible over the buzz

artigo.texto: This town ain’t big enough for just one launch provider. On Monday evening, Cowboy Space pulled back the curtain on Big Iron—a launch vehicle whose upper stage is designed to remain in orbit as a megawatt-class data center. “What we want to do is put a lot of available power in orbit, in our case to power chips, to power AI data centers,” Cowboy Space COO and Chief Legal Officer Joseph Yaffe told Payload. “The most efficient and most effective way to do that is to build our own vehicle to get us into space.” Cowboy is also opening Big Iron to outside customers—who can fly payloads that need up to a megawatt of power—through a program dubbed Big Iron Express. “Launch capacity is at a premium right now, if available at all,” Yaffe said. But many of the alternatives—Big Iron included—have yet to fly, and government customers “want to see a completed rocket,” Yaffe said. Horsepower check: Big Iron is no lightweight. To move fast and keep costs down, the team turned to proven architectures, and designed for existing infrastructure. - The 86 m stainless-steel vehicle is sized to be transportable by road. - Each vehicle is designed to carry 15,000+ kg to sun-synchronous orbit. - Nine liquid-oxygen and methane “Clydesdale” engines will power the first stage—each providing 300,000 lbs of thrust. Cowboy tested part of the Clydesdale at NASA’s Stennis Space Center last week. A ~30-person team built and tested its combustion chamber in 90 days, and the company is “almost a year ahead of schedule,” Yaffe said. Rather than being discarded, the upper stage joins Cowboy’s constellation. Once deployed in dawn-dusk orbit, each sat will measure 132 m by 73 m and carry five racks of NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs. Two-trick pony: To make every kilogram sent to orbit count, many of Big Iron’s parts take on a second job once they’re in orbit. - The rocket’s skin becomes the data center’s radiator; - Ammonia propellant works a double shift as coolant; - Nitrogen that pressurizes the second stage also deploys the solar wings. “If you build a small satellite with GPUs on it, you’re going to have to put radiators on it,” Yaffe said. “And so you’re paying for that same metal twice to lift it into space.” Hold your horses: Cowboy got its first taste of orbit with Reason-1, a laser power beaming demo sat that launched Oct. 1 aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18. Yaffe said the first beaming attempt will likely happen in the next few weeks, and testing so far has turned up “zero red flags.” Reason-2—slated for launch in 2027—will run GPUs in orbit for commercial and government customers, including a NOAA effort to process weather data in space. Cowboy is targeting Big Iron’s first flight in 2028. From there, it’s off to the races to scale Stampede, its planned constellation of up to 20,000 sats, pending FCC approval. “We just still have a lot of executing to do,” Yaffe said.

artigo.texto: Local officials in many parts of Connecticut are not waiting for the national data center boom to come to them. Earlier this month, for example, the East Lyme Zoning Commission voted unanimously to adopt an indefinite ban on all data center development, one of the first such blanket prohibitions in Connecticut. The ban, which went into effect on Saturday, came before anyone had announced even the faintest plan to construct a data center in the coastal town. “It seems like all over the country, they’re trying to figure out the effects of pollution, energy consumption, chemical runoffs,” Anne Thurlow, the chairwoman of East Lyme’s Zoning Commission, said during an August meeting. “I think it’s a good thing to ban them until we know more about them,” Thurlow added. “It could always be reversed if the town wanted to.” East Lyme is one of around half a dozen municipalities that have taken preemptive action to block data center development, either through temporary moratoriums or a complete ban, according to a review of public meetings and records by The Connecticut Mirror. Moratoriums have been passed in communities big and small, suburban and rural. New Haven passed a one-year moratorium in September, with an exemption for the city’s existing quantum computing hub. Morris, a town in the Litchfield Hills with fewer than 3,000 residents, has a two-year ban. “The Connecticut case is quite interesting because many other places in the country, when we see these protests and opposition, either something has started or something is already there,” said Subodha Kumar, a professor of statistics, operations and data science at Temple University’s Fox School of Business. But in Connecticut, he said, political pushback has formed well ahead of actual plans for development. “Connecticut has never been that attractive, frankly speaking, for data centers,” Kumar said. The development of large “hyperscale” data centers in Connecticut, and to a greater extent in New England, has been stymied by the high cost of electricity, along with the need to access to utility infrastructure and large plots of land to house thousands of servers, which can easily cover several football fields. In 2021, Connecticut lawmakers fast-tracked legislation to lure data center developers by promising to waive sales and use taxes for projects that invest at least $200 million in the state (or $50 million for projects located within certain state-designated enterprise zones). To date, the only project to take advantage of that exemption: Cigna’s $386 million renovation of an existing data center in Windsor. Thurlow said the effort in East Lyme was driven, in part, as a reaction to a proposal to erect a massive new data center facility next door in Waterford, which is home to the Millstone Nuclear Power Station. The planned facility would have drawn its power directly from Millstone, a setup known as co-location. But local pushback and years of delays ended up killing that project, according to Waterford First Selectman Robert Brule, who told CT Mirror last month that he and the town were no longer interested in hosting data centers. “We’d rather produce the energy now than produce a project that sucks up the energy,” Brule said. The Department of Economic and Community Development, which oversees the data center tax incentive program, said it has reviewed only two applications under the program since it began and none this year. The credit has become an issue in the gubernatorial election, with Republican candidate Sen. Ryan Fazio arguing the tax incentive should be ended. A spokesperson for Gov. Ned Lamont said the governor was open to discussing changing or eliminating the credit, adding that the tax incentive was never intended for large AI data centers and “should be clarified to ensure it is never used by a hyperscale data center and that data centers bring their own power.” The law also exempted qualified projects from local property taxes but requires developers to enter into a host fee agreement with any municipality in which a data center is located. Randy Collins, a lobbyist at the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities, said developers argued it would be “economically unfeasible” to invest millions of dollars into the necessary equipment for data centers without offsetting some of the taxes. But despite a handful of towns successfully negotiating host fee agreements, Collins said developers have been slow to actually take advantage of the tax breaks. “If you look at the resources and requirements going in, they’re not just going to be popping up everywhere,” Collins said. Still, the issue has drawn considerable attention. Democrats in the state Senate say the moment requires new policy, with Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff announcing this week that he intends to introduce legislation next session that would create a statewide moratorium on new data centers. The proposal was initially outlined in a CT Mirror op-ed in September. “We think there should be rules of the road. We think there should be a moratorium,” Duff told reporters during a Thursday morning press conference in Groton. “We think we should better understand what electric and water and other types of problems are.” The public concern around data centers, he added, is something worth listening to. “We’re seeing people across our state and across our country who are really upset over the proliferation of data centers coming in, literally in people’s neighborhoods,” Duff said. “We should not have these in people’s neighborhoods.” Duff said there is a clear partisan divide over data centers. artigo.texto: General Motors is backing a sodium-ion battery push aimed at making electricity storage cheaper for utilities and data centers. Peak Energy, a sodium-ion battery startup backed by General Motors through its investment arm GM Ventures, announced on October 23 that it had raised $108 million in an oversubscribed Series B funding round. GM Ventures led the round, with participation from LG Technology Ventures and other investors, to support the company’s expansion into grid and data center energy storage. The startup plans to expand manufacturing, fulfill more than $1 billion in existing customer orders, and bring its passively cooled battery storage systems to the data center market. Its platform eliminates active cooling equipment, which the company says can reduce storage costs and energy waste. The funding builds on a partnership announced June 10. GM will develop next-generation sodium-ion cells at its Michigan battery laboratories and retain exclusive manufacturing rights, while Peak Energy will integrate the cells into its stationary storage systems. A battery built for the grid The partnership focuses on grid storage rather than electric vehicles. Stationary batteries have different requirements from vehicle batteries, making cost, reliability, and safety more important than packing maximum energy into a small, lightweight package. Lithium-iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries currently dominate stationary storage. Peak Energy is pursuing sodium-ion as an alternative that uses more abundant, potentially lower-cost materials. More from Energy See All GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, Kurt Kelty, said the chemistry suits the application. “At GM, we know that the application should determine the battery, and for grid-scale stationary storage, sodium-ion is the right solution,” Kelty said. “Peak is already demonstrating the value of sodium-ion through their innovative energy storage platform, and together we’re working to push those benefits even further with our next-generation cell – helping deliver more reliable, lower-cost energy storage at scale for the US grid,” he added. Removing active cooling equipment Peak Energy’s approach extends beyond battery chemistry to the equipment surrounding the cells. Conventional LFP storage systems use active cooling to manage operating temperatures. That equipment adds components, consumes electricity, and increases system complexity. The company says its sodium-ion platform operates with passive cooling, eliminating the need for those systems. According to the company, the platform can lower energy storage costs by 20 percent compared with conventional systems while delivering more than 99 percent uptime. These figures are company-reported and have not been independently verified. Peak Energy also estimates that replacing conventional LFP storage with its technology could reduce annual battery-storage energy waste across the US by up to two terawatt-hours. That projection concerns potential savings from broader deployment, rather than energy already saved by installed systems. Manufacturing for rising electricity demand The new funding will support Peak’s manufacturing expansion as utilities add storage alongside renewable generation and electricity demand grows. Data centers represent another target, particularly as AI infrastructure increases power demand. Peak Energy plans to bring its passively cooled storage platform to that market while working through its existing customer orders.

artigo.texto: Opinião Data centers e a fome por recursos Tao e Gao referem que um data centre hiperescalável típico pode utilizar 11 a 26 milhões de litros por dia, apenas para arrefecimento A economia digital está cada vez mais dependente dos data centres (ou centros de dados), infraestruturas altamente consumidoras de eletricidade e de outros recursos. Em setembro de 2026, segundo dados divulgados pela Forbes Portugal, os países europeus com mais data centres eram o Reino Unido (568), a Alemanha (533), a França (393) e a Espanha (219). Portugal apresentava 46. Os data centres, vitais para suportar a evolução da economia digital e, em particular, da Inteligência Artificial, são responsáveis por diversos impactes ambientais. Consumiram cerca de 1,5% da eletricidade mundial em 2024. Segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia, este consumo poderá mais do que duplicar até 2030. Dependendo do local onde são instalados e da origem da eletricidade que os alimenta, podem também contribuir para as emissões de gases com efeito de estufa. Têm ainda uma enorme pegada hídrica. Em determinadas regiões, até 57% da água utilizada para arrefecimento pode provir de fontes potáveis. Tao e Gao referem que um data centre hiperescalável típico pode utilizar 11 a 26 milhões de litros por dia, apenas para arrefecimento. Segundo Tao e Gao, existem várias medidas que devem ser consideradas. Em primeiro lugar, aumentar a utilização de fontes de energia renovável para alimentar os data centres. Em segundo lugar, devem ser priorizadas tecnologias de arrefecimento mais eficientes, que reduzam o consumo de água, bem como soluções para recuperar e reutilizar o calor residual. Em terceiro lugar, a informação sobre as emissões e outros impactes ambientais destas infraestruturas deve ser pública e transparente. Finalmente, a localização dos data centres deve considerar a capacidade a capacidade dos territórios em fornecer os recursos. A localização não pode ser determinada apenas pela disponibilidade de terrenos ou pela proximidade de infraestruturas digitais, tem de considerar o ambiente e os cidadãos.

artigo.texto: New alliances offer hope to battery swap sector By Cao Yingying | China Daily | Updated: 2026-10-26 09:24 As China's electric vehicle energy supply competition pivots toward ecosystem dominance, a string of major battery-swapping alliances has formed to address the sector's long-running hurdles of fragmented standards and hefty up-front infrastructure investment. BAIC and CATL signed an agreement on Thursday to deepen battery-swapping cooperation and build a unified battery swap ecosystem. According to the agreement, BAIC will roll out adapted models across its multiple brands to connect to CATL's EVOGO solutions. Earlier last week, Huawei-affiliated Yinwang Intelligent Technology signed a cooperation agreement with CATL and CATL's battery-swapping subsidiary CAES to codevelop a smart battery swap ecosystem. The alliance will link vehicle, station and cloud data, enabling EVs fitted with Huawei's Qiankun intelligent driving system to autonomously locate swap stations, drive into position, align and complete a 99-second battery swap before departing. Local media reports state the three partners plan to launch five swappable EVs by 2027. The first model will be by Epicland, a joint brand developed by Dongfeng and Huawei. Aistaland, a Huawei-GAC marque, also has swappable vehicles in its pipeline. As of Sept 30, CATL had built 2,520 EVOGO swap stations covering 200 cities across China's 31 provincial-level regions, more than doubling its network from December 2025. The battery provider targets 3,000 stations by year-end. Even so, vehicle development has lagged station expansion. CATL has released over 20 EVOGO-compatible models from partners including FAW, Changan, BAIC, Chery and GAC. Most carry price tags below 150,000 yuan ($22,470) and target commercial fleets, with low uptake among private buyers. The new partnerships are expected to speed up the rollout of battery-swappable EVs for private users. Tong Zongqi, general manager of the Open Service Platform at the China Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure Promotion Alliance, said battery manufacturers' push into swapping primarily aims to boost battery shipments and deepen ties with automakers. Combined with battery graduated sequential utilization and recycling, the business model closes the industrial value chain. For battery makers, swapping acts not merely as a sales channel but as a critical source of life-cycle battery operation data, Tong added. Nio, China's pioneer of consumer battery swapping, operated 4,186 swap stations and provided more than 120 million such services by mid-October. Its fifth-generation stations serve its Nio, Onvo and Firefly-branded cars. Since 2023, Nio has inked battery swap cooperation agreements with Changan, Geely, JAC, Chery, FAW and GAC. Yet these partners have not launched compatible vehicles to date; non-Nio vehicles on its network remain mostly fleet-focused. In late September, Nio and Geely signed a strategic deal covering charging and swapping, solidifying cross-shareholdings in their energy businesses. Geely Holding Chairman Li Shufu said last week at an industry conference that the tie-up avoids redundant infrastructure build-out. "There is no need for Geely and Nio to build separate systems, so we joined forces," Li said. The battery swap industry still faces fundamental headwinds: steep up-front capital expenditure, long payback cycles, cross-brand battery incompatibility and low adoption by private motorists. Batteries make up roughly 40 percent of an EV's total cost. Capacity degradation and poor residual values remain major deterrents for buyers. Battery as a Service, or BaaS, decouples battery costs from vehicle pricing and pools battery packs for shared use, easing consumer concerns over long-term battery performance decay. Ji Xuehong, director of the Automotive Industry Innovation Research Center at North China University of Technology, noted that business models like BaaS transfer battery ownership from consumers to operators, cutting up-front purchase costs. CATL Chairman Zeng Yuqun forecast China's future EV energy replenishment market will evolve into three parallel tracks: private home chargers, public fast chargers and battery swap stations.

artigo.texto: County Supes Approved Major Use Permit in September By Jacob Aere / kpbs / October 22, 2026 San Diego County and developers of a solar and battery storage project in East County are facing a lawsuit alleging the project’s environmental review was insufficient. The suit was filed in San Diego Superior Court last week. It focuses on the Starlight Solar project near the town of Boulevard. The county Board of Supervisors approved a major use permit for the development for last month. The 588-acre project, which includes a solar farm and a 868 megawatt-hour battery energy storage system, has faced community pushback. The suit, filed Oct. 15 by a group calling itself the Back Country Community Alliance for Responsible Development, was brought under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). “This is CEQA action brought under the California Environmental Quality Act. And what we’re alleging is that the Environmental Impact Report that was prepared and certified by the county was inadequate,” said Jamie Hall, the group’s attorney. The lawsuit seeks to suspend all activity on the project “pending full compliance with CEQA and with the requirements of law.” A major concern the suit raises is the potential for lithium-battery fires. “My client doesn’t believe the county adequately analyzed those impacts, they didn’t analyze the evacuation routes sufficiently, they didn’t assess whether there was enough water for this particular project,” Hall said. Boulevard residents previously told KPBS they are concerned about the proximity of the battery storage containers to homes and a school. Fires producing toxic gas have broken out at battery storage facilities in Otay Mesa and Escondido in recent years. “We don’t think we’ll have a fire and if we do we have enough safeguards in place,” said Jim Whalen, the Starlight Solar project’s land use consultant. Whalen went on to say that the lawsuit lacks merit. “I don’t think the lawsuit has any merit, number one. We will be addressing the allegations going forward. We’re going to try and see if we can settle,” he said. He pointed out that projects like Starlight Solar help meet state and county green-energy mandates. “The county has to approve renewable energy projects at scale, that’s a given. ‘Where do they go,’ is the only question. We think we’ve done the best job fitting a large project into an area with the least number of people being affected,” Whalen said. A county spokesperson would not comment, citing the pending litigation.

artigo.texto: BYD Lifts on Sector Tailwind as Battery Roadmap, Seagull Launch and Brazil Permits Set Up October 30 Test Published on 10/25/2026 at 09:10 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD shares climbed 4.4% in Hong Kong on Friday, riding a broad rebound across auto and lithium-battery names rather than any company-specific catalyst. The advance followed losses in the prior session and reflected a friendlier market backdrop for the whole sector — a distinction that matters when weighing what actually drove the stock. Europe Sales Offer an Operating Anchor Reuters reported Thursday that BYD's European sales rose in September, with Chinese automakers collectively gaining market share on the continent. That gives investors an operating reference point beyond the short-term sector bounce. Still, a sales increase on its own says nothing about the profitability of the European business. Trade policy belongs in the same frame. Reuters also reported a provisional agreement between the EU and China to limit Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid exports. For shareholders, volume growth and potential export restrictions now sit side by side. The deal is preliminary and should not be read as a final settlement. Technology Priorities Confirmed, Not Delivered On an investor platform today, BYD said it is prioritizing megawatt fast charging, a next-generation Blade Battery and integrated body-battery technology. The distinction is critical: the company is confirming its technological direction, not reporting a completed development milestone or a concrete launch date. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? No performance figures for the announced programs were disclosed. BYD said it will formally update the market once applicable disclosure obligations kick in, so no near-term product launch can be inferred from the statement. The message underscores how central battery and charging technology are to the development plan, yet it offers no basis for quantifying added revenue or earnings. Separating technological potential from commercially proven success remains the key task for valuation. Seagull Refresh Puts Charging Tech on the Road Already-launched products are a separate matter. On Tuesday, BYD began selling the second-generation Seagull in China at an entry price of CNY 65,900, with Flash Charging versions starting at CNY 75,900. That puts fast-charging hardware into more affordable segments rather than reserving it for premium classes. The caveat is infrastructure: advertised charging power depends on compatible stations, so the vehicle's technical capability alone does not guarantee the same charging speed at every plug. For equipped variants, BYD quotes a 10% to 70% charge in 5 minutes — figures that describe the Seagull on sale, not the next-generation development steps discussed today. A European launch of the new Seagull has not been confirmed, so the Chinese sales start implies no European volume contribution; execution in the home market is the near-term focus. Brazil Doubles Down as Analysts Split on Margins Fitting the international growth story, Reuters reported Friday that BYD is seeking approvals to double the annual capacity of its Brazilian plant to 600,000 vehicles. Alexandre Baldy said investments have already exceeded 5.5 billion reais, and BYD is targeting a local component share above 50% by the start of 2027. Both figures are goals, not current production capacity or achieved localization. BYD at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. The expansion push meets a more cautious read on the business from parts of the analyst community, which cite weak domestic demand, higher input costs and policy uncertainty. Barclays, by contrast, keeps an "Overweight" rating and points to global expansion, while flagging softer domestic volumes after subsidy cuts and amid tougher competition. The divergence makes clear that growth opportunities alone do not answer the question of future profitability — the economic proof behind the development strategy remains the central yardstick. The next scheduled disclosure is October 30, when BYD is due to report third-quarter 2026 results. That date offers the first real opportunity to weigh the model offensive and international expansion in financial terms. Until then, Friday's gain looks chiefly like a recovery within the sector. artigo.texto: OPINION| by Danny Bixby, Springfield In his first encyclical, or “letter to the faithful,” Pope Leo focused on an issue that’s been a hot topic in Springfield and across Missouri: how to protect our communities from the environmental, social, and economic harms caused by AI data centers. As a Christian, I find myself agreeing with the Pope. In fact, I think the concerns he expresses feel familiar to many of us, regardless of religion: damage to our environment; unchecked development controlled by a few powerful tech companies; exploitation, prioritizing profit over human dignity. His words were top of mind when I saw that our elected officials in Jefferson City are going “all in on nuclear power” to meet the extraordinary demand from new AI data centers – despite people in Springfield and across the state saying NO to rampant data center development. My common sense quickly kicked in – who’s going to pay to build all of these nuclear reactors? It’s not the tech billionaires developing these hyperscale data centers, or the corporations profiting from them. It’s us. That’s right – even though 68% of Missourians don’t want data centers in our communities and nearly 60% of Missourians worry about being able to afford utilities, Jefferson City politicians passed legislation this year clearing the way for data centers by letting power companies raise our utility bills to cover the cost of building these new plants. It doesn’t take much digging to uncover how we got here. A small handful of special interest megadonors has been buying influence in Jefferson City to get even richer at the expense of our water and energy, our jobs, and our way of life. Right here in Springfield, where voters will soon choose between Rep. Betsy Fogle and Rep. Melanie Stinnett to be our new state senator, all you have to do is follow the money to see where the candidates stand on the issue: Betsy Fogle voted against letting power companies charge families to build new nuclear power plants. Melanie Stinnett voted YES on the bill – YES to forcing us to pay for nuclear plants that “have to be built to provide the power that we need for the data centers” according to the bill’s sponsor. I added it up, and Stinnett has gotten over $1 million in campaign cash (through her campaign committee and the Heart of SGF PAC, which is aligned with her) – over 70% of it coming from corporations and special interests, including those that could profit from data center development. I’ve been fortunate enough to live in Springfield for 26 years. I’ve put down roots here. It’s where I met my wife; where we raised our four daughters; where I served as a pastor and started my own business. I want to spend the rest of my days waking up to a view of God’s green earth – not server farms. That’s why I’m voting for Betsy Fogle for state senate. I trust her to stand up to Big Tech and make sure our communities have a say when it comes to what gets built in our backyard and who gets the bill. Submit a letter to the editor.

artigo.texto: BloombergNEF forecasts energy storage additions to reach 188 GW/535 GWh in 2026 and 209 GW/638 GWh in 2027 It expects annual additions in India to exceed 6 GW in 2026, supported by tender-driven procurement Analysts highlight that rising solar penetration and supply-chain localization policies are reshaping deployment and battery manufacturing Global energy storage installations are set to reach a new record in 2026 with 188 GW/535 GWh, forecasts Bloomberg New Energy Finance (BloombergNEF). The market is expected to set another record in 2027, with annual additions reaching 209 GW and 638 GWh. In its latest energy storage market outlook, BNEF forecasts 2026 global additions to represent a 45% year-on-year (YoY) increase in GWs. Analysts attribute the expected growth to rising solar penetration, government policies promoting storage and growing demand for electricity. Deployment is now expanding beyond China and the US, as India, Australia, and several European markets accelerate battery adoption, they point out. China, the US, and Australia are expected to account for 62% of global additions in 2026. China’s energy storage market remains strong despite the withdrawal of a policy mandating storage for renewable projects. New measures, including output-firming requirements for standalone solar and wind projects and a 300 GW storage target by 2030, are supporting growth. The storage market grows in the US thanks to tax credits and on-site energy storage demand from data centers, while India’s tender-driven annual additions will likely exceed 6 GW of total installations this year, up from a 'few hundred megawatts' last year, according to BloombergNEF. Deployment is also spreading to new markets as countries seek to integrate more renewable energy, improve grid flexibility, and strengthen domestic battery supply chains. Several European countries are also expected to make larger contributions in 2026. Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, France, Greece, the Netherlands, and Ukraine are among the markets forecast to reach gigawatt-scale annual additions. In 2027, Spain, the UAE, Chile, and Japan are expected to accelerate deployment, supported by power market fundamentals, diversified revenue stacks, and utility-led procurement activity. The growing share of solar power in electricity generation is increasing the need for storage. Batteries can store surplus electricity when generation is high and release it when demand rises, or solar output falls. By the end of 2025, approximately 69 GW of energy storage power capacity, equivalent to 196 GWh of energy capacity, was paired with around 299 GW of solar capacity globally, according to the analysts. China accounts for a substantial share of solar-plus-storage installations. Solar curtailment and the decline in electricity prices during periods of high solar generation are among the factors encouraging storage deployment in markets such as the US, Australia, and Chile. However, the trend is spreading, with countries including India, Mexico, and the Philippines introducing regulatory or auction-linked requirements to promote battery integration with renewable energy projects. BloombergNEF expects renewable energy projects paired with storage to remain an important source of deployment growth in the coming years. The US has introduced tariffs and incentives to support domestic battery production, alongside restrictions affecting equipment and supply chains linked to China. The European Union and Japan are also addressing supply-chain security and cybersecurity concerns. These policies could make market access more difficult for some Chinese suppliers. In response, Chinese equipment manufacturers are increasingly exploring markets with fewer restrictions, including the Middle East, Latin America, and sub-Saharan Africa. India, South Korea, and Brazil have also introduced measures intended to encourage domestic production and the use of locally manufactured components, although their approaches are less stringent than those in the US, according to BNEF. In terms of technology, despite growing interest in alternative battery technologies, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is expected to remain the primary battery chemistry for energy storage over the next decade. BNEF attributes its expected dominance to cost competitiveness, long cycle life, and an established supply chain. Sodium-ion batteries are also gaining attention amid rising prices for LFP materials. They offer advantages such as a lower risk of fire and the ability to operate across a wide temperature range, potentially reducing cooling requirements and auxiliary energy consumption. However, limited manufacturing scale and challenges in competing on cost remain barriers to wider adoption of sodium-ion and other non-lithium long-duration storage technologies. BNEF expects cumulative global energy storage capacity to grow approximately tenfold by 2036 compared with the end of 2025, reaching around 3 TW of power capacity and 11 TWh of energy capacity.

artigo.texto: CATL's Market Share Slips to 40.9% as Buybacks and Swap Deals Underpin a Sentiment-Led Bounce Published on 10/25/2026 at 08:10 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL shares climbed 7.8% on Friday, lifted by a broad recovery across Chinese and South Korean equities rather than by any fresh company announcement. Media accounts attributed the move to shifting trading flows and a rotation back into previously sold-off sectors, framing it as a mood-driven countermove following steep losses rather than confirmation of a fundamental turnaround. Battery-linked names and other growth sectors helped drive the afternoon rebound in China. Third-Quarter Profit Misses Expectations The rally follows a Tuesday earnings release in which CATL reported a third-quarter 2026 net profit of 21.2 billion yuan, up 14.5% year on year. According to Reuters, that marked the slowest earnings growth in nearly two years. Revenue for the same quarter rose 58.6% to 165.2 billion yuan, yet both the top and bottom lines fell short of analyst expectations, Reuters reported. Management pointed to product mix as well as consumption-tax and export-tax-rebate effects when explaining per-unit profitability. Reuters also noted that CATL's share of China's traction-battery installation market stood at 40.9% in September, down from 49.8% in January. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Nine-Month Figures and Buyback Activity For the first nine months of 2026, CATL posted revenue of 442.14 billion RMB and a net profit of 64.53 billion RMB. Alongside those results, the company repurchased 3,488,600 A-shares on Wednesday for roughly 800 million RMB, according to its own disclosures, then added a further 2,271,000 A-shares on Thursday for about 499.9 million RMB — buying back stock on two consecutive trading days. A mandatory disclosure to the Hong Kong exchange put the Wednesday tranche at 3.49 million A-shares for around 800 million RMB. Battery-Swap Partnerships and Network Targets Chinese industry coverage tied the battery sector's recovery to several catalysts beyond the buybacks, including partnerships built around battery swapping. On Wednesday, CATL and the Shaanxi Transportation Holding Group signed a strategic cooperation agreement covering the electrification of commercial vehicles, battery-swap stations for heavy trucks, energy storage and charging infrastructure along highways — a collaboration spanning multiple corners of transport infrastructure. CATL, its Chocolate Swap unit and Huawei subsidiary Yinwang also agreed on Monday to link their systems technically, according to media reports. Huawei's intelligent-driving systems are to be connected with CATL's battery-swap ecosystem, with the planned vehicle-to-station workflow designed to complete a swap in 99 seconds. Reuters additionally reported on CATL's plans to expand its battery-swap network for heavy trucks. The company is targeting 900 stations in China by the end of the year, rising to 2,000 by 2027 — concrete build-out goals that sit alongside the newly signed cooperation agreements. artigo.texto: Superexcesso de data centers de IA até 2028? O que a SemiAnalysis diz sobre a oferta de GPUs e restrições de energia A supercapacidade dos centros de dados de IA pode se tornar uma preocupação significativa até 2028, pois a rápida expansão da infraestrutura gera incerteza em relação à oferta de GPUs, disponibilidade de eletricidade e demanda por computação. Em sua pesquisa de 19 de outubro de 2026, a SemiAnalysis projetou mais de 50 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade adicional de centros de dados globais em 2027, levantando questões sobre se a produção de semicondutores poderá acompanhar a construção. O possível desequilíbrio pode afetar a Nvidia, grandes provedores de nuvem e investidores que financiam o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura de IA. No entanto, as atuais escassezes de eletricidade e a forte demanda por serviços de inteligência artificial complicam as perspectivas. Compreender a relação entre capacidade de centros de dados, disponibilidade de chips avançados e requisitos futuros de computação é essencial para avaliar os riscos financeiros e as oportunidades de crescimento do setor. SemiAnalysis alerta para possível supercapacidade de data centers de IA até 2028 A empresa de pesquisa de semicondutores SemiAnalysis alertou que os centros de dados de IA podem enfrentar supercapacidade até 2028, à medida que a construção de infraestrutura acelera e as restrições de fornecimento de semicondutores evoluem. Em seu relatório de 19 de outubro de 2026, a empresa previu mais de 50 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade adicional de centros de dados globais em 2027. O líder da pesquisa, Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros, destacou posteriormente a possibilidade de que o desenvolvimento de centros de dados possa acabar superando a disponibilidade de hardware de computação avançado. O alerta refere-se a um possível desequilíbrio entre a capacidade da infraestrutura e o fornecimento de chips, e não a uma redução confirmada na demanda por inteligência artificial. SemiAnalysis prevê mais de 50 GW de capacidade de data centers em 2027 Em seu relatório de 19 de outubro, Datacenters 2027: The Year of Acceleration, a SemiAnalysis elevou sua previsão de expansão de capacidade para 2027 de aproximadamente 43 GW para mais de 50 GW. A pesquisa identificou mais de 24 GW de capacidade de data centers em construção avançada em 40 grandes complexos, com a maioria dessa capacidade prevista para ser entregue durante 2027. Muitas dessas instalações já estavam mais da metade do caminho na construção, com equipamentos elétricos e de refrigeração instalados. Os achados sustentam as expectativas de expansão substancial da infraestrutura de IA, embora a atividade de construção projetada não garanta que todas as instalações se tornem operacionais conforme o cronograma. A SemiAnalysis baseou suas projeções em monitoramento da construção em nível de edifício, atividade de desenvolvimento de hyperscalers, compromissos de locação e indicadores de implantação de equipamentos. Grandes empresas de tecnologia, incluindo Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta e Oracle, contribuíram para o aumento da demanda por instalações de computação em grande escala. Os desenvolvedores também estão adotando construção modular e sistemas elétricos pré-fabricados para reduzir os prazos dos projetos e diminuir a necessidade de mão de obra. Essas melhorias podem acelerar a adição de capacidade, mas as condições de financiamento, conexões elétricas e disponibilidade de equipamentos permanecem como fatores importantes que influenciam as datas reais de conclusão. O risco de superoferta de data centers de IA depende da oferta de chips e da expansão da infraestrutura Durante uma discussão em 20 de outubro de 2026, o pesquisador da SemiAnalysis Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros destacou a relação em mudança entre a disponibilidade de GPUs e a oferta de energia elétrica para centros de dados. Em alguns mercados, obter GPUs tornou-se mais fácil do que garantir energia suficiente para operá-las, deixando a infraestrutura elétrica como uma grande restrição à implantação. No entanto, à medida que os desenvolvedores expandem instalações e introduzem geração de energia no local, a indústria poderia enfrentar um gargalo diferente. Chips de lógica avançada, memória de alta largura de banda e capacidade de fabricação de semicondutores podem se tornar cada vez mais importantes para determinar quão rapidamente novos centros de dados podem ser equipados com sistemas de IA operacionais. O risco potencial de supercapacidade de data centers de IA em 2028 surgiria se as instalações concluídas excedessem a oferta disponível de equipamentos de computação adequados. Os operadores poderiam, consequentemente, enfrentar infraestrutura elétrica, de refrigeração e de edifícios subutilizadas enquanto aguardam a instalação de GPUs ou componentes de suporte. Tal descompasso poderia atrasar a geração de receita e aumentar a pressão financeira sobre projetos intensivos em capital, mesmo que a demanda por serviços de computação de IA continue crescendo. Se esse cenário se materializar dependerá da produção de semicondutores, da comissionamento das instalações, da disponibilidade de eletricidade e das necessidades de computação dos clientes. O aviso da SemiAnalysis permanece como uma perspectiva condicional, e não como confirmação de que a infraestrutura global de IA entrou em um ciclo de superoferta. Restrições de oferta e energia da GPU criam novos gargalos na infraestrutura de IA A rápida expansão da inteligência artificial está exercendo pressão crescente sobre as redes elétricas, a fabricação de semicondutores e a infraestrutura de computação avançada. Embora as empresas estejam investindo pesadamente em aceleradores de IA e novas instalações, a disponibilidade de GPUs sozinha não determina quanta capacidade de computação pode se tornar operacional. Os data centers exigem eletricidade confiável, refrigeração de alta densidade, equipamentos de rede e memória especializada para suportar cargas de trabalho modern

artigo.texto: PERU — Jason McClure, an apple farmer in Miami County, said he didn’t have any plans to run for political office this year. But that changed when the Miami County Plan Commission voted in May to give a favorable recommendation to a data center ordinance and lift a temporary moratorium on the projects. Hundreds of residents attended the meeting to speak out against it. That included McClure, who wants to reinstate the moratorium. The day after the meeting, he went to the courthouse to file as an independent to challenge two-term Republican County Commissioner Fred Musselman, who serves on the board and voted to pass the ordinance. “It was the straw that broke my back to get into the race,” McClure said. “Enough is enough. My neighbors are showing up and they’re not being heard.” ‘This election’s boogeyman’ As proposals to build hyperscale data centers rapidly ramp up across Indiana, the controversial developments have become the defining issue in many local races where elected officials are considering the issue. Voters are asking whether candidates for county commissioner and council seats support or oppose data centers. For some, the answer will determine their vote, according to Chad Kinsella, director of Ball State University’s Bowen Center for Public Affairs. “Data centers have kind of become this election cycle’s boogeyman,” he said. “It seems to be that everybody hates them and is terrified that one’s going to show up in their vicinity.” At the beginning of the year, Indiana had 38 operational data centers and 37 more under construction or planned for development, according to the University of Virginia’s Weldon Cooper Center for Public Service. A number of large-scale projects have been proposed or approved since then, including in Kokomo, Hobart, Wheatfield, Frankfort and Sullivan County. Nearly 70% of likely voters in Indiana say they oppose construction of new data centers, according to a Free Press Indiana Poll conducted by Bellwether Research. Just 18% said they supported more construction and 13% were unsure. Shannon McFarland, who lives in Peru, which is located in Miami County, said she strongly opposes a data center anywhere in the county. She said that’s the only reason she’s voting for McClure, the independent candidate who wants a moratorium. “Most of this town does not want them here,” McFarland said. “I will absolutely vote for McClure.” In rural Jasper County, commissioners in June unanimously approved a development agreement with Amazon to build a $7 billion, 304-acre data center campus near Wheatfield. Resident Shawna Reid said she strongly opposes the project and wishes she could vote against Rein Bontreger, the incumbent Republican commissioner on the ballot, but he’s running unopposed. With no option to vote for an alternate candidate, Reid is pushing her state legislators to draft a law to allow Hoosiers to vote out commissioners for “serious misconduct” before their term is up. “If you don’t have a say in pulling them out of there if they have committed some travesty while they’re in office, that’s not cool,” Reid said. Guardrails or bans? Voters will decide But some county commissioners running for office are banking on voters who are more open to data center developments showing up at the polls. Angela Henzman, the Democratic candidate for LaPorte County commissioner, said she has concerns about data centers, but thinks an outright ban or moratorium isn’t the answer. The issue is top of mind for residents there. Amazon is building a $1 billion data center campus in the city of La Porte, and Google has plans to build a 70-acre project in Michigan City. Henzman said she’s pushing for any new projects to be built in an industrial park in the county under tight restrictions aimed at protecting residents and the environment. “There’s a small group of people who will say, ‘I’m 100% against that,’” Henzman said. “But then there are so many people along the spectrum that are saying, ‘I understand they’re here. I just don’t want them on farmland, or near my kids’ schools or near my home.’” Jody Slabaugh, the Republican running for the LaPorte County commissioner seat, said he thinks most voters are against any more data centers coming. He’s proposing a moratorium on new developments — something 32 other counties around Indiana have adopted. “There’s definitely some that are going to say, ‘No, I don’t want a data center, and I’m not voting for anybody who says they’re going to put one here,’” Slabaugh said. A poll released this month commissioned by the American Infrastructure Alliance found a majority of Americans prefer stricter data center guardrails over moratoriums. Nearly 55% of voters said they favor allowing data center construction if the company pays for its own electricity needs to protect ratepayers and guarantees it will protect environmental resources. Less than a third (31%) of those polled called for outright bans. Musselman, the Republican incumbent in Miami County facing off against independent McClure, said he doesn’t regret passing the controversial data center ordinance there. He said it creates reasonable guardrails to protect residents while still reaping projects’ economic benefits, like new jobs and increased tax revenue. Musselman said they’ll find out soon whether more residents support his approach over a straightforward moratorium on the developments. “I guess that’s what Nov. 3 is going to tell,” he said. “If I lose, I was wrong in how I read the community. If I win, I must have been right. I don’t know how else to say it.” FPI News reporter Carson Gerber covers pressing issues throughout the state and how local communities are tackling those challenges. artigo.texto: O ciclo de investimentos em inteligência artificial, a temporada de resultados do terceiro trimestre de 2026 e a entrada de capital estrangeiro na B3 dominaram a pauta de estrategistas na semana, segundo compilação do InfoMoney. Entre os pontos analisados estão as projeções da XP para o capex das oito maiores empresas americanas — que podem chegar a US$ 1,8 trilhão até o fim da década —, o papel dos fundos imobiliários na expansão dos data centers e o ingresso de R$ 10,1 bilhões de investidores externos no primeiro pregão depois do 1º turno. Capex de IA e o gargalo da execução A equipe de estratégia da XP avaliou os aportes de capital das companhias ligadas à inteligência artificial para identificar pressões operacionais, oportunidades e as teses de posicionamento mais defensáveis. O levantamento projeta que as oito principais empresas dos Estados Unidos concentrem US$ 1,8 trilhão em investimentos até o encerramento desta década, montante que redesenha as perspectivas do setor de tecnologia e exige leitura cuidadosa dos reflexos sobre as carteiras. A infraestrutura física exigida por essa corrida coloca os data centers no centro do ecossistema. O Brasil aparece como candidato natural a receber parte desse fluxo graças à matriz elétrica limpa, à capacidade energética instalada e à posição geográfica, e os fundos imobiliários surgem como veículo para o investidor acessar essa frente de infraestrutura digital. 3T26: receita cresce, lucro quase parado Em um ambiente macroeconômico desfavorável tanto no Brasil quanto no exterior, a nova safra de balanços deve trazer números contidos. As estimativas consolidadas apontam avanço de 7,2% na receita líquida e de 12% no Ebitda na comparação anual, enquanto o lucro líquido tende à estabilidade, com alta de apenas 0,5% no conjunto de companhias acompanhadas — desempenho que esconde disparidades relevantes entre as áreas analisadas. Na avaliação de ativos específicos, o cobre ganhou peso na tese da Vale (VALE3). Após o Vale Base Metals Day e o Investor Tour realizado no Canadá, analistas concluíram que as reservas atuais sustentam a meta de 700 quilotoneladas anuais até 2035, deslocando o debate da disponibilidade de recursos para a capacidade de entregar os projetos. Big techs e o fluxo de R$ 10,1 bilhões Nos Estados Unidos, a divulgação de resultados das empresas associadas à inteligência artificial trouxe um quadro heterogêneo. SpaceX e Meta ficaram acima do consenso do mercado, enquanto a Tesla apresentou dados levemente desfavoráveis, pressionada pela queda do faturamento na divisão de energia. No mercado local, o relatório mensal Fluxo em Foco mostra que os aportes externos ganharam tração em outubro e atingiram R$ 10,1 bilhões no primeiro pregão após o 1º turno. O documento detalha as posições e o espaço para novos ingressos em renda variável caso o cenário mais otimista se confirme.
