artigo.texto: EMA seeks industry proposals to scale up energy storage Submissions are due by 29 January 2027. The Energy Market Authority (EMA) has launched a consultation paper, calling on the industry to propose technologies, business models, and projects for energy storage systems (ESS) that can be commercially deployed at scale. The development comes as Singapore aims to triple its energy storage capacity from about 350 megawatt-hours to around 1 gigawatt-hour by 2030. Electricity demand is expected to grow rapidly over the next few years, driven by new large loads such as semiconductors, data centres, and the electrification of the transport system, according to EMA. The ESS can respond quickly to fluctuations in solar generation and other supply disruptions to help maintain the power system’s stability. Electricity stored in ESS can also be released should there be high demand in some areas, reducing the strain on the electricity network. Smaller ESS in homes, businesses, and electric vehicles could be coordinated to collectively support the country’s power system, including through arrangements known as virtual power plants. “Singapore’s need for flexibility in the power system is growing,” said Puah Kok Keong, chief executive of EMA. “We would like to partner [with] companies to turn promising ideas into commercially viable energy storage solutions that can be deployed at scale,” he added. EMA said it will work with the industry and relevant agencies to improve access to energy market information and review existing rules. It will also develop requirements for how ESS operate and enable them to be centrally controlled when needed, depending on their size and role in the power system. The authority is also seeking industry interest in forming an industry-led energy storage workgroup to share experiences, develop practical solutions, and address common barriers to ESS deployment. The consultation paper is available on the EMA website, and parties are invited to submit their views and proposals by 29 January 2027 to [email protected].

Atribuição de responsabilidades para o recebimento e processamento de procedimentos administrativos relacionados a créditos de carbono especializados nas áreas de Indústria e Comércio, Construção, Agricultura e Meio Ambiente. (Hochiminhcity.gov.vn) – O Comitê Popular da Cidade de Ho Chi Minh emitiu um documento atribuindo a responsabilidade pelo recebimento e processamento dos procedimentos administrativos relacionados a créditos de carbono especializados nos setores de Indústria e Comércio, Construção, Agricultura e Meio Ambiente. Para os quatro procedimentos, o registro/ajuste de projetos no âmbito do mecanismo nacional de troca de créditos de carbono (código 1.014136); alterações nos participantes do projeto (código 1.014131); cancelamento do registro do projeto (código 1.014132) e emissão de créditos de carbono no âmbito do mecanismo nacional de troca de créditos de carbono (código 1.014133) são realizados da seguinte forma: Para créditos de carbono especializados sob a responsabilidade de gestão estatal de um departamento que administra um setor ou área específica: o Departamento de Indústria e Comércio, o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente e o Departamento de Construção são designados para processar os dossiês e assessorar o Comitê Popular da Cidade para revisar e aprovar os resultados da resolução desses procedimentos, de acordo com suas respectivas áreas de gestão. Para créditos de carbono multissetoriais sob a responsabilidade de gestão de dois ou mais departamentos/setores: o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente assumirá a liderança, coordenando-se com o Departamento de Indústria e Comércio e o Departamento de Construção para processar os dossiês e assessorar o Comitê Popular da Cidade na aprovação dos resultados para os setores relevantes; o Departamento de Indústria e Comércio assumirá a liderança, coordenando-se com o Departamento de Construção para processar os dossiês dos setores sob sua gestão; os departamentos relevantes precisam coordenar-se e fornecer feedback por escrito em tempo hábil para garantir o andamento do processamento dos dossiês e são responsáveis por questões técnicas. O Comitê Popular da Cidade atribui ao Centro de Serviços Administrativos Públicos da Cidade, subordinado ao Gabinete do Comitê Popular da Cidade, a responsabilidade de receber, processar e devolver os resultados dos procedimentos administrativos. Caso surjam dificuldades que ultrapassem sua competência, as unidades devem encaminhar as informações ao Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente para obter auxílio. Veja os detalhes aqui. artigo.texto: CCUS: Eliminando gargalos para alcançar a meta de emissões líquidas zero. A tecnologia de captura, utilização e armazenamento de CO₂ (CCUS) abre caminhos para a redução de emissões nas indústrias, mas exige a superação de obstáculos relacionados a marcos legais, capital e infraestrutura. Na manhã de 27 de outubro, sob a direção do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente , o jornal Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, em colaboração com o Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas e o Instituto de Petróleo do Vietnã (VPI), organizou o workshop “Tecnologia de Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de CO₂ (CCUS): Uma Solução para Promover o Net Zero no Vietnã”. Estrutura legal completa, avalie com precisão o potencial O Sr. Luong Quang Huy, Chefe do Departamento de Gestão de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Proteção da Camada de Ozono (Agência de Alterações Climáticas), afirmou que o período de 2026 a 2030 foi identificado como um período de redução acelerada das emissões, enquanto se aperfeiçoa simultaneamente o quadro operacional do mercado de carbono. De acordo com o roteiro, o Vietname pretende operar oficialmente uma bolsa de créditos de carbono a partir de 2028, criando uma ferramenta adicional para apoiar a concretização das metas climáticas. Neste contexto, a Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de Carbono (CCUS) é significativa para as indústrias que têm dificuldade em reduzir as emissões através de soluções convencionais. Esta tecnologia permite a captura de CO₂ das fontes de emissão, que pode então ser utilizado ou transportado para um local adequado para armazenamento. Segundo o Global CCS Institute, em 31 de julho de 2026, haverá 113 projetos comerciais de captura e armazenamento de carbono (CCS) em operação no mundo , 59 em construção, 308 em fase avançada de desenvolvimento e 352 em fase inicial de desenvolvimento. A capacidade de captura de CO₂ dos projetos em operação é de aproximadamente 68 milhões de toneladas por ano, enquanto os projetos em construção têm uma capacidade total de cerca de 56 milhões de toneladas por ano. No entanto, a implantação comercial do CCS depende não apenas da disponibilidade da tecnologia, mas também de um arcabouço regulatório e de licenciamento claro, do acesso a locais de armazenamento, da garantia de fluxos de receita e de mecanismos adequados de alocação de riscos ao longo de toda a cadeia de valor. Para o Vietnã, a necessidade de reduzir as emissões nos setores de energia, cimento, aço, química e petróleo e gás exige pesquisa em soluções adaptadas às características específicas de cada setor. O Vietnã possui fontes concentradas de emissão de CO₂, potencial de armazenamento em diversas bacias sedimentares e campos de petróleo e gás offshore em declínio, além da experiência, dados geológicos e capacidades técnicas da indústria de petróleo e gás. Esses são fundamentos cruciais para avaliar a viabilidade do desenvolvimento de CCUS (Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de Carbono). O Dr. Nguyen Huu Luong, especialista sênior do Instituto de Petróleo do Vietnã, afirmou que o Vietnã possui potencial para armazenar CO₂ em três bacias sedimentares principais: Cuu Long, Nam Con Son e Song Hong. Segundo ele, a Petrovietnam realizou uma avaliação preliminar do potencial de armazenamento de CO₂ em 34 campos de petróleo e gás offshore. Em 2011, o Vietnã realizou a injeção de CO₂ no campo de Rang Dong. No entanto, o potencial geológico não se traduz automaticamente na viabilidade da implementação de um projeto comercial. Cada local precisa ser inspecionado, avaliado e verificado quanto à capacidade de armazenamento, capacidade de absorção de CO₂, integridade do reservatório e condições de monitoramento de segurança a longo prazo. Você também pode gostar Um passo institucional importante é a Lei do Petróleo nº 10/2026/QH16, aprovada pela Assembleia Nacional em 23 de agosto de 2026 e em vigor desde 1º de março de 2027, que adiciona disposições sobre captura e armazenamento de carbono associados às atividades de petróleo e gás. No entanto, para a implementação prática, é necessário esclarecer melhor as normas relativas a levantamentos, seleção de locais, licenciamento de injeção, operação, monitoramento, encerramento de projetos e responsabilidades a longo prazo. O Dr. Nguyen Thanh Tung, Vice-Diretor do Instituto de Petróleo do Vietnã, acredita que as novas regulamentações fornecem uma base legal inicial para que o Vietnã faça a transição da pesquisa potencial para a implementação gradual de projetos. No entanto, essa é apenas uma condição necessária. O arcabouço legal deve abranger todo o ciclo de vida do projeto e esclarecer as responsabilidades de todas as partes envolvidas em cada etapa. A equação entre custo e infraestrutura determina o potencial de comercialização. Além do arcabouço legal, a eficiência econômica é uma das condições decisivas para o desenvolvimento da CCUS (Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de Carbono). Os custos de captura, transporte, uso e armazenamento de CO₂ precisam ser equilibrados com a receita proveniente de produtos que utilizam CO₂ e com o valor econômico da redução de emissões, incluindo a possibilidade de registro de créditos de carbono, caso as condições aplicáveis sejam atendidas. Segundo o Dr. Nguyen Thanh Tung, um projeto só pode ser implementado em escala comercial quando possui um modelo de negócios viável e um fluxo de receita suficientemente estável para compensar o investimento, os custos operacionais e os riscos. Isso requer um mecanismo para determinar taxas de serviço adequadas, compromissos de longo prazo das fontes de emissão e um plano claro de alocação de riscos entre as partes envolvidas. O Sr. Le Van Nghi, Presidente e CEO da QIS Global, observou que o Vietnã possui vantagens decorrentes de seu potencial de armazenamento de CO₂ offshore, experiência na indústria de petróleo e gás, capacidade em projetar, adquirir, fabricar, comissionar e operar projetos industriais, além de uma rede internacional de cooperação tecnol

artigo.texto: The Pittsburg City Council voted unanimously to place a 45-day moratorium on new data center development following a heated meeting, though residents say the temporary pause does not go far enough to stop a controversial project. The vote targets the next two phases of the Avaio data center project, proposed at the former Delta View Golf Course. The city approved the project's first phase in 2024, which is not affected by the temporary halt. Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are About two dozen demonstrators turned out outside City Hall to protest the development, raising concerns over potential health risks and the project's proximity to homes, schools, and a church. “It’s right by a church, it’s right by a school, I live in close proximity, I’m worried about the illnesses,” said Pittsburg resident Marta Rodrigues. The tension carried inside when demonstrators interrupted the start of the council meeting, prompting a temporary pause. Police escorted the protesters out of the chambers, and the meeting resumed with public comment. Residents continued to press the council during the public comment period, with one commenter stating, "What part of no don’t you understand. I can spell it out for you it’s N-O." Another speaker added, "We can build a future without an industrial power plant besides the playground, protect the places where our children grown up." Councilmembers acknowledged the community's apprehension following the pushback. Local “We hear that there’s a lot of concern….a lot of fear of what it could mean…for city of Pittsburg,” said Councilmember Jelani Killings. The local pushback arrives just days before next week’s election, with Proposition 45 adding another layer of controversy to the debate. Opponents fear the ballot measure could streamline environmental reviews and make it easier to move certain data center projects forward. “It guts our environmental and public review…very broad definition of broadband internet projects,” said Woody Little of Clean and Healthy California. However, a legal analysis from the California Chamber of Commerce challenges that argument, stating that conventional data centers would not qualify under the measure because they do not provide mass-market retail internet access directly to customers. Next Steps The 45-day moratorium takes effect immediately. While the council could consider extending the pause before it expires, development on the first phase of the Avaio project remains unaffected for now.

artigo.texto: Did Ukraine's data center strikes affect Russia's bot army? We now have better evidence. Pro-Russian accounts targeting Ukrainians on Facebook and Telegram sharply declined after Ukrainian drone strikes on Yandex data centers, according to a new report from a Ukrainian government agency. It’s the most direct evidence so far behind a claim that went viral last week, but it falls well short of proving it. The report comes from Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD), which operates under the country’s National Security and Defense Council. It was published Oct. 15, and United24 Media covered it on Oct. 17. The CCD used software from the Ukrainian security firm Osavul to track accounts it flagged as showing "signs of inauthentic behavior." According to Osavul's website, the firm "builds AI-powered risk intelligence for hybrid threats." According to United24, the CCD analyzed 22,664 messages from 5,201 accounts posted between Oct. 6 and 12, across 26 topics in Ukraine’s information space. The report found two sharp drops in activity, each following a strike that fully shut down a Yandex facility. On Oct. 8, the day a fire took Yandex’s data center in Sasovo, in Russia’s Ryazan region, offline, messages fell 83.6 percent, from 4,032 to 660. You May Also Like The number of active accounts fell by a similar share. Activity rebounded past pre-strike levels by Oct. 10, but on Oct. 12, a day after a strike fully halted operations at a Yandex data center in Vladimir, messages fell by 42.6 percent and active accounts dropped by 41 percent. A smaller group of 98 accounts that posted pro-war propaganda, conspiracy theories, or calls for violence followed the same pattern. The CCD concluded that strikes on data centers can significantly disrupt Russian influence networks, but the effect appears to be short-lived. Mashable was unable to verify the CCD’s findings independently. Before publication, we emailed Osavul to request the underlying dataset, the criteria it uses to flag inauthentic behavior, and any information about where the accounts were hosted. Osavul did not respond by publication time. The report never defines "inauthentic behavior." While the term is quite broad, some general signals that researchers typically attribute to bot accounts include newly created profiles, unusually high posting volume, blank or AI-generated profile photos, and activity across many unrelated political narratives. Without Osavul’s criteria, it’s unclear whether these accounts are automated, run by coordinated humans, or a mix of both. Still, if the numbers hold up, they point to something real. The CCD argues that the drops show strikes on data centers can significantly constrain Russia’s information operations by disrupting the automated networks behind them. However, the agency also acknowledges how quickly the accounts came back, suggesting the disruptions were "substantial but short-lived." Why it matters The findings arrive after a week of overheated claims. Last week, Mashable looked at viral claims that Ukrainian drone strikes on Yandex data centers had knocked Russia’s bot army offline. The conclusion we and other outlets reached was that the data behind those claims couldn’t support them. That claim spread like wildfire on social media, amplified by European officials and even backed up by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, President Zelenskyy said "everyone noticed" a drop in Russian bot activity. Social media users echoed similar observations about the seemingly stark decline in pro-GOP and pro-AfD posts after the strikes. It was an easy idea to believe, given how platforms like Facebook and X incentivize and reward polarizing political ragebait, and Russia’s online influence operations are well-documented. The claim also seemed to have supporting data. United24 Media, the Ukrainian government-run outlet whose reporting drove much of the conversation, cited an analysis by The Deep Dive of Cloudflare Radar data. That data showed automated traffic from Yandex’s network had nearly vanished by Oct. 11. As Mashable reported at the time, that data couldn’t support the claim. "Automated traffic" means any request that software, rather than a person, sends to a website, and most of it is mundane. Yandex, often called "Russia's Google," runs the Federation's biggest search engine, so its network constantly sends out crawlers to index the web. Knocking its data centers offline would stop that traffic, whether or not a single troll account went quiet. We found no published evidence tying influence campaigns on social media to Yandex servers, and United24 acknowledged the same limitation. Cloudflare has since published its own analysis. It said its data doesn’t appear to support claims that the strikes crippled social media manipulation, though it couldn’t rule out a connection. Zelenskyy’s office has also narrowed his remarks. According to BBC Verify, his office said the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity. He has a Master's in Journalism from the University of North Texas and is a proud orange cat father. His writing has also appeared in PC Mag and Mother Jones. artigo.texto: MOUNTAIN HOME, Idaho — Mountain Home neighbors are raising concerns about a proposed data center, but the project faces a major obstacle: the city's current zoning regulations don't allow it. WATCH: Where the proposed Mountain Home data center project stands The proposal from Weitz & Co. outlines plans for four three-story data center buildings at the Bennett Ranch Industrial Campus, totaling approximately 3.4 million square feet. The development would also include power generation, backup power systems and cooling infrastructure. Despite the scale of the plans, the project remains just a proposal, with no formal application submitted to the city. In a letter addressed to company owner Dan Weitz, Mayor Rich Sykes said, "On October 20, 2026, [Weitz] dropped off at Mountain Home city hall three copies of what appears to be a proposal," but has not submitted a land-use application, conditional use permit or building permit. "It makes me feel a whole lot better knowing that it's just an idea right now and not something that has been approved and stamped and is going through," Mountain Home neighbor Christine May said. RELATED | Thousands of acres of public land south of Boise eyed for new data center Still, the size of the proposal and its potential impact have some neighbors worried. The developer said, in their project overview documents, its closed-loop cooling system would be designed for minimal water consumption, and an agreement dating back to 2005 would allow the site to connect to the city's water system. But the proposal doesn't spell out what that agreement allows. "All the money in the world will not buy you a glass of water if there isn't any, and we have to think about that," Mountain Home neighbor Lizabeth Braun said. Some neighbors question whether a project this size belongs here at all. "I just don't think they need to be here in Mountain Home. They can try elsewhere," Mountain Home neighbor Evan Peterson said. "I just think that there's a lot of reasons why we shouldn't have a data center in the middle of town surrounded by houses," May said. Months before this proposal showed up at City Hall, Councilman Scott Harjo went to the Planning and Zoning Commission, raising concerns about data centers, including their potential water use. "I'd like to have an answer for that before they come knocking, quite frankly," Harjo said. Now, someone has come knocking. The mayor's letter said the city has been working since early July to define and categorize data centers in its zoning code. Right now, the city said, "Data center is neither a permitted nor conditional use in any zone in the City," meaning they're currently prohibited under city code. READ MORE | Inside Meta’s new Kuna data center built for AI But some neighbors aren't convinced it'll stay that way. "Just judging by their previous reactions to things, I think it probably stands a pretty good chance of getting approved," Braun said. "It's scary when you think about it." "I don't want to see them get walked over. I don't want to see us as a community get walked over," Peterson said. The city said no formal application has been submitted, but the developer can still work with staff and pursue approval once the proper zoning rules are in place. artigo.texto: Beijing, 26 out (Xinhua) -- A integração da China entre tecnologias digitais e finanças verdes está abrindo novas oportunidades para a cooperação global na transição de baixo carbono, disseram os participantes na Conferência Anual 2026 do Fórum da Rua Financeira, em Beijing. Sob o tema "Construindo um ecossistema aberto, colaborativo e inclusivo para o desenvolvimento financeiro global", o evento de quatro dias foi encerrado na semana passada. Ele reuniu participantes nacionais e internacionais, tanto online quanto presencialmente, para discutir o desenvolvimento financeiro e a cooperação diante dos desafios econômicos globais. "Nos últimos anos, vimos o mercado de finanças verdes da China crescer várias vezes", disse Ma Jun, presidente do Instituto de Finanças e Sustentabilidade em Beijing. "A integração das finanças digitais e verdes criou muitas oportunidades de crescimento e ajudou a impulsionar os investimentos transfronteiriços." Esse crescimento ganhou reconhecimento internacional. " A China melhorou a qualidade do ar ao desenvolver uma economia circular e construir uma sociedade ambientalmente amigável", disse Yaseen Anwar, ex-presidente do Banco Estatal do Paquistão, em um fórum paralelo. Ele acrescentou que a capacidade instalada de energia eólica e solar do país continua a crescer, enquanto produtos verdes, como veículos de nova energia (NEVs), lideram globalmente. Dados divulgados pelo Ministério da Ecologia e do Meio Ambiente mostram que a capacidade instalada de geração de energia renovável do país atingiu 2,455 bilhões de quilowatts no primeiro semestre deste ano, representando 60,7% de sua capacidade total instalada de geração de energia. A China ocupa o primeiro lugar mundial tanto na produção quanto nas vendas de NEVs há 11 anos consecutivos. Nos últimos anos, a China tem oferecido amplas oportunidades para o investimento verde global e a transição de baixo carbono, aplicando tecnologias como big data, blockchain e IA para melhorar a governança das finanças verdes, modernizar as estruturas industriais e aprimorar o meio ambiente ecológico. O Banco da China emitiu títulos verdes no âmbito da Iniciativa Cinturão e Rota para apoiar grandes projetos verdes, como usinas fotovoltaicas de grande escala em países parceiros. Espera-se que esses projetos forneçam às comunidades locais um abastecimento estável e de longo prazo de energia renovável limpa. O mercado de carbono é uma importante ferramenta política para lidar com as mudanças climáticas por meio de mecanismos de mercado e para acelerar a transformação verde abrangente do desenvolvimento econômico e social. O volume acumulado de negociação de cotas de emissão de carbono no mercado nacional de carbono da China ultrapassou 1 bilhão de toneladas, de acordo com dados do Ministério da Ecologia e do Meio Ambiente. A experiência da China no desenvolvimento de seu mercado de carbono também oferece lições com as quais outros países podem aprender. "Os compromissos da China em relação às emissões de carbono e o desenvolvimento de seu mercado de carbono têm dado uma contribuição enorme para a ação climática global", disse Charles Bowman, copresidente da Força-Tarefa de Finanças Verdes Reino Unido-China. "A cooperação em finanças verdes entre a China e o Reino Unido tem promovido a transformação econômica, a conservação da biodiversidade e o desenvolvimento sustentável em ambos os países", acrescentou ele. Essa cooperação também está se estendendo aos parceiros da Iniciativa Cinturão e Rota. Muitos deles estão implementando ativamente políticas verdes e sustentáveis, ao mesmo tempo que mobilizam capital. "A China adaptou serviços para diferentes regiões, incluindo a promoção da aplicação de instrumentos de finanças verdes e do desenvolvimento de mercado, a realização de pesquisas aprofundadas sobre políticas verdes e o avanço dos mecanismos do mercado de carbono", disse Cheng Lin, chefe do Escritório do Secretariado em Beijing para os Princípios de Investimento Verde para a Iniciativa Cinturão e Rota. Especialistas observaram na conferência que, como as tecnologias digitais e inteligentes remodelaram profundamente o setor financeiro nos últimos anos, potencializar as finanças verdes com essas tecnologias é um caminho fundamental para o desenvolvimento sustentável global. "As tecnologias digitais e inteligentes podem oferecer um importante apoio às finanças verdes, superando gargalos na coleta e análise de dados e monitoramento e avaliação de riscos", disse Zhang Bei, vice-chefe do departamento de pesquisa do Banco Popular da China. À medida que os eventos climáticos extremos se tornam mais frequentes, tecnologias como sistemas de informação geográfica, sensoriamento remoto por satélite e grandes modelos de linguagem podem ajudar a avaliar com maior precisão como diferentes regiões e grupos populacionais estão lidando com as mudanças climáticas, identificar prioridades para a adaptação e direcionar o financiamento para as áreas com maiores necessidades, observou Zhang. O papel cada vez mais importante da tecnologia digital nas finanças verdes da China deve beneficiar mais parceiros globais em seus esforços de desenvolvimento sustentável. Mari Elka Pangestu, vice-presidente do Conselho Econômico Nacional da Indonésia, disse que a China é líder em tecnologias limpas. Ela expressou esperança de aprofundar a cooperação com parceiros chineses além do investimento de capital, por meio do estabelecimento de mais joint ventures, do aumento da produção local e do fortalecimento da transferência de tecnologia. O 15º Plano Quinquenal da China (2026-2030) prevê a expansão de produtos e serviços financeiros verdes e o incentivo a maiores investimentos no desenvolvimento verde e de baixo carbono.

artigo.texto: The San Diego City Council today is expected to approve Mayor Todd Gloria’s proposed temporary ban on large data centers Tuesday, but it likely would do almost nothing to stop a potential data center near the Midway District that developers have been exploring. Our MacKenzie Elmer recently broke the news about a 400-megawatt data center that Manchester Financial Group has considered building on U.S Navy land. If built, it could possibly be the largest data center in all of California. Because it’s federal land, the Council is essentially powerless. But it’s not just that. President Trump is encouraging data centers. He has ordered the Secretary of War to identify military sites that could house large-scale data centers, like the one proposed. At today’s meeting, councilmembers will vote on whether to put an emergency ordinance in place that would pause all pending applications for data centers for 45 days. The Council can keep renewing the ban for a total of 20 months. The goal is to use that time to come up with regulations for how data centers might fit within city zoning. Gloria said at an event last week that without new regulations, it would be almost as easy to permit a data center as a warehouse. Supe Candidate Clarifies Where He Stands on County Sales Tax District 5 Supervisor candidate Kyle Krahel is trying to set the record straight about his stance on Measure B, a proposed countywide half-cent sales tax increase on this year’s ballot. At our Politifest North County even this month he took a bold and very clear position in support of it, but the Union-Tribune reports that he said he was opposed to the measure six months ago. Krahel told our Tigist Layne it was all a misunderstanding. Krahel is a Democrat running against Republican Rebecca Jones, who is the mayor of San Marcos, to serve on the county Board of Supervisors. Krahel didn’t stutter at Politifest when he said “people are going to die on our streets” if Measure B fails, explaining that it will be difficult to provide essential services to the region’s most vulnerable people without that extra revenue. That’s because the federal government has been rolling out massive cuts to food benefits, health care coverage and many safety-net programs as part of its “Big Beautiful Bill.” During an online candidate forum in April, Krahel said he was opposed to Measure B. But he told Voice that wasn’t the case. He thought the moderator had asked each candidate if they generally support sales tax increases, and his answer was no. But when it comes to Measure B, he said, he was in support of it then and still is today. “I am generally skeptical of any tax increase, especially regressive taxes like sales taxes, partly because it hurts working families,” Krahel said. “I didn’t realize that it was that specific question. I supported Measure B before that actually, but yes, I support the need for us to backfill fiscally the cuts that are coming.” Save the Date: Brews and News Our Brews and News Live Podcast is happening in two weeks on Tuesday, Nov. 10, and you don’t want to miss it! It’s all going down at 6 p.m. at Soda Bar. Whether you’re an avid listener of San Diego’s most popular public affairs podcast, or you’re hoping to come meet our team of journalists over a beer, Brews & News will be an awesome opportunity to get all the inside scoop on current San Diego happenings. Join the pod team with special guests Julie Roland and Mason Herron for this live recording at Soda Bar. Spots are limited. Grab your ticket now to be part of the celebration! This is a public 21+ event. Valid ID is required at the door. Reporter’s Circle and Editor’s Circle members (annual giving $500+) receive two free tickets. Please email membership@voiceofsandiego.org to redeem your tickets or for any questions. In Other News - A new audit revealed that San Diego’s backlog of 7,000 streetlight repairs, and the long waits to get them fixed, can be attributed to questionable management and weak oversight of electricians. artigo.texto: What to Do About the Coming Glut of AI Data Centers Mark MacCarthy / Oct 27, 2026 There is a current shortage of AI data centers, but that shortage is temporary. More AI data centers will be built than will be needed to satisfy future AI compute demand. The industry is in the throes of a familiar bubble, where more investment flows into constructing facilities for a new technology than can be supported by customer demand. This has happened before with railroads and internet communications facilities and is happening again now with AI data centers. An oversupply is usually followed by a contraction — prices and supply collapse until an equilibrium is restored. But in this case the overexpansion of AI data centers is so large that the contraction is likely to have substantial macroeconomic consequences, a rapid decline in stock values and economic activity across the economy. This sequence of a recession following an overexpansion is also a familiar pattern established by the earlier overexpansion of railroads and internet facilities. Regulation can serve several purposes other than preventing the coming AI data center crash. Policymakers generally know how to protect electricity ratepayers from paying the costs of providing service to AI data centers and picking up the bill for stranded transmission and distribution facilities no longer needed to supply AI data centers. Policymakers are moving toward AI safety regulation needed to protect against dangerous AI experiments by AI developers. Congress should begin a series of hearings on the liability of AI developers and deployers for damages caused by AI models and agents, and a system of insurance needed to make sure victims of these mishaps can be compensated. Policymakers must also begin to address inaccuracies and unreliability of AI models, especially in consequential areas such as providing health information to the public. Along with collaborators, I will be addressing these issues in upcoming commentaries. Unfortunately, the system of governance in the US does not provide policy tools to prevent the coming oversupply-contraction cycle in AI data centers. Generally speaking investors are free to put their money where they feel they can earn the largest return, even if the collective result is an economic crash. Policymakers should be aware, however, of the industry dynamics that are leading to this outcome, even if there is little they can do to stop it. AI data centers today and tomorrow Chips are the key physical elements in an AI data center. Strung together in elaborate layouts of ever-increasing density within enormous physical structures, they are the devices that AI companies use to train and operate their AI models. There are shortages of chips, especially memory chips, and prices for these scarce items are soaring. But the major cloud computing companies, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have been able to secure a steady supply of chips from providers like Nvidia and have begun to develop chips of their own. In addition to chips, data centers costs include land, design and engineering expenses, construction of physical structures, power, cooling facilities, and networking expenses. Together with Meta, the three major cloud companies are expected to devote roughly $750 billion to capital expenditures this year alone, almost all of it focused on these AI infrastructure expenses. Often independent developers build and operate data centers specifically designed to handle AI workloads and lease them to cloud computing tenants or directly to AI developers. One of these “neocloud” providers, CoreWeave, for example, has Microsoft, OpenAI and Meta as leading customers. The leading AI companies, including Anthropic and OpenAI, have been scrambling to secure adequate compute through contracts with companies operating data centers and providing chips. Anthropic said it expects to spend at least $518 billion over the coming decade building AI infrastructure with six partners including the big three cloud computing companies, Google, Microsoft and Amazon, according to a confidential IPO prospectus. Including chip deals with companies like Broadcom means that Anthropic’s future AI infrastructure costs top $600 billion, according to its draft S1 prospectus, a figure confirmed by the formal release of its prospectus on October 26. There is a widely recognized shortfall in current data center capacity. As Wall Street Journal reporter Asa Fitch noted, “A data-center crunch is coming.” According to a recent Morgan Stanley analysis, estimated global demand for data center capacity will be “about 56 gigawatts next year, with just 51 gigawatts of new facilities being energized.” In 2028, estimated demand climbs to 86 gigawatts, but “only 68 gigawatts of computing power come online.” Protests against data centers have the potential to slow data center expansion to meet this unmet demand. Texas and New York have halted the construction of new AI data centers and Pennsylvania and Oregon have imposed new limits. Heatmap reports the “cancellation” of $260 billion worth of data center projects in 2026. Some of this is a healthy shakeout. Utilities have known for some time about “phantom” data centers, where companies operating data centers ask utilities for power they might not need, sometimes because they file the same energy requests with several utilities at the same time. But new requirements on potential data center customers have begun to purge utility wait lists of phantom data centers. Despite protests and moratoria, data center expansion still seems to be on track. The industry analysis firm, Semianalysis, estimates that data center capacity will double in 2027 compared with 2026. The ultimate driver of this demand for AI data centers is increasing usage of AI services, mostly by enterprises, but also by individual users. artigo.texto: Absolar vê data centers como solução para curtailment Entidade cobra do presidente reeleito Lula a regulamentação do Redata e investimentos nas redes elétricas para viabilizar novos projetos no Brasil A Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (ABSOLAR) defendeu a atração de data centers como parte da solução para aproveitar a energia renovável cuja geração é cortada (curtailment) no Brasil. Em posicionamento divulgado após a reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a entidade cobra do presidente reeleito a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), planejamento energético e investimentos nas redes de transmissão e distribuição. Segundo a associação, 17,2% do potencial de geração solar e eólica do País foi cortado no primeiro trimestre de 2026. A ABSOLAR relaciona esses cortes à falta de demanda e de capacidade de armazenamento da eletricidade disponível. Na avaliação da entidade, a instalação de data centers pode trazer novas cargas capazes de consumir parte dessa energia. A manifestação ocorre após Lula mencionar as fontes renováveis como um dos fatores para atrair investimentos em infraestrutura digital no discurso da vitória. “O Brasil reúne condições privilegiadas para transformar sua matriz renovável em vantagem competitiva, inclusive na atração de data centers, indústrias eletrointensivas, fábricas de hidrogênio verde e eletromobilidade”, afirma Rodrigo Sauaia, CEO da ABSOLAR. Redata e infraestrutura elétrica A associação aponta a regulamentação do Redata como uma das medidas necessárias para avançar nessa agenda. O regime prevê contrapartidas relacionadas ao uso de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão e depende de regulamentação do Poder Executivo para produzir efeitos. A entidade também ressalta que a atração de empreendimentos precisa ser acompanhada de planejamento energético e de expansão das redes elétricas. Segundo a ABSOLAR, a infraestrutura de transmissão e distribuição está entre os gargalos relatados por grandes consumidores que avaliam investimentos no Brasil. Data centers integram uma das três propostas apresentadas pela associação ao governo federal, aos governadores e ao Congresso Nacional para o período de 2027 a 2030. Batizada de “Energia que Emprega”, a iniciativa reúne ainda indústria eletrointensiva de baixo carbono, hidrogênio verde, eletrificação, eletromobilidade e planejamento da transmissão. A entidade associa esse conjunto de medidas à viabilização de 18 gigawatts (GW) em novas usinas solares. Leilões de baterias No curto prazo, a ABSOLAR considera os dois primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade para contratação de sistemas de baterias, previstos no comunicado para 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026, o primeiro teste da agenda energética após as eleições. A associação pede definição das condições de custeio dos certames e defende contratações anuais de armazenamento. Na avaliação da entidade, as baterias podem dar flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico, mitigar os cortes de geração renovável e reduzir a necessidade de acionamento de termelétricas. A presidente do Conselho de Administração da ABSOLAR, Bárbara Rubim, também cobra previsibilidade regulatória e ressarcimento aos empreendimentos que tiveram a geração cortada. Entre as reivindicações estão incentivos para projetos de armazenamento, um marco legal próprio para a atividade e redução da carga tributária sobre baterias, que, segundo a associação, chega a 84,8%.

artigo.texto: The U.S. government's new designation of helium gas as critical for artificial intelligence and data centers may spur drilling projects in Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. "Helium is essential to producing the semiconductors and advanced technologies that power our economy. By designating helium as a critical material, we are taking another step toward securing our supply chains, creating American jobs, and ensuring the United States leads the world in energy and technological innovation," U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced Oct. 23. Reasons for the critical-material designation were outlined the same day in a four-page Federal Register notice. It stated that growing AI infrastructure in the United States will depend on the ability of the nation to produce semiconductors. "Helium's unique properties make it indispensable to semiconductor production, with no viable substitutes in many critical applications. The United States has significant domestic deposits of helium-rich natural gas to support growing industrial demand," the Department of Energy noted. What Is Helium? Helium is one of seven types of "Noble Gases" named as such because they don't have normally have chemical reactions with any other gas or substances. (Other types of these inert gases include helium, krypton, neon and radon.) "Noble gases are the least reactive elements in the periodic table, and they condense out of the air at very low temperatures. They are therefore extremely difficult to trap at temperatures above freezing," according to DOE. Helium (which is non-toxic and lighter than air) has no odor or color. A byproduct of extracting natural gas, helium has multiple high-tech uses including in use in quantum computing, air-to-air missile guidance systems, medical MRI machines, cardio-pulmonary resuscitation pumps for heart surgery, fiber-optic cables, blimps, deep sea diving and leak testing natural gas infrastructure. Domestic Helium The most recent U.S. Geological Survey assessment of helium stated that in 2025 there were 29 plants producing various types of helium domestically. In addition, Texas had three underground cavern storage sites for helium. "In 2025, six new helium operations (three in New Mexico and one each in Colorado, Kansas, and Montana) began producing helium in the United States. A helium storage cavern was brought online in Beaumont, TX, which was able to store excess helium production," stated a 2026 mineral commodity summary for helium. USGS estimated that last year's sales of Grade-A helium (99.997% helium or greater) and gaseous helium (above 98% helium) amounted to $970 million.

artigo.texto: To pitch a 'My Turn' guest column, email jdalessio@news-gazette.com. MAHOMET — A few weeks after public backlash led the village of Mahomet to end preliminary talks with a data-center developer, the village board is set to vote on a resolution calling on state lawmakers to protect the Mahomet Aquifer from data-center development. The board will vote tonight on whether to approve the resolution, which would authorize Mayor Jason Tompkins to sign and send identical letters on the subject to state Sen. Chapin Rose, R-Mahomet, and state Rep. Chris Miller, R-Hindsboro. “On behalf of the Village of Mahomet Board of Trustees, I write to express our support for efforts through legislation to protect the Mahomet Aquifer including the requirement of a closed-loop cooling system for data-center developments,” the proposed letter from Tompkins states. “We further urge the legislature to resolve this important issue during your fall veto session or during (the lame-duck) session in January.” The village of Mahomet announced on Sept. 28 that it was in talks with Clean Cloud Energy about a potential data-center project in “a rural area west of Champaign” that falls within Mahomet’s extraterritorial jurisdiction. One week later, the village announced the end of those discussions amid public opposition, including concerns about transparency and the potential impact on the aquifer. Documents released by the village on Sept. 28 following a Sept. 14 Freedom of Information Act request by Mahomet resident John Bambenek show that Clean Cloud Energy began talking with Mahomet officials about the project in December. The village entered into a nondisclosure agreement with the company in early 2026 but was released from the agreement on Sept. 16. Individuals who signed NDAs include Village Administrator Patrick Brown, Village Planner Abby Heckman and Economic Development Specialist Austin Shufflebarger. The village board discussed data centers during a study session last week, Tompkins said. “One of our trustees, Trustee (Bruce) Colravy, felt that it would be appropriate for us to acknowledge the work that Senator Rose is doing as far as for the protection of the aquifer,” Tompkins told The News-Gazette. “… That is something that I believe our entire board is very committed to. And it’s a very important resource, and so we were just lending support to Senator Rose in his efforts.” “I just feel like the NDA, the data center and there seemed to be some disregard, then, for how that might impact the aquifer — or at least perceived disregard,” said Colravy, who has a degree in natural resources and helped found the Upper Sangamon River Conservancy. “And so I wanted to do something to try to clear that up.” He doesn’t like the idea of data centers being located over sole-source aquifers but added that he’s not sure if banning this is legally an option. The proposed resolution states that the village supports legislation that would prevent data centers from using groundwater from the Mahomet Aquifer and require alternative cooling methods such as “reclaimed water, surface water, or closed-loop or air-cooled systems.” Andrew Rehn, director of climate policy at Prairie Rivers Network, said in a previous interview that closed-loop cooling systems for data centers do not consume as much water as evaporative cooling systems, though they do use more electricity. Colravy supports the requirement of closed-loop cooling systems but would like the language about reclaimed water and surface water to be removed from the resolution. “I think you can create some environmental problems with that as well,” he said. “As you may know, the Sangamon River, we put processed wastewater back into the river, but that water is not waste. It is used by wildlife until it gets to Decatur, ends up in their lake, then it’s used for recreation and it’s also their water source. So when you take from that, you’re also taking from downstream.” Tompkins acknowledged that the protection of the aquifer was a concern that the village heard from members of the public after announcing that it was in initial talks with Clean Cloud Energy. “Had the data center ever gotten to a point of an official proposal by a developer, we would’ve been very adamant about that, making sure it’s a closed-loop system and that all measures to protect the aquifer would be put in place,” he said. According to Prairie Rivers Network, the Mahomet Aquifer is the sole source of drinking water “for nearly 1 million people across 14 counties in Central Illinois.” Clean Cloud Energy previously said in a public statement that it would use “zero water” to cool the proposed project near Mahomet. “The coolant is an engineered solution that will be trucked on-site with a small amount of water that may be used during the initial fill,” company officials said. “The only potable water used would be for the needs of the employees in the building — sinks, bathrooms, and canteen — just like any other business or manufacturing facility.” “As a business, we only do closed-loop, air-chilled cooling that uses no water,” Clean Cloud Energy CEO Raj Keswani said in a previous interview. “Evaporative cooling is, in our view, not a responsible way to develop data centers.” However, community members remained concerned about the project’s potential impact. And despite the village’s decision to end talks with the company, Mahomet officials have still been criticized by some in regards to how the discussions were handled. “The last couple study sessions, there (have) been comments about the project,” Tompkins said. “Obviously, we have listened to those items. We have taken them very seriously. And we felt the letters to legislators was a good first step as far as acknowledging that we do recognize the importance of the aquifer. We also, in future study sessions, will be discussing NDAs, how they work and what policies we may have going forward on those.” Colravy said he was first told that the company had app

artigo.texto: Alto valor das baterias e mercado ilegal de peças multiplicam furtos e roubos de carros elétricos em São Paulo Foram 186 ocorrências de janeiro a julho de 2026 contra 62 no mesmo período do ano passado Os carros elétricos e híbridos entraram na mira dos ladrões no estado de São Paulo, e os casos de furtos e roubos cresceram 200%, segundo levantamento feito pela empresa de rastreamento de veículos Ituran para O GLOBO. A empresa analisou dados de roubos e furtos da Secretaria de Segurança Pública (SSP) e registros que identificam as marcas e os modelos envolvidos nas ocorrências, o que permitiu calcular a evolução dos crimes envolvendo carros elétricos e híbridos. Foram 186 ocorrências de janeiro a julho de 2026 contra 62 no mesmo período do ano passado. Veículos a combustão, no entanto, ainda são responsáveis por praticamente 99% desse tipo de crime no estado: houve mais de 56 mil ocorrências entre janeiro e julho deste ano. - Infecções, falhas na assistência e inconsistências em prontuários: Tudo sobre a morte de seis bebês em hospital de SP - Vídeo: Clube da Esquina, local histórico para a MPB, é vandalizado com tinta vermelha em Belo Horizonte; polícia investiga A Polícia Civil encontrou desmanches clandestinos focados em carros elétricos principalmente da montadora chinesa BYD, em ao menos duas ocasiões, na Zona Leste da cidade de São Paulo. Delegados da unidade especializada em roubos de veículos ouvidos pelo GLOBO apontam que ainda não identificaram pelas peças provenientes de crimes nas fiscalizações a desmanches legalizados — aqueles que revendem peças de veículos apreendidos ou leiloados, por exemplo. Se até 2025 a maior parte dos casos envolvendo carros elétricos ou híbridos era de roubos com uso de violência, em 2026 o cenário apontou para uma alta de furtos. Especialistas ouvidos pela reportagem afirmam que os ladrões aprenderam a quebrar as barreiras de segurança desses modelos. O principal alvo dos criminosos são as baterias, informam seguradoras e delegados. A peça chega a corresponder a 50% do valor dos carros — os modelos citados na reportagem, quando novos, variam entre R$ 120 mil a R$ 250. Também estão na mira dos criminosos itens para reposição, como para-choques, retrovisores e portas, que têm alto custo e são escassas no mercado nacional. Os dados apontam que o modelo que mais aparece nos boletins de ocorrência é o BYD Dolphin, seguido do Toyota Corolla Cross híbrido. As versões mais visadas têm entre dois e cinco anos de fabricação. Essa fatia responde por 47% dos casos. O Toyota Corolla Cross não é o modelo híbrido mais vendido atualmente, mas a demanda por peças de reposição aumenta à medida que a frota envelhece. Incidência na capital A capital paulista concentra a maior parte dos casos registrados no estado, com 137 ocorrências. Um engenheiro de 67 anos, que pediu para não ser identificado, teve um BYD Dolphin Mini furtado na Zona Leste. No dia 14 de julho deste ano, um domingo, por volta das 7h40, ele estacionou o carro na Avenida Secondino, na Vila Prudente, e quando retornou ao local, no fim de tarde, não o encontrou mais. O carro tinha rastreador, e o proprietário conseguiu localizá-lo num endereço a cerca de 20 minutos de distância, em Sapopemba, também na Zona Leste. A vítima acionou a polícia, que identificou no local uma loja de peças automotivas aparentemente ilegal. Os policiais encontraram ali um alçapão, que dava acesso a um porão, onde se depararam com peças do carro do engenheiro, como o para-brisa, além do motor de outro veículo com registro de furto, também da BYD. Cinco pessoas foram presas em flagrante. — O furto me causa medo e apreensão até hoje. A estrutura montada para o desmonte do meu carro era bastante organizada e profissional, se é que posso utilizar essa palavra — diz o engenheiro. — Não existe sistema (antifurto) seguro. É só questão de tempo para (criminosos) descobrirem as brechas Outro desmanche clandestino foi encontrado em agosto passado durante uma operação do 42º DP do Parque São Lucas que investigava uma quadrilha especializada no furto de veículos elétricos. Policiais civis bateram na porta da casa de um homem apontado como membro do grupo, no bairro Vila Ema, para cumprir mandados de busca e apreensão, quando se depararam com uma dezena de peças automotivas, entre portas, capô, para-choques e volantes. Os policiais conseguiram identificar uma porta de um BYD Song Plus que havia sido furtado dois meses antes. O homem que morava no local foi preso. O principal foco desse grupo eram as baterias dos carros. A equipe da delegacia ainda tenta desvendar como funcionava a cadeia de receptação da quadrilha e os possíveis compradores desses componentes. Uma tentativa de roubo a dois BYDs na Zona Sul de São Paulo quase terminou em latrocínio em novembro do ano passado. Era manhã de uma sexta-feira na região do bairro do Ipiranga quando três homens conseguiram entrar na residência de um casal e ficaram à espreita na garagem, onde os carros eram carregados. Sem conseguir ligar os automóveis, eles esperaram os proprietários aparecerem. O primeiro alvo, a mulher, foi surpreendida pelo trio quando descia as escadas em direção à garagem. Um dos homens, armado, a derrubou e apontou a arma para a boca da vítima, pedindo que ela ficasse quieta. Ela gritou, e o ladrão atirou. O disparo a atingiu de raspão a pálpebra e a testa da vítima. A movimentação foi percebida pela vizinhança, que chamou a polícia. Os criminosos desistiram de levar os veículos e começaram a buscar outros bens. Após roubarem um celular e as chaves da casa, eles foram contidos por vizinhos e pela Polícia Militar durante tentativa de fuga. Entre janeiro de julho deste ano, 83% das ocorrências envolvendo carros elétricos e híbridos foram furtos. Até 2025, nesse mesmo intervalo, a dinâmica criminal era diferente: 59% dos casos eram roubos, com abordagens diretas e uso de violência contra as vítimas. — Em 2025, nossa percepção é que (os elétricos e híbridos) ainda eram novidade,

artigo.texto: Data centers are using more water than at any point in the internet era, and the question of why is the top trending technology story on October 27, 2026. WSLS and TechRadar both put the topic in front of readers this week, and the explanation starts with one fact of physics. Nearly all the electricity that powers server hardware ends up as heat, and someone has to remove it. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, U.S. data centers directly consumed approximately 17.4 billion gallons of water in 2023, up from an estimated 5.6 billion gallons in 2014. Eric Sjostedt, a Virginia Tech researcher, summed up the core problem for WSLS on October 26: “At its core, data centers produce a lot of heat. It’s getting rid of that heat that uses so much water.” That sentence explains why data center water use keeps climbing even as chips get more efficient per calculation. More computing in a smaller space means more heat per rack, and the cheapest way to move heat outdoors is often to let water evaporate. This analysis walks through the mechanics, the numbers, the tradeoffs and the money. It also separates what the record confirms from what it does not. The AI build-out now underway echoes earlier infrastructure booms, a pattern we examined in our look at the AI infrastructure race and its old boom echoes, and water is one of the places where that history shows up first. No single facility, product or company drives today’s headlines, so this piece treats the story as an industry-wide trend. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Why Data Centers Use So Much Water: The 17.4 Billion Gallon Baseline The best anchor for any discussion of why data centers use so much water is the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimate. The lab puts direct U.S. consumption at roughly 17.4 billion gallons in 2023. That is water the facilities themselves take in and lose, mostly through evaporation in cooling systems. It does not include the water used to generate the electricity that runs the buildings, which is a separate and larger conversation we cover below. A year-over-year headline number hides how the use is distributed. Water consumption depends on how each site rejects heat outdoors, and that varies widely by design and climate. Facilities that lean on fans and outdoor air generally use less water but more electricity. Facilities that lean on evaporation generally do the opposite. LBNL’s figure is therefore a national blend of many different engineering choices rather than a per-building constant. The growth rate matters as much as the level. Going from 5.6 billion gallons in 2014 to 17.4 billion in 2023 means direct consumption rose roughly 3.1 times in nine years. The same arithmetic implies compound growth of about 13 percent a year over that span. Those two derived figures are our own calculations from the laboratory’s published endpoints, not numbers the lab reported, but they give readers a feel for the pace. Congress has taken notice of the topic. The Congressional Research Service published a primer titled Data Centers and Water: Frequently Asked Questions, which signals that lawmakers want a plain-language baseline before they write rules. Heat Is the Real Problem, Not Thirst Servers do not consume water the way a factory consumes a raw material. They consume electricity, and the electricity becomes heat. According to the LBNL reporting summarized in the research for this story, nearly all of the power drawn by IT equipment is converted to heat that must be removed to keep chips from overheating. Water enters the picture only because it is a very good way to carry that heat away. Matt Green, president of Brucker HVAC Solutions, told Network World why operators accept the water bill: “The reason why we evaporate water is because it’s a very effective way to cool.” The statement is blunt, and it captures the engineering logic. Evaporation moves a large amount of heat for each unit of water, so it keeps fan and compressor loads low. Green also drew a comparison with ordinary buildings. In the same Network World interview he said that office cooling uses a tolerable amount of water, but that data centers are “basically power plants in reverse,” and that the heat they generate demands substantially more water than a building of the same footprint would normally use. The comparison helps explain why a data center can look modest from the street and still dominate a local utility’s demand forecast. The heat load is also continuous. Offices empty out at night and homes cool down in winter. Servers run around the clock, and the AI hardware now filling new halls runs hot at all hours. Cooling plants therefore operate at high duty cycles, and any system that depends on evaporation pulls water every day of the year, with peaks in summer when outdoor air offers the least free cooling. How Evaporative Cooling Works and Why Operators Pick It In an evaporative system, warm water or refrigerant loops carry heat from the server floor to a cooling tower or similar device outside. There, a portion of the water evaporates and takes heat with it. The remaining water cools down and returns to the loop. The evaporated portion is gone, which is why engineers call it consumption rather than withdrawal. Operators must keep topping up the system with fresh supply. The attraction is energy efficiency. The research gathered for this story notes that evaporative cooling is generally more energy-efficient than air-cooled or waterless systems, though it consumes more water. In a business where electricity is among the largest operating costs, that tradeoff usually points toward evaporation unless local water is scarce or expensive. artigo.texto: Segundo a CNBC, levantamento All-America Economic Survey da própria CNBC revela uma tensão política crescente nos Estados Unidos em torno da expansão da inteligência artificial: eleitores republicanos apoiam amplamente o desenvolvimento da tecnologia, mas muitos rejeitam a construção da infraestrutura necessária para sustentá-la perto de suas casas. O presidente Donald Trump tem tratado a corrida da IA com a China como imperativo de segurança nacional e pressionado por uma expansão acelerada de data centers e da rede elétrica que os alimenta. Entre apoiadores do movimento MAGA, quase 55% querem que as empresas sigam desenvolvendo IA avançada enquanto o Congresso trabalha em regras para o setor, ante 27% que defendem uma pausa. Apenas 29% apoiariam um data center a menos de 10 milhas de sua casa, enquanto 40% se opõem. Considerando todos os republicanos e simpatizantes, o apoio cai para 24%. No eleitorado em geral, 63% não querem um data center de IA por perto e só 13% são favoráveis. A resistência é maior entre democratas: 80% contrários e 4% favoráveis. A conta política A pressão tem obrigado Trump e republicanos em disputas acirradas a recalibrar o discurso do início do boom. Em Ohio, o senador Jon Husted, que em 2024, como vice-governador, anunciou uma expansão de US$ 10 bilhões da Amazon Web Services, agora promove um projeto de lei parado que obrigaria grandes instalações a cobrir seus próprios custos de rede e geração, em vez de repassá-los aos consumidores residenciais. Em agosto, o comitê republicano para o Senado alertou empresas de IA de que a rejeição a data centers ameaçava a reeleição de Husted e classificou o tema como um risco pouco notado para as eleições de meio de mandato, conforme reportou a Axios. No Texas, o governador Greg Abbott suspendeu licenças para data centers até a conclusão de revisões de impacto na rede elétrica e nos recursos hídricos, além de defender o fim de incentivos fiscais estaduais, menos de um ano depois de exaltar o estado como epicentro do desenvolvimento de IA. Na quarta-feira, Trump escreveu em publicação no Truth Social que os desenvolvedores deveriam pagar um dividendo financeiro às comunidades onde se instalam e gerar a própria energia. Questionados sobre a principal preocupação caso os republicanos mantenham o Congresso, 18% dos eleitores citaram a falta de regulação de IA e data centers, percentual empatado com a continuidade das ações militares no Irã. A pesquisa ouviu 1.000 eleitores registrados entre 14 e 18 de outubro, com margem de erro de 3,1 pontos percentuais. Sobre o ritmo da tecnologia, 52% dos eleitores querem o desenvolvimento de IA avançada pausado até o Congresso aprovar regras de segurança, ante 32% que preferem seguir adiante para acompanhar a China. Brad Carson, ex-deputado democrata e cofundador do Public First Action PAC, disse à CNBC que “muitas pessoas estão incomodadas com esses data centers”. A indústria rejeita a leitura: Dan Diorio, da Data Center Coalition, afirmou à CNBC que o setor gera empregos, investimento e arrecadação e que os operadores pagam pela energia que consomem.

artigo.texto: The Hayward City Council is temporarily halting the development of data centers. On Oct. 20 the city council approved an urgency ordinance that activates a 45-day moratorium. This stops the approval of data centers and gives the city time to work on researching their impacts. One resident worried about the impacts of STACK, a data center that’s under construction. “I’m very concerned about the new data center that is coming into our community. So about a mile and a half away from my house. From the evidence that we have seen from previous data centers, I’m a little concerned for myself, for my environment, for my home, things from property value, when these data centers come in, from environmental safety concerns, obviously, from water usage, from electrical grid usage. These are all big concerns for us.” According to the urgency ordinance, water is used to cool off servers that use a huge amount of power. Data centers impact air quality and cause noises from the equipment, like diesel generators. The city said a developer confirmed they are interested in potentially building two data centers that would be 90 MW (megawatts) each on Arden Road and Corporate Avenue, a half mile away from the city’s four data centers. The city plans to take a closer look at how air quality, water use, noise and electricity would be impacted by data centers. One resident said he wants a stop to new data centers. “I believe that it is a detriment to our community and to our health. If they are gonna throw money at us, they need to subsidize our power, our water and our medical bills, because they are taking that from us. They are making it more expensive on our power and water, and it’s costing our health.” One resident believed data centers won’t negatively impact the community. “So I think facts matter, critical thought matters and I think the fact is that there is no evidence in California or in the Bay Area that data centers have caused any harm,” he said. “We have CEQA, we have local laws. Those studies have been completed, and they’ve been evaluated to demonstrate that most of the claims made this evening are inaccurate.” The council can choose to extend the moratorium to 10 months and 15 days, which requires a hearing and decision from the council. That hearing is tentatively set for Dec.1.

artigo.texto: Maritime emissions specialist EmissionLink has called for a dedicated proportion of EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) revenues to be invested in onboard carbon capture trials and supporting port infrastructure, warning that the technology risks remaining commercially unviable without targeted financial support. Philippos Ioulianou (pictured), Managing Director of EmissionLink, believes Europe has an opportunity to accelerate the development of maritime carbon capture by directing emissions trading revenues towards full-scale demonstrations that establish whether the technology can deliver verified emissions reductions at an economically sustainable cost. The call comes as the IMO moves to develop interim safety guidelines for onboard carbon capture systems. While welcoming the initiative, Mr Ioulianou argues that regulatory progress must be matched by investment in the infrastructure, emissions accounting mechanisms and commercial arrangements necessary to make the technology attractive to shipowners. "Developing safety guidelines is an important step, but regulation alone will not persuade shipowners to invest in carbon capture," said Mr Ioulianou. "Owners need a credible business case, backed by verified emissions savings, workable carbon disposal arrangements and a clear understanding of the financial benefits. "Europe is well positioned to lead this work. Allocating a proportion of EU ETS revenues to onboard trials and port reception infrastructure would help establish whether carbon capture can become a commercially viable decarbonisation solution for shipping." EmissionLink is advocating investment in demonstration projects that assess every stage of the carbon capture process, from onboard collection and storage to offloading, transportation and permanent storage or approved use. Such projects should operate against clearly defined performance criteria and generate independently verifiable emissions data that can inform regulatory development and future investment decisions. However, EmissionLink cautions that onboard carbon capture is unlikely to be a practical solution for every vessel. Ships operating on fixed and predictable routes offer the most promising early applications, as operators can plan carbon storage capacity and establish offloading arrangements at designated ports. For vessels trading on irregular routes or spot charters, the logistical challenges are considerably greater, particularly where carbon reception facilities and onward transportation arrangements are unavailable. Technical suitability will also depend on factors including vessel age, available space, additional power demand and remaining commercial life. Ship owners and charterers must also resolve contractual questions surrounding additional fuel consumption, offloading delays and the allocation of regulatory compliance benefits. "Installing carbon capture equipment introduces responsibilities that extend well beyond the initial investment," Mr Ioulianou explained. "Shipowners must consider the operational impact, the demands placed on crews and who ultimately bears the additional costs. These questions need answering before the technology can be adopted with confidence." A further concern is the need for greater clarity around emissions accounting and regulatory recognition. While the EU ETS recognises qualifying carbon capture and permanent geological storage or chemical binding, practical monitoring, reporting and verification arrangements for maritime carbon capture remain underdeveloped. Mr Ioulianou also warned that shipowners should not assume carbon capture benefits recognised under the EU ETS will automatically provide equivalent compliance advantages under FuelEU Maritime, which regulates the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used onboard ships rather than absolute emissions. "Capturing carbon is not necessarily the same as delivering a verified reduction in emissions," he said. "Shipowners need certainty over how those savings will be measured, independently verified and recognised under the relevant regulations. Without that clarity, it becomes extremely difficult to justify the capital and operating expenditure." EmissionLink believes the period during which the IMO develops its safety framework should be used to advance commercial trials, emissions verification procedures and port infrastructure in parallel.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media Energy storage is taking off as the state moves to make development easier and more profitable, but the horizon isn’t all clear for the sector. Just outside Boston, a developer is getting set to build a 700-megawatt storage facility that is expected to dwarf every other battery project in New England. One town over, another energy company just closed on $850 million in financing to build a 250-MW battery. Down near the Rhode Island border, ground has been broken on a 200-MW storage facility that is expected to be up and running by the end of the year. These and roughly a half dozen other projects at various stages are taking advantage of policies Massachusetts has put in place to help reach its goal of getting 5 gigawatts of battery storage capacity online by 2030, with another 5 GW to follow by 2035. While several larger and generally sunnier states top the list for installed storage capacity — California boasts a whopping 23 GW — Massachusetts’ ambition and policies put it at the forefront of the push to get more batteries on the grid. Thirteen states have set procurement targets for battery storage, but Massachusetts’ total of 10 GW by 2035 is the highest. And its policy landscape is setting the state up for success, observers say. “Massachusetts is really a leader in this space,” said Erin Smith, energy and grid policy director for the Environmental League of Massachusetts. “We’re ahead of the pack as it relates to encouraging battery buildout.” Massachusetts has ambitious clean energy goals and some of the highest electricity prices in the country. Batteries, the state figures, can help with both. They can store energy when power is cheapest and cleanest — like on sunny days when solar farms are producing in abundance — then send it back onto the grid during times of heavier demand, cutting down on the need to generate pricier, dirtier power. Battery systems can also bolster resilience, reducing outages during increasingly extreme and erratic weather. “If we have storage on the system, we can deploy it at different times to manage our load,” said Elizabeth Mahony, commissioner of the state Department of Energy Resources. So for the past 11 years, Massachusetts has been working to encourage the development of large-scale batteries, beginning with the launch of the Energy Storage Initiative in 2015 under then-Gov. Charlie Baker (R). The state blew past its initial target of installing 1 GW of storage capacity by 2025, topping 1.6 GW. Progress has only accelerated since then, thanks to a trio of state policies making it easier and more profitable to locate batteries in the state. The Clean Peak Standard, which went into effect in 2020, is a first-in-the-country program that pays renewable energy facilities and energy storage owners to send power onto the grid during times of peak demand. It provides an additional revenue source that can make battery developments more financially viable. “Those credits are incredibly important to financing and developing these projects,” said Aaron Lang, a partner at Boston law firm Foley Hoag who counts several battery developers among his clients. New siting and permitting reforms that went into effect on July 1 are also making Massachusetts more attractive to storage developers by streamlining and speeding up the approval process, Lang said. The new rules give the state Energy Facilities Siting Board authority to approve large energy projects, including storage facilities with a capacity of 100 MW or higher, rather than making developers work with the disparate permitting processes of individual municipalities. Decisions must be made within 15 months of application. “It ensures we can bring more clean energy, including batteries, online sooner,” Smith said. The state has also undertaken a series of procurements aimed at securing large-scale storage capacity. In December 2025, Massachusetts selected four projects totaling 1.3 GW of capacity to move ahead to contract negotiations with the major utilities. A second solicitation received 35 bids before it closed earlier this month; selected projects are set to be announced in February. Together, these actions create a climate that storage developers can rely on, said Hans Detweiler, vice president of development for Jupiter Power, the company behind the 700-MW Trimount project just outside Boston, where construction is slated to begin next year. “Moving through permitting and state solicitations takes years, so developers need confidence that the policy framework will remain stable over that period,” he said. “The Healey administration has consistently supported a procurement process that brings cost-effective resources to the grid to reduce electricity costs for consumers.” Even with all the state’s efforts, however, barriers remain. Perhaps the most pressing is the cost of interconnecting major projects like these to the grid. In September, developers canceled plans for a 125-MW battery system in the town of Tewksbury, citing the unexpectedly high cost — $65 million — of the upgrades necessary to hook into the grid. And that number is on the low end. Grid operator Independent System Operator New England recently completed a study of likely interconnection costs for a number of proposed projects, most of which were battery developments sited in Massachusetts. Many of the estimates topped $200 million, “quite a bit higher than developers anticipated,” Smith said. “We have an older grid here in New England, and it genuinely does require some upgrade costs to accommodate the influx of batteries,” she said. “How to allocate grid upgrade costs is going to be a debate.” Many battery proposals are also running into ardent community opposition. Carsten Cramer, Chairman of the Executive Board of Borussia Dortmund: "SIGNAL IDUNA PARK is not only our iconic home but also a central element of our comprehensive decarbonization strategy. With the battery storage system, we are working together with RWE to complete a forward-looking energy concept that makes our solar power even more usable. We are pleased that our stadium will continue to stand for resource-efficient and innovative practices in the future." Dr. Markus Krebber, CEO of RWE AG: "With the commissioning of the battery storage system, the entire system—comprising the photovoltaic system and the battery—at SIGNAL IDUNA PARK is now fully operational. The integration of both systems allows us to use the solar power generated on-site even more flexibly—even when the sun isn't shining. The experts from BVB and RWE have breathed life and energy into our partnership through this project. This provides a solid foundation for further joint developments." As a Premium Partner and an important part of the "BVB Empowers" initiative, RWE will continue to support BVB in optimizing energy management at SIGNAL IDUNA PARK as part of this six-year partnership. The goal is to further increase the stadium's contribution to energy security, energy efficiency, and decarbonization.
