artigo.texto: Nuclear power plants were engineered to do one thing exceptionally well: generate electricity at a steady rate, around the clock. That design philosophy made sense for decades, but it is increasingly at odds with a grid that now shares space with solar and wind resources whose output rises and falls with the weather and the time of day. Researchers at the University of Central Florida’s Center for Advanced Turbomachinery and Energy Research (CATER) argue that thermal energy storage, or TES, could be the key to reconciling the two. In a study published in the Journal of Energy Resources Technology, Part A: Sustainable and Renewable Energy, the CATER team paired thermodynamic modeling with an economic analysis of how nuclear plants could operate in a shifting energy market. The paper, titled “Molten Salt Reactor Dispatch Optimization via Thermal Energy Storage: Coupled Thermodynamic Modeling and Rolling-Horizon Economic Analysis,” examines how a molten salt reactor equipped with TES could be dispatched more flexibly than conventional nuclear plants allow. The research team included doctoral research assistants Augusto Delavald Marques and Abhilash Prasad, postdoctoral scholar Shinjan Ghosh, associate professor Erik Fernandez, alumnus Marcel Otto, and CATER director Jayanta Kapat. The core problem the researchers set out to address is a mismatch between reactor design and grid demand. “Nuclear power needs to be flexible while nuclear reactors operate at a steady pace because grid demand varies throughout the day,” Marques says. “This is a challenge for power plants because they must adjust quickly to meet grid demand.” Traditional nuclear plants are not built to cycle rapidly on and off. When demand drops, operators face an unattractive choice: deliberately ramp down output, which can place mechanical stress on equipment, or keep producing electricity that the grid does not currently need. Both options carry costs, and both become more frequent as weather-dependent renewables claim a larger share of generation. TES offers a third path. Instead of forcing the reactor itself to follow demand, a storage system can absorb excess heat produced by the reactor and regulate how much of that heat is delivered to the power conversion side of the plant. When electricity demand is low, heat accumulates in storage; when demand climbs, the stored thermal energy can be drawn down to run the plant’s generation equipment. The reactor keeps operating at the steady pace it was designed for, while the plant’s electrical output flexes to match the grid. The flexibility has a financial dimension as well. Electricity prices fluctuate through the day as supply and demand shift, and the researchers’ rolling-horizon economic analysis was designed to capture how dispatch decisions play out under those changing conditions. “By storing the energy when demand and prices are low and using it when demand and prices increase, it can increase the value of the electricity produced,” Ghosh says. In effect, TES lets a nuclear plant sell its output when it is worth the most rather than when the reactor happens to produce it. The study’s focus on molten salt reactors reflects where the researchers see the opportunity. “As renewable power generation grows, the need for flexibility in nuclear plants has become more important,” Marques says. “The deployment of next-generation nuclear reactors in the US over the next few years, such as molten salt reactors, is an opportunity to incorporate TES and improve the integration of nuclear and renewable energy on the same grid.” It is worth emphasizing what the study does and does not show. The findings come from coupled thermodynamic modeling and economic analysis, not from an operating plant, so the results represent model-based projections of how a TES-equipped molten salt reactor could be dispatched and how such dispatch might affect revenue. Real-world performance would depend on factors the models necessarily simplify. For a country investing in both advanced reactors and large volumes of solar and wind, the CATER team’s analysis suggests that the heat leaving a reactor does not have to become electricity at the exact moment it is produced. Stored as thermal energy and released on schedule, it could give nuclear power the dispatch flexibility that modern grids increasingly demand, without asking reactors to do something they were never designed to do. artigo.texto: FUZHOU, China, Oct. 26, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- SCUDPower will showcase custom electric motorcycle battery solutions developed around different vehicle requirements at the 83rd International Motorcycle Exhibition (EICMA 2026), held November 3-8 at Fiera Milano Rho. The exhibit will show how its R&D and custom battery development platform helps OEMs translate a vehicle’s load profile, operating environment, packaging limits and performance targets into a battery system engineered and validated for the application. Electric motorcycles used for city commuting, off-road riding and high-speed performance place different demands on range, discharge power, durability and protection. Rather than applying one standard pack across vehicle platforms, SCUDPower develops robust solutions around each program’s unique requirements. That development approach is reflected in two closely connected priorities: - Safety and reliability for real riding conditions. Pack protection, BMS controls and thermal management are developed and validated against the mechanical, electrical and thermal stresses expected in the intended operating environment. - Customization for each vehicle platform. Multiple cell chemistries, pack architectures and system configurations give OEMs more options as requirements evolve. The lineup also includes high-energy-density semi-solid-state battery packs designed to support the range and power needs of high-speed e-motorcycle programs. Backed by 30 years of experience, SCUDPower supports this work with a nearly 300-member R&D team covering BMS, electrical and mechanical design, firmware, algorithms, testing and engineering services. "Our engineers do not begin with a fixed pack design,” said Awen Chen, R&D Vice General Manager at SCUDPower. "We begin with the motorcycle-what it needs to deliver and what it must withstand-then work with the OEM to build and verify the right solution.” That engineering work is supported by more than 600 invention and utility-model patents, including nearly 70 related to thermal management and thermal-runaway prevention. A 2026 research collaboration with Tsinghua University extends that work into high-safety battery-pack design, thermal-runaway prevention, early warning and state-of-health estimation. SCUDPower welcomes EICMA attendees to Hall 18, Booth H96 to meet its engineering team, discuss vehicle requirements and explore a battery development path tailored to their platform. About SCUDPower SCUDPower is a custom battery pack manufacturer serving established equipment brands and hardware startups across light electric vehicles (LEVs), smart home, robotics, consumer technology, medical, UPS and BBU applications. Its capabilities span custom engineering, testing, manufacturing and global service, supporting customer programs from concept development through volume production. In the LEV sector, SCUDPower has received recognition from customers including Ninebot-Segway and NIU Technologies. Learn more about SCUDPower’s battery development capabilities at www.scudpower.net. artigo.texto: Vantage data center plan draws questions ahead of Oregon vote Vote on Issue 25 decides whether to block construction of data center OREGON, Ohio (WTVG) - Vantage Data Centers held an open house Sunday at Clay High School, giving residents a chance to ask questions about its proposed $1 billion data center ahead of a vote on the project next week. Resident group opposes project United Neighbors of Oregon, a resident-led group, has spent the past few months working to prevent construction of the data center off Corduroy and Wynn roads. “We didn’t come this far to only come this far,” said Laura Davis, a volunteer with United Neighbors of Oregon. “They’re spending monies, thousands, hundreds of thousands of dollars on this campaign to try and buy their way into Oregon. But I keep saying Oregon is not for sale,” Davis said. Davis said she is concerned about the wetlands and the people who live near the proposed site. Vantage addresses energy, water questions Misty Allen, vice president of public policy for North America at Vantage Data Centers, said residents have raised questions about the project. “People want to understand the, where’s the energy coming from? How will that affect their energy rates? What about water use? And how is the data center going to use water?” Allen said. Allen said Vantage will purchase its own power and cover the necessary infrastructure costs. “When it comes to water use, we’re not going to use any more water than, say, a typical medium commercial office building. And we use closed loop water for chilling of the data center,” Allen said. Allen said the facility would use 22,000 gallons of water a day, the same amount used by 65 homes. She said Vantage checked with the city’s water plant and was told it has the ability to service that need. Open house draws mixed reaction Davis said she remains unconvinced. “They had some people in there trying to convince other people that this is the right thing for Oregon. But we were in there telling people, this is not the right thing for Oregon,” Davis said. Davis said Allen and Vantage staff gave her one answer she liked. “If we win this vote, they will pull out,” Davis said. “Obviously we would have to have conversations with city council and the folks who have been working on this development. But certainly, if the community doesn’t want us here, we’ll have to seriously consider not being here,” Allen said. What’s on the ballot Davis said the ballot language is confusing residents. Voting yes on Issue 25 supports amending the city charter to prohibit construction of the data center. Voting no on the issue opposes blocking the construction. artigo.texto: A data center under construction in South Brunswick is drawing environmental concerns from residents who said they only recently learned about the project, more than a year after local officials approved it. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) is currently reviewing an application from Sentinel Data Centers to install several backup diesel generators at the former Princeton Nurseries property on Rt-1. The agency has opened a public comment period as part of its permitting process. Many residents said they didn't become aware of the project until the state began to seek public input on the generator permits. However, the proposed data center received approval from the South Brunswick Planning Board in May 2025. "It's only been in the last month, maybe a little bit longer than that that people have truly been aware of it and been able to raise their voices," said Kingston resident Karin Gillespie. "If there is an opportunity to impact the diesel generators and think about some kind of an alternative to that, that would be great." The property is situated on the border of several towns including South Brunswick, Kingston and Princeton. “This is about more than one data center. It is about the health of our families, the protection of our air and water and the long-term future of our communities,” said Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman. “Pollution does not stop at municipal borders. The impacts of this project will extend far beyond South Brunswick, threatening the health and quality of life of residents across the surrounding communities." Though the approval for the data center was granted by the South Brunswick Planning Board, Princeton Mayor Mark Freda and the city council released a statement at the beginning of October in opposition of the backup generators. "When running, these generators will undoubtedly send emissions across municipal boundaries, often negatively affecting air quality and public health in Princeton’s residential neighborhoods and at two of our elementary schools. We urge DEP to deny the air permit application for the center in its present form," the statement said. The two candidates running to replace Coleman in November are also speaking out on the data center and the potential impacts for nearby residents. Adam Hamawy, the Democratic candidate running to represent New Jersey's 12th district said in a statement, "Our communities deserve the right to decide their own future, not have it dictated by billionaires and corporate developers. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection has a responsibility to protect public health, and that starts with denying this air permit.” His Republican challenger, Gregg Mele, also spoke to News 12 about the planned data center. “Residents deserve a complete, independently reviewed accounting of generator emissions, noise, water demand, and electricity infrastructure costs—including all planned phases," Mele said. "Developers should pay the infrastructure costs they create, and protections for neighboring communities must be enforceable." While the current state review is focused on the backup generators, some residents continue to call for the entire project to be reconsidered. "Maybe we can do what so many other communities have done. Maybe we can get them to not have this data center," said South Brunswick resident Janice Gossman. "A lot of people say it's too late. We have to try." For some neighbors, the debate is personal. Michael Van Pelt, who lives down the road from the site of the data center, said he worries about how the facility could impact his family, including his son, who has autism. "My son is very sensitive to sound," Van Pelt said. "His special education program is magnificent. His teachers are wonderful and if he loses that, I don't know what we're going to do."

artigo.texto: The Federal Government has pledged support for Cross River State’s maiden Climate Transition Plan, expressing its readiness to help the state attract climate finance, access emerging carbon markets and develop investment projects that combine environmental conservation with economic growth. The commitment came from the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) and the Federal Ministry of Environment at an inception workshop on the development of the plan, held at the State Library, Calabar. Director-General of the NCCC, Omotenioye Majekodunmi, said Cross River’s extensive tropical rainforests, biodiversity and other natural resources placed it in a strategic position to benefit from emerging opportunities in carbon trading, nature-based solutions and international climate financing. She stressed that Nigeria’s climate commitments could only translate into measurable results through effective implementation at state and community levels, where environmental protection must be accompanied by improved livelihoods and sustainable development. “Nigeria’s climate ambitions will ultimately be delivered at the state and community levels, where forests are protected, infrastructure is made more resilient, clean energy is deployed, and livelihoods are strengthened,” she said. “Cross River State has a particularly important role to play with its rich tropical rainforest, the biodiversity and significant natural capital. “The state has an opportunity to demonstrate that climate action, conservation and economic development can go hand in hand.” Majekodunmi explained that the greenhouse gas inventory, climate vulnerability and risk assessment, alongside other baseline studies being undertaken by the state, would provide the scientific evidence required to translate policy ambitions into practical interventions. According to her, credible environmental data and clearly defined projects would strengthen Cross River’s capacity to attract investors seeking measurable climate and development outcomes. “It will also position Cross River State to take advantage of the emerging opportunities in nature-based solutions, carbon markets and climate finance,” she said. “As Nigeria operationalises its national carbon market architecture and advances implementation of our NDC, we need new and strong state-level projects that are credible, investable and capable of delivering measurable results and ultimately improve incomes.” She assured the state government of the council’s commitment to ensuring that its transition plan aligns with national climate priorities and attracts the partnerships required for implementation. “The National Council on Climate Change stands ready to work with Cross River State to ensure alignment with national climate priorities and, importantly, to help translate this plan into implementation and investment,” Majekodunmi declared. Similarly, Director of the Department of Climate Change, Federal Ministry of Environment, Iniobong Abiola-Awe, described the initiative as another demonstration of Cross River’s leadership in environmental conservation and subnational climate governance. She said the state’s longstanding reputation as a major ecological destination, particularly its vast forest resources and biodiversity, made the transition plan an important framework for balancing conservation with development. “Cross River State has long been celebrated as Nigeria’s premier eco-destination and vital subnational vanguard for forest conservation. “By unveiling this important framework, Cross River State is once again proving its proactive leadership in subnational environmental governance,” she said. Abiola-Awe commended the state government for initiating baseline studies, explaining that reliable data would enable policymakers to establish realistic priorities, measure progress and develop interventions capable of delivering results. “We are highly encouraged to see that Cross River State is executing critical baseline studies, and these studies provide the precise empirical formula needed to translate plans to implementation,” she added. She assured the state of the ministry’s readiness to collaborate on relevant programmes. Governor Bassey Otu, represented by the Speaker of the Cross River State House of Assembly, Elvert Ayambem, said the transition plan would strengthen climate resilience, safeguard the state’s natural resources and create opportunities for sustainable economic growth under his administration’s People First agenda. He emphasised the need to protect the state’s ecological assets, including what he described as more than half of Nigeria’s remaining tropical rainforests, extensive mangrove ecosystems and rich biodiversity. Otu said the transition framework would provide a coordinated approach to addressing environmental vulnerabilities while ensuring that conservation efforts contribute meaningfully to economic development. Earlier, Director-General of the Cross River State Council on Climate Change, Edu Effiom, said the inception workshop marked the beginning of the technical process for developing the plan, including reviewing its preliminary draft and conducting baseline studies. She called on ministries, departments, agencies and local government councils to provide reliable sector-specific data and technical contributions to guide policy priorities, climate projections and implementation targets. Effiom stressed that climate action must go beyond policy declarations, insisting that environmental commitments should be integrated into government budgets and local development plans to ensure measurable results. The Federal Government’s intervention is expected to strengthen cooperation with Cross River in developing a climate transition framework capable of attracting investment while protecting the ecological resources on which many communities depend.

artigo.texto: Patna: Bihar is preparing to introduce specialised green energy courses in its higher education institutions, aiming to equip students with skills in renewable energy, electric vehicles, battery technology and other emerging sustainable technologies. The state’s Higher Education Department has prepared a proposal to introduce these programmes in line with the National Education Policy (NEP). The initiative is intended to align higher education with the growing demand for skilled professionals in the green energy sector. According to the proposal, the courses have been designed with assistance from experts from the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) and National Institutes of Technology (NITs), with an emphasis on industry requirements, research and practical knowledge. Undergraduate and Postgraduate Programmes Proposed The proposed framework includes both undergraduate and postgraduate degree programmes. Students will have the opportunity to study energy management, carbon trading and sustainable business models, alongside technical subjects related to clean energy. The department has also referred to University Grants Commission (UGC) guidelines and directed that the necessary preparations be made to introduce the courses. A separate department dedicated to green energy studies is also being proposed at universities. EVs, Solar Power and Battery Technology Among Key Subjects The proposed curriculum will cover a range of emerging fields, including: - Renewable energy and solar power - Wind energy management - Green hydrogen technology - Electric vehicle (EV) technology - Battery technology and advanced battery management - EV charging infrastructure - Carbon accounting and auditing - Green corporate practices and sustainable business models These subjects are expected to help students develop expertise in technologies and practices associated with the transition towards cleaner energy. Research to Receive Special Attention The proposed initiative also aims to encourage teachers and students to undertake research in green energy and sustainability. By introducing specialised programmes, Bihar’s universities could expand opportunities for academic research while preparing students for changing industry requirements. Potential Career Opportunities in the Green Energy Sector The proposed courses could help students pursue careers in renewable energy management, solar and wind power projects, electric mobility, battery systems, EV charging infrastructure, carbon auditing and sustainability consulting. However, the programmes are currently at the proposal and preparation stage. Details regarding participating universities, admission procedures, course fees and the launch schedule have not yet been specified in the supplied information.

artigo.texto: Space-Saving, Ultra-Quiet, and Powerful: Sigenergy Launches the SigenCube C&I BESS Source: GlobeNewswire MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Sigenergy, a global leader in AI-driven smart solar and energy storage solutions, today officially unveiled the SigenCube Commercial & Industrial Battery Energy Storage System (C&I BESS) ahead of All-Energy Australia 2026. Designed to address the core challenges of commercial deployments—such as limited space, noise restrictions, and heavy power demands—the SigenCube introduces industry-leading energy density, ultra-quiet operation, and robust overload performance to the global market. Simplified Deployment: Big Energy Doesn't Need Big Space Deploying commercial energy storage no longer means sacrificing massive amounts of valuable real estate. The SigenCube boasts an exceptional energy density over 220kWh/m², dramatically shrinking spatial requirements. In a 4MWh project, traditional solutions typically require over 80m² of land, whereas the SigenCube requires only 54.5m², successfully saving over 30% in overall footprint. Beyond saving space, the system is engineered for maximum installation efficiency. It features a highly integrated, compact architecture that combines the Power Conversion System (PCS), high-voltage components, and distribution units into a single cabinet. To scale up multi-megawatt projects easily, the SigenCube incorporates a built-in Energy Management System (EMS) in each cabinet, supporting up to 100 units in parallel without the need for external data loggers, complete with automated failover to prevent single points of failure. Once on site, deployment is streamlined through factory pre-commissioning and quick app-based setup, allowing technicians to complete basic configurations and diagnostics in just 3 to 5 minutes. Peak Performance: Quiet Operation Meets Heavy-Duty Power While traditional commercial storage solutions are often notoriously noisy—frequently causing disruptions that make normal conversation difficult for people nearby—the SigenCube completely redefines the acoustic standard. It stands out as the quietest commercial energy storage system available, maintaining noise levels below 60 dB at one meter, which is comparable to the ambient noise of a normal conversation. This allows businesses to install the system smoothly near office buildings, commercial centers, and residential-adjacent areas. Despite its quiet and compact design, the SigenCube packs formidable power capabilities. Whether handling the sudden inrush currents of industrial air compressors, conveyor drive systems, or motor-driven centrifugal pumps, the system prevents tripping and handles load spikes effortlessly. To ensure this peak performance remains stable and efficient over time, the system features predictive smart thermal management that continuously monitors real-time cell conditions and day-ahead load forecasts to optimize cooling. By dynamically adjusting coolant temperatures before load changes occur, it cuts auxiliary power consumption by up to 20% while actively mitigating calendar aging to help extend battery life. All-Round Safety: Multi-Layered Protection from Pack to System Safety forms the foundation of the SigenCube, featuring strong protections spanning from the pack level up to the entire system. Within the battery pack, the system utilizes high-temperature fire-resistant isolation design and reinforced six-sided insulation, backed by a dense configuration of 40 NTC temperature sensors monitoring 64 cells per pack (0.625 NTC per cell, which is much denser than the industry average). Additional pack-level safeguards include pressure relief valves, electrical insulation sheets, crash frames, high-strength crossbeams, leakage detection and optional aerosol fire suppression available for select regions. At the system level, the SigenCube integrates top explosion vents, smoke and heat detectors, emergency fans, cabinet-level aerosol suppression, and a water firefighting interface, supported by 8 layers of overcurrent protection for complete peace of mind. Optimized O&M: Lower OPEX and Effortless Maintenance Commercial and industrial energy storage is never a short-term investment, minimizing long-term operational and maintenance burdens is essential for maximizing project returns. The SigenCube is engineered for long-term reliability with exceptionally low maintenance requirements. It uses a special sealed cooling loop that delivers a 10-year coolant life, significantly reducing scheduled replacements. Additionally, its pack-level active balancing delivers a strong 7A balancing current—keeping battery strings uniformly balanced over years of operation and eliminating the need for periodic on-site SOC calibration. Grid-Forming Resilience for Every Scenario Commercial and industrial facilities constantly face unpredictable grid fluctuations, weak infrastructure, and unexpected outages—making robust grid-forming resilience essential. Beyond seamless switchover, the system delivers exceptional all-around grid support, including 100% three-phase imbalance handling under complex load conditions, robust fault ride-through during voltage sags and swells, and reliable MWh-level black start without external grid support. Furthermore, it incorporates advanced grid-stabilizing intelligence—featuring rapid reactive power response for voltage regulation, virtual inertia support to stabilize grid frequency, active power oscillation damping, and superior weak grid adaptation for stable, clean operation in high-impedance environments. artigo.texto: Samsung — o maior diferencial hoje para data centers que pagam mais por HBM não é só tecnologia, mas a previsibilidade da entrega: clientes premium estariam aceitando pagar até 25% a mais pela garantia de fornecimento e pelos ganhos de rendimento que a empresa vem reportando. Preço e comparação: quanto custa um HBM no mercado A cotação atribuída à Samsung para HBM aparece em $4,50 por unidade, frente a $4,00 para Micron e uma faixa de $3,60–$3,80 para SK hynix. Esse spread equivale a um prêmio de até 25% sobre o preço dos concorrentes. A diferença de preço ganha sentido quando se considera que a HBM4 da Samsung é mencionada como posicionada na faixa média-alta dos US$4, tornando-a até três vezes mais cara que a referência anterior de HBM3E em cotações comparativas. A Samsung tem uma cotação de $4,50 para HBM, contra $4,00 da Micron e $3,60–$3,80 da SK hynix, refletindo um prêmio ligado à capacidade de fornecer volumes estáveis e avanços na produção de HBM4. Vantagens industriais por trás do prêmio A capacidade da Samsung de aliar sua divisão de foundry e múltiplos nós avançados, como um 4nm maduro, tem sido apontada como fator que reduz defeitos e eleva a utilidade industrial, favorecendo yields superiores durante a produção de HBM4. Relatos de rendimento em torno de 80% para HBM4 e a possibilidade de conciliar recursos entre memória e chips não relacionados à memória são citados como razões práticas para a empresa manter preços mais altos, atraindo clientes sensíveis a risco de falta de oferta. O que você acha? Você considera justificável que data centers paguem um prêmio por garantia de fornecimento e yields mais altos? Para acompanhar mais, acesse nossa editoria. Perguntas Frequentes Por que a Samsung está cobrando até 25% a mais por HBM para data centers? A Samsung está cobrando até 25% a mais por HBM porque sua capacidade de produção e estabilidade de suprimento oferecem menos risco aos data centers, com cotações citadas em $4,50 frente a $4,00 da Micron e $3,60–$3,80 da SK hynix. Essa diferença reflete preferência por continuidade de entregas e rendimentos superiores. O que torna a HBM4 da Samsung mais cara que a HBM3E? A HBM4 da Samsung aparece posicionada na faixa média-alta dos US$4, o que a deixa cerca de três vezes mais cara que a referência de HBM3E citada. Essa precificação incorpora melhorias de rendimento (relatos de até 80%) e custos de processo em nós avançados, além da integração com sua foundry. A diferença de preço impacta o custo total de servidores e aceleradores: data centers que priorizam disponibilidade e performance podem optar por pagar $4,50 por HBM para reduzir risco de falta, enquanto outros podem escolher fornecedores mais baratos, como Micron a $4,00, dependendo de capex e estratégia de suprimento. © Diário da Mídia · Conteúdo protegido por direitos autorais — reprodução ou cópia proibida sem autorização. artigo.texto: Morro Bay City Council plans to ban battery storage plants October 25, 2026 By KAREN VELIE After a more than four-year battle, the Morro Bay City Council is planning to pass an ordinance on Tuesday in an attempt to ban battery storage plants that provide power to the state’s electric grid. Vistra Energy, a Texas-based energy company, has plans to construct and operate a 600 megawatt battery storage facility on approximately 24 acres of a roughly 70-acre site. However, residents, concerned the facility would endanger the public while negatively impacting tourism and the fishing industry, have battled against the proposed project for years. Legislation passed in 2022 allows applicants to skip local approvals. However, it requires approvals from both the California Energy Commission and the Coastal Commission. So, even if the California Energy Commission green-lights the battery storage plant, it would still need approval from the California Coastal Commission, which has criticized the project. In an Aug. 2, 2024 letter regarding Vistra Energy’s proposed project, the Coastal Commission outlined serious issues about the location of the project. In summary, they stated that the future hazards of flooding and sea level rise and the impact on the environmentally sensitive habitat area are acute. In the 2024 election, Morro Bay, residents largely supported a measure requiring voter approval for changes to some zoning on the waterfront. Vistra Energy decided to seek state approval while bypassing the city’s consideration shortly before the November election. On Jan. 28, 2025, the Morro Bay City Council voted for an urgency ordinance to temporarily halt the proposed battery storage project. The urgency ordinance, which was extended once, is set to expire on Jan. 28, 2027. Even if the city council enacts an ordinance banning battery storage plants in the city, Vistra Energy could ask the state to override the ordinance and permit the project. However, a large amount of the funding for the battery storage facility is slated to be provided through the Inflation Reduction Act, which included $369 billion in subsidies for renewable energy. “The Inflation Reduction Act is anticipated to provide the opportunity to realize material benefits to Vistra with respect to its renewables and energy storage projects, as well as provide strong price support via the nuclear production tax credit for its nuclear facilities, including those acquired through the Energy Harbor transaction,” Vistra Energy said in a first quarter 2024 press release. However, the Trump administration and the Republican-led Congress have frozen, and rolled back major provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act. Without subsidies and tax credits, it is unlikely Vistra Energy will move forward with its plan for battery storage in Morro Bay. Davidson County commissioners to consider 4-month moratorium on data center development Davidson County commissioners are holding a public hearing about a proposed four-month pause on data center development to address zoning and infrastructure concerns. Davidson County commissioners are considering a four-month moratorium on data center development to give leaders time to evaluate regulations and address concerns about infrastructure and environmental impact. In August, commissioners rejected a proposal for a six-month moratorium. The new six-page proposal outlines the reasons for the 4-month pause, citing concerns local and national about data centers’ electricity use, water supply issues, heat production and noise pollution. During the first two months, county leaders would consult experts about data centers, review the county’s land and utilities, and visit nearby data centers. In the final two months, they would consider potential zoning changes and possibly propose rules to regulate data center development. artigo.texto: Vertiv Simplifies High-Density AI Infrastructure Deployment Across Data Center Environments The new Vertiv™ SmartIT platform is a pre-engineered AI infrastructure solution based on NVIDIA MGX™ and OCP ORV3 architecture The scalable solution supports deployment in existing enterprise facilities, new builds, commercial spaces, colocation and hyperscale environments without redesign COLUMBUS, Ohio , Oct. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vertiv Holdings Co. (NYSE: VRT), a global leader in critical digital infrastructure, today introduced the Vertiv™ SmartIT solution, a pre-engineered architecture designed to simplify high-density AI deployments for enterprises, research institutions and colocation providers across existing facilities and new data centers. Previously deployed with NVIDIA to support the NVIDIA DGX™ GB300, the highest-performing, largest-scale AI system available for enterprises, the Vertiv™ SmartIT solution integrates rack infrastructure, DC power conversion and distribution, direct-to-chip liquid cooling, in-rack cooling distribution and monitoring in a factory-validated design. By integrating and validating these systems before shipment, Vertiv™ SmartIT helps reduce on-site integration complexity and connects to facility power and cooling infrastructure. The solution is available now for AI deployments globally. "AI is fundamentally changing the demands placed on data center infrastructure, requiring closer coordination across power, cooling and IT systems to support increasingly complex workloads," said Scott Armul, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Vertiv. "Vertiv™ SmartIT reflects our approach to solving that challenge by bringing these disciplines together in a factory-validated architecture. By combining Vertiv's expertise across critical infrastructure, we're helping customers simplify deployment, build greater consistency into their AI environments and establish a foundation that can evolve alongside their computing needs." Vertiv™ SmartIT helps customers address key deployment challenges, including: - Deployment timelines compress: Factory validation replaces on-site integration, limiting the commissioning scope to facility connections. - Multi-vendor coordination is reduced: Customers benefit from a single order, one partner and one architecture spanning rack, power, cooling and monitoring. - Existing spaces become AI-ready: Brownfield enterprise facilities and Class A commercial buildings can support AI-class density without full reconstruction. - Scalability becomes repeatable: The same building block supports growth from single rack to multi-rack deployments, without redesign between phases. - Operational visibility increases: Integrated leak detection, automated response and continuous monitoring provide visibility from rack to site, with these capabilities built into the solution from day one rather than assembled from separate vendor tools. Vertiv™ SmartIT is a scalable, pre-engineered infrastructure platform for high-density AI deployments, supporting NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, NVIDIA DGX™ Rubin NVL8 and NVIDIA HGX™ Rubin NVL8 on NVIDIA MGX™ and Open Compute Project (OCP) ORV3 architectures. Designed to scale from a single rack to multi-rack deployments, it enables customers to deploy and expand AI infrastructure within a common architecture while integrating power, cooling, monitoring and controls. Built-in monitoring, leak detection and support for Redfish, SNMP and Modbus simplify operations, while Vertiv™ Global Services supports deployment, commissioning and lifecycle management. Vertiv SmartIT can be deployed as part of a broader Vertiv infrastructure architecture, with complementary solutions extending integration and management capabilities beyond the rack. Vertiv™ SmartRun extends integration across the row, while Vertiv™ rack power distribution units (rPDU) provide power distribution and monitoring. Vertiv™ Unify provides integrated monitoring, analytics and controls across power and thermal infrastructure, including leak detection and coordinated response control. Together, these solutions help customers scale from individual Vertiv™ SmartIT deployments to larger AI environments. artigo.texto: Margalla Heavy Industries Limited (MHIL), a military-owned company, has signed an agreement with Chinese partners and local investors to set up a $2.25 billion lithium-ion battery manufacturing plant in Rawalpindi. Production is expected to begin six to eight months after the government approves the policy. Engineering Development Board (EDB) CEO Hamad Ali Mansoor told the media platform that feasibility studies are complete and the project awaits approval. He said the building is ready and the machines are installed. The project was signed in July with a Chinese company he described as one of the “top-tier manufacturers,” of China along with a local private-sector investor. He did not name either party. The facility will produce lithium-ion cells with an annual capacity of more than 1,000MW. The first factory will initially produce 200-300MW before reaching full capacity. The plant is located at Heavy Industries Taxila in Rawalpindi district. MHIL manufactures defence equipment, including battle tanks, armoured vehicles, unmanned drones and protective gear, as well as compact battery energy storage systems, EV buses and two-wheelers. The general manager for digital media in MHIL, Muhammad Ameen, was not immediately available for comment. Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-2031. The agreement follows the approval by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of the Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-2031. The policy awaits IMF approval over proposed tax incentives for the electric vehicle industry and their potential revenue implications. The EDB estimates that demand for battery energy storage systems (BESS) could reach 100,000MW by June 2030 if the economy grows by 5 percent or more. If GDP growth falls below 3 percent, demand is projected at up to 80,000MW. Mansoor said demand would come from households, commercial buildings, industry and electric vehicles, including two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, buses and trucks. Grid stabilization alone could require 3,000-5,000MW of battery storage. Meeting the projected demand would require four to five gigafactories, each costing around $1 billion to $1.25 billion. The government prepared a lithium battery manufacturing policy and submitted it to the Ministry of Industries in March. It awaits approval. The plan includes four major factories, three in the Lahore, Faisalabad and Rawalpindi divisions of Punjab and one in Karachi. Manufacturers would be required to export a specified percentage of production, though Mansoor declined to give the target before approval. He said the policy incorporates international safety and performance standards. Pakistan currently assembles around 3,000-4,000MW of batteries, along with parts such as motors, controllers and chargers. Mansoor said local manufacturing of all these parts will begin at 100 percent by next year.

Click here to purchase a paywall bypass link for this article The town of Bloomfield has banned data centers, joining a number of Connecticut towns that have blocked or restricted the power-hungry facilities, and went a step further by also barring battery energy storage. The Town Plan and Zoning Commission approved the zoning amendments without any opposition at its meeting Thursday. The commission itself proposed the changes. The new rules prohibit data centers “as a principal use, accessory use, or component of a mixed use in every zoning district.” Planning Director Jonathan Colman said the rules target the large standalone facilities going up around the country. He said the town wrote the definition broadly on purpose. “They are often referred to by other names and titles, often to try and avoid the regulations that may be in place in the community,” Colman said. Colman said the town had already received one informal data center proposal, for the northwest part of town, that would now be barred. In June 2025, New York-based Atlas Capital Group made an informal presentation to the commission about a possible data center at 132 Griffin Road North. The project called for about 900,000 square feet of data center space and a 127,000-square-foot substation on a vacant 44-acre former tobacco field. Companies can still run servers for their own operations as an accessory use, town staff said. The amendments create a separate category for offices and engineering sites where computers serve on-site employees. Staff said that use differs from a data center, which relies on backup generators, chillers and cooling towers. The changes also eliminated a provision that let the commission approve uses not specifically allowed in a zone. Now, if a use isn’t listed, it isn’t permitted. The vote came two days after East Lyme’s zoning commission unanimously banned traditional and AI data centers, along with data center accessory uses. In 2021, Connecticut lawmakers created tax breaks to lure data centers, letting the state exempt projects of at least $200 million, or $50 million in certain economic development zones, from sales and property taxes for up to 30 years.

County Director of Planning and Building Abraham Prado presented the draft ordinance, which staff recommended the commission approve and forward to the San Benito County Board of Supervisors for approval. But the commissioners indicated they believed the draft ordinance wasn’t nearly ready for their review yet because expert consultant Mike Nicholas’ report on his review of the draft had not yet been considered by the ad hoc committee of interested parties. Nicholas, a retired Kern County fire captain who has worked with state officials on creating BESS project standards, agreed to review the draft ordinance and provide recommendations. However, Prado told the commission Nicholas’ recommendations had not been added to the agenda prior to the meeting. Prado then proceeded to give a lengthy review of the proposed ordinance, including changes made at the ad hoc committee’s behest. He said the staff recommended the commission approve the ordinance and forward it to the supervisors to adopt. Commissioner Robert Gibson was quick to comment, “The staff recommendation is a little off. The ad hoc requested more time to work on the ordinance. artigo.texto: Vaisala, a global leader in measurement instruments and intelligence for critical environments, will showcase data center measurement and service solutions at DCD>Connect Virginia, November 3–4 at Lansdowne Resort & Spa in Leesburg, Virginia. At stand 58, Vaisala will feature two additions to its data center offering, Vaisala Indigo Supervisor and Vaisala Care for Data Centers, alongside the Origo product family. Together, these offerings help operators support cooling performance, energy efficiency, operational reliability and uptime. The Vaisala Indigo Supervisor is designed to simplify environmental monitoring as facilities expand. It enables up to 100 measurement points to be managed as a single system. The solution supports two independent daisy-chained probe networks with up to 50 probes per chain and integrates with building management systems through a single Modbus TCP connection. A local touchscreen provides dashboards, measurement visibility, alert management and calibration information. Web-based commissioning tools help teams deploy the system efficiently. Touchscreen-enabled probe replacement and CSV configuration export support maintenance and more consistent implementation across multiple sites. Indigo Supervisor is expected to be available in early 2027. Vaisala will also highlight Vaisala Care for Data Centers, a service portfolio that provides a structured approach to maintaining measurement performance throughout the lifecycle of a facility’s measurement systems. Designed for hyperscale, colocation and enterprise data centers, the portfolio includes Vaisala Care, Vaisala Care+ and Vaisala Commissioning Care. Available options include calibration services, expert support, replacement probe pools, service documentation, and commissioning-phase calibration and handover documentation. Subject to Vaisala approval, agreed verification scopes may also include selected third-party measurement devices. These services help operators manage calibration, verification and documentation needs across growing measurement networks. The Origo product family will also be on display. This modular platform of transmitters and compact probes supports HVAC measurement in data centers and other mission-critical facilities. Origo provides real-time measurement of temperature, relative humidity, carbon dioxide and dew point to support stable environmental conditions and efficient HVAC operation. Interchangeable probes allow teams to configure the platform for specific measurement requirements. Two probes can be combined in one transmitter to support multi-parameter monitoring while reducing device count. With ±0.1 °C temperature accuracy and ±1% RH humidity accuracy, Origo helps operators reduce unnecessary cooling while supporting the stable environmental control that critical spaces require. Visitors can meet with Vaisala at stand 58 during DCD>Connect Virginia to learn how its measurement instruments, monitoring architecture and lifecycle services help support the reliable and efficient operation of scalable, AI-ready data center infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Interferry has warned that further delays to carbon pricing for road transport could undermine the competitiveness of European ferry services, potentially encouraging freight to shift from sea to road despite the EU’s transport decarbonization objectives. In a statement issued, the ferry industry association raised concerns over ongoing negotiations concerning the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), arguing that differences in the timing of carbon pricing between maritime and road transport are creating an uneven competitive environment. According to Interferry, European ro-ro and ro-pax operators face an estimated €1 billion in annual ETS compliance costs, while road freight continues to benefit from delays to its separate emissions trading framework. Ferry operators face rising costs as road transport avoids ETS2 Since 2024, commercial passenger and cargo vessels of 5,000 GT and above calling at European ports have been included in the EU ETS, with the maritime sector’s obligations being phased in. In an exclusive interview with SAFETY4SEA, Mike Corrigan, CEO of Interferry, identified the difference in carbon pricing between maritime and road transport as the main reason behind the association’s call for an immediate halt to further phasing-in of the maritime EU ETS. The CEO had argued that the imbalance could undermine the EU’s environmental objectives by encouraging freight and passengers to move away from ferry services towards road transport. Interferry estimates that current compliance costs are equivalent to approximately €250 per tonne of diesel fuel for affected ferry operators. Meanwhile, the EU’s ETS2, has already been postponed from 2027 to 2028 and faces pressure from several EU member states for further delays. What is the EU ETS2? As part of the 2023 revisions of the ETS Directive, a new emissions trading system named ETS2 was created. Separate from the existing EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), this new system will cover and address the CO2 emissions from fuel combustion in buildings, road transport and additional sectors (mainly small industry not covered by the existing EU ETS). Johan Roos, Director of Regulatory Affairs at Interferry, said: “The burdens and challenges of decarbonization cannot be borne by individual sectors alone, and all transport sectors must be treated equally.” Risk of freight shifting away from ferry services The central concern is that uneven carbon pricing could have consequences beyond the ferry industry’s operating costs. Ro-ro and ro-pax services often compete directly with road transport for freight movements, particularly on routes where customers can choose between transporting goods by ferry or using an alternative land connection. According to Interferry, higher compliance costs make ferry services less competitive and can encourage freight customers to favour road transport. The association also argues that competitive pressure limits operators’ ability to pass additional costs on to customers, potentially reducing the funds available for investments in cleaner vessels and technologies. Such a development could conflict with EU efforts to encourage greater use of short-sea shipping as part of transport decarbonization. However, the extent of any resulting shift from sea to road has not been quantified in the statement, and the environmental consequences would depend on the routes and transport alternatives involved. Interferry calls for equal carbon pricing and reinvestment To address the imbalance, Interferry is calling for changes to the structure and implementation of ETS2. Furthermore, The association proposes separating road transport from building emissions under the framework, allowing carbon pricing for road freight to proceed independently of concerns over household heating costs. Alternatively, it argues that carbon costs should be applied consistently across competing transport sectors. Interferry is also calling for all revenues generated through maritime ETS compliance to be reinvested in shipping’s decarbonization, particularly through support for: - Sustainable marine fuels produced within the EU. - Cleaner vessel technologies. - Onshore charging infrastructure for ferry operations. According to the association, redirecting ETS revenues towards these measures would help operators invest in reducing emissions while addressing the financial pressures arising from compliance. The broader concern is that carbon pricing designed to support decarbonization could produce unintended consequences if competing transport modes face substantially different obligations. For ferry operators, the issue is therefore not only the cost of EU ETS compliance, but whether the regulatory framework provides consistent incentives for freight transport across sea and road.

artigo.texto: Home › Energy Storage ›GoodWe Launches ESA 125 kW/251 kWh BESS at REI Expo 2026 GoodWe Launches ESA 125 kW/251 kWh BESS at REI Expo 2026 GoodWe has launched its ESA 125 kW/251 kWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) for C&I applications at the Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo 2026, alongside showcasing its comprehensive energy storage portfolio spanning residential, commercial, and utility-scale segments. October 26, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey At the Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo 2026, GoodWe announced the launch of its ESA 125 kW/251 kWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), expanding its portfolio of energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial (C&I) applications. The ESA Series is suited to a wide range of use cases, including factories, commercial complexes and other grid-connected or off-grid applications. It integrates the Power Conversion System (PCS), battery cells, Energy Management System (EMS) and Battery Management System (BMS) in a single cabinet, which simplifies installation, operation and maintenance while allowing flexible capacity expansion. The system scales from hundreds of kilowatt-hours to multi-megawatt-hours, supporting up to 15 units in parallel for a total capacity of up to 3.91 MWh in on-grid scenarios. At the expo, GoodWe also presented a full range of energy storage technologies, from residential systems to large-scale utility projects. In the utility-scale energy storage segment, the company showcased AC ESS 2MW/4MWh, which offers a one-stop integrated solution with in-house-developed battery, PCS, EMU and MVS components in a 20-foot containerised design that enables easier transportation and fast deployment. With 90.5 percent round-trip efficiency, a 7 percent increase in lifetime energy throughput and an AC/DC-separated architecture, it improves project returns while enhancing safety and simplifying maintenance, the company stated. It further added that the UT Series complements this offering for large renewable energy projects and grid-connected installations. GoodWe also showcased its residential hybrid energy storage portfolio, featuring the ES Uniq + Lynx A G3 and ET LV + Lynx A G4 solution. Designed to integrate solar power, battery storage, and intelligent energy management, these solutions highlighted the potential for greater energy independence, efficient solar utilisation, and reliable power supply for modern homes. In the C&I segment, the company showcased the GT Series string inverter, which is designed to enhance productivity and deliver high power density in C&I applications. With 8/10 MPPTs, a high input current of 21A per DC string and a maximum efficiency of 99 percent, it increases overall yield with high-power PV modules. It also supports string-level monitoring and an optional PID (Potential Induced Degradation) recovery function for better module performance. Type II surge protection on both the AC and DC sides protects the inverter against lightning, giving C&I PV projects added safety, reliability and a stronger return on investment. Aniket Sawant, Country Head, GoodWe India, said, “As GoodWe celebrates 10 years in India, we remain committed to driving the country’s clean energy transition through innovative and reliable solutions. The launch of our ESA 125 kW/261 kWh BESS at REI 2026 reflects our continued focus on delivering advanced energy storage solutions across residential, C&I and utility-scale segments.” If you want to cooperate with us and would like to reuse some of our content, please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: O Rio Grande do Norte busca ampliar sua participação no mercado de centros de processamento de dados, mas ainda depende da instalação de cabos submarinos de telecomunicações para atrair empreendimentos de grande porte. Apesar dos avanços na regulamentação do setor e da disponibilidade de energia, o Estado aguarda uma definição do governo federal sobre a infraestrutura de conectividade necessária aos projetos. O tema foi discutido nesta sexta-feira, 23, durante a Data Center Conference, realizada na Federação das Indústrias do Estado do Rio Grande do Norte (Fiern), em Natal. Leia mais: FIERN recebe em novembro maior evento sobre produção industrial do RN A instalação de cabos submarinos é considerada uma das condições para viabilizar estruturas capazes de atender empresas nacionais e internacionais. Esses equipamentos permitem a transmissão de grandes volumes de dados entre diferentes regiões e países, com capacidade e velocidade necessárias às operações digitais. A expectativa do setor é de que a infraestrutura amplie a competitividade potiguar na atração de investimentos associados à inteligência artificial, computação em nuvem e armazenamento de informações. Leia mais: Alecrim celebra 115 anos com ações para fortalecer o comércio O gerente comercial da Mendes Holler, Gladson Mortoza, afirmou que a chegada da tecnologia poderá ocorrer no curto e médio prazos. Segundo ele, a disponibilidade de energia representa uma vantagem para o Estado, mas precisa ser acompanhada de infraestrutura de telecomunicações. “O Estado já possui oferta de energia. Com a expectativa da chegada de conectividade via cabo submarino, o Rio Grande do Norte abre a porta para atender às demandas daqui, de todo País e até mesmo internacionais”, afirmou. Leia mais: Prefeitura amplia acesso à qualificação profissional O presidente da Fiern, Roberto Serquiz, defendeu a ampliação das negociações para acelerar a conexão do Estado às redes internacionais. Ele lembrou que o Ceará já dispõe dessa infraestrutura, o que poderia facilitar a integração regional. “É uma etapa que nós precisamos trabalhar. Os cabos já existem no Ceará, então, a ligação com o RN se torna apenas um ponto de diálogo. Com essa conectividade, fechamos mais um ciclo para que, definitivamente, os investimentos cheguem ao RN”, declarou. Leia mais: Procura pela primeira CNH cresce 86% no RN A secretária-adjunta de Desenvolvimento Econômico do Estado, Emília Casanova, informou que o governo potiguar já possui estudos sobre possíveis áreas de instalação, mas depende de uma decisão federal. “Nós temos um estudo de atracação em áreas de interesse, porém, não houve ainda uma decisão do Ministério de Telecomunicações, a qual inclui uma definição sobre os locais de instalação. A gente não sabe se será somente em Natal ou se haverá uma conexão também na região da Costa Branca”, explicou. A indefinição mantém em aberto a localização dos futuros pontos de conexão e o cronograma de implantação. Além da disponibilidade de energia e telecomunicações, projetos de data centers exigem investimentos em sistemas de refrigeração, segurança operacional e fornecimento contínuo de eletricidade, fatores considerados na avaliação econômica dos empreendimentos. RN já tem regras para licenciamento ambiental A regulamentação dos centros de dados no Rio Grande do Norte avançou em setembro, quando o Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema) aprovou normas específicas para o licenciamento desses empreendimentos. Publicada no Diário Oficial em 25 de setembro, a Resolução nº 2/2026 estabelece critérios conforme o porte das instalações, o consumo de energia e os sistemas de refrigeração utilizados. A legislação prevê procedimentos simplificados para instalações menores e estudos ambientais mais abrangentes para estruturas de maior porte. Projetos classificados como grandes ou excepcionais, quando utilizarem sistemas abertos de refrigeração, deverão apresentar Estudo e Relatório de Impacto Ambiental (EIA/Rima). As exigências procuram estabelecer condições para a expansão do setor, considerando o consumo de eletricidade e os possíveis impactos sobre os recursos hídricos. No âmbito federal, a sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), em setembro, criou incentivos fiscais para investimentos em infraestrutura de processamento e armazenamento de dados. A medida contempla atividades relacionadas à computação em nuvem, inteligência artificial e processamento de alto desempenho. A demanda por esses empreendimentos também cresce no Nordeste. Levantamentos da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) identificaram interesse em mais de 30 projetos na região, com potencial de consumo de 8,3 gigawatts. A dimensão dessa demanda reforça a necessidade de planejamento da infraestrutura elétrica e de telecomunicações. *Matéria atualizada às 11h55

artigo.texto: O desenvolvimento de uma infraestrutura digital sob controle nacional, a expansão de data centers, o fortalecimento da inteligência artificial (IA) desenvolvida por empresas brasileiras e a digitalização de serviços públicos estão entre as propostas para o período de 2027 a 2030 registradas no plano de governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva apresentado ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) para a eleição de 2026. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Soberania digital expõe dependência externa e pressiona Brasil por política de cibersegurança Embora o documento indique diretrizes e iniciativas para o próximo mandato, nem todas vêm acompanhadas de cronogramas, orçamento específico ou metas quantitativas de execução. Vencedor no pleito de 2026, o documento possui traz capítulo dedicado à economia digital, o documento estabelece a soberania digital como diretriz e prevê o desenvolvimento de um ecossistema nacional de tecnologia, que abrange desde a cadeia de data centers até os serviços de computação em nuvem. O texto também propõe investimentos em infraestrutura computacional, pesquisa, hardware e software de alto desempenho, além de medidas para ampliar o uso da inteligência artificial na economia. Data centers e infraestrutura computacional soberana O plano prevê ampliar a capacidade brasileira de desenvolver, operar, regular e governar tecnologias estratégicas e infraestruturas críticas. A diretriz inclui a construção de um ecossistema nacional de tecnologia digital, com atenção à cadeia de data centers e aos serviços de nuvem, além do fortalecimento da inteligência artificial desenvolvida por empresas brasileiras. Para viabilizar essa estratégia, o documento propõe mobilizar investimentos, inovação, compras governamentais e parcerias entre empresas públicas e privadas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Também prevê avançar em uma infraestrutura computacional soberana, com supercomputadores desenvolvidos e operados por instituições nacionais. A expansão dos data centers e das infraestruturas de IA deverá, segundo o plano, ser acompanhada de salvaguardas socioambientais obrigatórias. Entre os pontos mencionados estão a eficiência energética, a utilização progressiva de fontes 100% renováveis e a avaliação dos impactos sobre os sistemas elétrico e hídrico e sobre as populações locais. O documento também estabelece que a instalação de data centers no Brasil deverá prever contrapartidas relacionadas ao conteúdo local e à oferta de capacidade computacional para o mercado interno. As medidas estão associadas à proposta de fortalecer a autonomia do país em tecnologias estratégicas e ampliar a participação nacional nas cadeias digitais. O plano, porém, não detalha nesse trecho o volume de investimentos previsto nem estabelece um cronograma específico para a implantação da infraestrutura. Inteligência artificial e desenvolvimento de tecnologia nacional A inteligência artificial aparece como um dos eixos da política para a economia digital. O programa prevê acelerar sua adoção no setor produtivo, com foco em agronegócio, saúde e serviços financeiros, além de levar a transformação digital às pequenas empresas e à economia popular. O texto também propõe investir em instituições públicas de pesquisa e desenvolvimento que já trabalham com IA e na indústria nacional de hardware e software de alto desempenho. A intenção declarada é ampliar a capacidade brasileira de desenvolver tecnologias e fortalecer os diferentes elos da cadeia digital. Outra iniciativa prevista é desenvolver e manter modelos de linguagem em português e em outras línguas, orientados a problemas do país. Para isso, o documento propõe uma plataforma nacional de dados destinada ao treinamento e à avaliação desses modelos, além do estabelecimento de regras e infraestrutura para a economia de dados. A formação de profissionais também integra a estratégia. O plano prevê desenvolver talentos para consolidar um hub nacional de competências digitais, articulando polos de inovação, universidades, centros de pesquisa e setor produtivo. O documento não especifica, nesse conjunto de propostas, quantos profissionais deverão ser formados, qual será o investimento destinado às iniciativas ou quais indicadores serão utilizados para acompanhar sua execução. Digitalização da indústria e indústria 4.0 A transformação digital da indústria é outro eixo do programa. O plano propõe ampliar a produção nacional em cadeias de valor consideradas estratégicas, fortalecer a posição do Brasil nas tecnologias relacionadas à indústria 4.0 e aumentar a incorporação de tecnologia aos processos produtivos. Entre as diretrizes estão a internalização de tecnologias, a verticalização de cadeias de produção, a digitalização ampla e a renovação do parque de máquinas industriais. O documento prevê priorizar setores de média-alta e alta intensidade tecnológica. A proposta conecta a digitalização industrial à política de desenvolvimento produtivo e à ampliação da capacidade nacional de produzir equipamentos, sistemas e soluções tecnológicas. Para o setor de tecnologia digital, esse eixo abrange oportunidades relacionadas a hardware, software, pesquisa e desenvolvimento e integração de tecnologias aos processos industriais. O programa, entretanto, não apresenta metas específicas de adoção de tecnologias digitais por segmento industrial nem um calendário detalhado para a renovação do parque de máquinas. Serviços públicos digitais e uso de IA pelo governo Na administração pública, o plano prevê ampliar o compartilhamento de infraestrutura pública digital entre os diferentes níveis de governo. A proposta está relacionada à cooperação entre União, estados e municípios para enfrentar diferenças de capacidade na prestação de serviços à população. O documento também prevê investimentos no Portal da Transparência para transformá-lo em uma plataforma inteligente baseada em dados abertos e inteligência artificial. artigo.texto: Overview: For predominantly Black neighborhoods already confronting pollution concerns, Memphis' abbreviated data center moratorium offers limited breathing room. Residents and advocates say the council's decision falls short of protecting communities from the environmental costs of AI expansion. The fray over locating more AI data centers in Memphis reached a small break Oct. 20, after a long, contentious City Council meeting in which a proposed 18-month moratorium on data-center development or expansion failed and a much shorter 135-day pause passed. “The Memphis City Council failed the people of Memphis and the mid-South tonight,” state Rep. Justin J. Pearson, a Democrat from the area, told WREG after the five-hour meeting that drew more than 400 people. LEARN MORE: A Billion-Dollar Data-Center Tax Break Along the Civil Rights Trail “The four-and-a-half-month moratorium, passed with rushed, piecemeal guidelines, was not what the people wanted,” he said. What Went Wrong Pearson, who is running for Congress in a district Republicans gerrymandered into existence, currently represents Boxtown, the historically Black neighborhood founded by freedmen in 1863. For much of the past two years, Pearson and many of his constituents have lived beside Colossus, one of Elon Musk’s three hyperscale data centers. Each data center Musk has developed in the Memphis area is located in predominantly Black neighborhoods. Pearson has made the fight against data center development a key component of his campaign. Even before the Memphis City Council met last Tuesday for a third and final vote on a proposed moratorium, the question was who would be allowed in the City Council chambers. Earlier in October, activists on both sides packed the room for the expected final vote. When the council voted to delay the decision, the meeting plunged into chaos, with heated exchanges between council members and moratorium supporters in the crowd. The council decided to delay the final vote to Oct. 20. But Pearson and five other residents who attended that meeting later received letters banning them from the next two meetings. A federal judge partly overturned the ban just hours before the council convened on Oct. 20. The moratorium failed on a tie vote. Many blamed the result on the absence of Council member Yolanda Cooper-Sutton, who co-sponsored the moratorium in August with two colleagues but missed the meeting because of a family emergency. At times, she has been a vocal critic of SpaceXAI and was at the center of the conflict during the last council meeting when she voted to delay the third and final reading of the moratorium ordinance. After verbally sparring with activists — and some fellow council members — Cooper-Sutton was suspended from her duties on two committees for 30 days. However, she was still eligible to attend and participate in this week’s pivotal meeting. Moritorium Fails, Pause Succeeds Before the vote, the original proposal for a yearlong moratorium was amended to 18 months. A shorter, 135-day pause on data centers was then introduced during the council session and was approved on a 7-5 vote. While no one seemed happy with the final result, the pause offers a brief window to figure out how to regulate data centers, which critics say consume massive amounts of power and water and pollute neighborhoods that are already fighting for cleaner air. Council members who supported the original moratorium were also frustrated. RELATED: A Massive Data Center Helped Topple a Mayor. What’s Next? “We had hundreds of people packed in there who waited for hours, Council member Jerri Green told CNN. “They’ve been pushing for this for over a year. They’re the people who are being deeply impacted by these environmental hazards.” Green said that the City Council had failed the people of Memphis. During the 135-day ban, the city will study how data centers affect residents and the resources they demand. Recommendations are also to follow on where future data centers can be located and how such facilities will be defined.

artigo.texto: Greenvolt Group, through Greenvolt Power, has agreed to sell two standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Poland to A&R Investments. The projects are located in Ełk and Turośń Kościelna in north-eastern Poland, and have a total installed capacity of 400 MW/1,600 MWh. Both projects were completed in the third quarter of 2026 and have received the required permits for use. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to the fulfillment of the applicable conditions. Furthermore, both Ełk and Turośń have secured 17-year capacity market contracts starting in 2028. Under these contracts, each project will receive a fixed payment for making 85 per cent of its capacity available to the system. The projects are also covered by 10-year tolling agreements, under which the batteries will be optimised and their flexibility traded in the power markets. Earlier, in October 2026, Greenvolt Power raised € 284 million in project financing for its 253.1 MW wind project in Gurbănești, located east of Bucharest, Romania. The project is currently under construction and is expected to begin commercial operations by the end of 2027.

artigo.texto: Lula cobra regulação de big techs e contrapartidas de data centers No discurso da vitória, presidente defende inteligência artificial brasileira e reserva de capacidade de data centers para o país. Em seu discurso feito ontem à noite, 25, após a confirmação da vitória pelo TSE nas eleições de 2026, o presidente reeleito Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defendeu a regulação das plataformas digitais, a atração de data centers com contrapartidas para o Brasil e o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial nacional em seu discurso da vitória. Ao comentar a disputa eleitoral, acusou empresas de tecnologia de interferência no processo e afirmou que crimes cometidos no ambiente digital devem receber tratamento equivalente ao dos praticados fora dele. “Essa eleição foi uma eleição em que a gente teve que vencer a intromissão vinda de fora para dentro, através de plataformas digitais”, afirmou. Na sequência, disse que será necessário regulá-las. O presidente também criticou o poder econômico e a tributação dessas empresas: “Nós não podemos ter empresas monstruosas de grana, ganhando milhões e bilhões, não pagando nenhum imposto para esse país, e tentando direcionar o resultado eleitoral desse país”. Vale lembrar que as empresas instaladas no Brasil pagam tributos locais, como ISS e IOF por remessa de capitais. Redes sociais sob fiscalização A cobrança ocorre em meio a apurações sobre as práticas de moderação das redes sociais. Em 19 de outubro, conforme noticiou o Tele.Síntese, a Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) notificou a Meta para explicar os critérios usados na suspensão de contas, remoção de conteúdos e restrição do alcance de publicações no Instagram e no Facebook. Denúncias com possível repercussão eleitoral foram encaminhadas ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral. O Ministério Público Federal também instaurou procedimento sobre a moderação da Meta e do X, a partir de uma representação de organizações que reuniram mais de mil relatos de bloqueios, remoções e suspensões durante o período eleitoral. Essas iniciativas apuram as práticas das empresas; não constituem, por si, comprovação da interferência denunciada pelo presidente. A regulação defendida por Lula encontra um cenário de mudanças nas obrigações das plataformas. No julgamento sobre o artigo 19 do Marco Civil da Internet, o Supremo Tribunal Federal ampliou as hipóteses de responsabilização por conteúdos de terceiros sem necessidade de ordem judicial prévia. Data centers com capacidade para o Brasil Na frente de infraestrutura, Lula defendeu aproveitar o potencial brasileiro de energia renovável para atrair data centers e manter dados no país. “Vão ter que deixar uma parte do data center para informações brasileiras”, declarou. A exigência tem correspondência no Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), elaborado pelo governo federal e sancionado em 15 de setembro após aprovação na Câmara e no Senado. As empresas habilitadas terão de destinar ao mercado interno pelo menos 10% do fornecimento efetivo de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados instalado com os benefícios do programa. O regime prevê suspensão de tributos federais sobre aquisição de equipamentos e componentes e estabelece contrapartidas de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. Também exige atendimento da demanda contratual de eletricidade com fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão e fixa requisitos de eficiência hídrica. O setor aguarda a publicação da regulamentação vai que listar os equipamentos isentos na importação. Inteligência artificial brasileira Lula também falou de inteligência artificial. Associou a formação em matemática e engenharia ao desenvolvimento de tecnologia nacional. Disse que não quer depender de inteligência artificial “chinesa ou americana” e que pretende desenvolver uma alternativa brasileira. A declaração retoma objetivos do Plano Brasileiro de Inteligência Artificial (PBIA). Em 20 de agosto, o governo anunciou uma nova etapa do plano, com investimentos em supercomputação, desenvolvimento de chips em arquitetura aberta e criação da Nuvem Brasileira,. O projeto de nuvem prevê a participação do governo e do setor privado no desenvolvimento de infraestrutura e tecnologia nacionais para armazenamento e processamento de dados. A proposta é reduzir a dependência de provedores estrangeiros em componentes críticos, adotar padrões abertos e interoperáveis e estimular fornecedores brasileiros. O pacote também prevê um supercomputador estimado em R$ 1 bilhão, a ser instalado no Parque Tecnológico Augusto Severo, da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte. A execução ficará sob responsabilidade do Laboratório Nacional de Computação Científica, com recursos do FNDCT e previsão de operação no final de 2027. Outra iniciativa anunciada foi o Centro Nacional de Transparência Algorítmica e IA Confiável, na UFMG, destinado a pesquisas e ferramentas para avaliação de segurança, riscos, transparência e vieses de sistemas de inteligência artificial.
