artigo.texto: Croatian company ENNA Solar has signed an agreement to acquire a solar power project with a battery energy storage system in Romania. The Medgidia project comprises a solar power plant with a planned installed capacity of 166 MWp and a battery energy storage system (BESS) with a capacity of 612 MWh. Subject to obtaining the required regulatory approvals, the project will further expand ENNA Group’s renewable energy project portfolio in the Romanian market, ENNA Solar, a member of ENNA Group, said. ENNA Solar has signed a share purchase agreement setting out the terms for the acquisition of a 100% equity stake in the Romanian special-purpose company CIC Grenn Energy Medgidia, which holds the rights to develop the photovoltaic plant and its associated BESS. The project covers 204 hectares of land Construction of the Medgidia project is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The solar power plant is expected to enter commercial operation and begin supplying electricity to the grid in the first quarter of 2028, ENNA Group stressed. Expected annual electricity generation amounts to 265,932 MWh. The completion of the transaction and the transfer of the equity stake to ENNA Solar are subject to approval by the competent Romanian authority responsible for screening foreign direct investment (FDI), and approval from the relevant competition authorities in the applicable jurisdictions. The project is located in the Medgidia area, in Romania’s Constanța county, and covers approximately 204 hectares of land. Napast: The deal reaffirms our ambition to expand significantly into Central and Eastern European markets “Medgidia represents a significant step forward in the continued development of ENNA Group’s energy portfolio and the strengthening of our presence in the sizable Romanian market. It also reaffirms our ambition to expand significantly into Central and Eastern European markets, where we see further investment opportunities,” Boštjan Napast, President of the Management Board of ENNA Group, pointed out. He noted that the company is interested in renewable energy projects that are at an advanced stage of development or ready for construction. First major investment outside of Croatia The Medgidia acquisition builds on ENNA Group’s existing investments in Romania. ENNA Solar has already acquired the Mihăilești solar power project, with an installed capacity of 87.52 MWp, which is now at an advanced stage of construction. The project also includes a 140 MWh BESS, with commercial operation expected to begin in April 2027. Back in late December 2025 ENNA started the construction of this solar power plant. It is the company’s first major investment outside of Croatia. It also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on renewable energy projects in Azerbaijan. The company operates in the sectors of energy and logistics.

artigo.texto: The next governor of Wisconsin will have plenty of work ahead of them once they are inaugurated at the state capitol in January. Wisconsin has a multi-billion dollar budget surplus, and voters surveyed by the most recent Marquette University Law School poll said some of the most important issues to them revolve around affordability, healthcare, taxes and data centers. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” invited both candidates for governor to sit down for one-on-one interviews about their positions on voters’ top concerns. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Republican Tom Tiffany’s campaign declined the invitation, citing his busy schedule of events. Democrat David Crowley joined WPR host Kate Archer Kent last Thursday to share his plans for the state if he’s elected governor. The following was minimally edited for clarity. Kate Archer Kent: We’re fielding questions from WPR listeners for candidates for governor, and one question that comes up a lot is about lowering everyday costs like groceries and gas. Wisconsin ended the last fiscal year with over $3 billion in surplus. What would you propose lawmakers do with that money? David Crowley: Well, the first thing we have to do is actually tackle the affordability crisis. No matter where you go in the state of Wisconsin, each community member lets you know that they can’t afford the groceries, how that has gone up, the diesel and the gas prices, as well as renting or owning a home. And so, first and foremost, we want to pass the minimum markup law, repealing that particular sales tax as it relates to gas. That’s 40 cents a gallon that each person is paying at the pump, and we want to make sure that we can lower those costs, not just at the pump, but that will help to lower costs also in our grocery stores because of the amount of gas and diesel that they are utilizing. It’s also about utilizing that surplus to buy down the property taxes. So many communities across Wisconsin have gone through referendum after referendum just to make sure that our schools have enough resources to make sure that our children have what they need to build upon that foundation of learning. Funding our public schools here in the state of Wisconsin would naturally ease the property tax pressures that many of our older adults are feeling while being on a fixed income. But we also have to tackle healthcare. So many people have seen their premiums double or seen their doctor’s office, their clinics and their hospitals close because a trillion dollars were cut from the Medicaid/Medicare program with the help of Congressman Tom Tiffany. So we need to make sure that we expand BadgerCare across this state, which will not only help those who are uninsured and underinsured, but this will help everybody who has insurance to help lower their costs and, more importantly, make sure that you can get access to care whenever and whenever you need it. Also for those who have families or those who want a family, we know that childcare is not just expensive; it’s not accessible. The more we can work with our childcare providers to provide the floor of funding that they need and make sure that we can provide a slot for every working family — that’s going to provide every working adult to enter into the workforce or make the best decision for them and their family to get ahead. KAK: One thing I didn’t hear on your list was whether you would put any part of the surplus to send tax refunds to residents. Gov. Tony Evers and lawmakers pushed that bipartisan deal earlier this year. Would you try for one again? DC: When it came down to that deal, if I was the governor, I absolutely would have signed it. But unfortunately, my opponent actually pushed back and convinced many of the Republicans not to vote for that deal. I know what’s important is that we work with our legislative leaders and the legislature in general to make sure that we can come up with a bipartisan deal that works for everyone. I am open to doing whatever we can to make sure that we’re providing relief for the hardworking Wisconsinites that can’t get ahead. KAK: Your position on data centers has shifted recently. Over the summer, you said Wisconsin should not repeal state data center incentives. More recently, you’ve said you would absolutely sign a repeal. What has changed? DC: I’ve always been open to reforming the sales tax exemptions that the data centers have been getting. If we were to get a bill that came to my desk, I absolutely would sign it. I believe in those reforms because we have seen not just billionaires but big tech companies who have already received $80 billion in tax breaks from the federal government — a bill that my opponent actually supported and voted for. People are struggling to put food on the table, struggling to afford their rent or to afford their mortgage, struggling to put gas into their tanks. We need to be providing relief for them, not for the billionaire tech companies who are steamrolling communities with these data centers. We have to make sure that if a community doesn’t want a data center, they shouldn’t be forced to have one. They need to have a seat at the table. On day one, the legislature and I are going to get right to work to make sure that we have those guardrails in place to protect our communities. KAK: Would those guardrails entail a pause, a statewide moratorium? DC: I think right now we are effectively in a de facto moratorium. I know that there was recently a lawsuit, and now we’re going to have our Department of Natural Resources conducting an environmental analysis about what these data centers can actually do to our environment, and so I believe that we should continue to have a pause while this process plays out. artigo.texto: Hopkins County Fiscal Court hosts public session on data centers MADISONVILLE, Ky. (WFIE) - Data centers drew another packed house Monday, this time inside the Hopkins County Fiscal Courtroom, as county leaders opened the floor for public comment on the facilities and their potential impact on the community. It’s a scene that’s become familiar across the tri-state in recent months, as data centers tied to the artificial intelligence boom have become a hot-button issue in county after county — and Hopkins County is no exception. County leaders said the meeting was designed to give residents an opportunity to raise questions, thoughts or concerns about data centers before any new ordinances or other proceedings move forward. One of many to speak, Hopkins County resident Michael Howard, didn’t mince words about the technology behind the facilities. “Data centers are infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence is the most dangerous technology that humankind has ever invented, bar none, including atomic power, including genetic engineering,” Howard said. Overflow From a Madisonville Meeting Monday’s meeting came just a week after the city of Madisonville hosted its own public comment session on a draft data center ordinance, and many of the same residents showed up again — some from Madisonville itself, even though Monday’s meeting was a county matter, not a city one. Several speakers used the opportunity to tie the issue directly to next week’s election, criticizing Madisonville’s city administration in the process. “Why in the world do we even want to consider a data center? The mayor stood up, I heard him on the radio, ‘I’m for data center.’ He stood up and said he was. So vote him out when the election comes up,” Hopkins County resident Billy McKinsey said, drawing applause from the crowd. “Vote him out.” Environmental and Quality-of-Life Concerns Beyond the political back-and-forth, many residents who spoke Monday raised concerns about the day-to-day impact data centers could have on the county — from water and electrical usage to noise pollution and the loss of farmland and other environmental effects. Several speakers also pushed back on the idea that the issue breaks down along party lines. “This isn’t a Republican or a Democrat issue. It’s a human issue. We are everyday young professionals, parents, grandparents who have started to research and understand this issue. And the more we learn, the more concerned we become,” Hopkins County resident Marie Moyer said. What’s Next Monday’s session was limited to public comment — no votes or formal decisions were made. But officials say the feedback collected will factor into future discussions, including any new ordinances Hopkins County may consider to regulate data centers going forward. The county’s meeting follows closely on the heels of Madisonville’s own effort to draft data center regulations. City officials there are considering an ordinance that would restrict data centers to General Industrial zoning districts, require them to sit at least 250 feet from homes, schools, churches and daycares, cap building height at 75 feet, limit nighttime noise to 50 decibels, and require developers — not other ratepayers — to cover the cost of utility upgrades needed to serve large facilities. That ordinance has not yet been adopted, and city officials have said it can still be revised ahead of any vote. Madisonville’s public comment period on its draft ordinance was limited to a combined 10 minutes, a restriction that frustrated many residents who felt it didn’t allow enough time for the number of people who showed up wanting to speak. With both a city ordinance and now county-level discussions underway, data centers are expected to remain a central issue in Hopkins County in the weeks ahead. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: By Ashley Murray States Newsroom SPRINGDALE, Pa. – Residents in a small southwestern Pennsylvania town are facing the prospect of a 47-acre data center facility on their doorstep. “Right here behind this fence is where they want to put up the data center, and as you can see, there’s houses right across the street, roughly 100 feet,” said lifelong Springdale borough resident Cathy Mager, stretching her arms to show the distance from the development site’s perimeter to a line of houses across Porter Street. “We don’t want it,” she told States Newsroom on Oct. 19. The scenario is playing out around the United States. Both Democratic and Republican candidates during the heated midterm election cycle have had to navigate deep voter resentment of the massive advanced computer server farm developments that will power artificial intelligence. “The issue has blown up over the last year,” said Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution’s Center for Technology. “It wasn’t that long ago politicians were fighting to bring data centers to their communities. Now these facilities are completely controversial, and many people don’t want them in their neighborhood. So public opinion has changed very rapidly on this issue.” 53 Years with a Power Plant Mager is among a few dozen residents in Springdale, in northeastern Allegheny County, who formed the group Save Allegheny Valley Environment to protest the proposed data center development on the community’s riverfront site of a coal-fired power plant that went offline in 2022. “We’ve already lived for 53 years under that power plant,” said Vicki Wanamaker, 66, a lifelong Springdale resident who lives about a 10th of a mile from the fencing around the site. She’s worried now about the noise a data center would bring to the neighborhood, with its water coolers running and backup diesel generators on site, and whether she would experience electricity shortages. Springdale’s council voted 5-2 in December to approve a conditional use permit for the project by Dynamo DC, a company with a Springdale-based address that “builds AI data centers on environmentally remediated brownfield sites,” according to its website. Residents are now asking Allegheny County to stop further land use plans. Dynamo DC spokesperson Brian Regli said the developers will use “acoustical shielding” to keep noise well below ordinance levels. The hyperscale data center will recycle 500,000 gallons of water in a closed-loop system to cool the servers, he told States Newsroom during an interview in late October. The facility is planned to handle up to 240 megawatts, which it will pull from a regional electricity grid, Regli said. Dynamo DC has not yet identified which company or contractors will actually use the data center. The company plans for the data center to go online by 2029. Regli said the company is exploring “environmentally conscious” fuels for the diesel backup generators. The amount of backup power needed for the site will ultimately depend on how the data center is used. Some uses “may need a fraction of the backup power that we put forward,” he said. “But you know, if this is a critical facility, let’s say it is being used by the military – which I doubt that the center would become that, but let’s use that as an example – you’re going to want to have as robust of a backup infrastructure as you can,” Regli said. Amie Downs, of Caveat Communications, which is providing communications for Springdale, said the borough “was able to negotiate a number of other provisions that benefit the community and its taxpayers that relate to noise, lighting, traffic, landscaping and other requirements, imposing stricter standards than the borough’s ordinances otherwise required.” Thousands of Data Centers Planned Data centers are a linchpin of the modern internet, but the scale needed for advanced computing is new. There are 1,394 data centers already operating around the United States, and they carry a combined capacity of 64,764 megawatts. As of October, 2,841 more data centers are planned and would add 413,152 megawatts of additional capacity, according to the energy market firm Cleanview’s data center project tracker. “What we’re seeing now is huge facilities that are being built. These are data centers that occupy the size of several football fields,” said West, who also publishes the progressive organization’s TechTank and is a senior fellow on governance studies. “They require a lot of energy. Some of them require water as well. So the size of the data centers creates public anxiety and worry.” Sixty-three percent of American adults say they don’t want a data center built in their community, according to a late August poll published by YouGov and The Economist. A CNN poll conducted in mid-September found nearly two-thirds of registered voters surveyed said AI and data center development will be an extremely or very important factor in their vote this midterm election. The poll also found a partisan divide: Democrats are 26 percentage points more likely than Republicans to say they’re very concerned about data centers, according to the results. From Trump on Down The issue is permeating politics and races at the federal, state and local levels. President Donald Trump on Wednesday wrote on his Truth Social platform that data centers “are mandated by me to make their own electricity.” “If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend.’ … MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!” he wrote. The statement is a pivot from his late August post, when he called opponents of data center developments “backwards and poor.” Resentment against the large-scale projects has become a dominant issue in hotly contested U.S. Senate races that will determine party control for the closely divided upper chamber. artigo.texto: Construction Of Military Data Center On Maui Alarms Residents The nearly $100 million facility would work in conjunction with seven proposed telescopes near the summit of Haleakalā. The lab and data center are expected to be completed early next year. The controversial telescopes that the military is seeking to build in a state conservation district atop Haleakalā would be remotely operated from a two-story, 56,000-square-foot laboratory and data center that is currently under construction in Kīhei. Federal officials from the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force finalized plans to build the nearly $100 million facility at the Maui Research and Technology Park around the same time that they proposed adding up to seven telescopes to the military’s existing space surveillance complex on the volcano’s summit. But while the telescopes have drawn intense public backlash, the Kīhei project flew under the public’s radar for several years. Environmentalists, Native Hawaiian advocates and other Maui residents have in recent weeks called attention to the planned South Maui facility and criticized the military for failing to more explicitly disclose its connection to the new telescopes planned for Haleakalā’s 10,000-foot summit. By introducing the two projects separately, federal officials were able to circumvent questions about their relationship and cumulative environmental impact, according to Hina Kneubuhl, an organizer with Protect Haleakalā, a collective of Hawaiian cultural practitioners, environmentalists, community leaders and others working to protect culturally significant landscapes. “They segment these projects, and it’s so deceptive. All of us who don’t have time to do this, were trying to catch them while we’re catching all of these balls flying in the air,” Kneubuhl said during an Office of Hawaiian Affairs community listening session on Maui earlier this month. Because the telescopes would be built on state land that has been set aside for the federal government, the project cannot move forward until military officials have completed an extensive environmental impact statement and review process that requires opportunities for public feedback. The Kīhei facility — called the Secure Integration Support Laboratory, or SISL — is being built on private property that the federal government purchased in 2023, so officials were only required to complete an environmental assessment, a less rigorous process than required for an environmental impact statement. According to the 2022 draft assessment, Air Force officials concluded that no significant adverse effects would result from building the facility. “Where is the transparency regarding its water and electricity demands?” Lisa Yamada said during the OHA meeting last week. “Our families, farmers and communities are already struggling for these precious resources. Our ʻāina and wai should not be sacrificed for military expansion.” “Our younger generations are rising to protect our kūpuna, our culture and our ʻāina.” Construction of the South Maui facility began in late 2024 and is expected to be completed early next year, according to the government contract awarded to Hensel Phelps. The project was designed to consolidate all of the U.S. Space Force 15th Space Surveillance Squadron’s operations across Maui from four facilities into one. It will include a high-performance data center, laboratories, a remote telescope operations center, offices, a conference center, warehouse space and associated infrastructure, according to an April 2023 design document. The draft environmental assessment did not include detailed information about the project’s water consumption, but it projected that consolidating the military’s operations would result in reduced water and energy consumption by the Air Force on Maui over the life of the facility. There would be additional “short-term minor adverse effects on potable water use,” during the early stages of the project, according to the document. Water for the facility would be supplied from an existing Maui County reservoir at the eastern end of Lipoa Road, and the draft environmental assessment proposed adding a new half-million gallon storage tank to increase capacity. It would also include an emergency 2,500-kilowatt generator, as well as a 12,000-gallon tank and three 20,000-gallon tanks to store a two-week supply of diesel fuel capable of powering the entire building in the event of an electricity outage. Some residents have raised concerns about storing such large amounts of fuel in the wildfire-prone area, especially because federal officials have not yet finished cleaning up a 720-gallon diesel fuel spill caused by a lightning strike at the Maui Space Surveillance Complex on Haleakalā in January 2023. There are also heightened public concerns about military fuel storage tanks after the Navy’s underground oil storage facility at Red Hill on Oʻahu leaked in 2021, poisoning tap water for thousands of residents and service members in the area. Like existing military operations in South Maui, the new facility would be connected to and receive data from the Maui Space Surveillance Complex on the Haleakalā summit via fiber optic cable, according to the draft environmental impact statement for the planned telescopes. Despite years of pushback from residents, federal officials have maintained that the military needs to build new telescopes and improve its space surveillance capabilities on Maui to track and identify threats among satellites and other objects orbiting the Earth above the Pacific. In addition to concerns about the potential negative impact on cultural and environmental resources, many community members have expressed worry that the military could use new facilities on Maui for war-fighting efforts and that the island could soon become a target for foreign adversaries. artigo.texto: Texas' rapidly growing data center industry could reverse much of the state's progress on air quality by the end of the decade, according to a new report released Tuesday. The air emissions report published by the Houston Advanced Research Center revealed that the industry's impact on air quality depends heavily on how data centers are powered. The outlook is far worse if the facilities rely on natural gas plants. "What we are showcasing here is that there is a significant increase in different pollutant emissions that needs to be addressed because otherwise this could have strong implications for the population and environment," said Carlos Gamarra, vice president for energy, air and IT for HARC, whose team produced the air quality impact scenarios. Between 2002 and 2024, Texas sharply cut its major air pollutants -- particularly from transportation, industry and the power generation sectors -- even as the state's population grew by millions and its economy roughly doubled, according to the report, which used federal and state agencies' data on air emissions. At least 288 data center projects are planned across the state, according to a recent Texas Tribune analysis. The scale of the projected data center build-out means that the sector's future emissions trajectory now depends heavily on how electricity is supplied. According to the report's modeling, emissions could plausibly range from a marginal increase to a reversal of two decades of progress in reducing air emissions. By 2031, the report projects that statewide nitrogen oxide emissions could rise 35% -- even under a cleaner "net zero" scenario where data centers connect to the grid and deploy wind and solar on site. Under a different scenario where data centers choose traditional on-site natural-gas power sources, those emissions could increase nearly 400%. Such emissions can damage the human respiratory system with long-term exposure, causing chronic lung disease. "We need to treat data centers as the industrial facilities they are ... to hold them accountable to the same industrial and power generation emissions standards that produced Texas progress," Gamarra said. The report's researchers argue that it's not too late to stop this outcome. Instead of relying on the cheapest, fastest power options, Gamarra said, Texas lawmakers and industry leaders have the opportunity to shape the state's air quality by choosing cleaner choices like renewable and wind and implementing regulation that could help reduce the impact. HOW DO DATA CENTERS IMPACT AIR QUALITY? Data centers need electricity to keep their servers running. Those servers also need cooling systems to avoid overheating, and some of the most water-efficient technologies use the most electricity to operate. As AI computing chips get more powerful and run at hotter temperatures, the need for cooling increases -- and that means more energy. Data centers can get that electricity in a number of ways. Historically, the most common method has been connecting to the Texas power grid. But there's a wait to get connected. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the grid operator, in the last two years received over 500 requests to connect large electricity users, many of which are data centers, compared to two dozen such requests the year before that, according to state records from this summer. Proposed data centers in Texas range from five to 11,000 megawatts in planned capacity, which reflects the maximum power an individual facility could use in any given moment. The estimated electricity that large projects could need from the grid added up to 439 gigawatts -- which would equal roughly a third of all the power generation in America. Gov. Greg Abbott has temporarily halted new data centers from connecting to the state's power grid pending an audit examining each facility's power demand, water and cooling use, public financial assistance and community impacts. Data center developers and operators that can't wait for a grid connection look for alternatives. "The challenge right now is for these data centers when they try to connect to the grid, they have long timelines, like three to five years, and they cannot wait," Gamarra said. "So they start deploying their own on-site energy systems, and they don't always pick the cleanest version of on-site generation because of timelines." He also notes that cleaner, more renewable technologies cannot always provide continuous energy to the data centers. Operators that choose cleaner technologies pay a higher price. GOING BACK ON TEXAS AIR QUALITY PROGRESS Researchers modeled how four power supply scenarios could affect air pollutant levels over the next five years, based on projections of data center energy demand. The report studied a number of scenarios, comparing pollution from data centers connected to the grid versus combinations of on-site generation, including natural gas, solar and wind. artigo.texto: O senador e candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) prometeu ampliar o saneamento básico no Pará, melhorar as condições de tráfego na Transamazônica e atrair investimentos em data centers para o Amazonas. As propostas foram apresentadas nesta sexta-feira (23), durante o debate presidencial da TV Globo, em confronto com o presidente Lula (PT). ✅ Siga o canal do Claudio Dantas no WhatsApp Ao falar sobre a falta de água tratada e de coleta e tratamento de esgoto, Flávio afirmou que pretende trabalhar em parceria com o governador eleito do Pará, Daniel, para ampliar a infraestrutura de Belém. “Eu me comprometo a ajudar Belém a fazer o maior programa de saneamento básico da cidade”, declarou. O senador relatou ter visto esgoto a céu aberto na capital paraense e criticou as condições enfrentadas por moradores que convivem com mau cheiro e falta de infraestrutura. Ele também prometeu atuar para melhorar o acesso a serviços básicos na Região Norte. Candidato critica situação da Transamazônica Flávio afirmou que pretende garantir o asfaltamento de trechos da Transamazônica e responsabilizou entraves ambientais do governo federal pelas dificuldades para executar as obras. Segundo o candidato, a falta de pavimentação prejudica o deslocamento de moradores e o transporte de cargas, sobretudo durante o período de chuvas, quando caminhões ficam atolados e comunidades podem enfrentar dificuldades de conexão com outras regiões. “Eu vou garantir o que você mais pediu, o direito de trabalhar”, afirmou, ao direcionar o discurso aos eleitores do Pará. A proposta integra o discurso do candidato em defesa da ampliação da infraestrutura e da redução de obstáculos ambientais e burocráticos a projetos de desenvolvimento. Zona Franca e data centers Para o Amazonas, Flávio prometeu manter a Zona Franca de Manaus e ampliar sua capacidade de atrair investimentos. O senador citou a instalação de data centers como uma oportunidade econômica e defendeu aproveitar recursos de gás natural para produzir fertilizantes no Brasil. A proposta busca associar a estrutura industrial da região a novos investimentos em tecnologia e energia. Flávio também afirmou que pretende reduzir a dependência brasileira de fertilizantes importados, utilizando matéria-prima disponível no país. O candidato ainda declarou que pretende garantir autonomia aos povos indígenas para decidir sobre atividades em suas terras, tema que provocou reação de Lula durante o debate. Saneamento tem meta legal para 2033 Ao criticar a situação do saneamento, Flávio afirmou que, por causa do atual governo, a meta de universalização teria sido empurrada para depois de 2050. A declaração, porém, exige uma distinção: o Marco Legal do Saneamento, instituído pela Lei nº 14.026/2020, estabelece como metas o atendimento de 99% da população com água potável e de 90% com coleta e tratamento de esgoto até o fim de 2033. . A existência de metas legais não significa que elas serão necessariamente cumpridas. Em julho de 2026, apesar do aumento dos investimentos desde a aprovação do marco legal, o ritmo de aplicação dos recursos ainda estava abaixo do necessário para universalizar os serviços até 2033. . Lula rebate propostas e defende preservação ambiental Na resposta, Lula acusou o grupo político de Flávio de defender medidas que, segundo ele, enfraqueceriam a proteção ambiental. O presidente citou a gestão do ex-ministro do Meio Ambiente Ricardo Salles e afirmou que a Amazônia pode gerar mais recursos com a floresta preservada do que com sua derrubada. Lula também defendeu a economia verde e o Fundo Amazônia, cuja retomada atribuiu ao atual governo. “Ele não conhece a Amazônia”, afirmou o presidente, ao contestar as propostas do adversário.

artigo.texto: What are data centers, and why are Arizona neighbors pushing back? PHOENIX (AZFamily) — The number of data centers in Arizona continues to grow, with more than 100 online and another 50-plus planned. As the facilities become more visible, opposition to them is also increasing. Neighbors turn out against projects From Glendale to Flagstaff, neighbors have turned out in force against proposed data centers. “People over profits,” one opponent said. In Flagstaff, one speaker said, “This type of land use is not comparable with our city.” In Ahwatukee, homeowners have come together, holding biweekly meetings as they continue to fight a planned data center near 48th Street and Chandler Boulevard. “We’re concerned that this is in the wrong place,” one homeowner said. “All of this is going to be affected on a daily basis.” What is a data center? Dr. Kevin Hamlen, a professor of computer science at the University of Texas at Dallas, described a data center as “a large warehouse or building or series of buildings that store computing infrastructure, servers, data storage areas.” Hamlen said the growing number of centers is mainly about efficiency. “As computing infrastructure grows there’s more of a cost, benefit reward for centralizing all of that storage and all of that computation,” he said. He noted the Zoom call we were on likely required a data center, since its servers record and process the call. Storage is only part of the function Hamlen said people often misunderstand data centers as simple storage warehouses. “So data storage is part of what they do. Most of them don’t simply store data,” he said. He said companies are assuming centralizing computing is more efficient, but there has not been enough research to confirm that. “We’re doing a lot of guessing right now, and I think that part of it is a bad idea,” Hamlen said. “We should have standards and rigorous studies.” Hamlen said the public is asking important questions and that more research needs to be done to help answer them. artigo.texto: Paris Marx’s new book couldn’t have landed at a better time. The longtime critic of Big Tech and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast has been thinking about data centers for years, and Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech's Data Empires comes out right as opposition hits a fever pitch. “I certainly didn't predict that it was all going to kind of come to a head as my book was coming out,” he says with a laugh. While data centers are playing a role in shaping US elections—they’re one of the issues that could decide key midterm races in less than two weeks—there’s a history of struggle around the world. Marx’s book takes the reader on a tour of the tech industry’s quest for power and its opposition, from antiwar protests targeting American computers during the Vietnam War, to more recent resistance in Ireland and Chile, and an alternative vision for the future of data centers in New Zealand. I caught up with him this week to talk about what he’s seen, and what could happen if the AI bubble pops. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. MOLLY TAFT: When did you decide to write a book about data centers? PARIS MARX: In the Netherlands and Singapore, they had moratoriums going back to 2019. But in 2022, there was a growing recognition of the demands of data centers in Ireland, on the energy grid in particular. There were huge quantities of electricity that data centers were starting to consume over there. The other story that really got on my radar was what happened with Google in The Dalles, Oregon. Google was really trying to hide its water use figures, to the degree that it got the city council to try to keep its water use figures secret. They kept that going for the better part of a year before the community finally got the actual numbers and found out that Google was using 29 percent of the water in the community. ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022. It became apparent that there's going to need to be a lot more data centers for generative AI. These places were already feeling the effects of significant data center construction, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities very soon. I feel like a lot of Americans think data centers just came out of the blue in the US over the past year or two, just in time to be this huge midterms issue. One thing I like about your book is that it shows us how other countries and communities served as early warning signs. Ireland was a real example of what can happen. Dublin had a moratorium passed back in 2021. It was actually the grid operator that said, “Hey, there are too many data centers. We do not have the grid capacity to connect any more of them.” In response to that, you had the industry moving to make sure it can still build data centers in Ireland. They can't get grid connections in Dublin, so they start looking at building in other parts of Ireland. They also looked at starting to tap into the gas network so they can use generators. Eventually, they start building dedicated gas power plants to power their data centers instead of connecting to the grid. The Irish energy grid is a public grid—only the public utility can build electricity lines. And data center companies actually lobbied for legislation that essentially allows private companies to build electricity cables. That obviously concerns a lot of people and presents questions about equity in the system. The gas stuff looks so prescient with what’s happening in the US now, where companies are racing to build these massive private gas power plants for data centers. [Data center operators] were getting these emission licenses from the Irish Environmental Protection Agency to be able to burn all these fossil fuels. The agency was warning that climate targets are going to be a lot harder to achieve now. When I started to see that happen in the US, I wasn’t surprised. I’d already seen the story play out before. But the scale of it is staggering, and how quickly it’s escalated. What happens to the physical infrastructure—from the gas plants to the data centers themselves—that's getting built out if this industry falls apart? Is there historic precedent for that? I think we're in an AI bubble. But what does the collapse of that bubble look like? They're planning to add all these data centers and all of these gas power plants in order to power the data centers. But there are issues with getting turbines, with getting chips, with getting different kinds of pieces of the puzzle for the data center itself. Are these even going to get built out before there’s a reassessment of the demand for AI? We often talk about the excess build-out of fiber capacity back in the dotcom boom and bust. But there was also a build-out of data centers—obviously a much earlier stage than what we're at now. A lot of data center companies went under. Companies like Equinix, which did survive, bought up a ton of data centers to be ready for when that capacity returned. But the issue we have now is that if data centers are being planned for AI use, and we’re operating under the assumption that the chips are going to have to be cycled out within a few years. Even if the data center is there, what makes it most valuable is potentially not going to be useful by the time that demand returns. Inevitably, even if the data centers don't come, then those gas plants will exist. They will be looking for new customers to justify their existence. I'm sure that people are not building them with the intention to just shut them down. You ended the book with a specific example in New Zealand of a community-led effort to create a more accurate speech-recognition model of the Māori language, using local cloud providers to host the data. I really liked this alternative vision of a non-extractive way to harness the powers of AI. Have you thought about what we could do to make some changes and how this build-out is going? artigo.texto: Technology competition among manufacturers is intensifying as makers of power banks, electric bicycles and electric scooters work to lower fire risks in products that consumers use every day. Manufacturers of battery-powered goods are rolling out products designed either to suppress heat buildup or to limit the damage from thermal runaway, industry officials said on the 25th, following a string of incidents in which power banks overheated or emitted smoke on aircraft and subways. Anker, a power bank maker, recently launched the MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro, which carries a smart cooling fan to address overheating. The device automatically detects charging and heat conditions and adjusts the fan's rotation speed to cut the heat generated during wireless charging. "Consumers have become sensitive to overheating recently, so we applied a cooling fan to improve it," an Anker official said. "It can reduce heat generation compared with conventional wireless charging, which tends to run hot." Personal mobility companies are also developing technology to strengthen battery safety. Alton applied lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP) batteries, which offer improved thermal stability, to its electric bicycles early this year. The company said LMFP batteries lower the risk of thermal runaway while improving range and charging life compared with conventional lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. Electric bicycles using the battery have accounted for 19% of Alton's total bicycle sales since their release, and the company's overall second-quarter revenue rose 29.1% from a year earlier. Electric scooter maker Gcoo unveiled the Upgrade Gcoo, a new model designed to vent internal gas to the outside when thermal runaway occurs, reducing the risk of explosion. Rather than suppressing battery overheating, the product focuses on minimizing damage once thermal runaway begins. Gcoo also operates a battery subscription service for electric bicycles that uses external battery swap stations instead of indoor charging. Users of the safety-focused service rose 391% in the first half of this year from a year earlier. As battery use spreads across daily life, safety technology to prevent fires is growing more important. Battery-related fires in South Korea, including those involving general batteries and capacitors, rose to 706 in 2025 from 543 in 2024 and 359 in 2023, roughly doubling in two years, according to the National Fire Agency. "Companies are developing technology to reduce the risk of thermal runaway, but lithium-ion batteries structurally carry risks of heat buildup and thermal runaway," said Chae Jin, a professor of fire and disaster prevention at Mokwon University. "Along with technology development, safety measures must be put in place so that thermal runaway can be dealt with quickly if it occurs in actual use."

artigo.texto: RES secures its first battery energy storage consent in Northern Ireland Mid and East Antrim Borough Council's Planning Committee approves RES's Ballyross project near Larne. According to the company, the site lies close to an existing substation and has limited visibility from local properties. British renewable energy developer RES announces that it has secured its first consent for a battery energy storage system (BESS) in Northern Ireland. Mid and East Antrim Borough Council's Planning Committee approved the Ballyross project. According to the company, the site is located on land approximately 2 kilometres south-west of Gleno and 8.5 kilometres south-west of Larne. Elsewhere in Europe, battery storage is also changing hands, with Greenvolt selling two projects in Poland to A&R Investments. A site close to the Ballyvallagh substation RES says Ballyross is located near the existing Ballyvallagh substation. According to the company, this proximity would support the efficient operation of the system while minimising the need for additional grid infrastructure. In the United Kingdom, storage questions also affect other sectors, as Cadent says UK CO2 storage rules effectively exclude biomethane producers. The company stresses that constraints on Northern Ireland's electricity system are increasing. In its view, clean, low-cost electricity can therefore be prevented from reaching consumers. Storage projects such as Ballyross would make better use of this electricity by storing it when generation is high and releasing it when demand rises. Landscaping and statements from RES The approved scheme includes a landscaping package that RES describes as substantial. New native-species planting is intended to help the development blend into the surrounding landscape. It is also meant to create wildlife corridors and pollinator-friendly habitat. Peter Deeney, Senior Development Project Manager at RES, says the company has contributed to Northern Ireland's energy future and economic growth since the early 1990s from its office in Larne. He describes securing consent for Ballyross, RES's first battery energy storage project to be consented in Northern Ireland, as an important milestone. According to him, battery storage is becoming increasingly important as Northern Ireland continues its transition to a low-carbon energy system. Mr Deeney adds that the site was selected in part because it has limited visibility from local properties. He says the new planting will further reduce that visibility. He thanks the local residents and stakeholders who engaged during consultation, whose feedback, he says, helped inform the landscaping plan and shape the project's final design. artigo.texto: Jason Padgett is convinced mathematics can reduce the need for data centers. Data centers are facilities that house computer systems, servers and related IT infrastructure to store, process and distribute large amounts of data. Padgett, a Carmel resident, was diagnosed with acquired savant syndrome after suffering a traumatic brain injury during a mugging in Tacoma, Wash. The aftermath allowed him to develop exceptional math and geometric visualization, which he applied to come up with his data center theory. It all comes down to black holes. “Black holes actually store data, and then they project what’s called probability waves, which are like waves in the ocean,” Padgett said. “When a bunch of waves overlap, they make a new wave inside a black hole.” Those waves create patterns, which he said can be linked through a process that looks like connecting the dots. Padgett said brains – and AI – process data in a similar way. “In the model I have been developing, many possible quantum paths interfere, some cancel out, and the strongest coherent path becomes the route to the readable result,” he said. “I began asking whether a computer could copy that basic idea: eliminate what does not fit early and follow the most efficient path to the answer.” He said finding ways for AI to process information in fewer steps could make a big difference. “Fewer unnecessary calculations can mean less work for computer chips,” he said. “At large scale, less work could mean less electricity, less heat to remove and less water needed for cooling. We believe we have an early proof of concept showing that some internal AI work can be reused and some repeated computation can be skipped. But this is still early, and the next step is much bigger than one person.” Padgett said a team is needed. “That means software engineers, AI and machine-learning specialists, mathematicians, physicists, hardware and data-center experts, researchers, business leaders, investors and people who know how to turn an early technical idea into something that can be tested at real scale,” he said. Padgett primarily works independently, but he has spoken at Science of Consciousness conference organized by Dr. Stuart Hameroff, an anesthesiologist and quantum consciousness theorist and researcher at the University of Arizona.

artigo.texto: Mário Nazzari Westrup* e Mariana Palandi** A interação entre o novo sistema de tributação sobre o consumo e o mercado regulado de carbono revela uma discussão que vai além da incidência tributária Enquanto empresas se preparam para a implementação da reforma tributária, outra transformação estrutural avança quase em silêncio: o desenvolvimento do mercado regulado de carbono brasileiro. À primeira vista, parecem ser agendas independentes, mas não são. Em poucos anos, ambas passarão a influenciar as mesmas decisões de investimento, precificação, competitividade e alocação de capital das empresas brasileiras. É nesse ponto de encontro que surge uma discussão ainda pouco explorada. Quando se fala em mercado de carbono, o debate costuma começar pela incidência da CBS (Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços) e do IBS (Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços) sobre a negociação de créditos de carbono. Porém, antes de discutir a tributação de um ativo ambiental específico, vale perguntar como um sistema concebido para tributar de forma neutra deve se relacionar com instrumentos regulatórios criados pelo próprio Estado para alterar incentivos econômicos. A neutralidade é um dos pilares econômicos da reforma tributária. A lógica de um IVA (Imposto sobre Valor Agregado) consiste em reduzir interferências sobre as decisões dos agentes econômicos, permitindo que empresas invistam, produzam e concorram sem distorções provocadas pela tributação. Quanto mais neutro o sistema, maior tende a ser sua eficiência econômica. Essa foi uma das promessas da reforma brasileira. Entretanto, a própria reforma reconhece que esse princípio é limitado – o IS (Imposto Seletivo) é prova disso. Em determinadas situações, o Estado opta por utilizar a tributação não para arrecadar mais, mas para modificar comportamentos, elevando o custo de atividades associadas a externalidades negativas. Quando o mercado não produz sozinho o resultado social desejado, a neutralidade deixa de ser um objetivo absoluto. O próprio texto constitucional e a legislação complementar instituíram regimes diferenciados e tratamentos específicos, evidenciando que a busca por neutralidade convive, legitimamente, com outros objetivos de política pública. O mercado regulado de carbono nasce da mesma lógica econômica, embora utilize um instrumento diferente. Em vez de aumentar o custo de determinadas atividades, cria incentivos para que a redução das emissões adquira valor econômico. Trata-se de uma solução baseada em preços e negociação, capaz de permitir que o próprio mercado reaja às alternativas para descarbonizar a economia. Nesse sentido, tanto o Imposto Seletivo quanto o mercado de carbono procuram enfrentar a mesma falha de mercado: a ausência de um preço adequado para os impactos ambientais das emissões. Sob perspectivas distintas, ambos alteram os preços relativos da economia: enquanto a reforma tributária procura eliminar distorções tributárias, o mercado regulado atribui um preço às emissões de carbono. Em ambos os casos, o objetivo final é melhorar a alocação de recursos e orientar decisões econômicas mais eficientes. No entanto, o que acontece quando um mesmo investimento recebe um incentivo para reduzir emissões, mas simultaneamente sofre um aumento de custo decorrente da tributação? Se ambos os instrumentos pretendem orientar as decisões privadas, é desejável que transmitam sinais econômicos coerentes. Caso contrário, parte do incentivo criado por uma política pública poderá ser neutralizada pela outra. A experiência internacional mostra que não existe uma solução única para essa interação, mesmo entre países que adotam diferentes versões do imposto sobre valor agregado. Em Singapura, desde 2022, a emissão, transferência ou venda de créditos de carbono não é considerada fornecimento de bens ou serviços para fins do GST (Goods and Services Tax), ficando fora de sua incidência. No Reino Unido, desde setembro de 2024 determinadas negociações de créditos voluntários passaram a estar sujeitas ao VAT (Value Added Tax), após o amadurecimento do mercado secundário. Já o Canadá adotou uma terceira solução: preservou a incidência do GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax/Harmonized Sales Tax) sobre negociações de permissões de emissão no mercado secundário, mas atribuiu ao adquirente a responsabilidade pelo recolhimento. Os diferentes modelos revelam que a questão não se resume à escolha entre tributar ou não tributar – o desafio está em definir como a tributação se integra ao desenho e aos objetivos do mercado ambiental. A diversidade dessas experiências não conduz automaticamente à conclusão de que créditos de carbono devam ser excluídos da incidência da CBS e do IBS. A reflexão é outra. Se a própria reforma tributária admite relativizar a neutralidade quando o objetivo é corrigir externalidades, parece legítimo discutir como essa lógica deve dialogar com um mercado regulado criado exatamente para alcançar a mesma finalidade por meio de um mecanismo distinto. Mais do que definir a incidência tributária sobre esses ativos, será importante evitar que instrumentos concebidos para induzir a descarbonização acabem emitindo sinais econômicos contraditórios aos agentes privados, reduzindo a efetividade das políticas públicas. Para as empresas, o desenho dessa interação poderá influenciar decisões de investimento, estratégias de descarbonização, precificação de ativos ambientais, estruturação de projetos e até a atratividade econômica de determinadas tecnologias. À medida que critérios ESG, financiamento climático e mercados ambientais se consolidam, a maneira como esses instrumentos públicos se articulam tende a produzir efeitos que ultrapassam o campo tributário. Nesse contexto, previsibilidade e segurança jurídica tornam-se elementos centrais não apenas para reduzir litígios, mas para permitir que empresas precifiquem adequadamente riscos, avaliem investimentos de longo prazo e ampliem o financiamento de projetos de transição climática. O Brasil vive um momento raro. Em

artigo.texto: Créditos de carbono florestal e a lacuna da voz das mulheres na governança. O processo de alteração e complementação de diversos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental está atraindo considerável atenção pública, especialmente as normas destinadas a aperfeiçoar o arcabouço institucional do mercado de carbono. No contexto geral da transição verde, a comercialização dos serviços de absorção e armazenamento de carbono prestados pelas florestas é vista como uma etapa estratégica, criando um recurso financeiro sustentável para a proteção florestal e, ao mesmo tempo, abrindo oportunidades para melhorar a qualidade de vida das populações locais. No entanto, por trás dos números relativos à área ou às despesas, surge uma questão profunda de governança: o estatuto e a voz das mulheres no processo de alocação e decisão sobre como utilizar esses fundos. Créditos de carbono florestal: da pegada do trabalho à realidade dos benefícios. Essencialmente, os créditos de carbono florestal são certificados que representam uma tonelada de CO2 (ou equivalente em CO2) absorvida e armazenada por meio de atividades de proteção, reflorestamento ou restauração florestal. Quando países ou empresas precisam compensar emissões, compram esses créditos. Os recursos do mercado de carbono, portanto, se tornam um fluxo de financiamento verde para regiões florestais. A relação entre créditos de carbono florestal e mulheres não se resume à distribuição de benefícios sociais, mas decorre de suas contribuições diretas para a criação de "bens" de carbono. Os créditos são calculados com base na quantidade de CO2 reduzida ou absorvida devido à melhor proteção florestal, vegetação mais densa e expansão da área florestal. Nessa série de atividades, as mulheres em áreas rurais e montanhosas são a força de trabalho silenciosa, porém direta, que mantém essa "fonte de absorção". Desde o plantio de sementes e o cuidado com as árvores recém-plantadas até a colheita controlada de produtos florestais não madeireiros para evitar a degradação do ecossistema, as mulheres participam de quase todas as etapas da conservação da biodiversidade. Um exemplo vívido disso é a história da Sra. Le Thi Thinh, uma mulher Pa Co da aldeia de A Nieng, comuna de Le Trieng 1, distrito de A Luoi 1, cidade de Hue . Ao se tornar membro do Conselho de Gestão Florestal Comunitária, superando estereótipos de gênero como "mulheres não podem ficar na floresta o dia todo" ou barreiras relacionadas ao cuidado infantil, a Sra. Thinh lidera com confiança patrulhas que gerenciam quase 1.500 hectares de floresta natural, utilizando habilmente a tecnologia SMART Mobile para coletar dados para a proteção florestal. Ao proteger diretamente as florestas e prevenir a exploração madeireira ilegal, os esforços e o conhecimento indígena de mulheres como a Sra. Thinh contribuem para o valor agregado gerado por cada crédito de carbono florestal. Enfatizando esse papel fundamental, a especialista independente em gênero, Nguyen Thi Lan, afirmou: "As mulheres podem ser grupos impactados negativamente pelas mudanças ambientais e pelos processos de transição, e ao mesmo tempo possuir o conhecimento, a capacidade e a habilidade para impulsionar a mudança." Você também pode gostar A implementação piloto do Pagamento por Créditos de Carbono Florestal (ERPA, na sigla em inglês) em seis províncias do centro-norte do Vietnã demonstrou que os créditos de carbono realmente chegaram à população, proporcionando uma fonte prática de financiamento complementar para a proteção florestal e a melhoria dos meios de subsistência. No entanto, o processo de pagamento em nível familiar também revelou uma lacuna de governança relacionada ao gênero. Devido às práticas legais e normas sociais vigentes, a pessoa designada como chefe de família que recebe os pagamentos geralmente é um homem. Quando a receita é transferida diretamente para uma conta ou entregue ao chefe de família do sexo masculino, permanece questionável se as mulheres – as trabalhadoras diretamente envolvidas na floresta – têm o direito de discutir, propor ou participar das decisões sobre como esse dinheiro será gasto. Quando as contribuições das mulheres geram diretamente receita de carbono, elas têm todo o direito e precisam ser reconhecidas como partes interessadas em igualdade de condições, com voz decisiva na governança e na alocação desse benefício econômico . O mecanismo de pagamento chega às famílias, mas ainda há pouca cobertura da mídia. A promulgação do Decreto 180/2026/ND-CP, em meados de julho de 2026, estabeleceu uma base legal unificada para os serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono florestal no Vietnã. Este documento regulamenta de forma abrangente tudo, desde o planejamento do projeto e a determinação dos resultados de redução de emissões até os métodos de pagamento. Os fundos arrecadados podem ser transferidos diretamente ou confiados ao Fundo de Proteção e Desenvolvimento Florestal, ampliando os beneficiários para incluir famílias, indivíduos e comunidades. Para os proprietários florestais que sejam famílias ou comunidades, o valor total recebido será reinvestido na gestão florestal e na melhoria de seus meios de subsistência. A política aproximou o financiamento verde das comunidades locais. No entanto, quando os fundos chegam às aldeias ou famílias individuais, surge uma realidade: a "família" ou a "comunidade" é considerada uma unidade coletiva. O fato de uma comunidade receber benefícios ou uma família receber pagamentos não reflete a estrutura de governança interna: quem participa diretamente das discussões e as mulheres têm o direito de decidir como essa renda será gasta? A especialista Nguyen Thi Lan enfatizou: "Uma abordagem neutra em termos de gênero, que trata todos igualmente, às vezes cria inadvertidamente desigualdades de gênero indiretas. A questão a ser considerada não é apenas se as mulheres participam, mas qual o papel que desempenham, se têm poder de decisão e se se beneficiam de forma justa." Embora

artigo.texto: Long-Duration Energy Storage Market to Reach USD 25.59 Billion by 2035, Growing from USD 5.80 Billion in 2025 - SRI London, UK - October 2026 | Strategic Revenue Insights Inc. - Rising renewable shares, long-duration procurement rules, coal and gas plant retirements and grid expansion in Asia are driving strong growth in long-duration energy storage. https://www.strategicrevenueinsights.com/industry/long-duration-energy-storage-market The Long-Duration Energy Storage market was valued at USD 5.80 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 25.59 billion by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 16.0%, according to Strategic Revenue Insights Inc. The report was prepared by lead analyst Thomas Müller. The research methodology combines primary interviews with relevant industry stakeholders, including utilities, independent power producers, storage technology developers and grid operators, with secondary data across the regions covered by the report. KEY TAKEAWAYS Market value is projected to rise from USD 5.80 billion in 2025 to USD 25.59 billion by 2035, at a CAGR of 16.0%. Pumped Hydro is the largest technology with a 41.00% share, while Hydrogen Storage is the fastest-growing technology at a 21.1% CAGR. The 6 to 8 hour class is the largest duration at 43.00% while systems above 24 hours grow fastest at 20.2%, Renewable Integration is the largest and fastest-growing application at 37.00% and 17.7%, and Utilities account for 58.00% of end use. Asia Pacific is the largest regional market with a 36.03% share, valued at USD 2.09 billion in 2025, while the Middle East and Africa is the fastest-growing region at a 17.5% CAGR. Named market participants include Voith Hydro, Siemens Energy, and Rongke Power. Full report access: https://www.strategicrevenueinsights.com/industry/long-duration-energy-storage-market GROWTH DRIVERS AND TRENDS Renewable share growth is the largest growth driver, adding an estimated 3.0 percentage points to the CAGR, followed by long-duration procurement rules in North America at 2.2 points, coal and gas plant retirement in Europe at 1.8 points, and grid expansion in Asia at 1.5 points. The source projects the market at USD 12.18 billion in 2030. Key trends identified in the report include duration becoming a product feature that buyers pay for, tenders that specify duration and let technologies compete, and new chemistries moving from pilot to utility projects in the middle years. Opportunities include capacity contracts for 8 to 24 hour storage, pumped hydro upgrades and new builds, flow and iron-air battery scale-up, and industrial heat and hydrogen storage. MARKET SEGMENTATION By technology, the market is segmented into Pumped Hydro (41.00%), Flow Batteries (19.00%), Compressed Air (13.00%), Thermal Storage (12.00%), Hydrogen Storage (11.00%), and Gravity Storage (4.00%). Pumped Hydro is the largest segment with an 11.6% CAGR, and Hydrogen Storage is the fastest-growing at 21.1%, followed by Flow Batteries at 19.4%. By duration, the market covers 6 to 8 hours (43.00%), 8 to 12 hours (30.00%), 12 to 24 hours (19.00%), and above 24 hours (8.00%). The 6 to 8 hour class is the largest segment with a 13.9% CAGR, and above 24 hours is the fastest-growing at 20.2%. By application, the market includes Renewable Integration (37.00%), Grid Stabilization (34.00%), Peak Shaving (20.00%), and Backup Power (9.00%). Renewable Integration is the largest and fastest-growing segment at a 17.7% CAGR. By end user, the market is divided into Utilities (58.00%), Independent Power Producers (26.00%), and Commercial and Industrial (16.00%). Utilities is the largest segment with a 14.7% CAGR, and Commercial and Industrial is the fastest-growing at 17.7%. REGIONAL OUTLOOK The report covers North America, Europe, Asia Pacific, Latin America, and the Middle East and Africa. Asia Pacific is the largest regional market with a 36.03% share, valued at USD 2.09 billion in 2025 and projected to reach USD 10.43 billion by 2035 at a 17.4% CAGR. The Middle East and Africa is the fastest-growing region at a 17.5% CAGR, rising from USD 348.00 million to USD 1.74 billion. North America holds 32.93% (USD 1.91 billion) with a 15.0% CAGR, Europe 22.07% (USD 1.28 billion) with 14.4%, and Latin America 3.00% (USD 174.00 million) with 16.4%. COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE The report profiles Voith Hydro (Germany, 9.0% share), which supplies pump-turbines and generators for pumped hydro plants; Siemens Energy (Germany, 7.5%), which supplies compressors, turbines, grid equipment and hydrogen electrolyzers; Rongke Power (China, 6.0%), which builds large vanadium flow battery systems for grid projects in China; Fluence Energy (US, 5.5%), which integrates storage systems and software for utilities and developers; Sumitomo Electric (Japan, 4.5%), which makes vanadium redox flow batteries for grid applications; and Hydrostor (Canada, 4.0%), which develops adiabatic compressed air plants in engineered caverns. Form Energy, Invinity Energy Systems, Energy Vault and ESS Tech are also covered. MARKET RESTRAINTS High capital cost reduces the CAGR by an estimated 1.9 percentage points, and revenue uncertainty subtracts a further 1.3 points. The report also cites falling lithium-ion costs for 6 to 8 hour systems, long permitting for pumped hydro, bankability of new technologies, and supply risk for vanadium and other materials. artigo.texto: Forest carbon credits and the women's voice gap in governance. The process of amending and supplementing several articles of the Law on Environmental Protection is attracting significant public attention, especially the regulations aimed at perfecting the institutional framework for the carbon market. In the overall picture of green transition, the commercialization of carbon absorption and storage services provided by forests is seen as a strategic step, creating a sustainable financial resource for forest protection while also opening up opportunities to improve the livelihoods of local people. However, behind the figures regarding area or expenditure, a profound governance issue arises: the status and voice of women in the process of allocating and deciding how to use these funds. Forest carbon credits: From the imprint of labor to the reality of benefit. Essentially, forest carbon credits are certificates representing one ton of CO2 (or CO2 equivalent) absorbed and stored through forest protection, reforestation, or restoration activities. When countries or businesses need to offset emissions, they buy these credits. The funds from the carbon market thus become a green financing flow into forestry regions. The link between forest carbon credits and women is not simply a matter of welfare allocation, but stems from their direct contributions to the creation of carbon "goods." Credits are measured based on the amount of CO2 reduced or absorbed due to better forest protection, denser vegetation, and expanded forest area. In this series of activities, women in rural and mountainous areas are the silent but direct workforce maintaining this "absorption source." From sowing seeds and caring for newly planted forest trees to harvesting non-timber forest products in a controlled manner to avoid ecosystem degradation, women participate in almost all stages of biodiversity conservation. A vivid example of this is the story of Ms. Le Thi Thinh, a Pa Co woman in A Nieng village, Le Trieng 1 commune, A Luoi 1 district, Hue city. Becoming a member of the Community Forest Management Board, overcoming gender stereotypes such as "women cannot stay in the forest all day" or barriers related to childcare, Ms. Thinh confidently leads patrols managing nearly 1,500 hectares of natural forest, skillfully using SMART Mobile technology to record data for forest protection. By directly protecting forests and preventing illegal logging, the efforts and indigenous knowledge of women like Ms. Thinh contribute to the added value generated by each forest carbon credit. Emphasizing this key role, independent gender expert Nguyen Thi Lan stated: "Women can both be groups negatively impacted by environmental change and transition processes, and possess the knowledge, capacity, and ability to drive change." You may also like The pilot implementation of Payment for Forest Carbon Settlements (ERPA) in six provinces of North Central Vietnam has shown that the carbon credits have truly reached the people, providing a practical source of supplementary funding for forest protection and improving livelihoods. However, the payment process at the household level has also revealed a gender-related governance gap. Due to prevailing legal practices and social norms, the person named as the head of the household receiving the payments is usually a man. When the revenue is transferred directly into an account or given to the male head of the household, it remains questionable whether women – the laborers directly involved in the forest – have the right to discuss, propose, or participate in decisions regarding how that money is spent. When women's contributions directly generate carbon revenue, they have every right and need to be recognized as equal stakeholders with a decisive voice in the governance and allocation of this economic benefit. The payment mechanism reaches households, but there is still a lack of media coverage. The promulgation of Decree 180/2026/ND-CP in mid-July 2026 has laid a unified legal foundation for forest carbon sequestration and storage services in Vietnam. This document comprehensively regulates everything from project planning and determining emission reduction results to payment methods. The funds collected can be transferred directly or entrusted to the Forest Protection and Development Fund, expanding the beneficiaries to include households, individuals, and communities. For forest owners who are households or communities, the entire amount received will be reinvested in forest management and improving their livelihoods. The policy has brought green finance closer to the grassroots level. However, when the funds reach villages or individual households, a reality arises: the "household" or "community" is considered a collective unit. Whether a community receives benefits or a family receives payments doesn't reflect the internal governance structure: Who directly participates in discussions, and do women have the right to decide how that income is spent? Expert Nguyen Thi Lan emphasized: "A gender-neutral approach, treating everyone equally, sometimes inadvertently creates indirect gender inequalities. The issue to consider is not just whether women participate, but what role they play, whether they have decision-making power, and whether they benefit fairly." Although current regulations require community consultation and ensuring a fair benefit-sharing mechanism, the guiding documents do not yet set separate reporting targets by gender. Financial planning forms only record the number of households, area, and total cost, leaving management agencies without sufficient real-world data to accurately assess women's participation. From practical transparency to the need for policy transformation. Practical experience from forest carbon finance programs in Vietnam shows that integrating gender considerations is entirely feasible. artigo.texto: Sumitomo Corp. is studying how battery energy storage systems operate alongside electricity trading in Leicester, England, to prepare for expanding the technology across Japan. The Japanese trading house gained operational insights from a site storing enough power for 160,000 homes for two hours. Sumitomo studies UK battery storage model as Japan eyes wider adoption Japanese trading house Sumitomo Corp. is studying how battery energy storage systems operate alongside electricity markets in Leicester, England. The project offers lessons the company will apply as it pushes for wider deployment of the technology across Japan. A facility outside Leicester houses 30 shipping containers packed with batteries and inverters. Together, the units can store enough energy to power 160,000 homes for two hours. The site demonstrates what large-scale battery storage looks like in practice. Sumitomo gained insight into how the system functions as part of an electricity grid and how that relationship shapes trading activity. The company is learning how stored energy flows back into the market and how pricing signals drive demand for storage operations. Japan has been accelerating its own battery storage ambitions. The country's power sector faces growing pressure to integrate renewable energy sources while maintaining grid reliability. Battery systems offer a way to store surplus generation and release it when demand peaks, smoothing supply without relying on gas-fired backup plants. Sumitomo's move reflects broader momentum in Japan toward commercializing battery storage at scale. Trading companies have been positioning themselves as operators of the technology, leveraging their existing networks and relationships with utilities and industrial customers. The Leicester project gives them a concrete reference point for planning similar deployments domestically. The company did not immediately disclose specific timelines or investment figures for its domestic plans. Industry observers expect Sumitomo to use the Leicester experience to shape proposals for utilities and large industrial consumers who want storage assets on their sites. The East Midlands facility represents one of several battery storage projects being developed by UK firms as the country navigates its own energy transition. Japan's experience operating such systems at commercial scale could prove instructive as the technology moves from demonstration to widespread adoption. Sumitomo's exploration of the Leicester site underscores how international knowledge transfer is becoming a practical tool for energy companies seeking to accelerate deployment in markets where regulatory frameworks and market structures still are being defined. For Japan, the lesson is straightforward: build the capability, study the operations, then scale. Sources: Nikkei Asia reporting, Oct. 26, 2026 Source:asia.nikkei.com

artigo.texto: By Devyn Lyon, FOX23 News TULSA, Okla. — Oklahoma regulators have moved a hearing on OG&E’s proposed rules for large electricity users to January, extending a case that could help determine how the costs of powering data centers are divided and whether other customers could be left paying more. The hearing, previously scheduled for November 3, is now set for January 12, 2027. The central question for households and small businesses is straightforward: as large customers connect to the electric grid, who pays for the power plants, lines and other equipment needed to serve them? OG&E filed the case to seek approval of a proposed “large-load tariff.” A tariff establishes the rates, and service requirements customers must follow. In this case, OG&E wants special payment requirements for very large electricity users, including data centers. Google is participating in the proceeding and advocating for changes to how those customers can obtain power. In emailed responses to FOX23, OG&E said its proposal is intended to protect existing customers from costs associated with bringing large users onto the grid. “Current customers should never pay for the impact of bringing large-load customers onto the electric grid,” the company said. Simply put, OG&E wants large customers to make financial commitments, so the utility’s other customers are not left covering costs if a project uses less electricity than expected cuts back or closes. The company said its proposal would require large customers to: - Pay for infrastructure built to serve them - Sign long-term, binding contracts - Pay substantial minimum bills, even if they use less power than expected - Pay fees if they reduce their commitments of leave early - Provide financial security to back up those obligations OG&E also argues those customers should contribute toward the costs of its existing power plants. There are proposed requirements, regulators must determine what rules to approve. Google wants large customers to have the option to buy electricity from independent generators while continuing to use OG&E’s grid to receive it. Google argues that approach could reduce the need for OG&E to build expensive new power plants. OG&E argues those arrangements could leave large customers paying less toward its existing plants while continuing to depend on the utility’s system. The company also says it must maintain reliable service when a customer’s outside power source is unavailable. Its concern is that costs could fall to other customers if the large user does not adequately pay for that backup. Buying electricity from another supplier would still involve using power lines and other grid infrastructure. The dispute is over which costs those customers would remain responsible for, and whether state law permits the arrangements being proposed. The hearing delay itself does not approve a rate of increase or decide how those costs will be divided. The potential impact comes from the rules regulators ultimately adopt. If large customers do not cover the costs assigned to serving them, other customers could face pressure to cover more. But, if outside power purchases reduce the need for costly new utility construction, that could also affect future costs. Those competing arguments are part of what the commission must evaluate. Neither side’s position establishes what will happen to an individual customer’s bill. OG&E said other parties’ proposals raised legal questions that should be addressed before the commission hears the evidence. The company said it wants those parties to explain what law allows large customers to buy electricity from third-party generators while relying on OG&E’s grid. OG&E said the additional time would allow those arguments to be considered before the hearing. FOX23 also asked whether the requested date was connected to Commissioner Todd Hiett’s term ending January 11, one day before the rescheduled hearing. The company said it was not, saying its request was driven by proposals introduced by parties. The proceeding is Oklahoma Corporation Commission Case No. PUD2026-000046. Customers can search for that number in the commission’s Electronic Case Filing system to review filings, testimony, and orders. The commission’s October 21 scheduling order is available here. The January hearing is the next opportunity to examine the proposals and evidence. Moving that hearing does not resolve the underlying dispute over who should pay.
