artigo.texto: BRAZORIA COUNTY, Texas (KTRK) -- A potential data center in Brazoria County is raising concerns among residents, who told ABC13 they're being left in the dark. Landowners in Damon said they noticed a company buying more than 400 acres along the Brazos River, which is when they started asking questions. On Sunday, residents held a community meeting to discuss what they've found out so far. "We got to fight. We got to stop it before it gets here," one resident said. They told ABC13 that the county district attorney's office held a meeting earlier this month and showed them a map of seven parcels of land that included solar panels and batteries. Residents said that infrastructure pointed toward the potential for a data center. "That means a data center which could have gas turbines, and that means 24 hours, seven days a week, 365 days a year, noise, lights, vibration," Christine Clark, a concerned citizen, said. Experts previously told ABC13 that Texas counties have few tools to stop these developments, particularly in unincorporated areas, where regulations and permitting hurdles are limited. SEE ALSO: Permits related to data centers issued after Abbott's halt directive, advocacy groups found Residents said they're concerned about what a potential project like this could mean for a place they say is rich in both wildlife and history. "It concerns the dignity of our ancestors, the preservation of Black family heritage, and our rights to continue caring for our land that has sustained our family for generations," one community member said. Residents said the company buying the land is CleanSpark. In January, CleanSpark announced an agreement to acquire up to 447 acres of land in Brazoria County that was "positioning the Company to develop a large-scale data center project." In its press release, CleanSpark called itself America's Bitcoin Miner, a market-leading data center developer. ABC13 reached out to the company for more information and is awaiting a response. This comes as data centers continue to expand across Texas. ABC13's data team found that, as of February, 429 data centers were in the state. They found 293 were already operating, and the rest are planned or under construction. Brazoria County residents hope the place they call home won't join that growing list. "We're not giving up," Clark said

artigo.texto: Brasil precisará de energia nuclear para data centers, diz setor Presidente da Associação de Atividades Nucleares defende que fonte é a melhor forma de assegurar fornecimento nos centros de processamento O Brasil não conseguirá absorver toda a demanda energética de data centers que deve chegar ao país nas próximas décadas sem considerar a geração de energia nuclear, afirma Celso Cunha, presidente da Abdan (Associação Brasileira para o Desenvolvimento de Atividades Nucleares). Em entrevista ao Poder360, o executivo disse que a energia nuclear “explodiu” no mundo inteiro, sobretudo por causa das aplicações em data centers, e é reconhecida como a melhor forma de assegurar o fornecimento ininterrupto de energia elétrica nos centros de processamento de dados. Executivos e representantes dos setores de infraestrutura digital e de energia elétrica vêm defendendo nos últimos meses que o Brasil tem capacidade de se tornar o principal destino de data centers na América Latina diante de um cenário de investimentos globais em inteligência artificial, computação em nuvem e capacidade computacional. Estimativas da Moody’s falam em um mercado que pode movimentar até US$ 3 trilhões no país nos próximos 5 anos. Na disputa por investimentos estrangeiros crescentes no segmento, o Brasil larga na frente dos seus vizinhos sul-americanos por causa da matriz predominantemente renovável e do potencial para combinar diferentes fontes de energia. Porém, é consenso no setor elétrico que a elevada demanda por energia desses empreendimentos ainda é um obstáculo a ser superado. Data centers são intensivos em consumo energético e precisam operar 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. Demandam, portanto, energia contínua, confiável e a preços competitivos. “Alguns milissegundos sem energia em um data center custam mais caro do que uma usina nuclear inteira”, diz Cunha. Segundo o dirigente da Abdan, a geração nuclear oferece todas as características necessárias para abastecer os centros de processamento de dados: é firme, ou seja, consegue gerar energia de forma ininterrupta, e mais limpa do que renováveis como eólica e solar, as principais fontes usadas por data centers. Assista à entrevista de Celso Cunha ao Poder360 (27min): “O Brasil tem um potencial enorme para atrair data centers e se fala em até 70 gigawatts até 2050, mas é humanamente impossível atender uma demanda dessa sem considerar a energia nuclear. O mundo todo está usando”, disse durante participação no Poder Entrevista, o programa de entrevistas do Poder360. O Brasil fechou o 1º semestre com cerca de 706 MW (megawatts) de capacidade instalada em data centers. “É tanta energia que se precisa que nós vamos precisar de todas as fontes. Não vai ser só do gás ou só do nuclear. Se nós quisermos atender aos data centers, nós vamos precisar usar toda a nossa criatividade, nossa capacidade”, diz o executivo. Para Cunha, a introdução da energia nuclear nos data centers passa pela utilização dos SMRs (Pequenos Reatores Modulares, na sigla em inglês), uma das tecnologias em ascensão no setor. São equipamentos com potência típica de 50 MW a 300 MW por unidade, bem menores que as usinas nucleares tradicionais. A principal vantagem dessa tecnologia é a fabricação modular. Os reatores são construídos em série dentro de fábricas e montados no local de operação, o que reduz custos e prazos de instalação. “Você pode comprar como se fossem geladeiras. Ele já sai certificado e você compra o 1º, o 2º, o 3º e vai colocando em paralelo no data center. Ele não entra todo de uma vez, você pode botar esses SMRs de forma fracionada, de acordo com a necessidade do cliente do projeto”, diz Cunha. NUCLEAR NO REDATA O setor de energia nuclear, segundo o presidente da Abdan, tem interesse em atender projetos que venham a ser habilitados pelo Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter), lei recém-sancionada pelo governo federal que institui benefícios fiscais para instalação de data centers no Brasil. O texto aprovado pelo Congresso e promulgado pelo governo ainda tem uma série de pontos pendentes de regulamentação, como a definição das fontes de energia que serão exigidas para empreendimentos interessados nos incentivos do programa. O projeto original estabelecia que só data centers abastecidos por energia 100% limpa poderiam receber os incentivos fiscais, mas uma alteração no Senado incluiu também fontes “consideradas de baixa emissão”. Como mostrou o Poder360, a mudança abriu espaço para o uso de gás natural, defendido pela indústria e pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia. Segundo Cunha, a discussão atualmente em curso sobre o gás natural não preocupa. A avaliação do executivo é que o texto considera o uso de energia nuclear, apesar de não citá-la diretamente. Uma portaria ministerial com a definição das fontes permitidas deve ser publicada nas próximas semanas.

artigo.texto: Bulgaria's grid battery capacity has doubled in a year, from 3 to about 6 gigawatts. Electricity exports this year reached 3.5 terawatt hours, 62% more than last year, according to the Association for Production, Storage and Trade of Electricity (APSTE). The figures came out on Friday, 23 October. The batteries store solar power during the day and feed it back into the grid in the evening, when demand is highest. In July and August, heatwaves strained the grids of neighbouring countries, which struggled to meet demand. Bulgarian exports helped them. How it all started: Bulgaria doubles power storage capacity as exports jump 62% On the busiest days, Bulgaria sent out up to 50,000 megawatt hours a day, said Dimitar Zarchev, head of the Central Dispatch Department at the Electricity System Operator (ESO). By his count, that is about 2,000 megawatts an hour on average, roughly what the Kozloduy nuclear plant in north-west Bulgaria produces. Some of the power went to Romania this summer. In August, Romania shut down a nuclear reactor because of drought and low water in the Danube, whose water cools the reactor's turbines. Power from batteries cut the need for hydropower plants, which usually cover the peak, so reservoirs kept their levels. The European Union gave €700m in grants for batteries in Bulgaria ($783.86m at a rate of 0.8930 euros to the dollar). Together with changes to the rules, the money also drew private investment. Battery storage is now critical, not a luxury but a necessity, said Nikola Gazdov, chairman of APSTE. Energy is costly in Europe, there are worries about supplies, and hotter summers are expected because of climate change. High prices this year fuelled anger that led to social unrest. Storing power for peak hours affects consumers' bills and softens the shocks linked to the US and Israeli war against Iran. Bulgaria has little oil and gas of its own and produces far less electricity than many other EU countries. More batteries will need a bigger grid. Fast growth has already narrowed the gap in power prices between the hour of charging and the hour of discharging. That means owners will earn less, and investors have less reason to put in money. At some point batteries may start to "eat" part of their own revenue, the Energy Ministry said in a statement. For that reason, it says, they should take part not only in trading between cheap and expensive hours, but also in balancing markets and grid services. In winter the days are shorter and solar plants produce less, so batteries will help less. Zarchev said Bulgaria will rely more on conventional plants than on stored renewable energy. Greece's solar capacity grew more than threefold between 2020 and 2025, according to data from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA). Batteries there lag behind, and the evening peak is covered with imported gas. Since 2023, Athens has held three auctions for stand-alone batteries, and the first of them were installed only in April. By the end of the year, total storage in Greece will reach 1 gigawatt, government data show, a small fraction of Bulgaria's capacity. Greek officials say another 5 gigawatts will be added by 2030. In the first half of the year, Greek households paid an average of €0.1967 per kilowatt hour before taxes and charges, against €0.1117 for Bulgarian households, according to Eurostat. The Greek energy ministry said in a presentation last month that it is working to build batteries faster with EU money, to bring down power prices. Manolis Karapidakis, chief executive of the Greek association of energy storage developers, says that with 6 gigawatts of working batteries, Greece's power system would be better balanced today. Consumers would feel that too, he says. The EU has tried for years to expand batteries, because the sun and wind do not supply power all the time. Progress is slow because of long waits for permits and grid connections. Batteries are expected to spread faster, especially in Germany, Britain and Italy.

artigo.texto: TN candidates for governor explain how they’d handle data centers if elected A recent Beacon Center poll shows most Tennesseans oppose tax incentives for data centers. What This Story Is About - Four Tennessee candidates — Lauren Pinkston, David Hatley, Marsha Blackburn and Jerri Green — outlined differing positions on how the state should regulate its roughly 60 operational data centers and 15 to 20 proposed facilities. Why It Matters - A new Beacon Center poll found 61% of Tennesseans oppose tax incentives for data centers, and candidates differ on whether to pause development, let local communities decide, or impose new regulations and rate structures. What Happens Next - Candidates including Pinkston, Hatley and Green have called for moratoriums at the state or local level while rules on noise, environmental impact, water use and utility costs are developed. For Context - Tennessee data centers include the xAI facility in Memphis and the DC Blox facility proposed near the Nashville Zoo. Catch Up - Green is already sponsoring a Memphis moratorium resolution on data centers, and Pinkston says she was the first candidate to call for a statewide moratorium. NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - Tennessee has about 60 operational data centers, with 15 to 20 more proposed, and candidates in this election have different views on how the state should handle their future. A new Beacon Center poll found 61% of Tennesseans oppose tax incentives to bring data centers to the state. Pinkston calls for statewide moratorium Independent candidate Lauren Pinkston said she was the first candidate to call for a statewide moratorium on data centers. “I was the first candidate to call for a statewide moratorium [on] data centers because the state has not offered good guidance to local governments on how we make sure that the working class is not paying for the development that these data centers require,” Pinkston said. Pinkston said companies, not taxpayers, should cover the infrastructure data centers need. “If you’re coming to Tennessee, regardless of your infrastructure, that you are paying for the infrastructure that you are forcing to be developed. So the roads, the schools, the water, you pay for that. Growth has to pay for growth,” Pinkston said. Pinkston said the state needs to define allowable noise levels in decibels and the environmental and drinking water impacts of data centers. “What are the impacts of the environment and the drinking water? All of those things need to be clearly defined so that local communities have better guidance. And we need to have a moratorium across the state until those things are decided upon,” Pinkston said. Pinkston said she would not want a data center in her neighborhood or built on farmland. “In my neighborhood? Absolutely not. And taking up farmland? Absolutely not,” Pinkston said. She pointed to the former Saturn plant, now a GM facility, near her home south of Spring Hill, which she said was required to be built half underground with its above-ground portion painted blue to blend with the sky and is now hidden behind cornfields. “Those are really innovative solutions that keep the community happy while also adding good economic growth to the community as well,” Pinkston said. Pinkston said she is interested in building data centers underground, saying they run about 17 degrees cooler and that the heat they emit could be captured to fuel greenhouses, growing products for the local market. Hatley wants pause on new deals Independent candidate David Hatley also wants to pause new data center deals. “You know, they scare me,” Hatley said. Hatley pointed to the Blue Oval and Starbucks deals in Tennessee as examples of agreements he said are not always good for the state. “I see my opponents saying we’re going to pay for Starbucks with a payroll tax that doesn’t even exist. You know, so that’s what we get in government. We get guys that get to the front of the line, influence the people. And these deals happen that aren’t always good for Tennessee,” Hatley said. Hatley said data centers could have economic advantages, but the state needs to pause. “I think we need to stop right now and pause because... we don’t want to wake up in 10 years and have this economic boom in the first few years and then pay for it later,” Hatley said. Hatley said governors elsewhere are calling for moratoriums, and companies are increasingly offering to pay property taxes and electricity costs. He questioned how Tennessee got into the current situation. “We’ve given 20-year tax abatements to Google and now all of a sudden everyone’s against it. We should have never let these in the first place come into town,” Hatley said. When asked about concerns in Memphis over the xAI data center, including water pollution, electricity use and effects on lower-income neighborhoods, Hatley said he would place more regulations on existing data centers. “Even if they want to come in and pay our property taxes, they want to come in and pay electricity, why are they doing that? Asking yourself, we need to be making sure that these things aren’t harmful to our environment. That’s more important than anything else outside of economics,” Hatley said. “The state has to have some guardrails. We have to guide these local municipalities into how to handle these data centers and ultimately let them vote,” Hatley said. artigo.texto: Located on land approximately 2 kilometres south-west of Gleno and 8.5 kilometres south-west of Larne, Ballyross is strategically positioned close to the existing Ballyvallagh substation. This will support the efficient operation of the system while minimising the need for additional grid infrastructure. As constraints on Northern Ireland's electricity system increase, clean, low-cost electricity capable of powering homes and businesses can sometimes be prevented from reaching consumers. Battery energy storage projects such as Ballyross can help make better use of this electricity by storing it when generation is high and releasing it when demand rises. By adding flexibility and supporting grid stability, Ballyross will help create a more efficient and resilient electricity system. “From our office in Larne, RES has been proud to contribute to Northern Ireland’s energy future and economic growth since the early 1990s” said Peter Deeney, Senior Development Project Manager at RES. “Securing consent for Ballyross, our first battery energy storage project to be consented in Northern Ireland, is an important milestone as we continue transforming the way energy is generated, stored and supplied. Battery storage is becoming increasingly important as Northern Ireland continues its transition to a low-carbon energy system. Projects such as Ballyross can help make the electricity network more flexible and resilient, so that more renewable energy can be stored and used when it is needed most.” The approved scheme also includes a substantial landscaping package. New native-species planting will help the development blend into the surrounding landscape while creating wildlife corridors and pollinator-friendly habitat that deliver additional biodiversity benefits. “Alongside its strategic location close to Ballyvallagh substation, the site was selected because it has limited visibility from local properties” added Mr Deeney. “The new planting will further reduce visibility while providing valuable resources for a wide range of flora and fauna. We would particularly like to thank the local residents and stakeholders who engaged with us throughout the development of Ballyross. The feedback shared during consultation helped inform our landscaping plan and shape the project’s final design.” Construction of the BESS is expected to take around 20 months. artigo.texto: In the battleground state of Pennsylvania, data centers have become a kitchen-table issue. This September, nearly two-thirds of likely Pennsylvania voters told The New York Times they either strongly or somewhat oppose the construction of data centers to support artificial intelligence. For Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is seeking reelection in November, the subject has become unavoidable. After proudly announcing Amazon’s $20 billion data center investment in the Commonwealth in June 2025, the governor signed an executive order in August restricting further data center development across the state and requiring local approval for new installations. The reversal, according to his press release, was informed by “many residents who have expressed their concerns to him directly, and to many more who have shared feedback.” Neither political party has “really figured out how to respond to the challenge” of rising voter discontent over the issue, according to Matthew Levendusky, a professor of political science and communications. Levendusky expects the pressure to keep building into the 2028 presidential race. “Data center construction has become a bipartisan issue,” Parrish Bergquist, an assistant professor of political science, said. Any electoral effect, she added, might be “an anti-incumbent effect rather than a partisan effect.” “This is why you see Shapiro coming out against them, because if people are mad about these things, they will vote against whatever incumbent they view as being responsible for building them,” Bergquist added. “At the city council, town council level, I think that could have implications on both parties.” Bergquist thinks the debate over data center construction is largely driven by concerns from residents. “People don’t like the disruption associated with construction, or they don’t like noise or disruption to their sense of place,” she said in an interview. “People are like, ‘this isn’t a thing that's going to benefit us,’” Bergquist said. “Why does it need to be built here?” RELATED: Penn Democrats hosts Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro ahead of Election Day New Penn center aims to tackle AI-backed cybersecurity threats Levendusky — who is also the Stephen and Mary Baran Chair of the Institutions of Democracy division — said that media coverage of data centers and AI as a whole has generally “been framed in a way that generates a sense of grievance.” On one hand, he explained, voters are told the rise of AI will reduce the value of higher education, eliminate white-collar jobs, and might even wipe out humanity. The data centers that power that very technology, he continued, “raise utility bills, pollute, and reduce the quality of life for neighbors.” “Who benefits?” Levendusky continued. “Mostly a few large companies and their billionaire founders. So, you have highly concentrated benefits and much more broadly dispersed costs — a recipe for people to feel aggrieved.” John Quigley, a senior fellow at the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy, said that while corporations have made “promises about the economic benefits of data centers,” those claims “don’t withstand scrutiny.” While data centers create temporary jobs during construction, he said they “hardly employ anybody” once fully operational. According to Levendusky, companies need to “figure out how to structure the benefits of these centers” so that they “outweigh the costs for communities.” State Sen. Anthony Williams (D-8), whose district includes parts of Penn, said he has heard pronounced concerns from constituents regarding larger data centers. Despite that public opposition, he said the facilities did “meet a need that the public may have.” “There’s a lot of ads and literature that’s been generated about who supports a data center, who does not, what data centers would do to a community,” Williams explained. “The actual substantive portion related to policy and bills – I don’t think we’ve spent much time on that at all.” Instead, Williams said that on a statewide level, discussions of data centers and AI were more “political fodder” than substantive policymaking conversations. These concerns could be amplified by a lack of regulation, according to Quigley, who explained that, so far, the data centers proposed in Pennsylvania largely rely on diesel backup generation. “A data center could be running several hundred generators, which, even with the best available technology, are going to be releasing significant amounts of NOx and particulate matter pollution, to say nothing of carbon dioxide pollution,” Quigley said. If inhaled, NOx, or nitrogen oxides, can cause respiratory harm — and even lead to the development of asthma. Professor of Earth and Environmental Sciences Michael Mann wrote in a statement that data centers are “massive sinks of energy and water” that “produce substantial waste and pollution.” Mann, who is also the director of the Penn Center for Science, Sustainability, and the Media, said the environmental impact of data centers had previously been mitigated by using renewable energy. The Trump administration, though, has moved to have data centers run on natural gas, which Mann argued adds to “carbon emissions when we need to be rapidly decreasing them.” According to Bergquist, there has not been a concurrent push for the development of renewable energy sources to support the centers. “We have to figure out how to be able to build clean and renewable energy capacity and distribution in ways that are just and fair and not environmentally detrimental, but that don’t delay things for longer than they need to be delayed,” she explained. Despite rising calls for a pause on construction, Pennsylvania does not currently have a data center moratorium. Philadelphia already houses eight data centers, though none are the hyperscale developments needed for AI. artigo.texto: Lebanon Lebanon Launches National Carbon Market Roadmap with UN Support Lebanese Environment Minister Tamara Al-Zein launched a national roadmap for the carbon market, backed by the UNDP and Climate Promise initiative, aiming to finance climate projects and reduce emissions. Environment Minister Tamara Al-Zein emphasized "the state's responsibility in opening opportunities for scientific advancement, planning, and cooperation among its institutions," stressing that "Lebanon cannot afford to waste more opportunities or subject its citizens' interests to political tug-of-war." She considered that "the seriousness of work is measured by providing financing conditions and implementing projects," clarifying that "this approach directly guides the Ministry of Environment in preparing a national roadmap for the carbon market, allowing for the assessment of financing opportunities for climate projects and building the necessary foundations to benefit from them." Al-Zein affirmed that "political disagreement does not exempt anyone from the responsibility of agreeing on sound management of public utilities." She stated: "Waste and energy files must not remain hostage to disagreements while Lebanese people pay the cost of stagnation with their health and livelihoods." She noted that "this initiative has an economic dimension related to Lebanon's need to expand sources of financing for its projects and attract investment in sectors capable of reducing emissions." She pointed out that "developing this path may enable mobilizing additional resources to implement environmental and climate priorities, linking international commitments with tangible economic opportunities." Al-Zein's remarks came after she launched the process of preparing the national roadmap for the carbon market, supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Lebanon and the "Climate Promise" initiative, based on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. To this end, Al-Zein chaired a technical working meeting attended by the Ministry of Environment team, the international expert on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement Dr. Axel Michaelowa, and the head of the National Solid Waste Management Authority. The discussion focused on opportunities for developing projects in the waste sector eligible to participate in international carbon markets, and the challenges facing them. Al-Zein explained that "the roadmap aims to assess the potential of converting emission reductions into financing and investment opportunities, including the possibility of selling carbon credits according to internationally accepted standards." She indicated that "potential revenues from these credits could constitute an additional resource for eligible projects, contributing to supporting their financing, enhancing their economic viability, and sustainability." She considered that "the importance of this path lies in making available economic value for achieved emission reductions, alongside their environmental benefit, which may enhance the attractiveness of investment in sustainable projects." She saw that "starting with the waste sector allows linking the handling of a daily crisis with opportunities for financing solutions and ensuring their sustainability." She noted that "improving the management of this sector and developing projects that reduce its emissions provide a basis for studying the possibility of benefiting from carbon financing to support them." Al-Zein affirmed that "the role of the Ministry of Environment goes beyond addressing existing damages to exploring economic and financial opportunities for climate action, and establishing scientific and institutional foundations to benefit from them," stressing that "clarity of rules and procedures constitutes a fundamental element in building the trust of funders and investors in projects that can be developed." She revealed that "consultations will expand to other sectors, particularly energy, in cooperation with the Ministries of Energy and Water and Finance, and specialized teams within the Ministry of Environment," clarifying that "the work will include identifying sectoral potentials, technical and financial requirements, and regulatory frameworks necessary for participation." She pointed out that "results of emission calculations and trajectory assessments indicate that Lebanon is moving in the right direction regarding its climate commitments, enabling the exploration of opportunities to benefit from carbon market mechanisms." She noted that "progress in reducing emissions does not automatically mean the availability of sellable credits," explaining that "benefiting requires project accreditation and proving, measuring, and verifying the reductions they achieve with integrity according to international rules, while preventing double counting and ensuring consistency with Lebanon's obligations under the Paris Agreement." Minister Al-Zein concluded that "the value of any climate financing is measured by what it enables in terms of actual projects that protect the environment and improve people's lives, and by what it adds in terms of capacity to finance solutions and ensure their sustainability," affirming that "the goal is to build a path that combines environmental impact, economic viability, and public interest."

artigo.texto: Remover obstáculos para localidades com reservas florestais elegíveis para a venda de créditos de carbono. Durante a discussão sobre o projeto de lei que altera e complementa diversos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental no Grupo 4 (composto pelas delegações da Assembleia Nacional da cidade de Dong Nai e das províncias de Quang Tri e Dien Bien), os delegados propuseram que os obstáculos relacionados aos créditos de carbono sejam resolvidos em breve, criando condições para que as localidades com reservas florestais tenham acesso ao mercado de créditos de carbono. Garantir a sustentabilidade e o controle da poluição da água. Dando especial atenção à política de tratamento de águas residuais domésticas, o Deputado da Assembleia Nacional Le Hoang Hai (Cidade de Dong Nai ) elogiou bastante o fato de que, no geral, o projeto de lei trouxe mudanças positivas para sanar as deficiências na gestão de águas residuais domésticas, tais como: o controle rigoroso do lançamento de águas residuais em fontes de água degradadas (Cláusula 2, Artigo 7), proibindo que novos projetos lancem águas residuais diretamente em corpos d'água superficiais que já atingiram sua capacidade de suporte (a menos que 100% sejam reciclados ou tratados para atender aos padrões de qualidade da água superficial); e a adição de mecanismos legais claros (Artigos 72 e 72a) que permitem a reutilização de águas residuais domésticas tratadas (para irrigação de plantas, lavagem de ruas, resfriamento, etc.). Segundo os delegados, a regulamentação pressionará as cidades e os grandes projetos a investirem em tecnologias mais avançadas de tratamento de águas residuais antes de as lançarem no meio ambiente. Ao mesmo tempo, mudará a mentalidade do "tratamento de resíduos" para a "exploração dos recursos hídricos", promovendo uma economia circular para as águas residuais. Contudo, ao analisar o Artigo 40 à luz da gestão efetiva da coleta e do tratamento de águas residuais domésticas e industriais, os delegados apontaram diversas deficiências, tais como: O projeto de lei não diferencia a natureza das águas residuais domésticas das industriais. As águas residuais domésticas (provenientes de escritórios, edifícios e áreas residenciais) apresentam vazão e concentração de poluentes (DBO, DQO, amônia, etc.) que variam significativamente de acordo com o horário do dia e a estação do ano. O licenciamento baseado em "vazão máxima" e "limites fixos de parâmetros", como ocorre com as águas residuais industriais, leva a situações em que o sistema de tratamento biológico de um projeto sofre sobrecarga biológica localizada durante os horários de pico, causando infrações administrativas devido a parâmetros que excedem os padrões, mesmo que a carga total diária de poluentes não ultrapasse o limite permitido. A próxima deficiência reside na identificação da "fonte receptora de águas residuais". Na realidade, muitos empreendimentos e áreas residenciais lançam águas residuais domésticas no sistema de drenagem comum da cidade ou do polo industrial (sem uma estação de tratamento centralizada), em vez de diretamente em rios e lagos. Enquanto isso, o ponto a, inciso 2, do Artigo 40, que exige a especificação da localização e da fonte receptora final de águas superficiais nas licenças ambientais, transfere a responsabilidade pelo controle da fonte receptora (a capacidade de vazão do rio ou lago) para os proprietários de pequenos empreendimentos, quando essa responsabilidade cabe às autoridades locais pela gestão da infraestrutura geral. Com base nas deficiências mencionadas, os delegados propuseram a revisão do regulamento do Artigo 40 (conforme alterado e complementado) para distinguir claramente as normas e os métodos de concessão de licenças de descarga de águas residuais domésticas (com base na carga total/média diária) das águas residuais industriais perigosas. Ainda sobre este assunto, o deputado da Assembleia Nacional Nguyen Minh Tam ( Quang Tri ) sugeriu que a agência responsável pela redação da lei considere a inclusão de regulamentações sobre investimentos em infraestrutura de proteção ambiental para áreas de produção, comércio e serviços concentrados que ainda não concluíram a infraestrutura de tratamento de águas residuais e resíduos. Você também pode gostar Com base na situação atual dos parques industriais e zonas de produção concentrada em operação em todo o país, em geral, e em Quang Tri, em particular (Quag Tri possui atualmente 31 polos industriais estabelecidos e em funcionamento), fica evidente a desigualdade na infraestrutura de proteção ambiental entre essas zonas e polos. Algumas áreas carecem de sistemas centralizados de tratamento de efluentes, enquanto outras instalações, mesmo em uso há algum tempo, apresentam sinais de desgaste e deterioração. Enquanto aguardam a conclusão e modernização da infraestrutura, as unidades de produção ainda precisam tratar os efluentes para atender aos padrões exigidos antes de descartá-los no meio ambiente e cumprir os procedimentos ambientais necessários. Para garantir a sustentabilidade e o controle da poluição a longo prazo, especialmente à medida que a escala de produção aumenta, a infraestrutura continua a se deteriorar ou o volume total de águas residuais excede a capacidade de recepção da fonte de água, os delegados propuseram que a lei seja alterada para definir com mais clareza os requisitos para projetos existentes de produção concentrada, negócios e serviços que ainda não atendem aos padrões necessários. Especificamente, os regulamentos estipulam um prazo obrigatório para a conclusão da infraestrutura de tratamento de águas residuais em zonas e polos industriais em operação que ainda não atendem aos requisitos; eles também especificam as responsabilidades de coordenação entre os investidores em infraestrutura e as instalações de produção quando águas residuais que excedem os padrões prescritos são lançadas no meio ambiente. artigo.texto: ANEEL, ONS e EPE revisam nota técnica com os quantitativos da capacidade remanescente para conexão de novos sistemas de armazenamento no LRCAP 2026 Documento encontra-se disponível nos portais oficiais das três entidades O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) divulga hoje, dia 26/10, a primeira revisão da Nota Técnica NT-ONS DPL 0095/2026. A versão incorpora a retificação, pela transmissora responsável, da informação sobre a disponibilidade física para novas conexões no barramento de 69 kV da SE Milagres e da capacidade de interrupção de curto-circuito de um dos disjuntores da SE Milagres, em 230 kV. Além disso, contempla ajustes textuais de caráter geral, sem alteração dos valores das margens dos barramentos candidatos. O documento apresenta os quantitativos da Capacidade Remanescente do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) para conexão de novos Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia nas instalações da Rede Básica, Demais Instalações de Transmissão (DIT) e Instalações de Interesse Exclusivo de Centrais de Geração para Conexão Compartilhada (ICG), inclusive para conexões indiretas por meio dos sistemas de distribuição, no âmbito dos LRCAPs de 2026 – Armazenamento Nacional e Armazenamento, conforme estabelecido nas Portarias nº 444/GM/MME/2016 e nº 136/GM/MME/2026. A divulgação dessa Revisão da Nota Técnica segue os procedimentos determinados pelo § 5º do art. 3º da Portaria MME nº 444/GM/MME/2016. Assim, o documento encontra-se disponível nos portais oficiais do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico, da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) e da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL). artigo.texto: O Google derrubou cerca de 400 mil árvores no norte da Finlândia para abrir espaço a dois data centers, os enormes galpões de computadores que sustentam serviços de internet e de inteligência artificial. Segundo reportagem do jornal britânico The Guardian, o desmatamento começou sem as avaliações de impacto ambiental exigidas por lei. No início de outubro, a autoridade ambiental do país mandou suspender as obras e o caso provocou uma onda de revolta entre os finlandeses. Os projetos ficam em Muhos e na vila de Otanmäki, a cerca de 100 quilômetros de distância. Os dois fazem parte de um investimento de € 13 bilhões (cerca de R$ 72,38 bilhões) do Google em infraestrutura de IA, o maior do tipo na história do país. O tamanho do desmatamento Em Muhos, o Google desmatou 330 hectares de floresta, uma área de 3 quilômetros de comprimento por 2 de largura, na qual havia cerca de 250 mil árvores. Segundo o Guardian, a empresa removeu até a camada superficial do solo e deixou no lugar um grande lamaçal, a 400 metros do rio Oulujoki. A ecologista Mari Annala, da Associação Finlandesa para a Conservação da Natureza (SLL), estima que outras 150 mil árvores foram derrubadas em Otanmäki. Moradores relatam que a água dos riachos próximos ficou marrom. Como o corte foi irregular, a madeira não pode ser vendida às serrarias. Por que o data center do Google foi suspenso Em 6 de outubro, a Autoridade Finlandesa de Licenciamento e Supervisão (LVV) enviou cartas ao Google e ordenou a interrupção temporária das obras nos dois locais. O motivo: a empresa não concluiu as avaliações de impacto ambiental antes de desmatar. O diretor do Google na Finlândia, Antti Järvinen, pediu desculpas, mas afirmou que a empresa agiu "com base no melhor entendimento que tínhamos da legislação na época". Em nota, o Google disse que parou os trabalhos, que vai cumprir todas as exigências e que pretende replantar árvores em 130 hectares em Muhos. Ambientalistas consideram a área pequena demais diante do estrago. "Pura arrogância" A reação foi forte. "Nunca ouvi falar de nenhuma empresa que tenha feito algo assim na Finlândia", disse ao Guardian Hanna Halmeenpää, presidente do conselho da SLL. "Eles compraram uma vasta área de terra e simplesmente começaram a desmatá-la. É pura arrogância e é inacreditável." Mais de 93 mil pessoas assinaram uma petição que pede regras mais rígidas para data centers e uma taxa para compensar as comunidades afetadas. O primeiro-ministro Petteri Orpo, que havia chamado a atração de investimentos de "prioridade máxima", classificou o caso como "um banho de água fria". Lobos na vila e medo de virar alvo Em Otanmäki, antiga vila mineira, moradores dizem sentir o impacto no dia a dia. "Tivemos lobos entrando na aldeia porque todos os animais selvagens saíram da floresta", contou Anni Ranta, de 53 anos, cuja família vive no local há gerações. Ela também teme o barulho das obras e que o data center transforme a vila em alvo da Rússia, país com quem a Finlândia divide uma longa fronteira. O biólogo Vesa Hyyryläinen, da SLL, afirma que pica-paus que faziam ninhos na floresta foram expulsos. Por que as big techs querem a Finlândia O país virou destino preferido para data center s, com 145 projetos em diferentes fases de planejamento. O clima frio ajuda a resfriar os computadores e reduz o gasto com energia, uma das maiores despesas desse tipo de instalação. A estabilidade política, a terra disponível e a energia renovável também pesam. A corrida da inteligência artificial acelerou essa procura. Treinar e rodar sistemas como o Gemini, do Google, exige milhares de computadores ligados o tempo todo e cada novo data center consome tanta energia quanto uma cidade pequena. Quem ganha com os data centers Parte dos moradores apoia os projetos pelos empregos e impostos locais, mas há quem questione o benefício para o país. "Na verdade, para a Finlândia, não há benefícios", afirmou Jussi Kangasharju, chefe do departamento de ciência da computação da Universidade de Helsinque. "São empresas internacionais que atendem clientes internacionais. A Finlândia arrecada muito pouco imposto corporativo." O Ministério do Meio Ambiente diz acompanhar o setor e estar pronto para propor mudanças na lei. O tema deve pesar nas eleições finlandesas de abril de 2027.

artigo.texto: Aurora City Council to vote on data center moratorium following community pushback Aurora's mayor made his opinion on pausing the data center discussion clear in writing. The answer is a resounding "no," Mayor Mike Coffman said, responding to a developer's letter to the city council. Vantage said it will evaluate locating the Trident data center on sites farther from residential neighborhoods if the city council agrees to a 90-day pause on any efforts to enact new legislative requirements on development. Mayor Coffman said, "We need to move forward 'NOW' with new guidelines that protect residential areas so that we don't have another Trident situation." The co-presidents of Join Unite, a nonprofit formed just weeks ago to oppose the Trident data center, hope the third time's the charm to finally put firm rules in place around data centers. "We are cautiously hopeful that that actually is what's happening behind the scenes. But we're dealing with billionaires and huge corporations," said Makayla Llanos, one of the organization's leaders. Monday, city council will decide whether to implement a data center moratorium. That follows the city council's rejection of a six-month moratorium earlier this year, with Coffman casting the tie-breaking vote to kill it. After an uproar from the community in mid-October, the council unanimously voted to approve the first reading of an ordinance keeping data centers from being built in areas zoned "mixed-use office/ institutional" near schools, homes and assisted living facilities. City leaders will vote on an indefinite moratorium on new applications. "I hope the city does not agree to those terms, and I hope the city stands up for themselves and for us," said Tara Miller, one of the leaders of Join Unite. A new moratorium would not stop Vantage from moving forward with the Trident data center because it's already been approved. Any moratorium proposed would need seven votes to pass because the effort previously failed and likely wouldn't go into effect until February.

artigo.texto: Trending Champion and Warren township officials plan a public meeting Nov. 4 to discuss what needs to be on the books to handle a data center if one were to locate in either township. Champion Trustee Chairman Doug Emerine said to date, the Champion zoning department has not been approached by anyone about a data center. He said the township zoning board is working on guidelines and has been reviewing what Hubbard Township and other communities have done. Emerine said one property that has been discussed is the former Copperweld Steel property off state Route 45 that straddles both townships. He said the 360-acre site has one-third of the land in Champion and two-thirds in Warren Township. Emerine said of the available properties in Champion, that one would be the one to locate a data center on, and the zoning department needs to be prepared. “Right now we need to get as much information as we can on data centers. I am not sure what Warren Township officials want to do, but we need to get together and discuss this,” Emerine said. He said if a data center or any other large business were to express interest in locating in Champion, there would be public meetings to keep residents informed. “No matter what, there will be a data center located somewhere in Trumbull County,” Emerine said. Warren Township Trustee Ed Anthony said he agrees with Emerine that the Copperweld property would be the one where a data center would possibly locate. “It is prime property because of the available land and being by the river, which would provide water, but we have not received any inquiries,” Anthony said. He said the property does have many cleanup issues and there is litigation still on the property. Anthony said the township’s zoning board has been reviewing what to include in the zoning codes. Anthony said a joint meeting is being planned for 6 p.m. Nov. 4 at the Champion administration building. Also, Champion officials approved providing between $6,000 and $7,000 for the road department to do drainage upgrade work this year on Marshall Road. Emerine said the money will cover the costs for materials and supplies needed for the work. In another matter, Vanessa Teuscher found a bulletin and a service schedule from Dec. 1, 1985, when the township cemetery chapel was dedicated. She had the two items framed and they will be placed inside the chapel.

artigo.texto: A weaker ETS puts €90 billion in green investment at risk The review of the European Union's Emissions Trading System, or ETS, is now underway to bring the mechanism in line with the EU's new climate target: a 90% cut in net greenhouse emission by 2040 compared with 1990 levels. Yet that goal appears far off today. The ETS has helped decarbonize the power sector, but the EU urgently needs to drive investments in hard-to-abate sectors, where fossil fuels still dominate. Europe's carbon market is the very foundation of its climate policy. By putting a price on carbon dioxide, the cap-and-trade system gives industries a steady incentive to invest in alternative production methods, be competitive and reduce emissions. The ETS also generates large revenues that can fund climate and clean energy projects. A proven tool The carbon market cannot transform industry on its own. The right enabling conditions, whether in energy, infrastructure or markets for clean materials and products, are critical. But it is an essential industrial policy, and not a new one. For two decades, it has guided capital across many sectors. Following the price signal, companies are spending tens of billions of euros to switch to low-carbon or even net-zero processes. Where is new money going? Increasingly, into decarbonization. In 2025, large European companies put €313 billion into Taxonomy-aligned activities, and those with credible transition plans added a further €182 billion, according to the latest Report on Monitoring Capital Flows to Sustainable Investments, published by the Platform on Sustainable Finance, an advisory body to the European Commission. Clean power, green steel and net-zero cement: The future is already taking shaped. Mixed signals Despite the carbon market's positive economic and environmental impact, proposals now under negotiation threaten to derail the business models of companies that underpin Europe's long-term competitiveness and jobs. The Commission has tried to navigate pressures from industries and countries still heavily reliant on expensive and polluting fossil fuels while maintaining momentum toward the green transition. The aim is to avoid penalizing front-runners that have already invested in decarbonization. Nonetheless, the proposal includes several technical but far-reaching changes. It lowers the linear reduction factor, the annual rate at which the emissions cap shrinks. It also adds free allowances and creates a role for unproven international credits and carbon removals. On top of this, the European Parliament's draft report would weaken the market even further, potentially injecting more uncertainty into the outlook for the carbon price. A €90 billion shortfall According to a new study by Strategic Perspectives and Veyt, the Commission's proposal would blow a gigantic financial hole in Europe's climate plans. Industries covered by the ETS would spend €90 billion less on decarbonization technologies by 2040 than under current law, a drop of more than a quarter. In absolute terms, the Netherlands would be hit hardest, with its total halving to less than €20 billion. Germany would lose €15 billion and Italy €12.5 billion. The further softening proposed in Parliament's draft report could widen the gap even more. Recent reports by businesses and investors identify predictable price signals and policy coherence as key factors in their decisions. Europe will require hundreds of billions of euros a year, most of it from businesses and investors willing to commit capital at scale. In energy-intensive sectors such as steel, projects must be planned at least 10 to 15 years ahead. The jury is in: Diluting the ETS rewards high-emitting competitors and in the end punishes front-runners. A stable and robust carbon price is non-negotiable for European industrial leadership. Europe needs an agreement on an effective system that drives investment in industry. artigo.texto: Senator Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson have both embraced calls for guardrails on data centers ahead of the Maine Senate race, as polling finds that Maine voters are skeptical of their construction in the Pine Tree State. The midterm elections have been defined by the debate over artificial intelligence (AI) powered data centers, as a growing number of Americans—and Mainers—say they do not want to see them built in their communities. Collins has generally walked a fine line on data centers, voting for the Ratepayer Protection Act and calling for more local control over the issue. Meanwhile, Jackson has been highly critical of data center developers and has called for the state to implement a moratorium on their construction. The issue could be impactful in the race, which is one of a handful of toss-ups that could determine whether Democrats or Republicans control the Senate after the midterms. Proponents of data centers believe they are an important economic lifeline for communities that have the potential to create jobs. Critics, however, have raised numerous issues with data centers, including their impact on the environment, water usage, their potential to drive up electricity bills and noise pollution. In Maine, a state with a culture that values conservation, several municipalities have implemented moratoriums on data centers, as they are “very unpopular” in the state, Mark Brewer, professor of political science at the University of Maine in Orono, told Newsweek. “An exception might be old mill towns that have lost their mill but still have much of the infrastructure in place,” he added. The data center debate was on display during a viral moment in the final debate between the two candidates when a data center protester briefly disrupted while Collins was speaking. Collins said the protester was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” to which Jackson responded, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” During an October 13 debate, Collins said that the two candidates are “not that far apart on this particular issue” during a discussion about data centers. Here is a look at where the two candidates stand on the matter. Susan Collins Position on Data Centers Collins touted her support for the Ratepayer Protection Act, which required states to consider establishing standards for when data centers and other large electricity users connect to the grid, during the debate. “I voted and cosponsored a bill that the Senate considered just last month to put guardrails and encourage states to adopt guardrails on the construction of data centers. That included making sure that they have no impact on electric rates, very important for a state like Maine with the fourth highest electric rates in the country due to Troy’s policies,” she said. The senator said she believes the issue is decided locally. “There may be a former mill site, as Governor [Janet] Mills has said, where a data center would work out all right because there is a source of power and water, but in many other places, they would not work well,” she said. A spokesperson for Collins pointed to her statement about the Ratepayer Protection Act when reached by Newsweek. “Maine families and small businesses are already paying some of the highest electricity costs in the nation,” Collins said. “The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act ensures that they will not pay an even steeper bill by directing state utility regulators to consider standards that would make high-volume users like AI data centers offset their own costs. Mainers should not have to pay the bill for data centers’ power generation, transmission lines, and energy infrastructure.” Newsweek’s AI scorecard rates Collins as “Leans AI Skeptic.” Troy Jackson's Position on Data Centers Jackson has been much more critical of data centers. During the October 13 debate, Jackson said data centers have the ability to “create some jobs,” but that data centers being built in Maine cannot increase electricity rates or hurt the state’s water quality. “I want to make sure that we know what the data is. How they are using it, and there has to be real parameters, real guidelines to how we’re going to do this,” Jackson said. “I’m not really supportive of data centers, but I understand they’re maybe something that we have to deal with.” Jackson said data centers must be slowed down so people can better understand their development. “I am very much in favor of making sure the federal government or the state of Maine puts guardrails on these things because I don’t want the billionaires, again, writing the rules and making our communities worse off than they are right now,” he said. While campaigning for governor earlier this year, Jackson criticized Mills for vetoing a moratorium on data center development in the state. “Once again, we’re seeing power and influence coming into this state and ruining things for us Mainers. We needed a pause on this because it takes our power. It takes our water. There’s health effects. We need regulations because we don’t know what they’re doing without data, our information. We don’t know all the health effects to our kids,” he said. Newsweek reached out to Jackson's campaign via email. How Maine Voters View Data Centers Data centers are unpopular in Maine, according to polls. Only 29 percent of Mainers support the construction of data centers in the U.S., compared to 66 percent of whom oppose their development, according to a poll from The New York Times and Siena University of 619 voters from September 15 to 22. Forty-one percent of respondents said they believed Jackson would do a better job on data centers, compared to 39 percent who said they trusted Collins more on the issue, according to the poll, which had a margin of error of plus or minus 5.4 percentage points. artigo.texto: The Power Challenge Behind Hyperscale AI Expansion The number of new AI data center projects being announced continues to far outpace the number delayed by local opposition. The power grid is straining under the ambitions of hyperscale AI data center developers. Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Google have increased their data center investment roughly tenfold over the past eight years, according to Industrial Info Resources (IIR). Up from a combined $64 billion in 2018, their announced spending is expected to exceed $700 billion this year. “Twelve straight months of new project announcements with spending running consistently elevated indicates a structural, multiyear theme of digital infrastructure buildout that is set to continue for the foreseeable future,” said Shane Mullins, an analyst with IIR at the Data Center World Power event in September 2026. Community Opposition Grows, but Project Momentum Holds The rapid expansion of data center development, fueled in large part by AI demand, has whipped up a growing wave of community resistance. According to IIR, more than 500 data center moratoria are on record across 42 states. New Jersey and Michigan lead with 41 and 36, respectively. New York has enacted a statewide ban on new data centers larger than 50 MW, at least temporarily, while Texas has paused new grid interconnections as it works through about 200 GW of requests. “$130 billion in projects were rejected in Q1 of 2026 alone, more than the total rejected for the whole of 2025,” Mullins said. “The number of opposition groups has more than doubled over the past year.” Even so, resistance has slowed only a fraction of the broader AI infrastructure buildout. Capital continues to pour into the sector. IIR data show at least $400 billion per month in newly announced data center projects globally since April 2026, with May exceeding $650 billion. That has pushed cumulative capex beyond $7 trillion. In the US and Canada alone, that pipeline amounts to roughly $4.75 trillion and more than 4,250 planned or in-progress data center projects. Texas accounts for nearly $1.25 trillion of that total. Altogether, more than 400 GW of new data center load is in planning, and almost 100 US sites are being designed for at least 1 GW. Where Will the Power Come From? The scale of the challenge is already visible. The US now has 53 GW of operational data center load, up from 23 GW in 2023. Another 42 GW has been approved or is under construction. That could push data center electricity demand from 35 GW in 2024 to 125 GW by 2030. Grid planners have struggled to keep up. In 2022, US planners projected that the country would need 24 GW of additional electricity demand within a decade. By 2025, that forecast has climbed nearly sevenfold, to 166 GW. As a result, hyperscalers and other developers are increasingly being pushed to build, own, or co-develop power generation. Gas turbines remain the preferred option for projects that need to scale beyond 1 GW. But turbine manufacturers are facing capacity constraints of their own. GE Vernova, Mitsubishi Power, and Siemens Energy are sold out of larger turbines through 2029, with some orders now stretching into 2031. All three are expanding production, while other suppliers are offering fuel cells, reciprocating gas engines, and jet engines as faster alternatives. “If you need more than 300 MW and the utility queue says 2034, building or contracting for your own gas plant is the fastest and most certain path to power,” Mullins said. Natural Gas Reemerges in the AI Power Mix AI data center growth has reshaped the North American power market. In 2022, wind and especially solar were ascendant, and some analysts predicted the end of gas turbine sales in North America. Solar project announcements continue to rise, but so does interest in natural gas generation and battery energy storage systems (BESS). IIR estimates that $228 billion in new natural gas power plant projects are currently in play. Hyperscalers and AI data center developers are, in practice, largely power-source agnostic. Most organizations want clean energy, but the need for reliable power now is taking precedence. That has contributed to renewed investment in coal plants scheduled for retirement, as operators seek to keep them running for a few more years. Older natural gas plants are also being upgraded to increase output. “Natural gas is filling the AI data center demand gap, with 347 grassroots, expansion, and conversion projects,” said IIR analyst Britt Burt. “Gas is the fastest, most reliable path to new dispatchable capacity.” According to IIR, the North American power industry could attract more than $1.5 trillion in investment across nearly 7,000 planned projects. But the story is not only about gas. Nuclear energy now accounts for 111 projects worth $311.4 billion, including 61 small modular reactors (SMRs) as well as several nuclear plant restarts. Meanwhile, renewables continue to expand. One of the fastest-growing combinations is solar paired with BESS, which extends solar’s usefulness beyond sunset and improves dispatchability. IIR counts 701 BESS projects worth almost $200 billion. Wind development has slowed, and offshore wind may continue to fade in the US, but onshore wind remains active. Speed to Power Is Reshaping Energy Strategy The same set of constraints is shaping every energy source: interconnection delays, labor and equipment shortages, grid congestion, limited transmission capacity, and increasing community opposition. In that environment, data center developers are pursuing whatever path offers the fastest, most reliable route to power at the required scale. “AI and data center buildout, reshored manufacturing, and an aging generation fleet are driving electricity demand growth not seen in a generation,” Burt said. “This is one of the broadest capital cycles the US and Canadian power sectors have seen in decades.”

artigo.texto: Belkin introduced a 10,000mAh USB-C model at 220g and a 5,000mAh MagSafe Qi2 version, both using semi solid-state cells in premium aluminum bodies that weigh less than conventional lithium-ion packs. Belkin has released two new power banks built on semi solid-state battery technology, cutting weight without sacrificing capacity. The 10,000mAh model weighs 220 grams — roughly 20 to 80 grams lighter than comparable lithium-ion packs — while the 5,000mAh MagSafe version prioritizes thinness for direct iPhone attachment. Semi solid-state cells replace part of the liquid electrolyte with a gel-like substance, reducing the need for heavy protective casing. That translates to a denser energy package in a smaller footprint. Both units feature aluminum shells that feel cold to the touch and resist the heat buildup common in plastic-bodied competitors. The 10,000mAh unit delivers up to 60W over USB-C, enough to charge a MacBook Air at near-full speed. A small integrated display shows remaining capacity in real time. Belkin lists it at $89.95 on Amazon. The 5,000mAh MagSafe model supports 15W Qi2 wireless charging and snaps magnetically to the back of any iPhone 12 or newer. At roughly half the thickness of Apple's discontinued MagSafe Battery Pack, it slides into a pocket with the phone attached. The trade-off: no kickstand, no display, and a slight overhang on the new iPhone Duo's bottom edge. Belkin prices it at $69.99. Early hands-on impressions note the weight difference is immediately apparent when picking up either unit. The 10K model fits a jacket pocket without the usual brick sensation; the 5K model disappears against the phone. Both charge via USB-C and support pass-through, so the bank and a connected device can recharge simultaneously. Belkin says the semi solid-state chemistry also improves cycle life, targeting 1,000 full cycles before capacity drops to 80 percent — roughly double the rating of standard lithium-ion packs in this class. The company has not disclosed whether the cells come from a new supplier or an existing partner's updated line. Both power banks are shipping now through Amazon and Belkin's direct store. artigo.texto: The Aurora City Council did not pass a moratorium on data centers for the second time on Monday night. For the indefinite moratorium to go to a re-vote, it would have needed two-thirds of the councilmembers to vote “yes.” Alison Coombs, Ruben Medina, Alli Jackson, Amy Wiles, Gianina Horton and Mayor Mike Coffman voted in support. Recommended Stories Curtis Gardner, Rob Andrews, Stephanie Hancock, Francoise Bergan and Angela Lawson voted in opposition. It was the second time the council had voted on a data center moratorium, with the first being in an Aug. 10 meeting. It was shot down with opposition from Coffman, Andrews, Bergan, Gardner, Hancock and Lawson. According to council rules, it requires a two-thirds vote to bring back a resolution that was previously voted down. Coffman changed his vote Monday, saying voted against the first moratorium because it had a fixed time frame of six months, whereas the new moratorium would be indefinite. If the moratorium had passed, the city would have halted on accepting development applications for new or expanded data centers. “There is considerable interest and concern among residents within the city that Data Centers have the potential to create an unmanageable burden on critical energy and water resources,” the resolution read. After Monday night’s vote, the mayor said he would bring the matter forward again. During Monday night’s study session before the regular meeting, the council moved forward with zoning changes that would require data centers to be at least 750 feet away from residentially zoned districts. If the regulations pass at a future regular council meeting, data centers would be outright banned within 750 feet of residential zones, up for conditional approval from the council between 750 feet and a half mile and use-by-right a half mile or farther from residential zones. “Our current regulations are really ill-equipped,” Coffman said Monday, adding that a third of Aurora is undeveloped. Councilmember Gardner countered that while there is a lot of undeveloped land in Aurora, not all of it has the power infrastructure to support a data center. Last week, Vantage Data Centers officially agreed to seek alternative sites for the Trident Data Center. Company officials also asked the council to pause on any new data center rules until then. “The answer is a resounding ‘NO,’” Mayor Coffman wrote in a Facebook post Thursday in response to the request, saying the city needs to move forward “now” with data center regulations. Trident Data Center is the latest project by Vantage, which has 30 data centers in 12 countries. The company submitted the application for Trident to the city on Aug. 25, 2025. As currently proposed, the data center would stand two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by the developer through the city’s development portal. The current proposal puts the data center at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue. Those plans have already been through two formal city reviews, and a third is already underway, a city spokesperson told The Denver Gazette. Some residents of surrounding Green Valley Ranch communities, including The Reserve, a 55-plus area, oppose the data center, saying they worry about negative health impacts, declining home values and utility use. Vantage representatives have countered that they take measures to mitigate impacts to surrounding communities, saying their goal is to be a “responsible neighbor and steward of local resources.” Broadly speaking, supporters argue that data centers bring jobs and investment to local communities, as well as new tax revenues and that actions like moratoriums drive away businesses and ultimately hurt the economy. Supporters also insist that cultivating and growing data centers in America has positive repercussions for national security — that, in this technological race, the U.S. should not concede dominance to countries like China. Critics raise worries about energy, arguing that large data centers should pay for their electricity. They also point to water use, noting that much of the West is in a prolonged drought and data centers could exacerbate the situation. Others say data centers bring noise and other forms of pollution, as well as reduce property values and therefore should be built away from residential or urban centers. Meanwhile, a political split is emerging in how cities and counties deal with data centers. The Colorado jurisdictions that recently approved data center construction are conservative-leaning, while cities calling for or imposing moratoriums are more progressive.

artigo.texto: Retiree Eileen Castle hasn't been able to enjoy her backyard since a data center moved in next door in Lowell, Massachusetts, bringing noise, fumes, dust and water mist. But a few streets away, contractor Louis Haas is grateful to Markley, the company running the facility, for redeveloping an abandoned site he says was rife with drug use. Dubbed "the Dungeon" by some locals for the imposing black silhouette it casts over a residential neighborhood of this old milling city, those opposing views encapsulate how data centers are polarizing communities across the United States. Republican-governed states, with their looser regulations, host most of the country's current AI build-out. But in liberal-leaning New England, some feel betrayed by their elected representatives, while others fear being left behind if the industry is curbed. Over the din of construction behind a spiked fence, Castle, 82, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) her great-great-grandparents bought the property. But since the data center moved into a disused pasta factory a decade ago, "We have had nothing but noise. We have dust, dirt. We have all kinds of mist" from the adjoining cooling towers, which she fears could carry Legionnaires' disease. Noxious fumes made a long interview outdoors impossible, and she lamented that her grandchildren can no longer swim in her small pool. "I think every once in a while that maybe I should sell my house," she says, but adds her property value has plummeted. "The Markley Group serves more than 600 clients in Massachusetts and connects the digital infrastructure that powers our economy, our schools, and the everyday needs of our community," Markley Group CEO Jeff Markley said in a statement to AFP. The company said its backup diesel generators run only for five-minute tests each week and, thanks to abatement efforts, produce "about 44 decibels of sound, quieter than a soft conversation three feet away." It said it tests its water twice a year for Legionnaires' disease and has planted 2,000 trees. In 2015, the city council gave Markley a 20-year property and personal property tax break estimated at $77 million, the Lowell Sun newspaper reported at the time. Enthusiasm has since cooled. In March, the council unanimously passed a 360-day moratorium on construction and expansion of commercial data centers, though Markley's 352,000-square-foot (32,700-square-meter) site was grandfathered in. Residents represented by the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) and others have sued to challenge its expansion, which included increasing the number of generators to 27, and won a temporary injunction in August. CLF attorney Adam Reynolds told AFP that it is the "compounding effect of pollution that's really significant" in a historically industrial area. Markley has supporters. Haas, 50, who supplies coffee to a major tech company, said the boom had been good to contractors like him. "I'm a big liberal, I'm a Democrat. But I'm also pro-jobs and pro-economy," he told AFP. Markley said it employs more than 100 full-time staff in Lowell, a third of them local. On top of that, over 100 unionized trades workers work on campus. Another backer, Sarah Bibeau, a 43-year-old single mother of two who works in the defense sector, told AFP the company had been "kind and considerate," fixing roads and offering favors ranging from yard work to free Red Sox tickets. Detractors include Jake Fortes, a 44-year-old travel agent who founded the group "Honest Future for Lowell" and whose property sits on the fence line. "We're getting steamrolled by this company. So some of us have taken it to task," Fortes told AFP. Like Castle, he feels let down by Democrats, including state Gov. Maura Healey, who signed a sales tax break for data centers into law but then paused new applications this year, a reversal that illustrates the party's dilemma. Luz Marte, a 38-year-old lab technician, bought her house a year ago, without realizing the site was a data center. "It sounds very loud, like an airplane is going to take off," she told AFP as her 3-year-old son played. Her home insurer recently moved to triple her premium, which she believes is linked to Markley buying a building even closer to her property. "This is a home I bought for my son, to grow up, feel alive, and have a future," she said. "Now I'm doubting that idea."

artigo.texto: Article Summary - ComEd data shows that the cost of connecting 30 data centers to the utility’s grid will cost upwards of $3 billion. Some of the spending has already been completed, with the rest of the investments to be made by 2031. - The data center developers have paid $721 million in deposits for the infrastructure needed to connect to the grid. Utility watchdogs warn that Illinois households and small businesses could end up footing the bill for the gap. - ComEd disputes the advocates’ conclusion, saying it has been proactive in protecting customers from data center costs, including by securing $1.1 billion in credit that can be collected if the projects do not materialize as planned. This summary was written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story. CHICAGO — Data centers have been the focus of growing debate across the U.S., facing a push for regulation that would require operators to pay for the energy and water resources they use, among other proposals. But beyond paying to generate new energy, consumer advocates warn that the costs of infrastructure to connect data centers to ComEd’s grid will be paid in part by households and small businesses in northern Illinois — something the utility disputes. Records filed by ComEd in an ongoing regulatory matter show that new infrastructure and system upgrades needed to connect 30 data centers to the grid will cost $3.1 billion. Some of those projects are already connected, with the rest expected to come online by 2031. Developers of those data centers have paid $721 million in advance deposits, just under 25% of the total cost, an amount that consumer groups including the Citizens Utility Board and Environmental Law & Policy Center say could leave a potential shortfall of $2 billion to be spread across regular customers’ bills. “Ordinary households should not foot the bill to provide power to data centers,” said Nick Wallace, a senior associate attorney with the environmental law center. “ComEd and the (Illinois Commerce) Commission can protect ratepayers and the grid by requiring data centers to pay for 100% of their power supply and infrastructure investments.” ComEd contends that the consumer groups’ analysis overlooks $1.1 billion secured by lines of credit that guarantee rate payments from the data centers for 10 years. Electricity delivery The $3.1 billion in costs comes from two components of the electricity delivery system: transmission and distribution. Both include using poles and wires to move electricity from one place to another, but at different stages in the process. Transmission lines carry high-voltage electricity long distances along highways and across state lines from power plants to local substations where it can be reduced into lower-voltage electricity. Distribution lines then carry that electricity to the homes and businesses that use it. The data center connection costs are split roughly equally, with $1.6 billion expected in transmission costs and $1.5 million in distribution costs. The transmission costs for several individual projects each exceed $100 million, with one project alone expected to cost $289 million and another expected to cost $269 million. Max Leichtman, ComEd’s director of economic and workforce development, said only the distribution costs are an appropriate apples-to-apples comparison for the $721 million in deposits. Some of those projects won’t come online until 2030 or 2031 and are in early stages of development, so the full cost of equipment needed has not been calculated, he added. “The deposits that today stand at $721 million may continue to increase as these projects move forward and become more mature and more well-defined,” Leichtman said. “That doesn’t mean that’s all we’ll ever collect.” Leichtman said any remaining distribution costs would not be spread among all customers, but rather between similar types of customers in the large-user rate class. Consumer advocates, though, say the data center developers cannot be taken at their word to pay the bills. “These data centers are some of the wealthiest corporations in the world,” CUB spokesperson Jim Chilsen told reporters. “They always say, ‘Trust us, we’re going to pay our energy bills,’ but Illinois customers can’t afford to take big tech’s word for it.” Reducing speculation Hyperscale data centers’ requests for energy usage are often understood to be largely speculative. The massive projects — often operated by multibillion-dollar tech companies looking to compete in the race for artificial intelligence — sometimes place duplicate requests with different utilities, meaning some do not come to fruition. The projects have also faced growing opposition from local communities in recent years, causing many to withdraw. ComEd, in cooperation with Illinois and federal regulators, has sought to weed out speculative requests that drive up energy demand prices by requiring deposits for large customers and requiring them to sign long-term contracts known as transmission security agreements, or TSAs, that require customers to provide a line of credit guaranteeing payment of transmission rates for 10 years, even if the project does not materialize. Regulators approved ComEd’s TSA requirement in 2025, meaning that projects after that point have them in place. Of the total $1.6 billion in planned transmission costs, ComEd has $1.1 billion protected through transmission security agreements. Nineteen of the 30 projects pre-date the TSA requirement. Implementing the TSAs has also resulted in “substantial attrition” of data center requests in ComEd’s queue, Leichtman said. Payments now or later Like many of the utility watchdogs, ComEd also endorses the idea that large-load customers like data centers should be directly allocated the cost of their projects. The electric utility has proposed a new approach in which it would directly assign rates to individual data centers based on their costs rather than assigning costs within groups
