artigo.texto: ACME Solar Holdings Limited has commissioned an additional 17.91 MW/74.323 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) component for its Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) project in Rajasthan. The new installation was commissioned on October 23, 2026, with its commercial operation date scheduled for October 25, 2026. The project is being developed through ACME Sigma Urja Private Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of ACME Solar Holdings Limited. It is located in Village Neemri, Tehsil Rawatbhata, in the Chittorgarh district of Rajasthan. The BESS installation forms part of the project’s planned total discharge capacity of 250 MW/1,069 MWh. With this latest commissioning, ACME Solar Holdings has increased its cumulative commissioned battery energy storage capacity to 71.640 MW/297.292 MWh. The development represents further progress in implementing the energy storage component of its FDRE project. Battery energy storage systems play an important role in supporting renewable energy integration by storing electricity and making it available when required. These systems can help address the variability of solar and wind power generation by enabling electricity generated during periods of high renewable output to be used during periods of lower generation or increased demand. For FDRE projects, energy storage is particularly important because it helps developers deliver electricity according to scheduled requirements. Combining renewable energy generation with battery storage can improve the flexibility and reliability of power supply while supporting the integration of clean energy into the electricity grid. The commissioning of the additional BESS capacity brings ACME Solar Holdings closer to completing the planned storage capacity associated with the project. The company has now commissioned a cumulative 71.640 MW/297.292 MWh of battery storage capacity against the project’s total planned discharge capacity of 250 MW/1,069 MWh. The remaining capacity is expected to be commissioned in phases as project implementation progresses. The expansion of its commissioned storage portfolio reflects the company’s continued efforts to develop renewable energy projects supported by energy storage infrastructure. As India increases its renewable energy capacity, battery storage is expected to become increasingly important in managing fluctuations in generation, improving grid flexibility, and supporting the delivery of reliable electricity. artigo.texto: Trump says tech companies should pay Georgians thousands to host data centers ATLANTA, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - President Donald Trump said local communities should have approval power over booming data center projects and receive significant financial benefits from tech companies to offset their impact. Trump said in an exclusive one-on-one interview Saturday backstage in Perry that developers have the resources to support host towns. The rapid spread of energy-intensive data centers has become a flashpoint across Georgia, sparking voter pushback over rising electric bills and straining regional power grids. Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson previously broke with Trump on the issue, insisting local city and county leaders must have veto power over where campuses are built. Trump said he agrees with Jackson on local approval, arguing the solution to neighborhood resistance is simple: tech companies need to open their checkbooks. “I agree with that. No, I agree with that. And I think locals should be paid a lot of money for data centers,” Trump said. “When a data center goes in, I’ve seen it, people are very unhappy. All of a sudden, a data center decides to pay a community in the form of taxes, in the form of whatever — and all of a sudden, the same people love what they’re doing.” Trump acknowledged the global race for artificial intelligence, noting China is aggressively building competing infrastructure. He insisted tech giants have the capital to compensate local families directly. “We have to have them because you know who likes them? China,” Trump said. “China wants data centers, and they’re building them rapidly, and we’re beating China. But the data centers, they have money. They can pay local communities a lot.” Speaking before thousands in Houston County, Trump urged Georgia communities to demand substantial cash payouts. “And as far as data centers, we don’t want to get controversial,” Trump told the crowd. “The community that they’re being built in, they’re great. They give you a lot of money and everything. Ask for a lot of money. Tell them to pay you $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 for everybody that lives in the community. They’ll do it. You just gotta ask.” Trump cited an example in Louisiana where he claimed developer payouts flipped neighborhood opposition into support. “I saw one case in Louisiana where they were really fighting ... and then the company, I think it was Meta, they agreed to pay everybody $10,000,” Trump said. “And they went from, ‘we will not have it,’ to ‘do you have any more you want to bring?’ I’m telling you, just pay. Pay the people. Give them the money. They have so much money.” Trump then turned to Jackson on stage to address their policy alignment. “Do you agree with that, Rick? They’ll be very happy,” Trump said as Jackson looked on. “Rick’s a little bit tentative on that one. But no, they’ll be very happy.” The rally also served as the backdrop for major economic news. Backstage, Trump revealed to Atlanta News First that Audi plans to build its first U.S. manufacturing facility roughly 20 minutes from Perry. Gov. Brian Kemp later confirmed the German automaker will invest $4 billion in the Middle Georgia Megasite in Peach County, creating an estimated 4,500 jobs. U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., who is running for U.S. Senate, added that federal funding will ensure the Port of Brunswick is fully dredged to handle automotive exports from the new plant. Trump also addressed the U.S. Department of Justice’s notification that it is sending federal election monitors to six Democratic-majority Georgia counties, including Fulton, DeKalb and Gwinnett. Facing criticism from local election boards that the federal presence could intimidate voters, Trump defended the deployment. “They want to watch. You know, in Fulton County, you know that disaster,” Trump said. “They’re not going to do anything other than watch ... we want to all have honest elections.” On stage, Trump repeatedly targeted Democratic opponents, calling U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff a “radical-left extremist” and criticizing former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms over crime rates. Jackson echoed the sentiment, telling voters that “bad mayors don’t make good governors.” Trump suggested that if Jackson and Collins win, he would respond to calls to send the National Guard into Atlanta, which he labeled a “dangerous hellhole.” The Perry stop marked Trump’s second Georgia rally in recent weeks, aimed at energizing rural voters as early voting continues across the state. artigo.texto: Notícias O que a energia nuclear pode oferecer aos data centers O crescimento da inteligência artificial, da computação em nuvem e dos serviços digitais amplia a demanda por energia elétrica. Nesse cenário, a energia nuclear pode contribuir para o abastecimento de data centers, oferecendo geração contínua e baixa emissão de carbono. A possibilidade de integrar pequenos reatores modulares (SMRs, na sigla em inglês) e microrreatores a sistemas que combinam diferentes fontes de energia foi apresentada pela superintendente do IPEN, Isolda Costa, em evento realizado no Instituto de Engenharia, em São Paulo. Os SMRs podem atingir até 300 megawatts elétricos (MWe) por módulo, enquanto os microrreatores geralmente têm potência de até 10 MWe, conforme referências da Agência Internacional de Energia Atômica (AIEA). Essas tecnologias ampliam as possibilidades de fornecimento de energia em diferentes escalas, inclusive para instalações menores ou em locais com limitações de acesso à rede elétrica. A implantação dessas soluções exige avaliar fatores como demanda energética, custos, prazos, segurança, licenciamento, combustível, disponibilidade de água para resfriamento e gestão de rejeitos. A integração com fontes renováveis e sistemas de armazenamento também pode fazer parte do planejamento. A contribuição do IPEN O IPEN pode contribuir para o avanço de estudos sobre a aplicação da energia nuclear em data centers no Brasil, com pesquisas em materiais e formação de competências técnicas. Entre as possibilidades estão o fornecimento de energia nuclear pela rede elétrica, o planejamento de polos digitais associados a projetos de pequenos reatores e a avaliação de microrreatores para demandas localizadas. A viabilidade de cada alternativa depende de estudos técnicos e econômicos, além da disponibilidade de infraestrutura e de profissionais qualificados. A energia nuclear pode ampliar as opções para atender ao crescimento da infraestrutura digital com fornecimento firme e baixa emissão de carbono. O desafio é identificar as aplicações adequadas e demonstrar sua viabilidade para as necessidades brasileiras. Sem energia, não existe nuvem. A infraestrutura que construímos hoje precisa sustentar o mundo digital das próximas décadas.

artigo.texto: Power Brookfield Boosts Global Role in Batteries, Data Centers Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $80 billion worth of active and proposed projects worldwide from Brookfield and its subsidiaries Released Tuesday, October 27, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Two major acquisitions announced this year by Brookfield point to where the company is building out its presence, both in North America and globally: the battery-storage and data center markets, with the latter finding a new foothold in the Middle East. Charging Up the Battery Sector Brookfield Corporation, the parent company of Brookfield Asset Management Limited and Brookfield Renewable Partners, is broadening its role in the battery-storage and data center markets through its recent acquisitions of Aypa Power and Oaktree Capital Management, respectively. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $80 billion worth of active and proposed projects worldwide from Brookfield and its subsidiaries, including more than $28 billion worth focused on renewables, as well as more than $11 billion worth from Aypa. According to Industrial Info Resources data, Brookfield Renewable already is party to about $18.5 billion worth of battery energy-storage system (BESS) projects in development; the addition of Aypa, the largest stand-alone battery-storage developer in North America, will take that number to nearly $30 billion. Aypa's ongoing projects include two Canadian stand-alone BESS units that started construction over the summer: a unit in Elora, Ontario, which is designed to hold up to 211 megawatts (MW), and the Hedley unit in Jarvis, Ontario, which is designed to hold up to 200 MW. Both units will utilize lithium-ion containers and are set to wrap in the second quarter of 2027. The primary customer for both projects is Ontario's Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO). Industrial Info Resources offers more information on these units in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Plant and Project databases, where readers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in reports for the Elora and Jarvis projects. Brookfield Renewable's own projects in this field include the Star Dairy Solar Plant in Paris, Texas, which comprises 149 MW of generation from photovoltaic (PV) panels and a 205-MW BESS unit. The project, which is managed by X-Elio North America Incorporated, which Brookfield acquired in 2023, is set to begin construction early next year. Subscribers can learn more from a plant profile and a detailed project report. Aypa currently is owned by The Blackstone Group, which announced earlier this year it would sell its subsidiary to Brookfield for an enterprise value of about $7 billion. For more information on this deal and Blackstone's own fortunes, see October 23, 2026, article - Blackstone Upbeat on Long-Term Outlook for U.S. Data Centers. By the Numbers - More than $80 billion: Total value of active and proposed projects worldwide from Brookfield and its subsidiaries - More than $11 billion: Total value of active and proposed projects across North America from Aypa - About $7 billion: Enterprise value of Brookfield's acquisition of Aypa from Blackstone Eyeing a Global Role Brookfield's expansions go beyond the power-generation market. The company recently acquired the remaining 26% stake in Oaktree, giving it full ownership of a firm that can provide it with a broader slate of global financing and credit solutions. The deal also establishes the U.S. as Brookfield's biggest market, accounting for nearly half of its total revenue. The Oaktree acquisition already is bearing fruit: Brookfield is in the process of opening a new office in Doha, Qatar, bolstered by its strengthened global credit platform. Brookfield already manages roughly US$20 billion of assets within the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council, according to the company. That amount could be doubled through Brookfield's emerging partnership with Qai, a subsidiary of Qatar Investment Authority that focuses on AI infrastructure projects in Qatar and abroad. The Qatar deal complements Brookfield's increasing global approach to the data center market. One of its portfolio companies, DCI Data Centers, is preparing to expand of its Eastern Creek Data Center in New South Wales, Australia, to improve cloud data services in the region. The facility already handles 11 MW of load, and the expansions will bring it up to 64 MW. Subscribers can learn more from a plant profile and project report. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects from Brookfield worldwide. Key Takeaways - Brookfield is broadening its role in the battery-storage and data center markets through two recent acquisitions. - Aypa's BESS projects include two Canadian stand-alone BESS units that started construction over the summer. - Brookfield's acquisition of Oaktree complements its increasing global approach to the data center market. artigo.texto: As rack densities climb toward 1 MW and beyond, traditional low-voltage alternating current (AC) architecture is being pushed into territory it wasn't originally designed to handle. A primary reason the industry is increasingly looking toward 800 VDC to support the next generation of high-density compute. But the bigger question isn't whether direct current (DC) can power these new racks. It's where the conversion to DC should happen and how much of the traditional power architecture is still necessary. Sidecars offer a bridge to 800 VDC One near-term answer is the sidecar, a power-conversion unit positioned next to the compute rack. Sidecars give operators a practical way to introduce 800 VDC racks into facilities built around existing low-voltage AC distribution. Rather than redesigning the facility, operators can convert AC power to DC beside the rack. That makes sidecars an important bridge between today's infrastructure and emerging DC compute. But much of the existing electrical architecture remains in place. Power still moves through transformers and low-voltage UPS infrastructure before another conversion takes place near the rack. Each stage introduces losses and nearly all of that lost energy ultimately turns into heat, putting more pressure on the cooling system to remove it. SMA's white paper models the difference. In the architecture studied, delivering 1 MW through a traditional AC system with rack-level conversion results in approximately 80 kW of power loss per megawatt delivered to the rack. Converting medium-voltage AC to 800 VDC outside the building and distributing DC directly reduces that loss to approximately 20 kW. At data center scale, the difference becomes more than significant. Moving power infrastructure outside Efficiency is only part of the equation. Data center operators are also under pressure to maximize one of their most valuable resources: white space. A native DC architecture takes a different approach. Instead of generating 800 VDC beside the rack, conversion from medium-voltage AC to DC happens once, outside the data center building. Native 800 VDC is then distributed throughout the facility. Much of the supporting electrical infrastructure can move outside as well, including power-conversion equipment, switchgear and energy storage. Inside, the architecture becomes more simplified: compute, cooling and DC busway. There are fewer conversion stages, fewer pieces of electrical equipment and more room for compute. Rethinking redundancy and energy storage Any new data center architecture still must meet demanding resilience requirements. DC creates new options. A rack can be supplied by two independent DC paths, each capable of carrying the full load. During normal operation, both can remain active and share the load. Unlike AC sources, DC sources don't have phases that must be synchronized. With the appropriate protection architecture, both sources can continuously supply the rack, potentially eliminating the need for a traditional transfer event. Sharing the load between two paths also reduces current on each path, helping lower electrical losses without sacrificing redundancy. Moving energy storage outside the building can expand its role. Instead of primarily waiting to provide backup power, storage integrated into an external DC power system can help smooth large power swings from AI workloads, provide ride-through during grid disturbances and control how quickly a facility returns to full power following an event. Depending on the system and market, storage could also support other grid services. Designing power around compute Sidecars have an important role as data centers begin adopting 800 VDC. They provide a practical way to deploy new compute infrastructure without rebuilding existing electrical systems. But the longer-term opportunity is bigger than changing the voltage delivered to the rack. Moving conversion outside the building and distributing native DC can reduce conversion stages and electrical losses, free up valuable space for compute, simplify redundancy and give energy storage a more active role. For an industry racing to add enormous amounts of computing capacity, those aren't incremental changes. They represent an opportunity to rethink data center power architecture from the grid to the rack.

artigo.texto: Georgia leaders call on EPA to curb diesel generator emissions at data centers U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock and U.S. Rep. Hank Johnson called on the Environmental Protection Agency to immediately begin regulating the emissions of diesel generators that many data center operators are using for backup power and during peak times of electricity demand, arguing that the pollution poses significant harm to surrounding communities. In a letter dated Oct. 22, the Georgia Democratic leaders criticized the EPA for failing to oversee the generators, hundreds of which are being used at data center sites in Georgia alone. Even if the generators operate within state emission standards, their collective nitric oxide emissions would more than double that of Georgia Power’s two large coal-fired power plants, they wrote. artigo.texto: Moms in Western Henrico lead opposition to proposed Goochland data centers HENRICO, Va. (WWBT) - A group of mothers in Henrico are working to inform neighbors about proposed data center developments planned across the county line in Goochland. The women live in Henrico, near the Goochland County line. They are opposing data center campuses that could be built a few miles from their homes. “I feel like it’s just way too close to too many families,” Courtney Dare said. Last November, Goochland county officials approved it’s Technology Overlay District, an area zoned specifically for data center development. A pre-application was recently filed to build the Tuckahoe Tech Park, a nearly 900-acre data center campus along Route 6/Patterson Avenue. It would sit in a part of the Tech Overlay District known as ‘TOD West.’ That means it needs a conditional use permit to be built and would have to go through a public approval process. Back in the summer, when early plans were filed for the tech park, 12 On Your Side spoke with homeowners in the Mosaic at West Creek neighborhood in Goochland, who also live close to proposed Tuckahoe Tech Park. Regulatory filings by Dominion Energy to the SCC show developers have expressed interest in a few other data center projects that could be built by-right in the TOD. It includes a 1,000 acre campus within miles of where these moms live. One of the moms involved, Jennifer Butner, said her top concern is the back-up diesel generators used at these facilities. “They will have hundreds of generators that frankly the county will properly have very little control over when they are run,” Butner said. “And those generators are going to be within a mile of my children’s elementary school and my neighborhood and they’re going to be breathing in toxic fumes.” In addition to air quality concerns, the group said it is worried about noise, light pollution and the impact on home values. “There’s really been a lack of awareness in Henrico even though a lot of Henrico residents are going to be directly impacted,” Dare said. The group held a meeting last week to inform people about the proposals. Hundreds of neighbors attended, including elected officials from both Henrico and Goochland. A Goochland County spokesperson provided the following statement to 12 On Your Side when asked about the meeting: “We welcome the feedback and perspectives of all residents and interested stakeholders, including our neighbors in Henrico, on the important issues impacting Goochland County.” The group said it plans to continue its efforts, including attending the upcoming meetings with county officials in both Goochland and Henrico. “I personally think that it just needs to all slow down and I think the best way to do that is a moratorium. If that’s not possible, I want my state assembly members to put more of a restriction on where these data centers can be located,” Butner said. “We want to do whatever we can to protect our kids,” Robertson said. Goochland County is currently facing a lawsuit over the Tech Overlay District. Per the county’s website, there was a hearing on October 20 in Goochland County Circuit Court over the county’s request to dismiss the lawsuit. A ruling on the hearing has not been made yet. The Goochland Board of Supervisors also approved a motion on September 1 to re-examine what’s included in the TOD. It’s unclear how that review will affect projects proposed for the area. artigo.texto: The European Commission's new legislative package "Fit for 55" still needs to be approved by the EU member states and the European Parliament, but its main goals are already known and cover many key areas of the European Union's policy and economy. This is stated in an article by Iryna Stavchuk, Deputy Minister of Environmental Protection and Natural Resources of Ukraine. As is known, in July the European Commission published the "Fit for 55" legislative package aimed at revising the EU's current climate and energy targets for 2030. The package strengthens eight existing pieces of legislation and proposes five new initiatives across a range of policy areas and economic sectors: climate, energy and fuels, transport, buildings, land use and forestry, which will help achieve the set goal in the most effective way. Revision of the EU Emissions Trading System "Experience in recent years has shown that emissions trading is an effective and cost-efficient mechanism for reducing emissions, and the revenues it raises by auctioning emission allowances can be used by countries to support the transition to cleaner production and stimulate innovation," Stavchuk stressed. As noted, the "Fit for 55" package includes a proposal to lower the overall emissions cap further and increase the annual rate of reduction by gradually cutting the number of CO2 emission allowances (including free ones) granted to companies under the EU ETS. This should lead to a higher price per tonne of emissions and thus encourage companies to reduce emissions. It is also proposed to phase out free emission allowances for steel companies and sectors covered by CBAM, as well as for airlines, while including maritime shipping in the system from 2023. The argument is that a single ship produces as much carbon emissions as 8,000 cars a day. In addition, the EU intends to create a separate new emissions trading system for road transport and buildings heating and to start applying it from 2026. Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) One of the new proposals in the document is the creation of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which will set a price on imports of a limited number of polluting goods based on the carbon emissions generated during their production. "This measure is aimed at protecting European businesses from environmental dumping and preventing "carbon leakage" in situations where European companies want to relocate outside the EU to avoid paying for CO2 emissions. The mechanism is also intended to encourage industry outside the EU and to encourage the EU's international partners to take steps in the same direction," the Deputy Minister emphasised. She noted that CBAM will operate in addition to the European Emissions Trading System, but instead of allowances, special CBAM certificates will be introduced, which importers will buy in the EU according to the volume of emissions generated in the production of their goods. Certificate prices will be calculated on the basis of the average auction price of EU ETS allowances. CBAM will initially apply to imports of fertilisers, electricity, cement and metallurgical products (iron, steel, aluminium) and will take into account only direct emissions from production. As noted, these are the sectors with the highest CO2 emissions and high trade intensity, which creates a risk of "carbon leakage" to other countries. CBAM applies to companies from all non-EU countries, except those that participate in the European Emissions Trading System or have a national ETS linked to the EU one. This applies to members of the European Economic Area and Switzerland. At the same time, it is noted that Ukraine can count on special conditions, namely an exemption from CBAM in the energy sector. "The preamble of the document notes that as soon as third countries are closely integrated into the EU electricity market through market coupling, technical solutions should be found to ensure the application of CBAM to electricity exported from such countries into the customs territory of the Union. If no technical solutions can be found, third countries with market coupling should benefit from a temporary exemption from CBAM until 2030 at the latest, only for electricity exports, provided certain conditions are met. However, these third countries must develop a roadmap and commit to introducing a carbon pricing mechanism with a price equivalent to the EU ETS, and must commit to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050, so as to align it with Union legislation on the environment, climate, competition and energy. This exemption should be withdrawn at any time if there are grounds to believe that the country concerned is not fulfilling its commitments or has not adopted an ETS equivalent to the EU ETS by 2030," Stavchuk said. Changes in the transport sector As noted, the EU wants to ban the registration of new petrol and hybrid cars in the EU from 2035. It also plans to tighten CO2 emission standards for cars and vans, which will accelerate the transition to zero-emission mobility. From 2030, average emissions of new cars must fall by 55%, and by 100% from 2035, compared to 2021 levels. As a result, all new cars registered as of 2035 will be zero-emission. Under the revised Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation, the EU plans to ensure the necessary roll-out of interoperable and user-friendly infrastructure for charging and refuelling clean vehicles across the entire EU, keeping pace with market developments and guaranteeing that rural and remote areas are covered too. This is because consumers are increasingly buying electric vehicles. That is why it is proposed to build charging stations for electric vehicles every 60 kilometres along the EU's main motorways, and hydrogen refuelling stations every 150 kilometres. artigo.texto: Manejo adequado recupera pastagens e amplia estoque de carbono Experimentos de longa duração no interior paulista mostram que a intensificação moderada do pasto recupera a produtividade da terra e maximiza o sequestro de CO₂ Transformar pastos degradados em áreas férteis é um caminho prático para unir a produção pecuária à sustentabilidade ambiental. Experimentos de longa duração realizados no interior paulista revelam que ajustes simples no cuidado com o solo e na quantidade de animais não só recuperam a produtividade da terra, mas a convertem em um eficiente reservatório de carbono. Além de beneficiar o produtor, essa linha de pesquisa desenvolveu métodos mais simples e baratos para medir o carbono retido no solo, facilitando o futuro acesso de fazendeiros ao mercado de créditos de carbono. Os estudos fazem parte do Projeto Temático “Entendendo sistemas intensificados e integrados de produção: do mundo quântico à agricultura de baixa emissão de carbono”, apoiado pela Fapesp por meio do Programa Fapesp de Pesquisa sobre Mudanças Climáticas Globais, e coordenado pelo físico Ladislau Martin Neto, pesquisador da Embrapa Instrumentação, unidade de pesquisa da Empresa Brasileira de Pesquisa Agropecuária focada em unir a física, a química, a ciência dos materiais e as engenharias ao setor agropecuário. Para entender o impacto prático do manejo na retenção de carbono no solo, os pesquisadores compararam diferentes cenários de produção. As áreas avaliadas variaram desde pastagens degradadas –caracterizadas pela ausência de adubação e pelo pastejo contínuo do gado– até sistemas com diferentes níveis de tecnologia e intervenção. Esses modelos recuperados incluíram a chamada “intensificação moderada”, que combina a correção da acidez do solo, uso de fertilizantes e uma quantidade equilibrada de animais no pasto, e sistemas de alta intensificação, submetidos a irrigação artificial, doses elevadas de nitrogênio e uma grande densidade de gado. “Em uma das áreas estudadas, caracterizada como de moderada intensificação, o estoque de carbono no 1º metro do solo [a partir da superfície] aumentou de 102 para 162 toneladas por hectare entre 2011 e 2020 –um acréscimo médio de aproximadamente duas toneladas de carbono por hectare ao ano [em relação ao estoque da pastagem degradada]. Análises permitiram demonstrar que parte importante desse carbono adicional veio da própria forrageira [capim destinado à alimentação animal] cultivada na pastagem”, conta Martin Neto. A pesquisadora Patrícia Perondi Anchão Oliveira, que lidera o experimento, explica que o modelo vencedor em acúmulo de carbono (com doses moderadas de adubo e lotação equilibrada) não exige tecnologias inacessíveis. Pelo contrário, ele comprova a eficiência de uma fórmula familiar ao produtor brasileiro: a união de capins adaptados ao nosso clima com o gado de origem indiana, como o nelore. “Esse já é um caso de sucesso na pecuária brasileira, um sistema amplamente adotado pelos pecuaristas”, comenta a pesquisadora, ressaltando o potencial ambiental dessa base produtiva quando aliada ao manejo correto do solo. O objetivo dos pesquisadores foi descobrir não apenas quanto carbono havia sido acumulado no solo, mas como ele estava armazenado. Depois de mais de duas décadas de manejo, a pastagem apresentou 148 toneladas de carbono por hectare na forma de matéria orgânica associada aos minerais do solo, contra 92 toneladas na pastagem degradada. O resultado mostra o grande potencial de recuperação de áreas já convertidas para a pecuária. A relevância do achado está justamente em mostrar que é possível recuperar a qualidade de solos já degradados e aumentar sua capacidade de armazenar carbono sem que isso implique avançar sobre áreas de vegetação nativa. O título do projeto reúne duas vertentes que parecem, à 1ª vista, muito distantes. De um lado está o “mundo quântico”, no qual técnicas derivadas da física permitem investigar átomos, moléculas e interações entre a matéria orgânica e os minerais. Do outro, estão as extensas áreas de pastagens e o desafio de produzir com maior eficiência e menor emissão de gases de efeito estufa. É justamente a ligação entre essas escalas que orienta uma parte importante do projeto. “Trata-se de usar técnicas avançadas, como espectroscopias e outras, para pensar em uma situação real que beneficie simultaneamente o sistema produtivo e o planeta e motive a adoção pelo produtor”, diz Martin Neto. Segundo o pesquisador, os resultados –publicados na revista científica Geoderma– oferecem a perspectiva de remunerar produtores rurais pelo carbono adicional armazenado no solo de pastagens bem manejadas, por meio da geração e venda de créditos de carbono. Para isso, porém, é preciso demonstrar de forma confiável quanto carbono foi efetivamente incorporado ao solo e permanece ali. Onde o carbono se esconde Como explica Martin Neto, o solo é um ambiente extraordinariamente complexo. A matéria orgânica representa só uma pequena fração de sua massa, distribuída de forma extremamente heterogênea. “Saber que o teor de carbono aumentou, portanto, não responde a uma questão central para a mitigação climática. Esse carbono permanecerá ali por longo tempo ou será logo emitido para a atmosfera na forma de CO2?”, questiona o pesquisador. É preciso levar em conta que a matéria orgânica do solo se encontra em diferentes estágios de decomposição. Uma parte pode ser rapidamente metabolizada pelos microrganismos e devolver o carbono à atmosfera. Outra pode estabelecer interações com partículas minerais, especialmente argilas e óxidos de ferro e alumínio. Formam-se então associações organominerais que dificultam a decomposição e favorecem uma permanência mais longa do carbono no solo. “Hoje, sabemos pela ciência que um dos mecanismos mais importantes é justamente a associação da matéria orgânica com o componente mineral. Por meio de ligações e interações químicas, esse carbono pode ser retido por longo tempo. É isso que estamos procurando demonstrar”

artigo.texto: CCC chairs carbon markets panel The CCC’s chairmanship of the IACCM builds on its existing leadership functions in national climate policy and reporting. The Climate Change Commission (CCC) welcomes its designation as chair of the Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets (IACCM) under Executive Order (EO) 127, which establishes a governance framework for the Philippines’ participation in international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and in the Voluntary Carbon Market. Signed by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., EO 127 institutionalizes the country’s climate change mitigation efforts and seeks to unlock international climate finance. As IACCM chair, the CCC will guide inter-agency coordination and help ensure that carbon market policies support the Philippines’ Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), national greenhouse gas inventory, and climate transparency reporting obligations under the Paris Agreement. The Commission will also serve as the committee’s Secretariat and provide technical and administrative support. This move supports the direction set by the Philippine Development Plan 20230-2028, particularly Chapter 15 on accelerating climate action and strengthening disaster resilience. The chapter calls for stronger collaboration with the private sector and the international community to scale up sustainable and green investments. It also advances the transition to a low-carbon economy while promoting economic growth and resilience. “Carbon markets can help advance these goals by providing an additional channel for private capital and international climate finance. Credible carbon projects can support emissions reduction and other climate solutions. Clear rules and reliable accounting will help protect environmental integrity and give investors greater certainty,” said CCC vice chairperson and executive director Robert E.A. Borje. The CCC’s chairmanship builds on its existing leadership functions in national climate policy and reporting. As Secretariat of the NDC Technical Working Group, the Commission supports the assessment of sectoral policies and measures against the country’s NDC. It also supports the monitoring, reporting, and verification of NDC implementation and the fulfillment of national and international reporting requirements. Under Executive Order 174, s. 2014, the CCC serves as the overall lead agency for the Philippine National Greenhouse Gas Inventory. It coordinates and consolidates emissions data from sector lead agencies. This information provides an important evidence base for national climate policy and emissions accounting.

artigo.texto: How data centers became a bipartisan political issue in Wisconsin Data centers are a big issue across the country. As midterms approach, many look to the swing state of Wisconsin for lessons for how that issue could play out nationally. SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: In the center of the world... (CHEERING) PFEIFFER: ...That's where all sorts of Wisconsinites told me we were yesterday as they watched the Brewers win game one of the World Series. One of those people was Kristi Draver (ph). KRISTI DRAVER: Everybody knows it. Driving around Milwaukee, driving in from out of Milwaukee - everybody knows this is it, the center of the world, right here in Milwaukee. PFEIFFER: And I'm in Milwaukee today, hosting this program from NPR member station WUWM. Wisconsin, along with its Brewers fame, is known for its pivotal role in U.S. politics because of its rust belt geography and its urban rural divides. The midterms are 10 days from now, and Wisconsin is front and center on a contentious national issue, data centers. Many voters on the left and right dislike them, and midterm candidates are having to adapt. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) TOM TIFFANY: I have been consistent over the last year that we are not going to pay those subsidies to these companies. He just came around in the last week when he figured out, that's where the public is. I will not put my finger to the wind when making decisions like... PFEIFFER: That was the Republican contender for Wisconsin governor Tom Tiffany in this week's gubernatorial debate here. Just last week, the city of Milwaukee enacted a one-year moratorium on new data center construction. WUWM's Eddie Morales has been covering this, and he's with me in his station's studios right here in Milwaukee. Hi, Eddie. EDDIE MORALES, BYLINE: Hi, Sacha. PFEIFFER: What prompted this moratorium? MORALES: So there was a proposal to turn a vacant Walmart into a data center, and local community organizers - they rallied to stop that developer. Then residents mobilized in favor of a moratorium, with dozens coming to speak at city meetings. It's just one of several cities in Wisconsin to actually pause new data center construction. There are more than 50 different kinds of data centers already in Wisconsin, and the businesses who want to develop more say their projects will help stimulate the economy. PFEIFFER: This is definitely not the first time there's been backlash in Wisconsin to big tech companies coming in. Some of our listeners might remember the name Foxconn. Tell us about that history. MORALES: Yeah, so part of the reason why the anti-tech sentiment has been so quick and so strong here is because of that Foxconn deal. It was during President Trump's first term when he championed a massive project by the tech manufacturer Foxconn. The deal was supposed to bring more than 10,000 jobs to Wisconsin, and the state offered this substantial incentives package. But the company then dramatically shifted their plans. There was this public outcry, and it became a political mess for the governor's office, and it created this legacy of mistrust for Big Tech in Wisconsin. PFEIFFER: And, Eddie, as you know, the data center issue has even reached the governor's race. I've heard this week this ad with one candidate calling the other Data Center Dave - not a compliment. What's going on there? MORALES: Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany have accused each other of being too supportive of the data center industry, as we heard in that clip in your intro. Now, both candidates are trying to position each other as flip-floppers. PFEIFFER: There are different kinds of data centers. The new ones are the big hyper-scale ones people are concerned about, but I understand you've been on a tour of a different, more traditional one. What did you see? MORALES: Right, it was Potawatomi's Data Holdings. So that's on land that's owned by the Potawatomi tribe. And the building is really interesting. It has this design of a brick facade and fake windows that match the neighborhood's aesthetic. It's a 46,000-square-foot data center. It's small compared to the much bigger sites that are being built around the country for AI processing and that have been a little bit more in the public eye. The manager, Ryan Brooks - he took me on a tour, and while we were there, he told me that he's actually for the moratorium. PFEIFFER: The manager? - the management told you they're for the moratorium. MORALES: Mm-hmm. Well, he strongly supports data center regulations because he doesn't want more of the huge - what they call - hyperscale AI data centers versus his smaller data center, which has been operating for years. He's kind of worried about his business. RYAN BROOKS: The number of these large hyperscalers that are coming into town, the amount of power that they require - or coming into the state, even - the amount of power that they require is more than is planned by all the energy providers in your state. So someone's not going to make it. MORALES: So he thinks some of the other companies building the huge new sites don't have the community in mind, and he says his company is built on tribal land, so it's there to stay. But of course, his company does have its own incentives to take a position in this moment. PFEIFFER: Eddie, for communities who have been going through this, what have they learned? Any lessons here? MORALES: Well, Milwaukee, like in many places - it doesn't have the regulatory structures and the zoning laws in place to really manage the goals of huge new - of these huge companies who really want things done fast. And data centers, they can provide a lot of jobs, mostly construction jobs needed to build them, but then often it's just a very small number of jobs to maintain them. So different communities can offer a range of incentives to keep generating revenue like property taxes. But these centers can also create a lot of strain on a municipality's resources, and the public has been worried

artigo.texto: Researchers have synthesized strontium divanadate (SrV2O6) nanoparticles through a sol–gel method and reported that the material performs well in two demanding roles at once: storing electrical charge in supercapacitors and breaking down organic dye pollutants under light irradiation. The study, published in the journal Ionics, describes a pure crystalline structure with a uniform elemental distribution across the nanoparticles, a combination the authors identify as the foundation for the material's dual functionality. According to the study, the sol–gel preparation yielded nanoparticles with this uniform elemental distribution, giving the team a well-defined material to test in both electrochemical and photocatalytic measurements. On the energy storage side, the nanoparticles delivered high specific capacitance together with good rate capability, meaning the material retained its charge-storage performance as the operating conditions became more demanding. The authors characterize the overall energy and power densities as moderate, positioning the compound as a candidate rather than a finished electrode material. Two headline figures stand out from the electrochemical testing. The measured energy density reached a maximum of 3.14 Wh/kg, while the power density reached 1046 W/kg. The authors highlight the power figure in particular as evidence of the material's potential for high-power energy storage devices. The optical and electronic properties underpin the second application. SrV2O6 exhibited a band gap of 2.16 eV, which the study links to good light absorption and semiconducting behaviour. When illuminated, the material generated reactive oxygen species efficiently, and these reactive species, combined with favourable surface interactions, drove the photocatalytic degradation of two common organic dyes. Efficient charge separation within the semiconductor is cited as the mechanism that keeps the reactive species production going. The degradation results were substantial in the laboratory tests. The nanoparticles degraded 90 percent of methylene blue and 94 percent of brilliant green under light irradiation, performance the authors attribute to the reactive oxygen species generation and the favourable surface interactions between the dye molecules and the nanoparticle surfaces. The findings are measured observations from a laboratory study of the synthesized nanoparticles, not demonstrations in operating devices or field-scale water treatment. The abstract itself flags two practical limitations: relatively poor electrical conductivity and particle agglomeration. To push the electrochemical performance further, the authors point to controlling the particle morphology and minimizing agglomeration as promising strategies. Within the scope of the reported results, SrV2O6 emerges as a promising multifunctional material for both energy storage and environmental remediation applications, with the caveat that overcoming its conductivity and aggregation limits will determine whether that promise survives outside the synthesis laboratory. artigo.texto: Data Centers Bring Boom Times, But Will Gains Last? Data center projects can bring major capital investment to smaller markets, but lasting economic returns depend on realistic job expectations and protection against public cost exposure. Data center expansion is giving smaller US communities access to major investment opportunities, but it is also testing their ability to support power-intensive developments and secure lasting economic benefits. For local leaders, the calculation extends beyond the size of a construction budget or a headline investment announcement. Utility capacity, workforce availability, water resources, and the allocation of infrastructure costs can determine whether a project strengthens the local economy or leaves residents carrying expenses that outlast the initial building boom. A report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility and Heartland Forward examines these investment-readiness challenges across smaller communities. While the analysis addresses economic development broadly, it emphasizes the infrastructure and institutional capacity required to absorb major investment. “One of the central findings of our research is that attracting investment and generating lasting economic value are not necessarily the same thing,” Dominic Williams, a report author and senior expert at consulting firm McKinsey, told Data Center Knowledge. Looking Past the Headline Investment The report focuses on micropolitan communities with urban cores of 10,000 to 49,999 residents. Its framework assesses economic conditions, community assets and systems, and coordination among economic development institutions. Williams said smaller communities often have fewer institutions and less redundancy, making infrastructure or workforce gaps particularly consequential when a large project arrives. “Local leaders should take a comprehensive view of the costs and benefits associated with any potential investment, rather than focusing exclusively on the headline capital expenditure or the number of jobs announced,” he said. For data center proposals, that means distinguishing construction activity from ongoing employment and considering whether incentives or public infrastructure spending would produce greater benefits elsewhere. “A large construction project may generate substantial near-term activity but relatively fewer permanent positions once operational,” Williams said. Power Availability Pushes Development into Smaller Markets Developers’ search for sites they can bring online is widening the geography of data center investment, according to Sean Farney, vice president of data center strategy at commercial real estate services firm JLL. “With time-to-revenue driving site selection, the gulf between small and large cities vis-à-vis new development has shrunk considerably,” he told Data Center Knowledge. Power constraints, community opposition, and market saturation have pushed developers toward alternative locations. Farney pointed to activity in Abilene, Texas, Fort Wayne, Indiana, and Wisconsin’s Lake Michigan corridor. He argued that communities should account for spending generated by ongoing operations alongside construction and direct employment. Facilities require mechanical, electrical, and plumbing maintenance, as well as security, cleaning, and other services throughout their operating lives. “The spend just starts with construction,” Farney said. For local businesses, the opportunity includes securing recurring service contracts. Farney also identified spending on hotels, restaurants, and housing, as well as tax revenue and infrastructure improvements, as components of the economic benefits communities should evaluate. Measuring What Actually Stays Local Those opportunities require scrutiny of which benefits will remain in the community, Ruthbea Yesner, group vice president for worldwide public sector at analyst firm IDC, told Data Center Knowledge. “The deciding factors are power, broadband, and water, not land or tax appetite,” she said. Communities risk overextending themselves when they accept projects before utilities commit to supply and distribution upgrades required to support them. Water availability and workforce capacity also need to be assessed before development proceeds. Yesner cautioned against treating construction employment as a permanent expansion of the local jobs base. Workers may need to relocate to find comparable employment after a facility is completed, while direct operating teams can be relatively small. “My opinion is that small cities often undervalue what they are offering and potentially overvalue what they are receiving,” she said. Yesner recommended that communities enter negotiations with specific infrastructure priorities in mind. Local leaders should examine opportunities for electrical contractors, HVAC providers, fiber businesses, and other suppliers, while avoiding the assumption that broader industry-wide employment effects will necessarily materialize locally. Locking in Benefits Beyond the Build Yesner advised communities to use written infrastructure commitments, public reporting on resource consumption, and protections against stalled projects. Potential safeguards include incentive clawbacks, cost-overrun sharing arrangements, and bonds covering decommissioning and site restoration. Williams similarly recommended linking incentives to verified investment milestones and establishing developers’ responsibilities for infrastructure upgrades. “Communities should also consider how infrastructure investments can serve broader local needs rather than being designed exclusively around a single development,” Williams added. Workforce partnerships can extend the benefits. Developers, community colleges, and local employers can build pathways into electrical, technical, and maintenance occupations, while procurement arrangements can create opportunities for local suppliers. artigo.texto: AURORA | City council again delayed an indefinite moratorium on data centers, although the pause will not apply to the contentious Trident project, which is considering other locations. On Monday, a split council rejected the opportunity to vote on an indefinite moratorium, despite more than 50 people who signed up to speak in favor of the data center pauses. Council members Rob Andrews, Francoise Bergan, Curtis Gardner, Stephanie Hancock and Angela Lawson voted against allowing the council to reconsider the moratorium, while Mayor Mike Coffman and council members Alison Coombs, Gianina Horton, Alli Jackson, Ruben Medina and Amy Wiles supported the moratorium. Due to meeting procedure protocol, the council needed seven votes to discuss and vote on reconsidering a moratorium. The proposal was a pause on accepting data center applications until the city has implemented new regulations, but does not provide a specific timeline. It is the latest version of a moratorium after the council rejected a six-month pause in August. Following Monday’s vote, Coffman said he plans to bring the reconsideration back to council at the Nov. 9 meeting. Since the council voted against the reconsideration, members did not discuss the proposal. Council’s reconsideration is largely driven by the swell of public backlash against the planned Trident data center, which has applied to build near the Windler and Green Valley Ranch neighborhoods, including a senior housing community. City officials said the moratorium will not impact the Trident data center at its current location or any future location because the city has already accepted its application for development. Before the meeting, Vantage Data Centers, which is developing the Trident facility, requested the council pause new regulations for 90-days while the company looks for alternative locations. No other locations have been identified yet. “In the spirit of being a constructive partner and working collaboratively, Vantage is going to evaluate the technical and operational feasibility of locating the data center on sites further from residentially zoned parcels, where appropriate opportunities may exist,” Matthew Clark, senior manager of public policy for Vantage, said in the letter. In its letter, Vantage says new regulations, like the moratorium, could “hinder our efforts and lead to a negative outcome for both the residents of Aurora and Vantage.” Vantage previously said the company is working with Xcel Energy and the city to evaluate other locations to see if they meet the technical, energy and operational requirements needed for the facility. “At the same time, we continue to advance the current site, which is appropriately zoned for data center use and remains under review through the city’s established development process. No decision has been made to relocate the project,” Mark Freeman, vice president for global marketing at Vantage, said in a statement. “We remain committed to listening to the community and collaborating with local leaders and our partners as we evaluate the best path forward.” At the meeting on Monday, dozens of residents of Windler and Green Valley Ranch communities attended the meeting to support the moratorium and erupted in shouts of “Shame” after the vote. “We needed this moratorium and you all failed us,” Gary Zimmerman said, while his neighbors cheered in agreement. Beyond the moratorium, the council unanimously gave final approval to change which zoning data centers can build in to prohibit the facilities from the mixed use office-industrial areas. The change doesn’t impact Trident. Council discusses residential distance buffer At the study session before the regular meeting, council moved forward a residential buffer that bans data centers within 750 feet of homes and makes them a conditional use between 750 feet and a half-mile away from homes. As a conditional use, data centers looking to build within the specified range will be required to have public hearings and approval is dependent on meeting certain requirements. The proposal, put forward by Wiles, would allow data centers as a use by right if they were located in approved zoning and more than a half-mile from houses. As a use by right, data centers would go through an administrative approval process that does not typically require a public hearing. Data centers would still be limited to certain zoning, including industrial and airport zoning, and the residential buffer would serve as an additional setback from residents. The proposed setback distance is an increase from previous council conversations that focused on a 350-foot residential buffer. The new regulations also include a requirement for data centers to conduct noise modeling studies. Wiles’ suggestion was contentious among some council members, with Gardner, Bergan, Lawson and Hancock questioning how the buffer distance was calculated and whether the changes would impact Vantage’s ability to relocate. Vantage requested the city council pause new regulations for 90-days. City Attorney Pete Schulte said the buffer wouldn’t apply to existing applications and the city would consider any new location as an amended application, not a new one, so the regulations still wouldn’t apply to a different site. City Manager Jason Batchelor said the new regulations wouldn’t apply to several existing data centers, including JP Morgan Chase, QTS, Trident and data centers included in master plans. Additionally, the earliest the proposed residential buffer could be implemented would be in February, after Vantage’s 90-day request, Wiles said. artigo.texto: O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva destacou a matriz energética renovável do Brasil como trunfo para atrair data centers e construir uma inteligência artificial nacional em seu primeiro discurso após a vitória eleitoral no domingo (25). Durante o pronunciamento, o presidente afirmou que o país precisa deixar de apenas consumir tecnologia estrangeira para processar os próprios dados. “Eu não quero ficar dependendo da inteligência artificial chinesa ou americana, eu quero criar uma brasileira”, declarou Lula. Ele defendeu que empresas que se instalarem no país reservem parte da infraestrutura de computação para a demanda interna. Soberania digital e matriz limpa A estratégia vincula a abundância de fontes limpas no Brasil ao desenvolvimento da economia digital e da infraestrutura de ponta. O objetivo anunciado é impedir que a maior capacidade de energia renovável do mundo seja exportada como insumo bruto enquanto o país depende de centros de dados situados no exterior. Para o governo federal, a inteligência artificial deixa de ser uma promessa abstrata e passa a integrar a agenda de soberania tecnológica. Segundo a cobertura do setor, a meta é garantir que o processamento digital ocorra em território nacional, fortalecendo a pesquisa científica e o setor produtivo. Regras do Redata para o mercado interno A atração dessas estruturas tem base na Lei 15.504/2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter. O programa suspende tributos federais como PIS/Cofins, IPI e Imposto de Importação na aquisição de equipamentos para empreendimentos do setor. Em contrapartida, as empresas beneficiadas devem atender toda a sua demanda de energia por meio de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A legislação também estabelece compromissos diretos com a indústria e a pesquisa nacionais. Pelas regras do regime, ao menos 10% da capacidade de processamento incentivada deve ser destinada ao mercado interno, ao setor público ou a instituições de pesquisa. Além disso, as beneficiárias precisam investir o equivalente a 2% do valor dos equipamentos em projetos de pesquisa e desenvolvimento no Brasil. Os compromissos de atendimento e investimento podem ter redução de 20% para projetos instalados nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste. A medida busca descentralizar os investimentos e expandir a infraestrutura digital pelo interior do país.

artigo.texto: The Receipts: Air quality and representation fears rise with Taylor's data center AUSTIN, Texas — The Taylor City Council has approved a development agreement that could pave the way for a 664-acre data center campus just outside city limits, raising questions for neighbors who say they may feel the impact but have no voice in the process. CBS Austin has been investigating the proposed Taylor Technology Campus after residents reached out with concerns about noise, air quality and representation. Families living near the site say the project could alter the quiet, rural setting they have known for generations. "We wanted the fresh air, openness. We wanted a quiet life," said Connie Zycha, who lives directly across from the proposed campus. Zycha said her family has lived on their land for more than 140 years. "I won’t be able to sit in my front yard and watch the sunset. I won’t be able to watch the storms roll in or hear the train go by," she said. Neighbors near the site may attend council meetings and voice their opinions, but because the area is outside the city, they cannot vote in city elections. "We don't have a vote. We can't impact what they do," Zycha said. She added, "We don’t have a voice. We can’t yell at them and say, hey, we’re gonna vote you out. Because we can’t." Taylor officials said the agreement would allow the city to annex the land and apply specific regulations for the project. Daniel Seguin, executive director of community services for the City of Taylor, said the goal has been to deliver protections for people living nearby, even though they are outside city limits. "What our Taylor council has said is that their goal is to protect surrounding neighbors and the way that they were gonna do that is to negotiate for protections and ensure that this development is in city limits where regulations will apply," Seguin said. Seguin said the council worked to ensure the agreement included environmental protections and requirements for monitoring and enforcement. He explained that water for the data center would not be pulled from wells, addressing a concern raised by some nearby residents. "They will not be drilling wells. They're not gonna be accessing the aquifer beneath Taylor or impacting anyone's well water," he said. Air quality is also a major concern. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality said it has received Big Watt Digital’s application for an air permit for the campus’ natural gas electric generators but has not yet begun a technical review. Seguin said each natural gas generator will have its own air quality monitoring of the exhaust and the city is required to submit monthly reports to TCEQ. "Natural gas is unique in that it's one of the cleanest burning fossil fuels that is available, that exists," Seguin said. In an emailed statement, Big Watt Digital and PowerHouse Data Centers said the campus is being designed with dedicated on-site power generation and reclaimed-water cooling. They also pointed to noise limits, testing and property-line setbacks, and said they take neighbors’ concerns seriously. Carrie D’Anna, a community organizer with Halt Taylor Centers, said many questions still need answers. "People can’t make informed decisions without having information," D’Anna said. She added, "It’s not so much as control as responsibility. Because it impacts me, it impacts my family, it impacts the communities around me." The agreement also sets rules for water use and wastewater and limits noise at the property line to 65 decibels or the predevelopment baseline, whichever is higher. Seguin said the city will monitor compliance at the property line and that landscaping buffers are planned to lessen visible and audible impacts. "They're gonna be constructing berms along the property on the south side where the residents are. They're also going to covering those berms with multiple layers of planting," he said. Some residents remain frustrated that, despite the regulations, major decisions are being made without their ability to participate in city elections. Zycha said, "We have it less than a thousand feet from our home...The county commissioners are our voice. Not one has come to my property and asked me what I thought. Or sent a letter. What do you expect? We haven’t heard from them." Terry Pierce, a retired priest who lives nearby, said, "The problem here is that we need to regulate data centers and any other development in the city to build what is best for the neighbors, what is the best for children in this city." He continued, "If the air quality is such that kids can’t play outside. That is not a trade-off that is what we need here. It’s not a fair trade." D’Anna echoed concerns about the pace and transparency of the project. "Right now we have the intention that we are going to put, you know, regulations on it, but the ordinances and the agreements that we have made precede the amendments that they’re creating on behalf of us," she said. According to the city, the council posted the draft agreement online for public review ahead of the vote. Seguin said they work to reflect community input. "When community members have come and expressed concerns at a council meeting, then it came to the presentation, council members would directly parrot the community's questions back to the developers and back to city staff," he said. The council approved the development agreement on Oct. 8. Annexation remains a future step. Seguin said new zoning rules that specifically cover data centers are in development, but they would not apply retroactively to this project. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality will review air permit applications and monitor compliance for the on-site generators. Williamson County stated it cannot zone or prohibit data centers and has no authority over Taylor's annexation of the area. artigo.texto: Leilões de baterias podem fortalecer cadeia de energias renováveis no RN A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) deve aprovar e publicar nesta terça-feira (27) os editais dos leilões de armazenamento de energia previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro deste ano. Esses certames têm potencial para ampliar investimentos, reduzir cortes forçados de geração e aumentar a flexibilidade operacional no Rio Grande do Norte, segundo entidades do setor de renováveis. Segundo a Aneel, os editais vão considerar as sugestões recebidas durante a consulta pública, aberta de 30 de julho a 14 de setembro. Ao todo, foram registradas mais de 80 manifestações de empresas e associações do segmento. O processo ocorrerá em plataforma on-line, sob responsabilidade da Aneel e da Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE). O objetivo é contratar a disponibilidade de potência de sistemas autônomos de armazenamento de energia elétrica. O Leilão nº 05/2026-ANEEL será exclusivo para projetos que comprovem o uso de baterias fabricadas no Brasil, com verificação a cargo do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). Já o Leilão nº 06/2026-ANEEL permitirá a participação de sistemas que não atendam ao critério de fabricação nacional. Na avaliação do presidente do Centro de Estratégias em Recursos Naturais e Energia (Cerne), Darlan Santos, a realização dos leilões abre uma janela de oportunidades para o Rio Grande do Norte, que já conta com regulamentação ambiental específica para sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS). Segundo ele, a norma garante segurança jurídica e celeridade no licenciamento. “Diante desse cenário, o estado possui projetos com viabilidade para disputar o leilão. Diversas empresas geradoras com atuação no território potiguar já desenvolveram projetos voltados à hibridização de seus parques eólicos e solares com sistemas BESS e estão prontas para competir em dezembro”, esclarece. O diretor de Novos Negócios da Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (ABEEólica), Marcello Cabral, também avalia que os leilões podem atrair investimentos e favorecer a integração das fontes renováveis ao sistema elétrico brasileiro. Entre os fatores que sustentam essa perspectiva estão a bonificação locacional de 10% para projetos conectados a determinados barramentos estratégicos do sistema elétrico e o interesse demonstrado pelo mercado. Dados divulgados pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) apontam 6.091 projetos cadastrados, totalizando 296,8 gigawatts (GW) de potência, dos quais mais de 70% estão localizados no Nordeste. Esses números correspondem à etapa de cadastramento. A participação efetiva nos leilões dependerá da habilitação dos empreendimentos, ressalta Cabral. Entre as exigências para os certames, estão funcionalidades de controle de tensão e frequência e a operação na estratégia grid-forming, que permite aos equipamentos contribuir para a formação e a estabilidade da rede elétrica. Os contratos dos leilões terão duração de 15 anos, com início do suprimento previsto para 1º de agosto de 2028. Os sistemas deverão ter potência mínima de 30 megawatts (MW) e estar disponíveis para despacho centralizado pelo ONS por períodos de até quatro horas. A operação poderá ser solicitada duas vezes ao dia, com intervalo que permita a recuperação total da carga em até seis horas. A remuneração será feita por meio de receita fixa, dividida em 12 parcelas mensais. As condições para a contratação foram estabelecidas pela Portaria Normativa GM/MME nº 136/2026. Governo monitora processo O Governo do RN também acompanha o processo e avalia que os leilões podem contribuir para conter os cortes forçados de geração, conhecidos como curtailment, ao permitir que a energia excedente seja armazenada nos períodos de alta produção e devolvida à rede nos horários de maior demanda. Em nota sobre os certames, o Executivo estadual aponta que os contratos de 15 anos podem reduzir os riscos relacionados ao escoamento da energia e estimular investimentos privados em parques híbridos, que combinam fontes eólicas, solares e baterias. O governo destaca ainda que a implantação desses sistemas pode fortalecer a cadeia local de fornecimento, operação e manutenção, atraindo empresas de engenharia eletroeletrônica, integração de sistemas e gestão digital de cargas. A expectativa é de criação de empregos técnicos qualificados, tanto durante as obras quanto na operação e manutenção dos equipamentos, além do estímulo ao ecossistema de inovação e transição energética do estado. Para Darlan Santos, a consolidação dos projetos BESS também “pavimenta o caminho” para a atração e instalação de datacenters no RN. Ele pondera, porém, que a competitividade e a viabilidade econômico-financeira dos empreendimentos dependem da solução de questões tributárias. “Torna-se urgente a resolução da cobrança do ICMS incidente sobre os sistemas de baterias, por meio da inclusão definitiva desses equipamentos no Convênio ICMS 101/97, garantindo isonomia fiscal com os demais componentes das fontes eólica e solar”, completa o presidente do Cerne. A Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar), diz que embora o armazenamento não resolva isoladamente o problema do curtailment, sua integração ao sistema elétrico pode ampliar a flexibilidade operacional, melhorar o aproveitamento da infraestrutura existente e criar condições mais favoráveis para novos projetos de geração limpa. “Os leilões também representam um passo fundamental para a consolidação do mercado brasileiro de armazenamento de energia, com potencial para ampliar a escala dos projetos, reduzir custos e desenvolver uma cadeia nacional de fornecedores, equipamentos e serviços especializados”, afirma a entidade.

artigo.texto: O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) destacou o potencial brasileiro de energia renovável para atrair data centers ao país em seu primeiro discurso após a vitória nas eleições presidenciais, na noite de domingo, 25 de outubro. Reeleito para um novo mandato de quatro anos, Lula também defendeu o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial nacional e a destinação de parte da capacidade dos centros de processamento de dados para atender à demanda brasileira. “Temos que aproveitar o potencial energético de um país que talvez seja o que tenha mais capacidade de energia renovável”, afirmou o presidente, ao defender a instalação de data centers no Brasil. >> Relembre os planos de Lula para o setor energético Lula disse ainda que as empresas terão de reservar parte dessas estruturas para informações brasileiras. A declaração ocorreu durante um trecho do discurso dedicado à educação e ao desenvolvimento tecnológico. “Eu não quero ficar dependendo da inteligência artificial chinesa ou americana, eu quero criar uma brasileira”, afirmou. O presidente também defendeu investimentos na economia digital, na economia verde e na economia criativa, ao apresentar prioridades para o próximo mandato. Redata foi citado A atração de data centers faz parte da política do governo federal. Em setembro, Lula sancionou a Lei 15.504/2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), com incentivos fiscais para a instalação, modernização e ampliação dessas estruturas no país. O programa prevê a suspensão de tributos federais na aquisição de equipamentos e componentes utilizados nos empreendimentos, incluindo PIS/Cofins, Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI) e Imposto de Importação, observadas as condições previstas na legislação. Para acessar os benefícios, as empresas deverão atender à totalidade de sua demanda de energia elétrica por meio de contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução a partir de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A legislação também estabelece critérios de sustentabilidade e eficiência no consumo de água. Outra contrapartida prevista no Redata é a disponibilização ao mercado interno de pelo menos 10% dos serviços de processamento, armazenagem e tratamento de dados instalados com os incentivos. A capacidade poderá ser comercializada no Brasil ou cedida a instituições científicas e tecnológicas e ao poder público. A lei permite substituir essa obrigação por um investimento adicional equivalente a 10% do valor dos equipamentos adquiridos com o benefício fiscal em projetos de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. Independentemente dessa alternativa, as empresas deverão destinar 2% do valor das aquisições incentivadas a projetos de pesquisa e desenvolvimento tecnológico no país. Os compromissos de atendimento ao mercado interno e de investimentos em pesquisa poderão ser reduzidos em 20% para empreendimentos instalados nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste.
