artigo.texto: O mercado global de colocation para data centers deve crescer de US$ 124,47 bilhões em 2026 para US$ 222,97 bilhões em 2031, com taxa de crescimento anual composta (CAGR) de 12,4% no período. A projeção é de um estudo da MarketsandMarkets, que aponta a expansão da computação em nuvem, o aumento do volume de dados e a transformação digital das empresas entre os fatores que sustentam a demanda pelo serviço. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – AbraCloud pede regulamentação acelerada do Redata O modelo de colocation permite que empresas utilizem instalações de terceiros para hospedar seus equipamentos de tecnologia, com acesso a energia elétrica, refrigeração, conectividade e infraestrutura física, sem precisar investir na construção e na operação de data centers próprios. A modalidade também atende organizações que buscam ampliar sua capacidade de processamento de acordo com as necessidades do negócio. Segundo a análise, a adoção de ambientes híbridos e multicloud contribui para ampliar a procura por instalações que ofereçam conexões diretas com provedores de nuvem, redes de telecomunicações e outras plataformas digitais. Ao mesmo tempo, o crescimento das aplicações de inteligência artificial (IA) e computação de alto desempenho (HPC) aumenta a necessidade de infraestrutura com maior densidade de potência, sistemas avançados de refrigeração e disponibilidade energética. TI de uso geral concentra a maior participação Entre os segmentos analisados, a infraestrutura voltada à TI de uso geral deve manter a maior participação no mercado durante o período projetado. A categoria abrange cargas de trabalho tradicionais de processamento, armazenamento e redes, utilizadas em aplicações como sistemas de gestão empresarial (ERP), gestão do relacionamento com clientes (CRM), virtualização, bancos de dados e hospedagem de sites. Essas aplicações demandam disponibilidade de energia, refrigeração, conectividade e continuidade operacional. A expansão de ambientes híbridos, que integram infraestrutura própria, colocation e serviços de nuvem pública, também contribui para a procura por esse tipo de instalação. Embora as aplicações de IA e HPC estejam ampliando a demanda por capacidade computacional, a TI de uso geral continua representando uma base mais abrangente de cargas de trabalho corporativas, segundo o estudo. Hyperscalers devem registrar crescimento mais acelerado Os hyperscalers, grandes provedores de serviços de nuvem e plataformas digitais, devem apresentar o crescimento mais acelerado entre os grupos de usuários finais considerados na pesquisa. A expansão dos serviços em nuvem, das plataformas digitais e da infraestrutura voltada à IA aumenta a necessidade de capacidade de processamento e armazenamento em diferentes regiões. Nesse contexto, o colocation permite ampliar a infraestrutura sem depender exclusivamente da construção de instalações próprias. O modelo também possibilita a entrada em novos mercados e a aproximação de clientes e ecossistemas digitais. Para atender a esse segmento, os fornecedores precisam oferecer grandes volumes de capacidade, disponibilidade de energia, refrigeração compatível com cargas de alta densidade e conectividade de rede. América do Norte lidera o mercado A América do Norte deve continuar concentrando a maior parcela do mercado global de colocation durante o período analisado. A região conta com uma infraestrutura consolidada de data centers e redes, além da presença de grandes empresas, provedores de nuvem e hyperscalers. Nos Estados Unidos, os principais polos citados pela MarketsandMarkets incluem Northern Virginia, Dallas-Fort Worth, Atlanta, Phoenix, Chicago e Silicon Valley. A disponibilidade de energia e as restrições para novos empreendimentos, entretanto, levam fornecedores a avaliar localidades fora dos centros tradicionais. A capacidade de garantir terrenos, fornecimento elétrico e infraestrutura de conectividade está entre os fatores que podem influenciar a expansão dos operadores. Entre as empresas mencionadas no levantamento estão Equinix, Digital Realty, NTT DATA, QTS Data Centers, KDDI, Iron Mountain, China Telecom e CyrusOne. A pesquisa considera diferentes modalidades de serviço, incluindo colocation tradicional e gerenciado, escalas de atendimento de varejo (retail) e atacado (wholesale), além de cargas de trabalho de TI de uso geral e aplicações de HPC e IA. O estudo também avalia o impacto da inteligência artificial generativa sobre o setor até 2031. Participe das comunidades IPNews no Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, X e WhatsApp

artigo.texto: Após quase uma década respeitando os limites de eficiência energética, a Samsung está se preparando para uma reestruturação significativa da duração da bateria em sua linha de celulares de ponta. Resultados de testes técnicos recentes mostram que a próxima série Galaxy S27 apresentará um grande avanço na capacidade de armazenamento de energia, resolvendo o problema da duração da bateria que tem sido uma das principais preocupações dos usuários de smartphones topo de linha. Vazaram as especificações da bateria de 5.700 mAh do Galaxy S27 Ultra: um salto histórico após 7 anos. Os dados de certificação confirmam que o Galaxy S27 Ultra e o S27 Pro terão capacidades de bateria aprimoradas de 5.700 mAh e 5.200 mAh, respectivamente, combinadas com a tecnologia de carregamento rápido de 60 W. Dados técnicos da agência de certificação Safety Korea e do sistema de padrões 3C obrigatório na China confirmaram oficialmente as especificações das novas baterias para a próxima geração de smartphones topo de linha. De acordo com essas informações, espera-se que o Galaxy S27 Ultra, o modelo mais sofisticado da linha, apresente uma bateria com capacidade nominal de até 5.700 mAh. Isso representa um aumento de aproximadamente 14% em comparação com os 5.000 mAh que permaneceram constantes por várias gerações. Não apenas a versão Ultra, mas também a nova variante chamada Galaxy S27 Pro possui uma bateria de 5.200 mAh. A fabricação e a produção dessas duas baterias são de responsabilidade da subsidiária Zhuhai CosMX Power Jinwan. Pressão competitiva e mudanças nas estratégias de segurança. Desde os problemas de superaquecimento da série Galaxy Note 7, a Samsung tem aplicado consistentemente uma filosofia de segurança rigorosa aos sistemas de bateria de seus dispositivos móveis. Por sete anos consecutivos, a empresa manteve uma capacidade de bateria padrão de 5.000 mAh para os modelos Galaxy S Ultra, visando otimizar a dissipação de calor e garantir a estabilidade mecânica. No entanto, o mercado de celulares entrou em uma fase de intensa competição, com outras marcas elevando os limites de armazenamento de energia a níveis sem precedentes, como exemplificado pelo Honor X80 Pro Max com sua bateria de 11.000 mAh. Para reduzir essa diferença, mantendo a segurança, a Samsung integrou gradualmente materiais de silício-carbono ao sistema de armazenamento do Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra e Galaxy Z Flip 8. Embora a quantidade desse material em modelos dobráveis anteriores fosse cautelosa e pertencesse ao grupo tradicional de íon-lítio, essa plataforma abriu caminho para uma maior densidade de energia no Galaxy S27 Ultra. A potência do hardware incluída na nova geração. Além da capacidade de bateria aprimorada, o Galaxy S27 Pro promete oferecer especificações poderosas para otimizar a duração da bateria. O dispositivo possui uma tela de 6,47 polegadas, um sensor de câmera principal de 200 MP e duas opções de processador de última geração: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 ou Exynos 2700, dependendo do mercado. Ambos os modelos suportam carregamento rápido com fio de 60 W, mantendo um desempenho de carregamento comparável ao do Galaxy S26 Ultra. No geral, a atualização simultânea de uma bateria de 5.700 mAh para um processador de última geração ajudará a série Galaxy S27 a estabelecer um padrão mais elevado de desempenho duradouro no segmento de dispositivos premium.

artigo.texto: Building the Future, a new pro-data center super PAC, is spending more than $1.5 million to back Kansas state Sen. Ty Masterson, a Republican, in the state’s battle for governor, a person familiar with the spending said Monday in details first shared with NBC News. Building the Future is an offshoot of the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, backed by AI heavyweights and arguably the leading super PAC promoting industry interests in the midterm elections. Earlier Monday, The New York Times reported that Building the Future is also set to spend about $1.5 million in advertising to boost GOP Sen. Darline Graham in the South Carolina Senate race. In August, Build American AI, a nonprofit that is also in the Leading the Future network, announced a multimillion-dollar ad campaign in Kansas, Ohio and Wisconsin seeking to boost preferred policies to govern data center growth. At the time, it announced the formation of the political group, Building the Future. The group said in August it would back candidates who support “responsible policies that strengthen and protect communities, preserve water resources, and prevent rate hikes on electricity bills, while ensuring American leadership in AI and creating good-paying jobs for American workers.” Opposition to data center development has been intensifying for months, with the sprawling structures needed to power the AI boom becoming a key issue for voters across the country. Kansas is one of the only Democratic-controlled governorships that Republicans have a shot at flipping this fall. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report lists the race as leaning Republican. The state also features a competitive Senate contest between Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton. In a statement Monday, Holscher called Masterson a “stooge for Big Tech” who wants “to put a data center on every corner and in every cornfield.” FOR SUBSCRIBERSBenjamin Netanyahu battles for political survival FOR SUBSCRIBERS6 key takeaways from Anthropic’s IPO filing FOR SUBSCRIBERSBenjamin Netanyahu battles for political survival FOR SUBSCRIBERS6 key takeaways from Anthropic’s IPO filing “It’s also why he’s going to give them tax breaks while everyday Kansans’ costs go up,” she added. “These billionaire CEOs know that I won’t do their bidding, and that’s why they’re spending millions to beat me. But I’ll keep fighting for guardrails on data centers, and I’ll always put Kansans first.” Masterson did not immediately provide comment for this article. Data centers have been a hot issue in both Kansas and South Carolina, as well as other states across the country. In Kansas, Masterson has opposed moratoriums and defended a 2025 law he voted for that provided sales tax exemption for data center investments. Holscher voted for that law, too, but has since called for a statewide moratorium on the developments. In South Carolina, Graham has framed the investments as necessary for national security while expressing support for local control over their construction. Annie Andrews, Graham’s Democratic opponent, has called for a moratorium on new projects and labeled Graham as “Data Center Darline.”

artigo.texto: Rockford advances proposed regulations for potential future data centers Draft rules would address water use, electricity demand, noise, pollution and infrastructure impacts ROCKFORD, Ill. (Rockford News First) - Rockford officials approved moving proposed data center regulations to the city’s Zoning Board of Appeals for a public hearing Monday night, advancing an effort to establish permanent rules for the large computer facilities. The proposal follows a temporary moratorium approved by the City Council in August. That moratorium paused the processing and final approval of new data center applications while city staff reviewed how the facilities could affect Rockford. The vote does not represent final approval of the regulations. Instead, it moves the draft rules to the next step in the city’s zoning process, where the Zoning Board of Appeals will hold a public hearing and consider the proposed amendments. Data centers are large facilities that house computer servers used for cloud computing, artificial intelligence, online services and data storage. They can require significant amounts of electricity, water and cooling equipment. City staff recommended treating data centers as their own land-use category rather than as a general type of high-technology facility under Rockford’s existing zoning ordinance. The proposed regulations would require new data centers and significant expansions to receive performance-based approval. Eligible sites would be limited to appropriate industrial areas with adequate infrastructure. Developers also would need to provide detailed evaluations of a project’s potential effects on electrical service, water supply, wastewater, transportation, stormwater and emergency response. The draft rules call for closed-loop or other resource-conserving cooling systems designed to produce nearly no wastewater discharge from heat exchange equipment. Water use was a major focus of the city’s review. Rockford’s water system serves about 52,000 customers and produces an average of approximately 16.5 million gallons per day, with a systemwide production capacity of about 60 million gallons per day. City officials noted that available systemwide capacity does not necessarily mean every location can handle the demand of a large industrial facility. Proposed data centers would be reviewed based on factors including average and peak water use, seasonal demand, fire-flow needs, required water-main improvements and potential effects on existing customers. The regulations also would require professional noise studies addressing normal operations, peak cooling conditions, backup-generator testing and, when appropriate, low-frequency noise. Noise levels would have to comply with Illinois Pollution Control Board standards. Backup generators would be subject to state and federal air-permitting requirements. Developers would have to provide proof of the required permits before receiving a certificate of occupancy. Other proposed requirements include enhanced setbacks and landscaping near homes, schools and parks; limits on lighting near less-intensive zoning districts; stormwater and flood-control reviews; and fire and life-safety plans addressing generators, fuel systems, batteries, hazardous materials and emergency access. Developers would be responsible for paying for required public infrastructure improvements, such as water mains, streets, traffic signals and storm sewers. The proposal also would require confirmation that ComEd or another applicable utility could reasonably provide the necessary electrical service. City staff said data centers could provide construction jobs, capital investment and additional property, utility and sales tax revenue. However, the facilities generally are expected to create fewer permanent jobs than traditional manufacturing facilities of a similar size. The proposed rules also would require each new data center to submit a decommissioning plan explaining how unused servers, cooling systems, batteries, electrical equipment and hazardous materials would be removed or handled if the facility closes. The draft regulations now move to the Zoning Board of Appeals for public input and review before returning through the city’s approval process. Copyright 2026 Rockford News First. artigo.texto: Xpanner Launches X1 Piling R6 Automated Pile Driving System for Solar and BESS Sites Xpanner has introduced the X1 Piling R6, a fully automated pile driving system aimed at utility-scale solar and battery energy storage sites, according to Solar Power World. The construction automation company said the system combines its automation stack with the Everstar R6 crawler base machine. Under the workflow described by the company, operators upload a pile plan, move the machine to the relevant row and press a single button. The X1 then travels to each pile, aligns and hammers it, and holds it plumb while the operator supervises remotely. The company said the machine uses high-precision GNSS antennas and receivers, precision sensors and an Xpanner-developed automation controller to reach each pile position and drive to the required location and elevation. Xpanner said conventional pile driving depends on a two-person crew plus separate survey, marking and preparation work, while the X1 consolidates those steps into one automated cycle run by a single operator who does not stand next to the mast. The automation stack is carried over from the company's PD10 platform, which Xpanner said has been deployed on more than 67 U.S. jobsites with more than 10 of the country's top engineering, procurement and construction firms. On the R6 base machine, the company said the X1 delivers a 45% faster cycle time than the prior generation. Henri Lee, co-founder and chief executive of Xpanner, said solar and BESS builders are under pressure to bring new power online for the grid and for data centers and cannot find enough skilled crews. He said the X1 allows one operator to drive each pile plumb with a single touch, keeps people away from the mast and logs each pile as it is installed, extending automation that EPCs already use on the PD10 to a more powerful and versatile machine. The system connects to Xpanner Connect, the company's web-based project dashboard. Project teams can load the pile schedule and coordinates, assign machines and set up a site in minutes, according to Xpanner. As the X1 works, it records each pile's position, depth and plumb and posts the data to a live project map, replacing manual counts, phone calls, spreadsheets and end-of-day reports. Managers can also monitor machine state, cycle counts and alerts across the fleet without visiting a site. The X1 Piling R6 launches commercially on Oct. 26, 2026, through the Xpanner subscription. A single agreement covers the machine, the X1 automation kit, Xpanner Connect and Xpanner On-Site Support, with service delivered directly by Xpanner from demonstration and site validation through training, operation and maintenance. During site validation, Xpanner reviews each customer's pile schedule to confirm reveal heights and embedment. Xpanner said future capabilities for the X1 Piling R6 will include screw driving and pre-drilling. - 1. artigo.texto: Seu navegador não oferece leitura em voz alta. A concentração de grandes estruturas de tecnologia na Região Metropolitana de São Paulo não é coincidência. Nas últimas duas décadas, o estado se consolidou como o principal polo de processamento e armazenamento de dados do país, atraindo investimentos bilionários de operadoras de telecomunicações, provedores de nuvem e empresas especializadas em colocation. Esse movimento ajuda a explicar por que tantas companhias, mesmo de outros estados, escolhem hospedar seus sistemas críticos na capital paulista ou em cidades do entorno. Escolha o Por Dentro de Minas como sua fonte de notícias no Google Novo recurso permite definir quais portais você quer ver. Receba conteúdo de quem você já confia. Concentração econômica e demanda corporativa O primeiro fator é simples: São Paulo é o maior centro econômico do Brasil. A região reúne sedes de bancos, seguradoras, indústrias, varejistas, startups e empresas de serviços que dependem intensamente de tecnologia. Quanto maior o volume de negócios, maior a demanda por processamento de dados, baixa latência e alta disponibilidade. Em vez de dispersar a infraestrutura por diferentes estados, muitos provedores preferem estar próximos de onde se concentra a maior parte dos clientes corporativos. Essa proximidade reduz tempo de resposta entre servidores e usuários finais, algo decisivo para operações financeiras, comércio eletrônico, plataformas de streaming e serviços em nuvem. Para uma corretora de valores, por exemplo, milissegundos podem fazer diferença em negociações de alta frequência. Já para um grande varejista digital, o atraso em consultas de estoque ou meios de pagamento pode significar carrinhos abandonados e perda de receita. Outro ponto é a presença de equipes técnicas e executivas na própria cidade. Quando as áreas de tecnologia e negócios estão baseadas em São Paulo, torna-se mais simples negociar contratos, acompanhar projetos de migração e realizar visitas de auditoria aos data centers. Essa dinâmica reforça um círculo em que a demanda local justifica novos investimentos em infraestrutura, que por sua vez atraem mais empresas. Infraestrutura de telecomunicações e rotas internacionais Além da força econômica, o estado conta com uma infraestrutura de telecomunicações mais robusta que a média nacional. A capital é um grande ponto de interconexão entre operadoras, provedores de internet e redes corporativas. Diversos backbones de fibra óptica se cruzam na região, permitindo redundância de rotas e maior capacidade de tráfego. Isso é fundamental para data centers que precisam garantir conectividade estável e de alta velocidade, mesmo diante de falhas em um dos caminhos. São Paulo também se beneficia da ligação com cabos submarinos que chegam ao litoral brasileiro. Embora os pontos de desembarque estejam em outros estados, como Rio de Janeiro e Ceará, grande parte do tráfego internacional de dados acaba passando por rotas que convergem para a Região Sudeste. Para provedores globais de computação em nuvem, isso facilita a integração entre suas estruturas no Brasil e data centers em outros continentes. A existência de pontos de troca de tráfego (IXPs) relevantes na capital contribui ainda mais. Nesses ambientes, diferentes redes se conectam diretamente, reduzindo o caminho entre provedores de conteúdo, operadoras e empresas. O resultado é menor latência e melhor desempenho para aplicações críticas. Não por acaso, muitos projetos de expansão de infraestrutura de internet consideram São Paulo como ponto de partida. Energia elétrica, riscos e desafios de infraestrutura Data centers consomem grandes volumes de energia e exigem fornecimento estável. A Região Metropolitana de São Paulo, apesar de enfrentar desafios típicos de grandes centros urbanos, oferece uma malha elétrica relativamente mais robusta que a de áreas menos desenvolvidas. Empreendimentos de grande porte costumam contar com múltiplos alimentadores, subestações dedicadas e sistemas de redundância com geradores e bancos de baterias. Ainda assim, a concentração de consumo traz desafios. A necessidade de garantir disponibilidade próxima de 100% leva os operadores a investir em projetos complexos de engenharia, com caminhos independentes de energia e refrigeração. A busca por certificações internacionais de confiabilidade, como Tier III e Tier IV, faz com que as instalações em São Paulo adotem padrões rigorosos de projeto e manutenção. Há também a questão do espaço físico. Terrenos em áreas centrais são caros e escassos, empurrando muitos projetos para regiões periféricas ou cidades vizinhas, como Barueri, Santana de Parnaíba, Osasco e Campinas. Nesses locais, é possível construir estruturas maiores, com salas técnicas modulares e áreas reservadas para futuras expansões. A proximidade com rodovias e aeroportos facilita a logística de equipamentos e o deslocamento de equipes técnicas. Clima de negócios, mão de obra e ecossistema tecnológico Outro diferencial está no ambiente de negócios. São Paulo concentra escritórios de fornecedores de hardware, software, serviços de nuvem e consultorias especializadas em infraestrutura. Esse ecossistema reduz o tempo de resposta para manutenção, atualizações e suporte, fatores essenciais em ambientes que não podem parar. A disponibilidade de mão de obra qualificada também pesa. Universidades, escolas técnicas e programas de formação em tecnologia abastecem o mercado com profissionais de redes, segurança da informação, engenharia elétrica e ciência de dados. Para operadores de grandes data centers, conseguir montar e manter equipes especializadas é tão importante quanto ter bons equipamentos. A presença de hubs de inovação, parques tecnológicos e comunidades de startups cria um ambiente em que novas soluções são testadas com rapidez. Isso vale tanto para ferramentas de monitoramento e automação quanto para iniciativas de eficiência energética e reaproveitamento de calor. Muitos projetos-piloto acabam sendo implementa

artigo.texto: As word spread about NAVWAR being considered as a potential site for a data center, the community immediately responded. A group rallied last week calling for those plans to be scrapped. Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7. Others, like Francisco Martinez, are open to the idea of data centers coming to San Diego. “People don’t want the things too close to the neighborhood, but on the other hand, it’s the present and the future and we need all of that to develop the next step forward in many things,” Martinez said. District 9 Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera, has been a vocal critic of the possibility of the U.S. Navy’s cybersecurity hub becoming what would be the largest data center in California. “The conversation that is happening in NAVWAR is a flashing red light, and we need to think about this as a threat and it can happen in San Diego and one that we need to get ahead of,” Councilmember Elo-Rivera said. Local He worries the project would impact San Diegans' energy costs and plans for affordable housing. Martinez thinks if the land is available, developers should be able to move forward. “If it’s a land that is open and has no use for anything else, they can put a bid. It’s fair,” Martinez said. The redevelopment plans extend beyond a data center. Ted Elridge, the project’s CEO, told NBC 7 that they are also exploring a medical center, a university and defense campus, along with a life sciences facility. Elridge also confirmed there have been early talks with energy providers but said there have been no negotiations or agreements. Since NAVWAR is federal property, Elo-Rivera is calling on congress to take the project off the table. This week, San Diego City Council is set to vote on a temporary moratorium on new data centers and the expansion of existing ones. “What we don’t want is a rush to submit permits and get projects going before rules are in place,” Elo-Rivera said. If approved, the initial moratorium would last 45 days, and the city council could vote to extend it once it expires. The moratorium would buy city leaders time while they work to establish regulations with clear guardrails for developers wishing to bring data centers to San Diego. Elo-Rivera said they have submitted a policy proposal and need to start drafting the law. He said they want to ensure the draft has no loopholes before it becomes permanent. Martinez hopes they’re able to reach an agreement that satisfies everyone while moving San Diego forward. “It’s a balance between new technology and new needs, and what people want around their neighborhoods,” Martinez said. Mayor Todd Gloria has signed an executive order to freeze any data center construction, marking what advocates described as a first step addressing concerns about the project. Poway was the first city in the county to ban data centers, earlier this month, citing air quality, noise and water-use concerns, as well as a lack of local long-term job creation because much of a data center is automated.

artigo.texto: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has announced the development of a groundbreaking battery technology that may play a crucial role in the United States’ plans for lunar exploration and could also transform the landscape of electric vehicle (EV) power sources on Earth. This innovative battery is designed to function efficiently at extremely low temperatures, which could enhance the operation of lunar rovers and other equipment under NASA’s Artemis program. According to reports, the newly developed “freeze-proof” solid-state battery has undergone successful thermal vacuum testing and has withstood temperatures as frigid as 274 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 170 degrees Celsius). The testing revealed that while the prototype batteries showed reduced performance at temperatures down to 112 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 80 degrees Celsius), they performed optimally in a range from negative 76 to positive 176 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 60 to 80 degrees Celsius). Such performance is vital for the moon’s South Pole, where temperatures can plummet to 328 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 200 degrees Celsius)—conditions that conventional lithium-ion batteries simply cannot endure. Traditional lithium-ion batteries operate by transferring lithium ions through liquid electrolytes, which can freeze in harsh conditions and pose significant fire risks due to their flammable nature. In contrast, solid-state batteries utilize solid electrolytes, providing a safer and more stable environment for lithium ion movement, enabling faster charging and reduced risk of failure in extreme temperatures. While the EV industry may not currently require batteries that can survive extreme cold, advancements in solid-state technology from NASA’s endeavors could significantly impact terrestrial applications. The research suggests that these battery innovations could lead to enhanced safety, temperature tolerance, and efficiency for various electronic devices, including electric vehicles, commercial drones, and grid-scale energy storage systems operating in tough climates. Specifically, these breakthroughs might allow for longer ranges in colder regions and during winter months for electric vehicles. In addition to battery technology, NASA is exploring collaboration with the United States Department of Energy to develop next-generation nuclear energy solutions that could propel a new era for deep space exploration. This initiative is perceived as a transformative approach for space missions, as nuclear power is expected to extend the range and operational capabilities of spacecraft and instruments. As NASA forges ahead with these ambitious projects, the implications for both space exploration and energy technology may define the future of both fields, paving the way for innovative discoveries and advancements.

artigo.texto: Advocates raise concerns over Nevada data center expansion, cite water and energy use Opponents point to fossil fuels and water cooling, while industry coalition touts closed-loop systems and renewables. RENO, Nev. (KOLO) - Advocates against data center expansion in Nevada came together on Monday to express concerns with continued construction in the state. Debra Hendrickson, climate advocate for the NV Chapter of American Academy of Pediatrics, questioned the approach: “If you agree that AI, that this is a worthwhile goal, why are you pursuing it in ways that are so destructive to the state and to the world?” Josh Dini, of the Walker River Paiute Tribe, cited water concerns around the Monarch Data Center in Lyon County: “It’s on private land. And our concern is the water.” Hendrickson also tied the issue to climate change: “We’re one of the fastest warming places in the country. And pumping all our goals for reducing our greenhouse gases to address the threat of climate change, which manifested itself this summer in wildfires at the north end of town that caused tens of thousands of people to evacuate. And across the west, we’re seeing this massive increase in wildfires.” The use of fossil fuels to power data centers was among the top concerns raised. Bri Schmidt, Nevada Conservation League, advocated for using existing rooftop solar to support the grid instead of new methane gas plants: “Instead, we’re spending millions on new methane gas plants in the proposed plan... when we have solar, we get over 300 days of sunshine in Nevada. There’s other options... These are solar panels that are already installed in our homes that people already have that could be helping to meet demand.” Tray Abney of the Nevada Data Center Coalition addressed renewable energy, pointing to Greenlink Energy’s plan to connect north and south grids: “Greenlink is Energy’s plan to connect the power grids north and south.” he explained. “These lines will go through a lot of areas where you can build renewables. You can do solar. You can do wind. You can do geothermal.” On water use, Abney said newer centers use closed-loop technology: “The new ones that are being built in Nevada, water is not an issue. I toured one the other day... that’s a completely closed-loop system... water and glycol that cools off their systems... If you can picture your car, you don’t ever have to add water to your car unless there’s some kind of a problem... That stays in there for pretty much the life cycle of the building.” He acknowledged older centers built 10 or 20 years ago use different technology. Copyright 2026 KOLO. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Table of Contents Chinese billionaire Robin Zeng, the founder and chairman of Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., has seen $14.9 billion wiped off his fortune since March after shares of the world's largest electric-vehicle battery maker fell sharply on weaker-than-expected earnings. Zeng, 57, is now worth about $38.3 billion, down from $53.2 billion in March. Nearly all of his wealth comes from his stake in CATL, the company he founded in 2011 in Ningde, in China's southeastern Fujian province. CATL shares have dropped 33% in Shenzhen and 25% in Hong Kong over that period. The decline deepened on Wednesday, when the stock fell more than 12% in both markets, its worst one-day selloff in more than a year. The Hong Kong shares traded as low as HK$368 ($47.30), their weakest level since July 2025. The company's market value has nearly halved since peaking in May. Profit growth slows The selloff followed third-quarter results released on Tuesday. Net profit attributable to shareholders rose 14.5% from a year earlier to 21.25 billion yuan ($3.16 billion), well short of the 41.2% increase analysts had expected and down from growth of 36.5% in the second quarter. Profit also fell 5.8% from the previous three months. Revenue rose 58.6% to 165.2 billion yuan ($24.6 billion), slightly below forecasts. Gross margin narrowed to 20.69%, the second straight quarterly decline. In the first nine months of the year, CATL earned 64.53 billion yuan ($9.6 billion), up 31.6%, on revenue of 442.14 billion yuan ($65.8 billion). Management blamed new tax costs. China reinstated a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries on Sept. 1 at a transitional rate of 2%, which is set to rise to 4% in September 2027. Separately, the export tax rebate on battery products was cut to 6% from 9% in April and will be scrapped on Jan. 1. Chief Financial Officer Zheng Shu said the consumption tax is built into product prices, so passing it on to carmakers means renegotiating contracts, and those talks are still under way. CATL said it hopes to "shoulder the costs together" with customers and is developing new products to protect margins. "Based on the significant fall in profit growth, it seems that the company itself has shouldered the bulk of them," said Kenny Ng, an analyst at Everbright Securities International. JPMorgan Chase & Co. cut its rating on the Hong Kong-listed shares to neutral and lowered its earnings forecasts, while keeping an overweight rating on the Shenzhen stock. Carmakers look for other suppliers Investors are also watching what Chinese commentators have called "de-CATLization," a push by carmakers to reduce their reliance on a single battery supplier. Li Auto and Xiaomi have started developing their own EV batteries, and Tesla added Sunwoda Electronic as a supplier this year. Industry data show CATL's share of China's battery market fell to 40.9% in September from 49.8% in January, while rival BYD's rose to 21.1% from 17.4%. Globally, CATL still supplied about 40% of EV batteries installed in the first half of the year, according to SNE Research, and counts almost every major carmaker as a customer. The company said growth of 20% to 30% in global demand for power and energy-storage batteries is achievable in 2027. Zeng, who holds a doctorate in physics, co-founded Amperex Technology Ltd. in 1999, making batteries for consumer electronics, before spinning off CATL to supply car batteries. artigo.texto: A empresa sul-coreana LS Eco Energy planeja investir aproximadamente 65 bilhões de won (US$ 49 milhões) por meio de sua subsidiária no Vietnã para construir uma linha de produção de supercapacitores destinados a centros de dados de inteligência artificial ( IA ). A empresa pretende iniciar a produção e o fornecimento em massa de supercapacitores a partir de abril de 2027, visando uma receita anual de 150 bilhões de won com este produto até 2030. De acordo com um comunicado de imprensa da LS Cable & System, datado de 26 de outubro, a subsidiária da LS Eco Energy no Vietnã, a LSCV, lançará um projeto de fabricação de supercapacitores para atender à crescente demanda de encomendas da LS Materials, uma subsidiária do mesmo grupo. A LS Eco Energy planeja fabricar produtos utilizando um modelo OEM, empregando tecnologia da LS Materials. Os supercapacitores são dispositivos de armazenamento de energia capazes de carga e descarga rápidas, ajudando a compensar as quedas instantâneas de energia em sistemas de geração de energia de células a combustível de hidrogênio. A demanda por esses dispositivos deve aumentar à medida que o investimento em data centers de IA e sistemas de fornecimento de energia relacionados se expande. Em 13 de outubro, a LS Materials assinou um contrato para fornecer supercapacitores no valor aproximado de US$ 51,5 milhões a um fabricante americano de células a combustível de hidrogênio. A empresa está negociando contratos adicionais este ano. A expansão da capacidade produtiva no Vietnã ajudará a LS Materials a diversificar sua base de fornecedores e a criar uma nova fonte de receita para a LS Eco Energy. Segundo a empresa, a LSCV pode utilizar o espaço ocioso da fábrica existente para construir uma nova linha de produção, reduzindo assim os custos iniciais de investimento. Os custos relativamente baixos de mão de obra e de serviços públicos no Vietnã também devem contribuir para a competitividade de preços. A LS Eco Energy afirmou que considerará investimentos adicionais dependendo do volume de pedidos. O projeto representa um passo rumo à expansão das operações da LS Eco Energy, do setor de fios e cabos elétricos para produtos de alto valor agregado que atendem à infraestrutura de data centers com inteligência artificial. Contudo, a meta de receita para 2030 ainda depende do progresso da implementação, da demanda de mercado e da capacidade de expansão dos pedidos.

artigo.texto: After a long discussion on data centers during the joint subcommittee on tax policy Monday morning, it appears tension remains between Senate Finance Chair Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, and House Appropriations Chair Luke Torian, D-Fairfax, after a hard-fought budget negotiation process earlier this year. “You know, I just want to reiterate my desire for us to have a third meeting,” Lucas said at the end of the meeting. “We’ve only had two meetings, and I’m not satisfied that we’ve been given enough information for us to make any substantial recommendations on tax policy.” Lucas and Senate Democrats were adamant that they wanted to end the sales tax incentive for data centers in Virginia earlier this year when legislators were negotiating Virginia’s new two-year budget. The House and Gov. Abigail Spanberger did not want to renege on the commonwealth’s commitment to the tax incentive, which is set to run until 2035. Ultimately, the incentive stayed, but a new tax on energy consumption was included, which is expected to generate $600 million annually. The negotiations were tense at times in public, with Lucas publicly calling out Spanberger and House Speaker Don Scott, D-Portsmouth, for supporting keeping the incentive. But since then, there has been no public animosity between the two chambers as Lucas deals with her own legal troubles and faces multiple federal indictments. However, on Monday, the tension resurfaced in Lucas’ closing comments at the meeting. She brought up an alleged poll Torian is conducting to gauge House members’ interest in holding another subcommittee meeting to discuss taxes on data centers. “I don’t know if you’ve gotten that poll done yet, but I know the members of the Senate… We’d like to see a third meeting, and we’d like to see it somewhere in the community, especially the communities that are impacted by data centers,” she said. “So, if the House colleagues do not see the importance of this work, I feel compelled to give the people what they want and work on this issue in our committee, including having a meeting on data centers.” Torian then responded to Lucas, who was seated directly to his right, before delivering his closing statement for the meeting. “Let me share with you that there will be a meeting, perhaps maybe a couple of meetings, and I’m not in a position to articulate to the public how that will proceed because I believe you and I had a conversation a couple days ago, and we’re supposed to be meeting after this meeting, so we can talk,” Torian said. “But I’d still like to have those meetings fast,” Lucas responded. Torian began to say something, but Lucas interrupted and said, “We’ll talk.” “Okay,” Torian responded. Torian and Lucas did not respond to a question asking for clarification from Virginia Scope after the meeting.

artigo.texto: Russian ministry recommends underground data centers following Ukrainian drone strikes Russia's Digital Development Ministry has proposed building data centers underground, camouflaged from the air, and fitted with drone defenses, Russian state-controlled media Kommersant said on Oct. 25, following several Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers. Guidelines for existing, planned, and under-construction facilities outline the protection standards for three tiers of data centers, including whether sites are placed above ground or underground, according to Kommersant. The top tier includes strategic sites whose loss could disrupt key state functions for an hour or more; the second tier includes sites supporting regionally or economically important systems, where outages could last four hours or more; and the final tier covers corporate data centers whose damage would not have wider consequences for the state, Kommersant said. Existing data centers should be protected by reducing their visibility from the air and by deploying layered defenses, including reinforced structures, electronic warfare measures, and drone defense systems. The announcement came after Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers, a Sberbank facility under construction, and a data center belonging to social media giant VK between Oct. 8 and Oct. 18. Russia's centralized digital infrastructure leaves Moscow facing two challenges: inflicting comparable damage on Ukraine and protecting its own data centers from further strikes. Serhiy Petrenko, former head of Yandex Ukraine, estimated that around 80% of Russia's data centers are concentrated in Moscow and the surrounding region — within reach of Ukrainian long-range drones. The consequences of Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centers could extend far beyond disrupted banking and online services, potentially setting back the country's AI development and affecting military technology. On Oct. 16, Kemerovo Oblast governor Ilya Seredyuk proposed housing data centers inside depleted open-pit mines and quarries, given their natural protection from aerial bombardment.

artigo.texto: A SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPACE) celebrou um compromisso vinculante de financiamento de até US$ 40 bilhões com uma entidade estruturada e gerida pela Apollo Global Management. A operação destina-se à aquisição e arrendamento comercial (sale-leaseback de infraestrutura) de unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs) e equipamentos avançados para centros de processamento de dados (data centers), segundo documento protocolado nesta segunda-feira (26) junto à Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). A assinatura do compromisso ocorreu no sábado, 24 de outubro, e prevê a compra direta dos chips e equipamentos de IA pela Apollo, que os alugará de volta à SpaceX mediante pagamentos trimestrais ao longo de aproximadamente cinco anos. Estrutura Operacional e Cronograma Financeiro - Entrega em Lotes: A infraestrutura de chips será entregue em fases, com os contratos individuais de arrendamento iniciando-se no primeiro semestre de 2027. Cada contrato individual terá maturidade de 5 anos a 5 anos e 3 meses. - Dinâmica de Pagamentos: As parcelas trimestrais serão efetuadas antecipadamente, compostas pela amortização do principal (equivalente a $1/20$ do custo financiado por lote) somada a juros com taxa anual fixa cobrada sobre o saldo devedor restante (cuja taxa de juros definitiva será fixada no fechamento de cada contrato). - Volume do Principal: O total amortizado de principal alcançará cerca de US$ 40 bilhões, excluindo juros e despesas acessórias. A SpaceX prevê concluir a formalização final dos termos até o encerramento de 2026. Desempenho Financeiro do 3T26 e Expansão em IA A operação de financiamento de infraestrutura vem no encalço de um balanço trimestral robusto, o segundo apresentado pela empresa espacial desde a sua oferta pública inicial (IPO) no início de 2026: - Lucro Líquido: Atingiu US$ 4,4 bilhões no 3T26. O lucro por ação (LPA) ajustado ficou em US$ 0,35, superando a estimativa de consenso do mercado (US$ 0,13 apurado pela FactSet). - Receita Líquida: A receita total disparou 161% no comparativo anual, alcançando US$ 14,6 bilhões (frente a consensos de US$ 12,87 bilhões). - Divisão por Segmentos: - Inteligência Artificial (IA): Gerou US$ 7,56 bilhões no trimestre. - Conectividade (Starlink): Faturou US$ 5,2 bilhões, impulsionada pela marca de 13,6 milhões de assinantes ativos. - Lançamentos e Sistemas Espaciais: Somou US$ 1,77 bilhão. Os investimentos em capital (capex) escalaram para US$ 19,6 bilhões no trimestre (ante US$ 6,9 bilhões no 3T25), refletindo a corrida acelerada por capacidade computacional e constelações de satélites de última geração.

artigo.texto: Charlotte City Council votes unanimously to extend data center moratorium CHARLOTTE, N.C. – Charlotte City Council voted unanimously on Monday to extend its moratorium on new data centers until October 18, 2027. The decision pauses new facility approvals to give city planners time to study the environmental impacts, high power consumption, and immense water demands these facilities require. Following that vote, District Four councilmember Renee Johnson issued a stark warning to council members, noting that 5.5 million square feet of “hyperscale” data developments are already actively under construction near residential backyards. Johnson stressed that because these projects were previously approved, they will completely bypass the city’s upcoming safety and zoning restrictions unless aggressive legal options are pursued. She says, “So I need to sound the alarm. We have two hyperscale developments. It’s actually 5.5 million square footage of data centers that are under, currently under construction that will not be subject to these provisions.” The city’s specialized task force will continue reviewing distance and noise impacts over the next 11 months, to determine how existing facilities can be forced to comply with local noise ordinances.

artigo.texto: Here's why data center campaign contributions to Nevada politics are rising Political contributions from companies with a data center footprint in Nevada are on the rise ahead of a legislative session where the industry is likely to face unprecedented scrutiny, a Nevada Independent analysis found. In May, Jessica Roy, the wife of Switch founder Rob Roy, gave $1 million to a PAC supporting Gov. Joe Lombardo (R). From July through September, companies with an existing or planned data center donated more than $100,000 to candidates and groups, the highest quarterly total in eight years (excluding the $1 million donation from Roy). More than 65 percent of this money went to Democrats. It's a notable development in donations from the industry, which has given about $17 million in donations to candidates and groups across the past two decades. More than 80 percent of this total came through Switch's efforts to pass an energy ballot initiative during the 2016 and 2018 election cycles. There was also a spike in the mid-2010s as Switch, a company at the center of Nevada's data center industry, eyed a lucrative tax break package. The data suggests that although these companies have shown a willingness to spend in Nevada politics, its presence remains nascent. With the issues around data centers showing no sign of going away, that appears to be changing. Ken Miller, a UNLV political science professor, said that data centers haven't had as much of a reason to consistently donate to Nevada officials and PACs. "A lot of times some industries need to keep up a high level of maintenance of donation because they need to ensure that regulations on them don't change or they don't move against the competing industry," he said. "Those are the types of reasons why you maintain very high levels of political spending and that that hasn't been the case for data centers until now." With its proximity to Silicon Valley and business-friendly tax policies, Nevada has emerged as a hotbed for data centers. So far, there are more than 80 data centers operating, under construction or planned in the Silver State, according to a tracker from More Than Just Parks, a group focused on protecting public lands. The Indy's analysis included any company with a planned or built data center in Nevada, as well as people tied to those companies. At the same time, the nature of Nevada's data center industry makes it difficult to directly link political donations to companies' data center activities. Outside of Switch, many of the most prominent political donors with a data center footprint are large tech companies. Many of these donations could relate to the company's operations outside of data centers. "Google, Microsoft, Verizon, these are all groups that have a variety of interests across different sorts of regulatory environments," Miller said. "They could really be anything." Switch's donations More than 90 percent of the political donations come from Switch, which has massive data center campuses in Las Vegas and the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center. The company's donations took off in the 2010s as it successfully sought to bring a data center tax break package to Nevada and supported a failed ballot initiative to end the state's energy monopoly. Switch has long supported members of both parties, with a slight lean for Democrats, who have long controlled the Legislature, except for the notable 2015 session when Republicans controlled both chambers and when the data center tax break bill passed. Up until this year, the company had donated about $840,000 to Democratic candidates and groups, compared with about $710,000 to Republicans, The Indy's analysis found. But the tides turned this year with Jessica Roy's $1 million donation to the pro-Lombardo PAC. Lombardo had previously not received any money from Switch as governor or gubernatorial candidate. He did receive $10,000 in 2018 from Stella Roy, Rob Roy's then-wife, while serving as Clark County Sheriff, and the company also gave Lombardo $1,000 in 2016. By contrast, the company gave about $130,000 to former Gov. Steve Sisolak's (D) gubernatorial campaigns and associated groups. Attorney General Aaron Ford (D), the Democratic nominee for governor, has pounced on the $1 million donation to Lombardo's PAC. Ford, who co-sponsored the data center tax break bill, has received about $35,000 from Switch over the years, but the most recent contribution was in 2021. Data centers have emerged as a prominent issue in the governor's race. Ford has pledged pausing the tax break program and banning water-intensive cooling technology statewide. Meanwhile, Lombardo has supported data centers — calling it the state's new "gold rush" — but has also curtailed the data center tax break program, requiring companies to cover their own power costs and ending relief on a tax that supports local schools. In a statement, Prerna Jagadeesh, a spokesperson for Ford's campaign, said that Ford "has a plan to rein in data centers" and accused Lombardo of catering "to the data center interests propping up his campaign." Switch did not respond to a request for comment about its spending habits. However, Missy Young, a senior fellow at the company, said during an IndyFest panel last week that "economic considerations" drive the company's political spending. As an example, she thinks Ford's pledge to end the state's "right to work" law could "potentially negatively affect economic development and growth." The money Switch gives to Nevada candidates pales in comparison to what it spent on the energy ballot initiative in 2016 and 2018. Following years of tensions with NV Energy, Switch left the energy utility and eventually threw its support behind a ballot question that would have required the state to adopt a competitive electric market. Altogether, the company poured more than $12.6 million to support the ballot question, topped off with a $10 million infusion of cash into a group behind the ballot question in 2018

artigo.texto: Rushin submits alternative data center plan as Pulaski County considers permitting rules LITTLE ROCK, Ark. (KATV) — Discussions around data center regulation remain a major talking point in the race for Pulaski County judge. Republican nominee Michael Rushin laid out his framework for data centers in the county as a proposed ordinance around data centers is on tomorrow night's Pulaski County quorum court agenda. The county's JPs will have a chance to override a veto that would regulate data centers in Pulaski County, and Rushin weighed in on the subject Monday afternoon in Little Rock. "I want to let everyone know that it is our firm belief that no local government is sophisticated enough to know what is right, what the right measure or balance is in terms of regulation or conversation might be at this point," Rushin stated in front of media on Monday. Rushin states that he has submitted his own plan for addressing data centers to the quorum court, one that he says will help avoid costly lawsuits. "Protecting the interests of Pulaski County residents, rate and taxpayers, without going to court should not be difficult, and with the plan I have submitted to the quorum court, it will not be." In September, Pulaski County judge Barry Hyde vetoed an ordinance that would establish new permitting processes for data centers in the county, including the AVAIO data center that is set to be built near Wrightsville. Rushin says it was the right move at the right time. "I thanked him for his veto, I thought it was a very wise decision, because he is trying to keep us out of a court of law, he understands what's at stake. My opponent only knows litigation, that's what he's done for his career." The ordinance was backed by Wendell Griffen, the Democratic nominee for Pulaski County judge. He defeated Barry Hyde in the March 3rd primaries and now faces Rushin in November's general election. Channel 7 News spoke to Griffen earlier this month about his stance on data center regulation, and he addressed Hyde's veto and what could happen after. "It only takes 9 JPs to override the veto--when that happens, that law will be effective immediately." Rushin believes that if this ordinance is overridden by the quorum court, it could clash with his framework if he were to be elected. "It would create a pretty big headache," says Rushin. "I still think that if it does become into law, it just creates too much of an opportunity for us to end up in litigation that would be for years and years and years." Rushin believes that any money or resources spent towards hypothetical litigation would be better spent on fixing county roads and infrastructure. Tuesday night's quorum court meeting will decide whether or not the county's Justices of Peace will override Hyde's veto on the ordinance. It will be the final determination on whether the ordinance that regulates data centers will pass.

artigo.texto: Polaris awards battery storage contract, advances $60 million Punta Lima project By THE STAR STAFF Canadian renewable energy company Polaris Renewable Energy Inc. has recently awarded a key supply contract to Trina Energy Storage Solutions for its planned battery energy storage project at Punta Lima in Naguabo, marking a major step forward in the island’s ongoing efforts to strengthen grid reliability through utility-scale energy storage. The company announced last week that it has executed an agreement with Trina Storage to provide battery energy storage systems (BESS) for the Punta Lima project, which is being developed under Puerto Rico’s Accelerated Storage Addition Program (ASAP by its acronym in Spanish). The program was created to accelerate deployment of large-scale battery systems alongside existing generation facilities to improve grid resilience and reliability. The contract award allows the project to move from the planning and contractual phase into equipment procurement and implementation, Polaris said. The Punta Lima facility will consist of a 35.7-megawatt (MW) battery storage system with eight hours of duration. Under the terms of its agreement with the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority (PREPA), the system will provide 71.4 MW of storage capability through two four-hour energy delivery blocks. Polaris estimates total project costs will range between $55 million and $60 million, including the battery system, medium-voltage transformer, fees and balance-of-plant infrastructure. The company said it plans to fund the investment with cash on hand. Once operational, the project is expected to contribute some $12.5 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, or EBITDA, during its first year of operation. The development is one of several storage projects being advanced under ASAP, which seeks to add battery capacity to Puerto Rico’s power system following years of reliability challenges, storm-related disruptions and generation shortfalls. Polaris’ U.S. subsidiary, Polaris Power US Inc., secured its place in the program earlier this year when it executed a battery energy storage standard offer agreement with PREPA on June 5. Under that agreement, the company will receive monthly fixed and performance-based payments for providing energy storage services, including capacity and grid support. Deliveries of battery containers from Trina Storage are scheduled for March and April 2027, with commercial operations currently expected to begin during the third quarter of 2027. The agreement has a 20-year term beginning on the project’s commercial operation date. “The execution of the supply contract with Trina Storage is a significant milestone in advancing our investment in Punta Lima, moving the project from its contractual framework into equipment procurement and implementation,” Polaris CEO Marc Murnaghan said in a statement. “This investment reflects our confidence in Puerto Rico’s long-term energy transition and our commitment to delivering critical storage capacity that will enhance grid reliability and resilience.” Trina Storage, a global utility-scale energy storage provider, has some 30 gigawatt-hours of battery storage projects either commissioned or under execution worldwide, including over six gigawatt-hours in Latin America and the Caribbean, according to the company. Toronto-based Polaris Renewable Energy operates a portfolio of renewable energy assets across Latin America and the Caribbean, including geothermal, hydroelectric, solar and wind facilities. The Punta Lima project represents a growing trend toward deploying long-duration battery storage resources in Puerto Rico, where regulators and policymakers have increasingly emphasized energy storage as a critical component of the island’s transition to a more resilient and renewable electric grid.

artigo.texto: From Inverters to Full-Scenario Energy Storage: A Guide to SolisStorage's Product Portfolio Press Release Date 10-27-2026 Product highlights and application coverage across the energy storage portfolio CALIFORNIA, CA, UNITED STATES, October 27, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- In the solar industry, Ginlong (Solis) Technologies is a name that needs little introduction. Founded in 2005 in Ningbo, Zhejiang Province, and listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange in 2019 (stock code 300763), the company has spent two decades in power electronics. Its inverter products have evolved through seven generations of technology, it has been named a "Top Inverter Brand" by EuPD Research for 11 consecutive years, its products are sold in more than 100 countries and regions, and its annual production capacity has reached 80 GW. What deserves closer attention today, however, is the board Solis has been laying out around its energy storage subsidiary, SolisStorage: in-house development of PCS, EMS and system integration technologies, a product range covering residential, commercial and industrial (C&I), and grid-scale applications, and Solis AI tying the hardware to electricity markets. This article walks through that portfolio from a product and brand perspective. Residential Storage: The FlexAIO Flagship Residential is the product line closest to end users, and its flagship is the FlexAIO all-in-one stackable high-voltage energy storage system. Its design logic revolves around two words: flexibility and reliability. 6 kWh and 9 kWh battery packs can be mixed, as can old and new batteries; a single cluster stacks up to 6 modules, up to 6 clusters can run in parallel, and capacity scales all the way to 324 kWh — so the system grows as the household does. Reliability is engineered in finer detail: A+ grade cells with a cycle life of more than 10,000 cycles, five-layer hardware redundancy protection as standard, and continued safe operation of the whole system even if a single battery pack fails. On performance, FlexAIO supports 200% PV oversizing to raise generation utilization, switches seamlessly between on-grid and off-grid in under 10 milliseconds, and handles 150% overload for 10 seconds in off-grid mode. Built for outdoor installation, it carries IP66 protection and C5-M anti-corrosion, and with battery heating and active cooling its intelligent thermal management keeps it operating from -20°C to 55°C. Installation takes as little as 5 minutes, and ongoing maintenance is handled through OTA remote upgrades. The product has also stood up to third-party scrutiny: in October 2026, FlexAIO received IEC 62619 and IEC 63056 IECEE CB certificates from TÜV Rheinland — the former covering industrial lithium battery safety, the latter covering safety requirements for residential energy storage systems. Through the CB scheme's mutual recognition framework, these two certificates clear compliance hurdles for market entry across multiple countries and regions. C&I Storage: The EverCore ESS Platform Approach C&I is the fastest-growing part of Solis' storage business. The first 50 kW hybrid storage inverters shipped in July 2025, the 125 kW model followed in December of the same year, and by October 2026 cumulative global shipments across the full 50–125 kW range had passed 3 GW — in under 16 months. Behind that growth lies the sheer diversity of C&I demand: some customers want to use more of their own solar generation, some need to manage peak demand, some prioritize backup power, and electricity market rules and project conditions vary widely from place to place. Kun Zhang, Product Center Director at Solis, puts it plainly: "Different markets require different power levels, system configurations and operating strategies. Our approach is to build a versatile product platform with a high level of adaptability." That platform approach is embodied in the EverCore Energy Storage System (ESS). It offers three cabinet capacities — 100.48 kWh, 120.57 kWh and 261.24 kWh — and can be paired with 30–75 kW inverters (for low-voltage grids) and 50–125 kW inverters (for standard-voltage grids). Under its AC-DC separation architecture, a single inverter can connect up to 6 battery cabinets in parallel, so capacity can be expanded without additional inverter investment. The 125 kW all-in-one model integrates PCS, STS, PV inverter, circuit-breaker protection and EMS into one unit, achieving seamless on-grid/off-grid switching in under 10 milliseconds without an external STS, while supporting both DC and AC coupling and 200% PV oversizing. Thermal management and safety are the baseline for cabinet-type storage. EverCore stays with air cooling, using a three-air-duct architecture that combines a patented diversion air duct with Coanda-effect airflow to improve heat dissipation efficiency by roughly 30% over conventional air cooling. It is designed to operate from -25°C to 55°C at altitudes up to 4,000 meters. On the safety side, EVE 314Ah cells (8,000 cycles at 0.5C, 70% capacity retention, internal resistance as low as 0.15±0.05 mΩ) are paired with a 15-layer protective system — including thermal insulation between packs able to withstand 1,000°C, and a three-stage fire-suppression mechanism of pack-level aerosol, cabinet-level aerosol and fire-fighting water channels. Further up the scale, EverCore units can be paralleled to 1.25 MW, reaching grid-scale applications such as peak shaving and frequency regulation. These products cover C&I scenarios ranging from factories and farms to shopping malls, hospitals and large residences. Where site space is limited, the modular FlexCore-ID (indoor) and FlexCore-OD (outdoor) are the alternatives — the former built around 20 kWh battery packs and 314Ah LFP cells, the latter designed for direct outdoor deployment. artigo.texto: Especialistas avaliam que potencial do RN poderá torná-lo polo de data center Felipe Salustino Repórter O Rio Grande do Norte reúne todas as condições para se tornar um polo de data center dentro da corrida global por este tipo de tecnologia. A avaliação é de especialistas ouvidos pela TRIBUNA DO NORTE durante a Data Center Conference, realizada pelo Grupo FRG na sexta-feira (23), na Federação das Indústrias do Estado (Fiern), em Natal. O encontro reuniu representantes dos setores de tecnologia, energia, infraestrutura, meio ambiente e engenharia para debater o tema na capital potiguar. A escolha do local para realização do evento se deu exatamente em função das condições que o estado possui para o desenvolvimento de investimentos do tipo. Tiago Fraga, CEO do Grupo FRG e presidente do Conselho da World Carbon Association (WCA), detalhou que o RN possui diversas aptidões para se tornar um protagonista nesse tipo de empreendimento. “Em primeiro lugar, destaco a questão regulatória e de licenciamento ambiental, com a aprovação da resolução nº 02/2026”, afirma. Ele ressaltou que grandes data centers necessitam de investimentos da ordem de R$ 1 bilhão. “Então, o investidor precisa de segurança regulatória e de facilidades para aprovação de licenciamento ambiental. O estado ajustou esses dois pontos”, destaca. Tiago Fraga aponta outro fator: a disponibilidade de energia que gera excedente. “Esses três fatores colocam o Rio Grande do Norte como protagonista na corrida por data center, que é uma corrida mundial”, completa. Os data centers são estruturas que abrigam equipamentos capazes de processar e armazenar informações utilizadas por empresas, serviços públicos e plataformas digitais. O funcionamento desse tipo de tecnologia depende de uma estrutura que envolve fornecimento de energia, conectividade, refrigeração e segurança, conectando diferentes áreas de conhecimento e atividade econômica. A conferência teve apoio da Fiern, da WCA, Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), Conselho Regional de Engenharia e Agronomia do Rio Grande do Norte (Crea-RN), Potigás, Neoenergia Cosern e Banco do Nordeste. Roberto Serquiz, presidente da Fiern, ressaltou que, diante do ambiente atual, a reunião das diferentes áreas no deabte sobre o tema serve para que o estado possa avançar na busca por soluções que possam aproveitar o excedente energético gerado. “O potencial que nós temos foi construído ao longo de 20 anos de geração de energia que nos trouxe o curtailment, um problema gigante. E as soluções são o armazenamento em baterias, o hidrogênio verde e o data center, as quais devem resolver o impasse entre a geração e o uso intensivo de todo esse potencial”, explicou. Um dos palestrantes do evento, Gladson Mortoza, frisa que o RN tem todas as condições de se tornar um polo de data center, com um núcleo semelhante ao que é observado no Ceará. “O Rio Grande do Norte tem oferta de energia limpa com custo razoável, está trilhando meios rápidos para licenciar esse tipo de empreendimento e possui um aquífero, que garante segurança hídrica”, frisou. “Então, existe toda uma pré-condição para que o estado se torne um polo de data center”, finalizou. Para Luis Tossi, vice-presidente da ABDC, o RN tem buscado um ambiente propício para esse tipo de investimento com regulação e licenciamento. Ele ressalta os impactos que esses empreendimentos provocam nas regiões onde são implementados. “A instalação de um data center de 100 megawatts gera de 6 mil a 9 mil postos diretos de trabalho durante a construção, que leva de 18 a 24 meses, e requer algo entre 600 e 800 empregos diretos de mão de obra altamente especializada, como engenheiros, tecnólogos e outros”, descreve. Há necessidade de conectividade via cabos submarinos Para os especialistas ouvidos pela reportagem, o Rio Grande do Norte tem dado passos importantes para investimentos em data center e deve seguir avançando nesse ambiente. A regulamentação do setor é um desses, mas ainda há a necessidade de conectividade via cabo submarino para a instalação de grandes empreendimentos. De acordo com Emília Casanova, secretária-adjunta de Desenvolvimento Econômico do Estado (Sedec), o Rio Grande do Norte ainda aguarda definição do Governo Federal para a instalação de, ao menos, um cabo. “Nós temos um estudo de atracação em áreas de interesse, porém, não houve ainda uma decisão do Ministério de Telecomunicações, que inclui, dentre outros pontos, uma definição sobre os locais de instalação”, disse ela. “A gente não sabe se será somente em Natal ou se haverá uma conexão também na região da Costa Branca”, completou a adjunta. O tema também integrou as discussões da Data Center Conference na sexta-feira, em Natal. De acordo com Gladson Mortoza, gerente comercial da Mendes Holler, empresa especialista em data center, a expectativa é de que a tecnologia chegue ao RN no curto e médio prazos e, assim, o estado deve conseguir instalar grandes estruturas capazes de atender às demandas regionais e globais. “Repito que o estado já possui oferta de energia. Com a expectativa da chegada de conectividade via cabo submarino, o Rio Grande do Norte abre a porta para atender às demandas locais, de todo país e até mesmo internacionais”, frisou gerente, que ministrou palestra durante o evento. artigo.texto: [SMM Cobalt Morning Meeting Summary] Raw material prices continue to decline, end-use demand is weak, and the market is under pressure At the start of this week, the industry chain remained in the doldrums overall, with raw material prices continuing to slide, end-use demand weak, and market purchasing sentiment cautious. Electrolytic metal prices temporarily stabilised, consolidating around 230,000 yuan/mt, with low imports and production cut rumours boosting market confidence, though supply-demand fundamentals had yet to improve. Sulphate prices continued to pull back, with some traders quoting close to 40,000 yuan/mt, and lower recycled raw material costs further weakened price support. Chloride and trimanganese tetroxide prices weakened in tandem, with downstream inventory high and purchasing demand insufficient. Actual transactions for metal powder fell to around 275,000 yuan/mt, and the market still faced downward pressure. The cathode material segment remained under pressure, with ternary cathode precursor processing coefficients weakening and operating rates declining at some enterprises; ternary cathode material order growth was sluggish, and November production schedules were expected to decline further. Consumer cathode materials were dragged down by sluggish end-use demand and falling raw material prices, prompting enterprises to proactively cut production, while inventory destocking remained slow. On the industry news front, XTC New Energy Materials (Xiamen) plans to invest 723 million yuan to build a project with annual capacity of 40,000 mt of LFP; GSP Automotive Group's solid-liquid hybrid battery production line debugging fell short of expectations. Overall, the market is expected to consolidate on a weak note in the near term, with price stabilisation contingent on demand recovery and inventory digestion.

artigo.texto: Financing battery energy storage: key legal considerations for investors and lenders At a glance Developers typically finance battery energy storage systems (BESS) through non-recourse project finance structures using an SPV. Their volatile, market-driven reve-nues set them apart from wind and solar projects. A BESS project’s bankability depends on its revenue model. Tolling agreements offer the greatest financing certainty, while fully merchant projects require significantly more equity and face stricter covenants. The regulatory framework affects project economics and requires legal assessment early in project development. A largely unrestricted grid connection, or at least a grid connection commitment, is fundamental to any BESS project. Equity is a key component of bankable BESS financings. Investors may earn higher returns, but they also bear greater risks, particularly because they rank behind lend-ers and depend on volatile revenues. Battery energy storage systems (BESS) rank among the key technologies of the energy transition. They add flexibility to the power system, help integrate renewable energy and open up new trading opportunities – from balancing energy through arbitrage to ancillary services. Financing them nonetheless remains challenging: unlike wind and solar projects, they lack long-term guaranteed remuneration. Revenues are volatile, market-based and hard to forecast. Whether a battery storage system proves bankable therefore also depends on how it is structured legally. I. Financing structures: project finance and the non-recourse principle BESS projects are typically structured as standalone project financings through a special purpose vehicle (SPV). The financing follows the non-recourse principle: lenders have no recourse to the shareholders and rely instead solely on the project’s cash flows and assets. Typical loan tenors run between seven and ten years. The crucial difference from conventional renewable energy financing lies in the revenue profile. Where wind and solar projects often build on long-term feed-in tariffs, BESS revenues track dynamic market prices. That drives higher equity requirements, more conservative valuations and shorter loan tenors. Typical features of the financing documentation for BESS projects include: - Sculpted repayment matched to the batteries’ degradation curve - DSCR covenants - Cash-sweep mechanisms and restricted-payment clauses - Augmentation reserves funding later capacity additions The security package typically includes a pledge over the shares in the SPV, an all-assets assignment of claims under the material project agreements, pledges over bank accounts and a transfer of title to the facility by way of security. The last of these matters especially because batteries count as movable assets so lenders cannot take a mortgage over them. Securing rights in rem over a site is all the more important: without robust land, access and cable rights (usually secured through first-ranking limited personal easements in favour of the SPV and the lenders) financing cannot be structured. Reviewing site security is therefore a standard part of legal due diligence and deserves early attention, given how much it can delay a project. II. Revenue models and bankability A BESS project’s revenues typically rest on three pillars: ancillary services (notably FCR and aFRR), peak shaving and avoided network charges, and wholesale arbitrage. In practice projects combine these sources through revenue stacking. Prequalification requirements, state-of-charge management and technical constraints, however, limit how far they can do so. The choice of revenue model decides whether a project is bankable: - Tolling agreements offer the greatest planning certainty: the project company makes its storage capacity available to a counterparty and receives a fixed or partly variable fee. - Fully merchant projects are in principle bankable, but lenders apply significantly stricter requirements: they limit gearing more tightly, require higher DSCRs and additional liquidity reserves, and expect developers to update their trading forecasts regularly. - Hybrid floor structures strike a middle path, with loan-to-cost (LTC) ratios of 55–65%, for example through optimisation contracts with minimum fees. Degradation is a factor that should not be underestimated: batteries lose roughly 2-3% of their usable capacity each year. The financial model should realistically reflect this technical risk, which should be mitigated through manufacturer warranties and an augmentation reserve. Beyond that, bankability requires technical due diligence, an independent revenue forecast, qualified project partners and confirmation that the project can obtain insurance. III. Regulatory framework The regulatory framework significantly affects a BESS project’s economics so developers must factor it into project development at an early stage. Grid connection: A grid connection is fundamental to financing any BESS project. Transmission system operators and, increasingly, distribution system operators use maturity-based procedures to allocate grid capacity. Developers should clarify availability, connection capacity, costs and deadlines early. Flexible connection arrangements can make it easier to connect a project, but they may restrict how the project can operate. The grid connection contribution also represents a material investment and site-selection factor, as reflected in recent Federal Court of Justice case law (2025). Exemption from network charges: Battery storage currently benefits from an exemption from network charges if it enters operation by 4 August 2029. The statutory deadline for new storage projects to qualify ends on that date.
