artigo.texto: BYD announced on October 26 that blind orders are now open for the second-generation Seal 07. The car was first unveiled by the regulatory filings on August 7th. Design and dimensions The new model continues the “Ocean Aesthetics” 2.0 design language and shares its overall styling with the Seal 08. The front features a wave-shaped split headlight arrangement and a closed grille. A LiDAR unit on the roof suggests the car may come with BYD’s God’s Eye B advanced driver-assistance system. Six exterior colors are offered: Pala Green, Aurora Pink, Sea Mist Purple, Liuguang Silver, Snow White and Obsidian Black. The car measures 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase that BYD says expands cabin space. Its rear uses a full-width taillight design derived from the Seal 08. Interior Inside, the Seal 07 adopts BYD’s latest design language. It keeps a large floating central display and a digital instrument cluster, and adds a new three-spoke steering wheel. The center console trim and air vent shapes have also been revised. Wireless phone charging and two cup holders remain in the front center console. Three interior color schemes are available: Yunxi White, Phantom Grey and Ningye Purple. The car also features a 20-speaker audio system. Seating includes zero-gravity front seats with massage, ventilation and heating functions. The rear has a large sofa-style bench. The 2,960 mm wheelbase is said to improve passenger space. Storage includes a 618-liter trunk and a 160-liter front trunk, described as the largest in its class. The Seal 07 will be offered in two powertrain options. The plug-in hybrid uses a 1.5T turbocharged engine rated at 115 kW and a drive motor rated at 160 kW (215 hp). It has a 38 kWh battery pack and a WLTC electric range of 245 km. The battery-electric version uses a drive motor with a peak output of 300 kW (402 hp), offers up to 718 km of WLTP range. Both versions will feature BYD’s second-generation Blade Battery, flash charging and DiSus-M suspension.

artigo.texto: Oregon residents debate Issue 25 during council meeting one week before vote on data center Supporters and opponents speak out ahead of vote on $1 billion data center OREGON, Ohio (WTVG) - Oregon residents voiced their opinions on a potential $1 billion data center one week before they vote on the issue. Residents say the language of Issue 25 is confusing. A yes vote supports a ban on a data center with a demand or peak load of 25 megawatts or greater. A no vote opposes that ban. Supporters cite financial benefits Ben Pfeiffer, a science teacher at Clay High School who has taught in the community for 28 years, said passing any kind of levy would be difficult given current economic conditions. “I think that we can agree that given the economic times we’re in, passing any kind of levy would be difficult. It doesn’t have to be this way,” Pfeiffer said. Pfeiffer said the data center could help avoid future financial strain on the school district. “Over 15 years, this commercial project is estimated to bring more than $100 million to Oregon City Schools. That includes $10 million in milestone payments over the next three to four years, and $7 million every year through a pilot agreement,” Pfeiffer said. Pfeiffer said the district would need to put forth an operating levy in 2028 unless the data center moves forward. He said the financial forecast has determined this revenue would offset the operating deficit and avoid a levy request for eight to 10 years. Melissa Mummert, an intervention specialist at Clay High School, also said the data center is necessary. “Our children are doing their part every day. Now we must do ours. We need to build an educational future defined by opportunity rather than program cuts and inspiration rather than reduced services,” Mummert said. Opponents raise concerns Those arguments did not sway several people in the audience who support Issue 25. Laura Davis, a volunteer with United Neighbors of Oregon, compared the district’s planning strategy to an unreliable financial gamble. “This planning strategy is like buying a car and hoping to make the payments when you win the lottery. There does not seem to be a plan B if the data center does not happen,” Davis said. Mary Crowley, who opposes the data center, cited concerns about artificial intelligence and data security. “We don’t want a data center. We don’t want unregulated AI. We don’t want surveillance technology. We don’t want our data being stolen and used against us. We don’t want our resources exhausted,” Crowley said. Those who spoke at the meeting are urging Oregon residents to research data centers before casting their vote. artigo.texto: Regulating data centers in San Antonio has boiled down to one choice. Should data centers be approved on a case-by-case basis or can they be built by-right, whenever they meet a set of pre-determined city standards? On Tuesday, the City of San Antonio’s Zoning Commission recommended a plan for regulating data centers. It gives San Antonio City Council, which will make a final decision next week, a fourth option for regulations after three were presented last week. All four use by-right, case-by-case or a combination of those approval processes. There are some clear starting points for any data center land-use policy in San Antonio. Data centers will only be built in industrial, commercial or manufacturing zones. They will also not be allowed over the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone. These rules are only for land use — regulations regarding power or water use would fall under CPS Energy and the San Antonio Water System’s authority. The city’s Development Services Department presented two initial options for data center rules. The by-right option allows data centers to be approved automatically once they meet a list of city requirements. The case-by-case policy would require each data center project in the city to be plead its own case in front of City Council. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones presented a third option last week, giving developers a list of citywide standards that developers could meet before they earn approval from City Council on a case-by-case basis. On Tuesday, the city’s Zoning Commission put forward its own recommendation. The committee of council member-appointed residents, which makes recommendations on land-use to City Council, outlined a policy that allows by-right data centers in some parts of the city , but not in others. San Antonio City Council will decide what the new rules will be at an Oct. 29 A session. The newest proposal On Tuesday, the Zoning Commission put forward its proposal for regulations. The commission’s policy proposal would allow by-right development in industrial areas, specifically the general, heavy, mixed and mixed heavy industrial districts, while there would be specific use authorization in business park, light industrial and general commercial zones. To build data centers by-right, developers would have to leave 350 feet of separation between data centers and residential or neighborhood buildings and have a 100-foot setback from their own property line. The rules also require downward-facing lighting, to prevent light pollution. The Zoning Commission also considered data centers that were already built; San Antonio currently has at least 19 data centers, according to the Texas Tribune. Sparrow said many previously built data centers would be non-conforming with new rules. They would be allowed to keep operating, he said, but they would not be able to expand or conduct extensive repairs unless they come into line with new policies. Commissioner John Bustamante recommended including an exemption for older data centers under the new rules, allowing them to finish expansions or phased construction. It was approved as part of the Zoning Commission’s recommendation. The Zoning Commission does not enact policies. Its recommendation will go to City Council members, who will consider it when making their decision. The first two options Councilman Ric Galvan (D6) got the ball rolling on data center regulations almost a year ago, when he submitted a request in October 2025 to start the policymaking process. Data centers have multiplied across Texas as larger facilities look to serve artificial intelligence needs. Galvan’s district has been a hotspot for their development within city limits. Staff from the city’s Development Services Department had four public meetings between May and September, where they discussed potential policies with stakeholders. “If you wanted to participate, you were invited,” said Logan Sparrow, assistant director at the DSD. “Not going to lie, a lot of those folks were from the [data center development] industry, but we certainly tried our best to include as many people as we could.” Developers have pushed for a set of clear requirements for construction. They see those rules as more stable, making investment and construction more dependable. That’s why they want by-right development, one of the first policies proposed by DSD. Developers could build a data center if they own the land and meet city requirements, which would include being 500 feet away from residential, school, hospital, day care and assisted living properties and a landscape buffer onsite. City officials are referring to this as Option 1. “Anytime we want to attract investment, there has to be consistency and predictability. They want to know the rules of the game,” said Stephanie Reyes, president of the Real Estate Council of San Antonio, who spoke in favor of by-right development on Tuesday. DSD staff also proposed case-by-case evaluations of data centers. That would require what’s known as a specific use authorization for each proposed data center. That means every data center would go in front of the Zoning Commission and City Council, which would lay out specific requirements for each data center. City officials are referring to this as Option 2. “It’s so important for you all to recommend to City Council this specific use authorization because it would give the public the opportunity to ask these questions and to give feedback and to share their concerns,” said Deedee Belmares, Clean Energy advocate for advocacy group Public Citizen. Public Citizen monitors data centers and informs residents about their development in San Antonio and across the state. On Wednesday, Belmares advocated for case-by-case evaluations of data centers, speaking out against DSD’s by-right proposal and the Zoning Commission’s latest recommendation. The Mayor’s proposal During an Oct. 14 City Council meeting, Jones shared what she called a combination of by-right and case-by-case processe

artigo.texto: RWE completes sale of shares in Five Estuaries Offshore Wind Farm 09.10.2026 RWE and Borussia Dortmund officially commissioned the new battery storage system at SIGNAL IDUNA PARK today during the Bundesliga home match against Eintracht Frankfurt. This marks the completion of the two partners’ joint energy concept for the stadium. Following the installation of the photovoltaic system on the roof of the BVB FanWelt and the completion of the world’s most powerful photovoltaic system on a stadium roof, the battery storage system has also become operational. The battery storage system has a capacity of 3.7 megawatts and can supply this output for just over an hour. The photovoltaic system, which was commissioned in December 2025, comprises 11,132 solar modules and has a capacity of more than 5 megawatts (MWp). By linking the battery to the new PV system, the electricity generated can be used even when the sun is not shining. With the new photovoltaic system, BVB can meet up to 45 per cent of SIGNAL IDUNA PARK’s electricity requirements. Dr Markus Krebber, Chief Executive of RWE AG: “With the commissioning of the battery storage system, the entire system comprising the photovoltaic plant and the battery at SIGNAL IDUNA PARK is now fully operational. Linking the two systems makes it possible to use the solar power generated on site even more flexibly, even when the sun isn’t shining. The experts from BVB and RWE have breathed life and energy into our partnership through this project. It provides a solid foundation for further joint developments.” Carsten Cramer, Chairman of the Executive Board of Borussia Dortmund: “SIGNAL IDUNA PARK is not only our iconic home, but also a central element of our holistic decarbonisation strategy. With the battery storage system, we are collaborating with RWE to complete a forward-looking energy concept that makes our solar power even more usable. We are delighted that our stadium will thus continue to stand for resource-efficient and innovative action in the future.” As a “Premium Partner” and a key part of the “BVB Empowers” initiative, RWE will continue to support BVB in optimising the energy management of SIGNAL IDUNA PARK as part of the six-year partnership. The aim is to further increase the stadium’s contribution to security of supply, energy efficiency, and decarbonisation. Images for media use (image rights: BVB) are available in the media library. Further information on the project can be found at: www.rwe.com/bvb

artigo.texto: - Data centers have become a topic of intense debate in Michigan as tech giants rush to build the computing facilities - A Bridge Michigan panel explored the tension between Michigan’s economic goals and the environmental realities of data centers - The discussion caps Bridge Listens, a yearlong experiment in reader-led journalism Michigan lawmakers are under intense pressure to regulate data centers more strictly as public opposition to the computing facilities becomes too strong to ignore. That’s a key takeaway from speakers on an expert panel at the inaugural Bridge Michigan Issues Summit at Marygrove Conservancy, titled “Innovation Collision: Balancing High-Tech Ambitions with Energy and Water Realities.” The half-day Issues Summit featured expert speakers on some of the most pressing issues facing Michigan ahead of the November election, from education outcomes to healthcare costs and housing affordability. The event capped Bridge Listens, the news organization’s yearlong focus on top issues identified by more than 6,400 Bridge readers in survey responses. Environmental topics including data centers ranked high on readers’ list of concerns. In response, Bridge has spent much of the year digging into Michigan’s data center debate, including reporting on candidates’ policy stances, documenting the public pushback and exploring Michigan’s strategy to absorb the facilities’ massive energy and water demand. More than 375 people attended the Issues Summit in Detroit, virtually or at a watch party at Alpena Community College. During the data center discussion, audience members heard from: - Brenda Stumbo, Ypsilanti Township supervisor - Michelle Martinez, director of the University of Michigan Tishman Center for Social Justice and the Environment - Erik E. Nordman, director of Michigan State University’s Institute of Public Utilities - Jeff Guilfoyle, senior strategist at Public Sector Consultants All agreed that intense pushback against data centers has begun to reshape Michigan’s policy landscape just two years after lawmakers first passed tax breaks meant to lure data center developers to the state. By exempting qualifying data centers from sales and use taxes, lawmakers “opened the floodgates” to development with little input from residents, said Martinez. It left many feeling “blindsided by the scope, the speed and the lack of channels to have a voice in the decision-making,” she said. The panelists offered differing perspectives about how the industry may shape the state, with some expressing concerns about negative environmental and quality-of-life consequences from data center development while others argued Michigan stands to reap meaningful returns from the multi-billion-dollar investments. In Saline Township, for example, annual property tax revenue from Oracle and OpenAI’s forthcoming Stargate data center will boost local tax revenue from a few hundred thousand annually to more than $10 million annually, said Guilfoyle, who has studied the potential economic benefits of data center development. “That’s a significant increase and that money is a driver in the community,” Guilfoyle said. The facility is also expected to employ 450 people permanently on-site while supporting thousands of temporary construction jobs. The promised benefits so far haven’t won over many Michigan residents, nearly two-thirds of whom oppose the building of data centers in the state, according to recent polling. Ypsilanti Township Supervisor Brenda Stumbo is familiar with that pushback, which she blames in part on lawmakers welcoming the industry to Michigan without consulting voters or local public officials who’d be left to negotiate the details with some of the world’s wealthiest companies. “It was rushed,” Stumbo said of Michigan’s process, “and we know as individuals, in our personal lives and professional lives, when you rush something, it doesn’t really go well.” Data center developers have since fanned out across Michigan looking for land and available energy. A single 1-gigawatt facility demands as much power as a large US city, prompting questions about how Michgian utilities can absorb the spiking demand without raising rates on residential customers. “It’s the million-dollar question,” said Nordman. And so far, the answer is unclear. In some areas, increased demand from data centers has helped tamp down on residential rates by adding a new customer to split the cost of maintaining poles, wires and power plants, Nordman noted. But in others, data center demand has outstripped existing capacity on the grid, creating a mismatch between energy supply and demand that has driven rates up. Michigan should be insulated from at least some of that rate shock, he said, because state policy prohibits utilities from forcing other customers to shoulder the cost of investments needed to serve data centers. Asked whether Michigan utilities can absorb data centers’ skyrocketing energy demand while still meeting Michigan’s mandate to transition to 100% clean energy by 2040, Nordman was less optimistic. “It will be challenging,” he said. “Very, very difficult. Because, when we put these laws in place, we had relatively flat demand growth … now we have to work twice as hard.” Even if Michigan utilities manage to meet the 2040 deadline, Martinez noted, data center demand in other states is likely to lead to new investments in fossil fuel infrastructure that drives climate change. “In Texas, they have a 424 GW backlog for data centers alone,” Martinez said. “The air that comes from Texas does not stay in Texas.” Watch the entire Issues Summit here:

artigo.texto: A specific kind of development has been assigned new Washington County zoning requirements: battery energy storage facilities. The county’s board of supervisors voted unanimously last week to put special permits in place for projects involving large industrial installations that store and distribute power to the electric grid. The regulations apply to storage facilities that have a capacity greater than 600 kilowatts per hour and, with the approval of a permit, they can be built only in light and heavy industrial zones. With the ordinance in place, the supervisors will have to vote to approve any battery energy storage projects. Lightshift Energy, an Arlington-based energy storage developer, has expressed interest in building one in Washington County, according to county officials. The projects would likely only be built in places near electrical substations, said Stephen Richardson, the county’s planning commission coordinator. “They don’t want to be very far away because you lose all your efficiency,” Richardson said. “You lose your current the longer the line is.” Combined with the new zoning restrictions, the only viable places would likely be in industrial parks, he said. There are three Appalachian Power substations around Abingdon: the Hillman Highway Substation, South Abingdon Substation and Arrowhead Substation. The power company also operates a major facility at Highlands Business Park near Glade Spring. Data centers have begun using energy storage systems to act as a buffer for voltage spikes and reduce reliance on diesel generators, and utility companies have begun to install them too. Earlier this spring, the Salem-based Blue Ridge Power Agency announced it was pairing with Lightshift to deploy energy storage installments across five sites in the region. In addition to the projects in Salem, Lightshift is also seeking federal approval for an energy storage installation at Highlands Business Park. The company is leasing a parcel there for $10,000 annually until it gets the proper permits, and then it plans to buy the property, County Administrator Jason Berry said by phone. It should be beneficial for anyone using the grid, Berry said, since the facility would be able to stabilize it and prevent blackouts. Appalachian Power uses the lines the facility would attach to, and its parent company, American Electric Power, also feeds power through those lines to multiple other states, he said. Lightshift declined to comment on the Washington County project. Once the company buys the property, the board of supervisors would have to vote to approve the development plans now that the stricter zoning regulations are in place. Though battery energy storage facilities require no onsite jobs, it would bring in more business property tax revenue for the county, Berry said. “For us, it’s more of a tax generator than a job generator,” he said. Other than Lightshift, there has been no other interest in battery energy storage projects in Washington County, Berry said.

artigo.texto: BYD FCB Ti 9 full-size SUV to launch post-Nov 15, Shark pickup enters China in December BYD’s Fang Cheng Bao brand will launch the Ti 9 full-size plug-in hybrid SUV in China after November 15, 2026, followed by the domestic debut of its Shark plug-in hybrid pickup in late November or early December. General Manager Xiong Tianbo announced the schedule, with Ti 9 display and test-drive vehicles expected at dealerships in late October ahead of launch. Fang Cheng Bao’s Ti 9 offers a six-seat layout and a 310 km electric range. The Ti 9 will become the flagship of Fang Cheng Bao’s Ti series, which targets the urban family segment with unibody SUVs. It measures 5,270 mm long, 1,999 mm wide and 1,880 mm tall, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase. Unlike the Bao 5 and Bao 8, which use body-on-frame construction, the Ti 9 adopts a monocoque structure and BYD’s DMS hybrid platform. The cabin has a six-seat, 2+2+2 layout with independent second-row seats. Equipment includes heating, ventilation, and massage functions across all three rows, a 30-inch panoramic front display, and a 21.4-inch ceiling-mounted, fold-down rear entertainment screen. The plug-in hybrid powertrain combines a 1.5-litre turbocharged gasoline engine rated at 115 kW (154 hp) with two electric motors producing up to 200 kW each. Together, they produce 400 kW (536 hp) and drive both axles. A 66.48 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery from BYD’s FinDreams Battery delivers a claimed 310 km of electric-only range under the WLTC test cycle. BYD also claims a total range exceeding 1,600 km with a full tank and fully charged battery. The Ti 9 comes standard across all trims with BYD’s DiSus-A air suspension with road-preview capability and the iATS (Intelligent All-Terrain System). It also features flash-charging technology and second-generation Blade batteries. Exterior options include six finishes: Flowing Light Gold, Universal Silver, Starburst Gold, Crimson Cloud Red, Deep Space Blue and Meteorite Black, with solid and two-tone options. BYD Shark pickup prepares for domestic launch in China Fang Cheng Bao plans to introduce the Shark plug-in hybrid pickup in China in late November or early December 2026. The model debuted in Mexico in May 2024 and has since entered international markets. China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) lists the domestic version as a light-duty multipurpose truck. It measures 5,457 mm long, 1,971 mm wide and 1,925 mm tall, with a 3,260 mm wheelbase. The cargo bed measures 1,520 × 1,530 × 515 mm. The filing lists a curb weight of 2,710 kg, a gross vehicle weight rating of 3,495 kg and a rated payload of 460 kg. The domestic Shark uses a 1.5-litre turbocharged gasoline engine, designated BYD476ZQF, with a net output of 135 kW (181 hp). Its all-wheel-drive system pairs a 170 kW front electric motor with a 150 kW rear motor, delivering a combined peak electric-motor output of 320 kW (429 hp). The listed maximum speed is 180 km/h. An LFP battery supplied by Xi’an FinDreams Battery powers the plug-in hybrid system. Available domestic regulatory specifications do not list battery capacity or electric-only range, so overseas figures should not be treated as confirmed specifications for the Chinese version. Pricing remains unannounced Fang Cheng Bao has not yet announced domestic prices or trim levels for either model. The Ti 9 targets family buyers seeking a large, six-seat plug-in hybrid SUV, while the Shark extends the brand into the pickup segment. Fang Cheng Bao is a premium BYD brand that sold around 126,000 cars in the third quarter of 2026, up 131% from the same period last year.

artigo.texto: Found an error? Report now Marcel Aumer, CEO and majority shareholder of Flexbase, is having a large battery storage facility built in Laufenburg, Aargau. Keystone FlexBase is building a technology center in Laufenburg, Aargau. At its heart is a battery that will one day help stabilize the power grid. But from the perspective of FlexBase CEO Marcel Aumer, this can only be the beginning. When the Keystone-SDA news agency visited FlexBase in mid-September, the large construction site in Laufenburg was characterized above all by a massive excavation pit and numerous cranes. In the future, a building 218 meters long, 80 meters wide, 25 meters deep, and 30 meters high will stand there, as Aumer explained. To blend into the landscape, the concrete structure will be clad with a blue photovoltaic system, as Aumer explained. This complements the often-blue skies of the Fricktal region. The system will be one of the largest PV facade installations in Europe and will have “a capacity of at least two megawatts.” However, according to Aumer, the PV system is out of proportion to the battery storage system being installed. Plans at the time called for 108 vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFB) with a maximum capacity of 1.2 gigawatts by 2029—equivalent to that of the Leibstadt nuclear power plant. According to FlexBase, the planned storage capacity of 2.1 gigawatt-hours corresponds to the electricity needs of 170,000 households over a 24-hour period. Unlike a lithium-ion battery, the VRFB model planned for Laufenburg is neither flammable nor explosive, as Aumer noted. The tanks are mostly filled with water, which also simplifies disposal. Furthermore, the vanadium dissolved in the water—which is used as an electrolyte—is reusable. There is virtually no degradation, and the service life of redox flow batteries is longer than that of lithium-ion storage systems, for which the disposal problem remains unresolved. The largest facility of its kind to date is located in China and began operations at the start of the year, as Rongke Power announced at the time. According to the company’s figures, its capacity and output amount to one gigawatt-hour and 200 megawatts—significantly less than what is planned for Laufenburg. From Aumer’s perspective, this is the technology for a sustainable future, and it is gaining ground worldwide. “I have clear goals in mind,” said Aumer. “The peaks caused by renewable energy need to be smoothed out.” This refers both to short-term fluctuations and to storing excess capacity during the day and releasing it at night when capacity is insufficient. “But we still have a long, long way to go before we can ensure a 24-hour, 356-day power supply from renewable energy sources,” Aumer said. He cited Europe as an example. In its Electrification Action Plan published in July, the European Commission cited a need for 200 gigawatts of storage capacity by 2030 and as much as 500 gigawatts by 2040. According to Aumer, the demand for power and capacity is enormous. “Our project is large, but our 1.2 gigawatts of power and 2.1 gigawatt-hours of capacity are just a drop in the bucket,” Aumer noted. However, he added, batteries cannot simply be connected to the grid at will. The grids are aging, and there is a lack of connection capacity. Expansion is difficult—partly due to objections. “It’s the only place to build something on this scale. There’s no other place like it,” Aumer said of the site. That’s because the Laufenburg star connects the Swiss power grid to the European grid—here, more than 41 cross-border lines provide access to the European electricity market. “I don’t have that anywhere else,” said Aumer. Aumer knows the location very well. Over the past ten years, he has been coming and going from the Stern in Laufenburg for work. He developed the idea for the project over the course of several years, drawing on his experience. When the property in Laufenburg went up for sale in 2023, he “knew within a second: This is it.” When it comes to finances, Aumer is keeping a low profile. He said the total costs would range from 2.5 to 5 billion Swiss francs. The money comes from private funds—but he does not want to publicly disclose his investors. The CEO revealed that he is the majority shareholder of FlexBase. However, he isn't doing it for the money—his passion project can only be realized in this location and in this way, as a campus that covers a wide range of subject areas. These include, for example, an AI data center above the Batterie and space for startups.

artigo.texto: Columbus data centers could pay more under proposed rate hike for high-usage customers COLUMBUS, Ohio (WSYX) — Columbus Water and Power reached its October 26 deadline to submit a proposed rate structure for high-usage customers. The proposal comes as utility costs remain a concern for Columbus residents and city leaders look for ways to ensure large customers cover the costs of the utilities being used. Columbus Councilman Christopher Wyche, chair of the Public Utilities & Sustainability Committee, said the city wants to identify customers whose water demand regularly puts additional strain on the system. “I think we want to have that flexibility to one, have conversations with customers who may face the surcharge, but two, as we are having those discussions, to find those who are peaking and surcharging on a regular basis, that they are in this methodology,” Wyche said during a Public Utilities & Sustainability Committee meeting on October 21. How would the new rates work? Columbus Water and Power Deputy Director Jon Lee said the proposed structure includes a high-demand surcharge for about 400 commercial customers whose water usage spikes above typical levels. “The purpose of the rate is straightforward. It is to more fairly recover the additional system capacity costs created by commercial customers whose water demand rises significantly above their normal usage,” Lee said. Lee said the utility must maintain enough capacity to meet periods of unusually high demand, including the treatment, pumping, storage and distribution needed to deliver water. “When a customer has unusually high peaks, we still have to maintain the treatment, pumping, storage and distribution capacity necessary to serve that peak,” Lee said. “The proposed surcharge will cover those additional costs.” Under the proposal, commercial customers using at least 100 hundred cubic feet (CCF) of water per month and meeting a peak-demand factor of 2.0 times their typical usage would qualify for the high-demand surcharge. One CCF equals 748 gallons, meaning 100 CCF is equivalent to 74,800 gallons per month. That number is roughly 15 times the average water usage of a single-family home. The proposed high-demand surcharge is $1.62 per CCF. According to Lee, about 426 customers would qualify under the current model, generating an estimated $6 million in revenue. “Based on our current modeling, approximately 426 customers would qualify with those parameters. Customers creating higher system capacity requirements should bear an appropriate share of those costs,” Lee said. The proposal focuses on water usage and infrastructure costs. It does not establish whether data centers or other large customers would face higher electricity rates under a separate structure. What could it mean for residents? City leaders say the goal is to keep customers with unusually high water and energy demand from shifting the additional costs onto the average homeowner. “We should be careful not to spread those extra costs onto households and businesses already relying on the system,” said Emmanuel Remy, vice-chair of the Public Utilities & Sustainability Committee. However, the proposed surcharge does not guarantee lower household utility bills or prevent future rate increases. The city has not indicated that residents would see immediate savings if the proposal is approved. The Water & Power Dept. also recommended changing its water capacity fees so new customers help pay for planned infrastructure projects, including the Home Road water treatment plant, rather than shifting those costs onto existing ratepayers. Customers who do not meet the proposed high-demand criteria would not be subject to this particular surcharge. If approved, the new charges are expected to begin in late 2027 or early 2028. What's next? Water revenue would shift some costs away from residential and small business customers, making their standard water rates about 1.6% lower than usual. While that would only slightly offset Columbus’ planned 18% water rate increase in 2027, it could help limit future increases as data centers and other high-demand users grow. Columbus Water and Power confirmed Monday that it submitted its rate recommendations to City Council. The department declined an interview before the council's public hearing on the proposal. The public hearing is scheduled for Thursday, November 12. The legislation is then expected to go before City Council for a first reading on November 16 and second reading on November 23. The proposal will need to move through the council process before the new rates can take effect.

artigo.texto: Kern CASA program electrifies first home with new appliances, solar and battery storage BAKERSFIELD, Calif. (KBAK/KBFX) — For one Kern County homeowner, a new set of home upgrades means more than new appliances. Maria Perez’s home is the first to be fully retrofitted through the Kern CASA Project, a program that helps qualifying families make energy and health-related improvements at no cost. Perez, who has asthma and lives on a fixed income, received a series of upgrades including an electric HVAC system, water heater, stove and dryer. Her home was also weatherized and equipped with solar panels and battery storage. Project Manager Brianda Castro said the work is designed to reduce the home’s reliance on gas while also addressing indoor air quality. “Simply just switching gas appliances to electric appliances and making sure that we remove any fossil fuel footprint with gas combustion from the home,” Castro said. Perez had previously received asthma-related services through the Central California Asthma Collaborative. Castro said that connection helped make her a strong fit for the project, which is also focused on reducing pollutants inside the home. “So, when you eliminate the use of gas in the home it eliminates those pollutants and so therefore it creates a healthier just air quality within the home,” Castro said. The cost of making those changes can be a major hurdle for families, Castro said, particularly for lower-income households that may not be able to afford newer appliances or larger home upgrades on their own. “And then lastly these appliances are also newer which means that they are not very affordable for the regular low-income household. the beauty about the programs that we offer to residents in low-income communities is that it has no cost to the homeowner,” Castro said. Perez said the improvements are especially meaningful because managing her asthma while living on a fixed income has often meant prioritizing household expenses over her own health needs. The first completed home is expected to be one of several. Castro said the project plans to complete upgrades at another 18 homes. The funding also included a workforce development component. Twenty Kern County residents were trained in skills related to home retrofits, and Castro said some have since worked on homes included in the project. Although applications for this round of Kern CASA funding are closed, Castro said her team continues to connect families with other programs that may help them qualify for similar home improvements.

artigo.texto: Wall Street's fastest traders are building data centers and backing chip startups to stay ahead in AI High-frequency traders like Jane Street and Hudson River Trading are now racing each other for AI computing power. The biggest firms are spending billions on cloud contracts, startups, and their own data centers, Bloomberg reports. Part of the reason is that they increasingly rely on machine learning to predict market moves. One executive estimates that compute spending is now ten to twenty times higher than it was before ChatGPT launched. XTX Markets is building a data center in Finland, and Jane Street runs one in Texas with more than 4,000 Nvidia GPUs. Hudson River spends $1 billion a year on AI, according to AI chief Iain Dunning, and signed a multiyear deal with CoreWeave. Jane Street went a different route. It invested $1 billion directly in CoreWeave and committed $6 billion to its computing services. Jane Street also led a funding round for chip startup Etched and became the first customer for its AI chip, which is supposed to deliver more performance by running at a lower voltage. According to Bloomberg, the industry sees rising costs and fast-aging chips as real risks. Executives like Jan Boomaars, CEO of Amsterdam-based high-frequency trader Optiver, still think doing nothing is more dangerous. artigo.texto: KARACHI: Pakistan’s military-owned Margalla Heavy Industries Limited (MHIL) has signed an agreement with Chinese partners and local investors to set up a $2.25 billion lithium-ion battery manufacturing plant in Rawalpindi, an official said on Monday, with production expected to begin within months of the government approving a policy for the sector, reports Arab News. The development comes as the South Asian country seeks to reduce its reliance on imported energy technologies and develop local manufacturing capacity amid growing demand for energy storage, electric vehicles and renewable energy. Lithium-ion batteries are central to storing electricity generated by solar and wind power and powering electric mobility, making domestic production a potential avenue for reducing import costs and attracting foreign investment. The gigafactory’s feasibility studies have been completed and the project is awaiting approval before it could start manufacturing, according to Hamad Ali Mansoor, CEO of the Engineering Development Board (EDB), an apex government body entrusted to strengthen the engineering base in Pakistan. “The building is ready, the machines are installed, so after the policy comes, the production will start within six to eight months,” Mansoor told Arab News, adding that Islamabad was working with Chinese and local stakeholders to invest in the multibillion-dollar project. “They are investing $2.25 billion in Pakistan.”Located at Heavy Industries Taxila in Rawalpindi district, MHIL manufactures defence equipment, including battle tanks, armoured vehicles, unmanned drones, protective gear, compact battery energy storage system and EV buses and two-wheelers. Arab News reached out to MHIL’s general manager for digital media, Muhammad Ameen, but he was not immediately available for comment.The development comes days after Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif approved the Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-2031, which awaits IMF approval over proposed tax incentives for Pakistan’s Electric Vehicles industry and their potential revenue implications. After the new EV-based auto policy takes effect, EDB estimates that Pakistan’s demand for battery energy storage systems (BESS) could reach as much as to 100,000 megawatts (MW) by June 2030. Building a local plant to manufacture lithium-ion batteries would be crucial for the cash-strapped country, which aims to shift its petrol-powered vehicles to EVs to save billions of dollars it spends every year to import fuel. Mansoor said the battery gigafactory project was signed in July with a Chinese company he described as one of the “top-tier manufacturers in China” alongside a local private-sector investor. He would not name the Chinese and local investors now. “They are manufacturing lithium-ion cells,” he said, adding that the facility would produce lithium-ion cells having a capacity of more than 1,000MW annually.EDB has estimated that grid stabilization alone could require 3,000-5,000MW of battery storage and that meeting the projected demand would require four to five gigafactories, each costing around $1 billion to $1.25 billion. “In our industry, we will have up to 100,000 megawatts of battery energy storage systems. This is a very large capacity. For this, we need four to five gigafactories,” the EDB CEO said.The first factory will initially produce around 200-300 MW before reaching its planned capacity of 1,000 megawatts, according to Mansoor. “If our economy grows by 5.0 per cent or more than 5.0 per cent of GDP (gross domestic product), then by June 2030, our demand will be up to 100,000MW,” he said.“And if our GDP grows by less than 3 percent, then our demand will be up to 80,000MW.” Mansoor said the demand would come from households, commercial buildings, industry and electric vehicles, including two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, buses and trucks.The government has prepared a lithium battery manufacturing policy that was submitted to the Ministry of Industries in March and is awaiting approval, according to the official. The plan includes four major factories, three in Punjab’s Lahore, Faisalabad and Rawalpindi divisions and one in southern city of Karachi, aimed at building domestic capacity for batteries used in electric vehicles and energy storage. The policy would require manufacturers to export a specified percentage of production, although Mansoor declined to provide the target before the policy’s approval.“We will manufacture it in Pakistan and export it,” he said, adding that the policy incorporates international safety and performance standards. Pakistan currently assembles around 3,000-4,000MW of batteries as well as parts like motors, controllers and chargers, but needs to move toward domestic manufacturing to avoid costly imports, according to Mansoor.“All these parts we [will] start manufacturing 100 per cent in Pakistan by next year,” he added.

artigo.texto: O mercado de carbono na encruzilhada da reforma tributária Falta de definição sobre a natureza jurídica dos créditos de carbono abre lacuna para interpretações diversas e incerteza sobre incidência dos novos tributos Atualizado A regulamentação da reforma tributária acabou criando uma contradição relevante para o mercado brasileiro de carbono. Ao instituir o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), a Lei nº 15.042/2024 buscou conferir tratamento tributário favorecido aos créditos de carbono, afastando a incidência de PIS e Cofins para estimular o desenvolvimento desse mercado estratégico. Entretanto, a disciplina do IBS e da CBS, introduzida pela Lei Complementar nº 214/2025, não reproduziu essa diretriz nem definiu expressamente a natureza jurídica desses ativos para fins de incidência dos novos tributos. A lacuna abre espaço para interpretações divergentes – se os créditos de carbono constituem ativo financeiro, valor mobiliário ou direito sujeito à tributação sobre o consumo – e cria um ambiente de insegurança jurídica justamente em um setor que depende de previsibilidade para viabilizar investimentos de longo prazo. Em determinadas interpretações, a carga tributária incidente sobre essas operações poderá alcançar cerca de 30%, comprometendo a competitividade do mercado brasileiro. A raiz desse impasse decorre da assimetria conceitual estabelecida pelo próprio arcabouço normativo. O artigo 14 da Lei nº 15.042/2024 estipula que os ativos do SBCE e os créditos de carbono configuram valores mobiliários apenas quando negociados nos mercados financeiro e de capitais sob regulação da CVM, enquanto o artigo 53 da mesma lei os qualifica como frutos civis nas iniciativas florestais. Em contrapartida, a Lei Complementar nº 214/2025 restringiu a não incidência de IBS e CBS aos títulos e valores mobiliários (artigo 6º, inciso VII), sujeitando a negociação de direitos e bens imateriais à regra geral do imposto sobre o consumo (artigo 4º). As alienações diretas de balcão – que concentram o mercado voluntário 2 ficam, assim, desprovidas de proteção tributária expressa. Com o término da desoneração do PIS e da Cofins em 2027, tais operações migrarão para uma alíquota padrão estimada entre 27% e 30%. Essa indefinição afeta toda a cadeia do mercado de carbono, alcançando empresas desenvolvedoras de projetos, produtores rurais, instituições financeiras, plataformas de negociação e companhias que utilizam créditos de carbono para cumprir metas de descarbonização. Além do aumento potencial da carga tributária, a ausência de regras claras tende a exigir revisões contratuais, provisões tributárias e reavaliações de investimentos até que haja posicionamento do legislador ou da Administração Tributária. A nosso ver, essa situação contraria os princípios da segurança jurídica, da neutralidade e da coerência normativa que orientaram a reforma tributária. Espera-se, portanto, que a regulamentação complementar ou eventuais ajustes legislativos esclareçam o tratamento tributário desses ativos, preservando a finalidade do SBCE e assegurando um ambiente regulatório compatível com a expansão do mercado de carbono no Brasil. O cenário é ainda mais sensível na aposentadoria ou cancelamento dos créditos pelas empresas compradoras. Sem a garantia de creditamento pleno no modelo não cumulativo, a tributação converte-se em custo à descarbonização. Cabe ao Comitê Gestor do IBS e à Receita Federal editar normas integradas que harmonizem o sistema fiscal com os princípios constitucionais de proteção ambiental inseridos pela Emenda Constitucional nº 132/2023. Sobre a autora Fernanda Rizzo é sócia da área Tributária & Aduaneira do escritório de advocacia Vieira Rezende.

artigo.texto: Democratic congressional nominee William Lawrence is calling for a federal moratorium on new data centers until regulations give communities greater control over development, saying opposition to the projects is bringing together voters across party lines. In a wide-ranging interview with Michigan Firsthand for The Livingston Post, Lawrence also outlined a gradual expansion of Medicare that could retain a role for private insurance, proposed a national infrastructure bank to finance housing, and endorsed legislation restricting transfers of offensive weapons to Israel. He also discussed his association with political streamer Hasan Piker, and his relationship with U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Lawrence faces Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett in the Nov. 3 election for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, which includes all of Livingston County. Advertising spending in the district has exceeded $61 million this election cycle, making it the nation’s costliest House race for advertising, according to WKAR and AdImpact data, as Democrats hope to wrest control of the U.S. House and Senate away from Republicans. Watch the full discussion with Lawrence on Michigan Firsthand, the YouTube podcast produced in partnership with The Livingston Post, by clicking here. Read our companion interview with Barrett in The Livingston Post and watch the full discussion on Michigan Firsthand here. A pause on data centers The Lansing resident and community organizer who defeated the former U.S. Ambassador Bridget Brink and former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam for the Democratic nomination argues that communities should not have to accept the projects to secure a prosperous future, particularly when the technology they support could displace workers. “We need to slow this down,” Lawrence said, calling for federal rules that would help communities “determine their own future rather than having it pushed onto us from above.” He described concerns over data centers as a bipartisan issue that surfaced in his meetings in Howell Township, Lyon Township, Mason and elsewhere with residents who shared concerns about electricity bills, water use and property values. “Unfortunately, there’s also been a lot of bipartisan support from the top down for supporting the interests of the big tech companies and data center developers,” he said. “I think people deserve to have a good future and a prosperous economy without just having to accept this deal that’s being pushed to us from Silicon Valley with no opportunity for local communities to determine their own futures.” Lawrence also acknowledged the state’s role in attracting data center developers through incentives such as tax breaks, and he criticized Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and state lawmakers for their handling of data center development. “I’ve been clear that I disagree with how the governor and the Michigan legislature has handled this issue,” he said. “And I think it really demonstrates that, again, this is an area where people from the grassroots have a lot in common: Democrat, independent and Republican.” Earlier this year, Attorney General Dana Nessel, in a previous interview with Michigan Firsthand for The Livingston Post, said that she thinks the Governor sold the legislature a “bill of goods.” A gradual expansion of Medicare On health care, Lawrence described Medicare for All as a goal reached through successive changes rather than an immediate replacement of the existing system. “It’s gonna be a step-by-step process,” he said. His proposed steps include lowering Medicare’s eligibility age to 55 or 50, adding dental, vision and hearing benefits and expanding coverage for long-term care. He also said reversing Medicaid cuts would be an immediate priority. Asked whether he still sees a role for private insurance, Lawrence said a public plan could provide baseline coverage while people purchase additional benefits. “I think that we can continue to have private insurance in some form,” he said. But he did not give a firm guarantee that people could keep their current insurance. Asked directly, he began with “most likely” before saying the answer would depend on the plan’s details and the transition. “What I’m clear on is that we need to have universal guaranteed coverage,” he said. Housing and tenant protections On housing, Lawrence proposed stronger tenant protections, including legal representation in eviction proceedings, alongside efforts to make construction and financing less expensive. He said he would co-sponsor existing legislation to establish a “national infrastructure bank,” with lending directed toward housing, water systems and transportation. “Now we can have a national infrastructure bank that still delivers profit to its investors and has a public purpose and can be targeted towards investments like housing,” he said. Lawrence said the goal should include housing affordable to middle-income residents as well as people with lower incomes, with opportunities for both renters and prospective homeowners. Tariffs and rising costs Lawrence also criticized President Donald Trump’s tariff policies, arguing that unpredictable changes make it harder for businesses to invest and families to plan. “You know, tariffs can be okay if it’s part of a consistent trade and industrial strategy,” he said. “But what the president is doing is he’s seemingly waking up in the morning and then just deciding what he wants the tariff rate to be – 55% or 40% or 25% or 5%, depending on his mood, or depending on the last of his advisors who happen to have his ear. That creates completely erratic business conditions.” Lawrence said Michigan families were paying an average of $5,000 more over the past year because of tariffs. The National Taxpayers Union Foundation estimated $23 billion in executive tariff costs on imports into Michigan from January 2025 through June 2026. That’s equivalent to $5,619 per household when divided by the state’s household count. Foreign policy

artigo.texto: Australian installers will get a closer look at Solis’ expanding battery storage range at All Energy Australia 2026. artigo.texto: Energy storage development plan for Green Belt between Busby and Thorntonhall Plans for an 86-acre long-duration energy storage development on Green Belt land between Busby and Thorntonhall are moving forward again. The proposed Busby Long Duration Energy Storage project would cover 34.9 hectares of land at Meikle Dripps Farm, roughly equivalent to 54 football pitches, close to Waterfoot Road. It would have a capacity of up to 150MW and store 1,200MWh of electricity, enough to operate at its maximum output for eight hours. Correspondence received by the Jackton, Thorntonhall and Busby Alliance LDES Action Group indicates that developers are now preparing to hold a statutory pre-application consultation before submitting the full plans. Consultants Cavendish Consulting have told campaigners that residents will be given an opportunity to see and comment on the proposals before an application for consent is lodged. No date has yet been announced for the consultation. The Scottish Government’s Energy Consents Unit continues to list Busby LDES as a “Pre Application” project. The live record names Apatura Project 22 Ltd as the applicant and confirms that no full Section 36 application has yet reached the determination stage. Documents already submitted as part of environmental screening give a clearer picture of the potential scale of the development. The site extends across six agricultural fields approximately 100 metres west of Thorntonhall and 250 metres south of Busby. The nearest residential property is immediately beside its southern boundary. The developer’s original screening submission modelled a development of up to 3,510 battery blocks. It considered container units around 2.6 metres high, with one potential configuration allowing them to be double-stacked. The accompanying landscape assessment said that could result in structures around 5.2 metres high, although the final design and technology had not been fixed at that stage. Frontier Power Energy Holdings acquired the rights to the Busby project and a separate 200MW scheme at Ayr from Apatura on 26 May 2026. Apatura said it would retain an active role in progressing both developments. Frontier now says Busby is expected to use long-duration batteries supplied by US manufacturer Eos Energy Enterprises, including its Z3 zinc-based technology, rather than conventional lithium-ion batteries. The company has also confirmed that Busby has received a Gate 2 notification through the National Energy System Operator’s reformed grid connection process. Gate 2 means a project has met NESO’s tests for readiness and can secure a place in the reformed connections queue, with a confirmed connection point and date. It is separate from planning permission and does not amount to approval for the development to be built. The Green Belt location is likely to remain one of the main issues when the full application is considered. The developer’s own landscape assessment says the Green Belt in this location helps maintain separation between East Kilbride, Busby and Clarkston, Thorntonhall and Waterfoot. It also acknowledges that developing the site would increase the urban influence on the landscape and result in an “unavoidable loss of openness” that would conflict with its Green Belt designation. South Lanarkshire Council reached a similarly conclusion during environmental screening. Its assessment said the project would be out of scale with the existing environment, describing it as a medium-scale development being introduced into a semi-rural area. Scottish Ministers subsequently determined that the development did not need to be accompanied by a full Environmental Impact Assessment. A future application is still expected to include detailed assessments covering aspects including landscape and visual impact, noise, ecology, flooding and drainage. Construction itself was estimated in the screening documents to take around 12 to 18 months, including work on the access, underground cables, fencing and landscaping. The transport assessment anticipates construction traffic using Waterfoot Road and Peel Road, including HGVs, light goods vehicles and “a small number of abnormal loads”. A public Core Path connecting Thorntonhall and Busby also crosses the site. The developer has proposed retaining and upgrading the route, although South Lanarkshire’s environmental screening states that the surroundings of sections of the path would be altered. The scheme has attracted sustained opposition in Busby, Thorntonhall and Jackton. Campaigners argue that energy storage infrastructure of this scale is inappropriate for agricultural Green Belt land separating established communities and have raised concerns about landscape change, construction traffic and noise. A Change.org petition opposing the Busby LDES development has now attracted 2,962 verified signatures. The petition states: “The BESS/LDES Local Action Group and the Jackton and Thorntonhall Community Council (JTCC) are fighting back against this development because of the dangers it poses - from fire risks and noise, to environmental damage and traffic. “While we acknowledge the importance of energy infrastructure, we believe this location is completely inappropriate and that safer, more suitable alternative locations should be considered.” The action group is also due to meet Scottish Labour South Scotland MSP Joe Fagan later this month as it prepares for the expected public consultation.

artigo.texto: With public distaste for data centers in Connecticut on the rise, residents in several communities are pushing for new restrictions even as the company looking to build one in Cromwell is stepping up its public relations effort. East Lyme’s zoning board last week unanimously prohibited any data centers from being built there, making the town at least the seventh in Connecticut to impose tougher rules. Morris, Trumbull, New Haven, Waterford, West Haven and Groton have all either banned new data centers altogether or imposed temporary moratoriums against them. Even so, Trumbull appears to be on track for the massive expansion of an existing data center. The $200 million cogNovum project would enlarge a former Nasdaq center in the town’s Merritt Boulevard office park. So despite the town’s newly enacted two-year moratorium against new centers, zoning officials are treating cogNovum as an expansion — and immune to the ban. A band of Trumbull residents this week tried to get their zoning board to adopt a new regulation adding expansions to the temporary ban, but were turned back. “We wanted a one-year moratorium against expansion of existing data centers,” opponent Richard White told WICC radio interviewer Melissa Sheketoff on her Melissa in the Morning program Thursday. “They voted against us 5-0.” In mid-summer, First Selectman Vicki Tesoro told residents that the project isn’t like the mega-centers that are proposed around the country. Developers want to put up a 10-gigawatt facility on more than 2,500 acres in Piketon, Ohio, for instance, and Meta and Blue Owl Capital are looking to build a 5-gigawatt center totalling 4 million square feet in northeastern Louisiana. “This is a renovation of a decades-old, existing data center — not the new construction of a hyperscale AI facility,” Tesoro told residents in late July. “Four main concerns rise to the top of my conversations with residents: electricity, noise, water, and expansion of the building’s footprint,” Tesoro said. “When it comes to these four things, I told the applicant directly: no increase in electrical draw beyond existing site capacity, no increase in noise, no increase in water use, no expansion of the building’s footprint. They have agreed to all four.” But the Trumbull AI Data Center Watch, an organization of opponents, is still fighting. Similarly, a group organizing against a potential 100-megawatt data center in Beacon Falls is connecting with local data center opponents in several communities, and recently started selling coffee cups, T-shirts and more to promote its message “Happy to not be on the map.” First Selectman Gerard Smith got blowback from opponents when he said the center would “put Beacon Falls on the map in a big way.” Meanwhile, a commercial real estate firm promoting plans for a data center in Cromwell said residents there haven’t heard enough about the proposal’s upside. The Algonquin gas pipeline runs through the Cromwell property and along with on-site fuel cells means the operation would be powered without taking anything from the electrical grid, according to Jay Morris of O,R&L Commercial, the real estate broker for landowner Gardner Nurseries. Although no formal application has been filed with the town, developers have signaled they want to put up a 1.2 million-square-foot, 300-megawatt data center on part of a 160-acre site off Geer Street. “This site is zoned for Industrial, and if this opportunity goes away it could be developed for manufacturing and distribution uses that could have much more building density, truck traffic and noise, and likely not seek to preserve open farmland,” Morris wrote in a letter to The Courant. “The developer has been meeting informally with local residents and has designed the preliminary layout to be set back far from the road and houses,” Morris wrote, saying the project would use only about a third of the acreage and leave the rest as open space. “Many of the national data centers are enormous, many 10x or more what is being discussed in Cromwell,” he wrote. A data center would add no burden to schools or other town services, wouldn’t require substantial water supplies, would generate no traffic after construction and would provide “substantial” local tax revenue, he wrote. “I believe if the public understood the benefits of this use in this location vs any other type of industrial development, they would welcome this opportunity,” according to his letter. Late Friday afternoon, however, Mayor James Demetriades posted a detailed zoning proposal from resident Juan Duque aimed at curbing data centers in Cromwell. It would set safety standards along with maximum limits on noise and vibrations; the Planning and Zoning Commission is scheduled to hear the proposed regulations Dec. 3. Of special relevance to the Geer Street project, the regulations would establish a cap of 100,000 square feet and require at least a mile buffer from any school. The Geer site is across the street from the town’s Woodside Intermediate School.

artigo.texto: In the first six months of 2026, Australia saw more clean energy generation capacity reach financial close and more large-scale battery storage capacity switched on than during the whole of 2025, according to the country’s latest biannual investment report. According to the Clean Energy Council (CEC)’s latest report, nine utility-scale batteries, worth $4.3 billion and representing 2.3 GW / 7.1 GWh of storage capacity, were switched on during the period. With these additions, the country surpassed the 2 GW / 5.1 GWh of battery storage capacity added during 2025. The report, Large-scale renewable generation and storage (January–June 2026), found that 12 generation projects, totalling 2.6 GW of new capacity, reached a final investment decision (FID) in H1 2026. This exceeded the 2.3 GW recorded across the whole of 2025, with solar farms and hybrid solar-and-battery projects leading the additions. Five generation projects, totalling 1.4 GW of new capacity and worth more than $2.8 billion, were commissioned during the first half of the year. These included the 756 MW first stage of Victoria’s Golden Plains Wind Farm, which is expected to generate enough electricity to power more than 400,000 homes. Renewable Investment Sustains Despite Economic Pressure Australia’s renewable energy investment performed strongly despite a challenging economic environment, strengthening the country’s energy security and helping deliver a more reliable and affordable electricity system. Clean Energy Council (CEC)' CEC Chief Executive Jackie Trad said the results demonstrate the resilience and growth of the clean energy industry despite significant headwinds. “Australian sun and wind cannot be cut off by conflict overseas. Each new solar, wind and battery investment helps make Australia more energy independent and economically resilient, shielding Australians from global fossil fuel price shocks and supply disruptions,” she said. “An increase in renewable generation and storage is already putting downward pressure on power prices, with wholesale electricity prices averaging $74 per megawatt-hour in the June quarter, down nearly 50 per cent on the same period in 2025.” Trad also said Australian-made clean energy would deliver more affordable and reliable electricity for households and businesses, alongside tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in investment and economic activity, particularly in regional Australia. Queensland Leads in Clean Energy Investment Queensland led the nation in clean energy investment, accounting for $9.6 billion and 4.5 GW of projects that were either at financial close or under construction. New South Wales, meanwhile, had the largest battery storage pipeline, at 4.3 GW / 11.2 GWh. “Queensland is leading the nation in clean energy investment, showing what can be achieved when world-class renewable energy resources are matched with investor confidence,” Trad said. “But the story is bigger than any one state or territory; across Australia, investors are backing the technologies they know will power our economic future and strengthen our energy security. “With $32.5 billion worth of generation and storage projects now under construction or at financial close, maintaining this momentum will require predictable approvals, timely transmission and long-term revenue certainty to help more projects, including onshore wind, progress into operation. “Australian-made clean energy will not only deliver more affordable, reliable electricity for households and businesses, but also tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in investment and economic activity, particularly in regional Australia,” she said.

artigo.texto: SALT LAKE CITY, Utah — It currently takes around four gigawatts of energy to power the entire state of Utah each year, but two planned data centers could more than quadruple that consumption. One in Millard County is working toward an energy capacity of more than 10 megawatts, while another in Box Elder County is targeting nine megawatts. And more are coming. But as Utah faces an energy deficit caused by increasing demand and decreasing supply, "there's not enough power in Utah to provide these data centers what they need,” notes Shon Hiatt, a University of Southern California professor who has studied Utah’s data center landscape. “Especially at this scale.” That's why many data centers under development in the state are now opting to bring their own energy. The move to what's sometimes referred to as “behind the meter” or “off-the-grid" energy comes after the Utah Legislature approved a new law last year that created an alternative process to provide power to large-load customers. "If they can't get it from the utility, Utah — with that law that just passed this session — basically says, ‘Oh, well then we'll give you permission to build your own power, bring your own,’” Hiatt said in an interview. His research for the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute found that seven data centers currently under construction will use nearly three times as much energy as all the ones that currently exist in the state combined. More than half of that energy will be “behind the meter.” Celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary’s controversial Stratos project in Box Elder County, for example, would tap directly into a natural gas pipeline near the Great Salt Lake called the Ruby Pipeline. Creekstone Energy, which is building what’s been billed as the “world’s largest data center” in Delta, plans to tap the Kern River Gas Pipeline and will also bring its own solar energy. While state law has greased the wheels, the “bring your own energy” movement also comes amid growing concerns nationally about how data centers could impact prices for ratepayers around the country. President Donald Trump called on hyperscale data centers in March to “build, bring, or buy” all their needed energy and to pay “the full cost of their energy and infrastructure, no matter what.” Abe Silverman, an assistant research scholar at Johns Hopkins University who focuses on energy markets and data centers, said there is "bipartisan" consensus that "data centers need to pay their own way.” “Grandma should not be subsidizing Google’s electric bill,” he said. The state hasn’t seen cost increases from data centers yet, according to Michele Beck, director of the Utah Office of Consumer Services. She told FOX 13 News that she believes Utah laws will continue to protect ratepayers from electricity rate spikes moving forward (though natural gas is a more complicated picture). “What SB132 has done is create pathways so that the data centers themselves can be responsible for procuring their power,” she said in an interview. “And then that helps to keep the shifts away from the regular customers.” But Olivia Douglas — a Bountiful resident who recently moved back to Utah from the northern Virginia area known as “Data Center Alley” — is skeptical the state will be able to mitigate the environmental and cost impacts of hyperscale data centers. "You can’t create energy out of thin air,” she said in an interview. “You can’t create water out of thin air. It has to come from somewhere. And then who’s paying for it?” WATCH: Hiatt, with USC, explains why data centers would rather not bring their own energy 'A geographically specific picture’ When Douglas and her family first moved to Prince William County, Virginia — a “beautiful area” with lots of trees — she had no idea there were data centers there. But as more came into the area, she started feeling their impacts. The construction boom increased traffic, she said, and the community began to feel “more industrial by the day.” Douglas, who recently moved back to Utah in part over concerns about quality of life and rising costs, also blames data centers for spikes in her monthly electricity bill. "Over the course of, I want to say, like five years, energy prices rose 30%,” she estimated. “Even within the last couple of months, I still am in contact with neighbors and they’re seeing even more increases — jumping $100, $200 a month in their energy bills.” Prince William County is home to at least 41 data centers, with 70 more on the way, according to the U.S. Data Center Map. (Research from the Kem C. Gardner Institute found, by comparison, that there are currently 48 operational data centers in the entire state of Utah.) While it can be difficult at times to parse the impact of data centers on energy prices, Silverman said there’s “pretty clear evidence” that they have contributed to rising costs in some regions, including in Virginia. But “it is very much a geographically specific picture,” he added. A Bloomberg analysis published last year found electricity rates spiked as much as 267% per month compared to the previous five years in areas near “significant data center activity.” But the Data Center Coalition, a group that represents the industry, points to reports showing rising energy costs are instead a product of inflation, grid modernization, natural gas volatility and other dynamics. Hiatt’s research found minimal data center impacts on energy prices in the United States between 2019 and 2025, though he stresses “that was looking backwards.” “Moving forward, though, I think we are at a risk,” he added. Experts agree the picture is particularly complex when it comes to questions about how data centers could impact the price of natural gas, a traded commodity that also heats homes. “I think the natural gas side will be trickier because so much of it is federally regulated or subject to market forces,” said Beck, with the Utah Office of Consumer Services, which advocates on behalf of ratepayers. artigo.texto: BYD's R&D Roadmap Meets a Cautious Earnings Reality Published on 10/25/2026 at 04:20 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD has laid out where it intends to spend its engineering effort next: megawatt fast charging, a next-generation Blade battery and integrated body-to-battery construction. The company confirmed the three priorities on an investor platform, a disclosure that sketches the direction of travel without committing to a single launch date or performance figure. That distinction matters for anyone trying to price the stock. BYD has restated a technological course, not reported a completed milestone. No output data accompanied the announcement, and management said it would publish progress once formal disclosure obligations kick in. Nothing in the statement points to a near-term product rollout, and nothing in it allows an analyst to book incremental revenue or profit. What the roadmap does and does not cover The message underscores how heavily battery and charging technology weigh in BYD's development planning. It stops short of offering a basis for quantifying future sales. Separating technical potential from commercially proven success remains the core exercise here. Products already on sale sit in a different category. The direction reaffirmed today is not a fresh market entry and should not be conflated with the charging specifications of vehicles already in showrooms. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? Seagull refresh shows execution on the ground Two days before the investor update, BYD launched the second generation of its Seagull in China. The line-up runs to five variants priced between 65,900 Yuan and 99,900 Yuan, with selected versions carrying particularly rapid charging capability. Flash Charging trims start at 75,900 Yuan — evidence that BYD is not reserving fast-charge hardware for its pricier segments alone. The caveat is physical rather than commercial: advertised charging power depends on compatible stations. A car's technical ceiling does not guarantee the same charging speed at every plug. For the equipped variants, BYD quotes a 10-to-70 percent top-up in five minutes. Those figures describe the Seagull technology on offer, not the next-generation development work flagged today. BYD has not confirmed a European launch for the new Seagull, so the Chinese sales start translates into no European volume contribution. For now, execution in the home market is what counts. The Seagull is not the only recent addition. BYD introduced the Da Han EV in China on 13 October, offering three versions priced from 235,900 Yuan to 275,900 Yuan. The two launches sit in very different price brackets and together round out a picture of steady product activity in China. Neither set of sticker prices says anything about demand or about the profit each model will generate. Brazil paperwork and the rally that wasn't about it Alongside the model cadence, BYD is pursuing a larger manufacturing footprint in Brazil. Reuters reported on Friday, citing the company, that BYD has begun seeking permits to double annual plant capacity to 600,000 vehicles. The procedural stage is the key detail: the targeted expansion is not the same as capacity already available. At the same time, the Brazilian unit was close to completing its stamping, welding and painting facilities — so the news bundles a permitting step for future growth with tangible progress at the existing site. BYD at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. Friday also brought a 4.4 percent gain in BYD shares, part of a broad recovery across lithium-battery and other automotive names. The friendlier sector backdrop, rather than any single company-specific trigger, was the dominant force. Investors are therefore better served separating the market move from the recent news on models and production. No direct link between the Seagull launch and Friday's share-price action has been established, and the rally on its own is no proof that the market is already discounting higher volumes or extra earnings from either the new models or the Brazil plan. Analysts split on the earnings risk Technological ambition is running into a more sober read on the business. One house cites weak domestic demand, higher input costs and political uncertainty as grounds for caution. Barclays, by contrast, keeps an "Overweight" rating and points to global expansion, while acknowledging softer domestic volumes after subsidy cuts and amid tougher competition. The divergence illustrates a simple point: growth opportunities alone do not settle the question of future profitability. Hard evidence on the economics remains the central yardstick, and it still trails the development strategy. Today's statement sharpens BYD's research priorities without removing those earnings risks. What will count is verifiable development progress and its conversion into sellable products. Absent performance data and launch dates, the next battery generation stays a development prospect rather than a secured earnings driver.
