artigo.texto: General Motors Co. in Detroit says it’s considering allowing battery technology startups to use its new, 500,000-square-foot battery development center in Warren when the facility opens in December. According to reports, Kurt Kelty, GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, says the automaker has held internal discussions about potentially opening the new facility to startups interested in learning battery cell manufacturing processes. This could provide smaller companies with access to capabilities that would otherwise require substantial capital investment. Despite these reported internal discussions, GM insists no decision has been made. The new, $145 million battery prototype facility is located at GM’s Global Technical Center in Warren. It’s designed to accelerate the development of next-generation battery technologies, including lithium manganese-rich (LMR) and sodium-ion chemistries. GM has announced a partnership with Peak Energy, a California-based energy storage system manufacturer, to develop and deploy sodium-ion cell batteries for stationary grid applications. Meanwhile, LMR battery technology has been tapped as a “big step” for GM’s proposed all-electric vehicle portfolio.

artigo.texto: Bondada Engineering Secures 20 MW/120 MWh VRFB BESS Order 27 Oct 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Bondada Engineering has received a Letter of Intent from Gujarat Industries Power Company for an engineering, procurement and construction package for a 20 MW/120 MWh Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System at GIPCL’s 165 MW natural gas power plant complex in Vadodara, Gujarat. The award also includes operations and maintenance services for 10 years. The project is scheduled for completion within 18 months of receipt of the notice of award. GIPCL is a domestic entity, and the disclosure stated that the contract does not involve any interest of Bondada Engineering’s promoter, promoter group or group companies. It also does not fall under related-party transactions. The order marks Bondada Engineering’s expansion into advanced energy storage technologies and complements its renewable energy engineering, procurement and construction portfolio. The company described the project as India’s largest grid-scale Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System project, positioning it in the long-duration energy storage segment. The company’s disclosure highlighted the growth potential of India’s energy storage market as renewable energy capacity expands and the need for grid stability increases. The Government of India has set a target of deploying approximately 236 GWh of battery energy storage systems by 2030, compared with current installed capacity of around 9.3 GWh. Bondada Engineering said the project would strengthen its position in the battery energy storage system sector and support its participation in India’s clean energy ecosystem. The company is expected to undertake the EPC scope and subsequent operations and maintenance obligations under the award from Gujarat Industries Power Company. artigo.texto: Dados do Banco Central mostram avanço de 9,2% em relação ao acumulado de agosto de 2025, enquanto energia renovável, mineração, petróleo e infraestrutura digital aparecem entre as áreas associadas ao interesse estrangeiro no país. O investimento direto no país chegou a US$ 86,6 bilhões no acumulado de 12 meses até agosto, com recursos ligados a atividades que vão de energia e mineração à infraestrutura digital. O resultado ficou acima dos US$ 79,3 bilhões registrados no mesmo recorte um ano antes. A série do Banco Central do Brasil mostra que o volume correspondia a 3,39% do Produto Interno Bruto e representa crescimento de aproximadamente 9,2% na comparação anual. Somente em agosto, os ingressos líquidos alcançaram US$ 7,4 bilhões. - Brasil reúne uma combinação difícil de ignorar: 90% da produção mundial de nióbio, segunda maior reserva conhecida de terras raras e uma agenda com os Estados Unidos que envolve tarifas, investimento e abastecimento industrial - Brasil tem um amortecedor entre dólar e inflação: estoques antigos, contratos fechados, concorrência e margens fazem a alta cambial atravessar importações e indústria antes de alcançar os preços pagos pelo consumidor - 88,0 nas expectativas contra 81,4 na situação atual: confiança melhora em outubro, mas a distância entre futuro e presente cresce enquanto o indicador financeiro das famílias recua ao menor nível desde janeiro - Brasil entra na reta decisiva de um tributo estimado em R$ 636 bilhões: TCU julga nesta quarta o cálculo da CBS, ainda sigiloso, antes de o Senado definir a alíquota para 2027 O resultado mensal reuniu US$ 9,3 bilhões em participação no capital, dos quais US$ 5,7 bilhões corresponderam a lucros reinvestidos. Houve, ao mesmo tempo, saídas líquidas de US$ 1,9 bilhão nas operações entre empresas relacionadas. O que entra no investimento direto O indicador não representa apenas dinheiro aplicado na construção de fábricas, parques de geração ou centros de dados. Ele reúne diferentes relações financeiras entre investidores estrangeiros e empresas instaladas no Brasil, incluindo aportes de capital, reinvestimento de lucros e operações entre companhias relacionadas. Por isso, os US$ 86,6 bilhões não equivalem ao valor de novas obras iniciadas no período. A própria composição de agosto mostra que parte relevante do fluxo veio de lucros reinvestidos por companhias que já operam no país. A dimensão internacional do movimento foi destacada pela agência EFE, que classificou o acumulado como recorde. A reportagem informou ainda que o Brasil havia sido, em 2025, o terceiro maior destino mundial de investimento estrangeiro, atrás de Estados Unidos e China, com base em dados da OCDE. A EFE também citou levantamento da Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Comércio e Desenvolvimento segundo o qual o Brasil recebeu 43% dos fluxos destinados à América Latina. Entre os setores associados ao capital estrangeiro aparecem energia renovável, mineração, centros de dados, indústria farmacêutica e madeira. A presença de atividades diferentes no mesmo recorte não permite concluir que os recursos tenham sido distribuídos de maneira uniforme. O valor agregado do Banco Central também não identifica, por si só, quanto cada um desses segmentos recebeu no período. Renováveis, minerais, petróleo e centros de dados Na área de energia, a composição da matriz elétrica brasileira aparece entre os fatores destacados pela agência. A reportagem informa que 88% da eletricidade do país vem de fontes renováveis, com participação da geração hidrelétrica e presença de fontes como eólica e solar. Essa característica também aparece relacionada à infraestrutura digital porque centros de dados exigem fornecimento elevado e contínuo de eletricidade. Cada empreendimento, porém, permanece sujeito a condições próprias de custo, disponibilidade de infraestrutura, licenciamento e cronograma antes de chegar à operação. O interesse em atividades ligadas à transição energética convive com investimentos em setores tradicionais. A EFE aponta minerais críticos e terras raras entre as áreas acompanhadas por investidores estrangeiros e registra, paralelamente, projetos vinculados à indústria de petróleo. O recorte reúne, portanto, atividades com características diferentes: geração renovável, recursos minerais estratégicos, óleo e gás e infraestrutura necessária aos centros de dados. A presença desses setores no mesmo fluxo não significa que todos estejam no mesmo estágio de implantação. Um anúncio empresarial, uma intenção de investimento, um aporte financeiro e a entrada em operação de um empreendimento representam momentos distintos. Essa diferença impede que o volume registrado como investimento direto seja tratado automaticamente como obra executada, contratação realizada ou nova capacidade produtiva já disponível. A referência temporal também limita interpretações políticas sobre o dado. A série utilizada pela EFE termina em agosto e, portanto, não representa uma reação à eleição de domingo (25) nem permite relacionar o fluxo registrado pelo Banco Central a acontecimentos ocorridos depois do período medido. Para avaliar o efeito do capital estrangeiro sobre a economia local, será necessário observar quais projetos avançam para etapas como construção, contratação, compra de equipamentos e início da produção. Os próximos dados mensais do Banco Central também indicarão se o volume acumulado mantém a trajetória observada até agosto.

artigo.texto: Italy continued to expand its solar and energy storage fleet in the third quarter of 2026, with 1.742 GW of new photovoltaic capacity connected, up 37% from the 1.269 GW installed in the same period of 2025 and 5% higher than in the previous quarter. In the first nine months of the year, the country added 4.834 GW of new solar capacity through 147,632 new installations, according to calculations by ITALIA SOLARE based on Terna’s Gaudì data, updated to September 30. By that date, Italy had 2,314,113 photovoltaic installations connected to the grid, with a total installed capacity of 48.347 GW. The number of new connections also increased during the third quarter, rising from 38,660 in the second quarter to 58,459 between July and September, an increase of 34%. Utility-scale solar drives new installations Growth in the Italian solar market is increasingly being driven by larger projects and commercial and industrial installations. Between January and September, the utility-scale segment, covering plants of at least 1 MW, added 2.241 GW through 473 new connections, accounting for 46% of all new photovoltaic capacity installed in Italy during the period. The commercial and industrial segment, covering installations between 20 kW and 1 MW, added another 1.697 GW through 11,905 new projects, equivalent to 35% of newly connected capacity. The residential market, comprising systems of up to 20 kW, added 897 MW through 135,254 new connections, representing 19% of the new capacity. In the third quarter alone, utility-scale projects added 858 MW, compared with 457 MW in the same quarter of 2025. Of this volume, 394 MW came from projects between 1 MW and 10 MW, while another 464 MW came from installations above 10 MW. The C&I segment reached 543 MW, up from 500 MW a year earlier, while residential additions increased from 312 MW to 341 MW. Paolo Rocco Viscontini, president of ITALIA SOLARE, said the third-quarter figures confirm continued growth in the Italian solar market, with large-scale projects playing an increasingly important role and the commercial and industrial segment maintaining a positive trajectory. The association nevertheless said the residential market remains an area to monitor after contracting in the first half of 2026 compared with the previous year. Sicily leads new solar capacity additions At regional level, Sicily ranked first for newly connected photovoltaic capacity in the first nine months of 2026, with 686 MW, followed by Lombardy with 644 MW, Piedmont with 498 MW, Veneto with 463 MW, Emilia-Romagna with 443 MW and Lazio with 432 MW. The composition of growth varied significantly by region. Of the 686 MW added in Sicily, 476 MW came from installations larger than 10 MW, reflecting the strong contribution of utility-scale projects. In Lombardy, by contrast, the commercial and industrial segment accounted for a significant share of new capacity, with 405 MW, while large-scale installations were largely absent. By number of new installations, Lombardy ranked first with 22,999 connections, followed by Veneto with 18,099, Emilia-Romagna with 13,405 and Sicily with 11,653. Italy approaches 20 GWh of energy storage The expansion of solar capacity is being accompanied by further growth in electrochemical energy storage. As of September 30, Italy had 984,829 connected storage systems, with a total capacity of 19.983 GWh and a combined power rating of 8.338 GW. Of this capacity, 12.552 GWh was associated with photovoltaic installations, while 7.368 GWh came from stand-alone storage systems. A further 57 MWh was linked to thermal power plants and 6 MWh to wind installations. During the first nine months of 2026, Italy connected 98,197 new storage systems, adding 1.953 GWh of capacity and 907 MW of power. Almost all new installations by unit count were batteries associated with photovoltaic systems: 98,186 units, representing 1.486 GWh of capacity and 773 MW of power. By contrast, just 11 new stand-alone storage systems added a combined 467 MWh of capacity and 134 MW of power, highlighting the significantly larger average size of these projects. Solar-linked storage capacity rises despite fewer installations During the third quarter, storage systems associated with photovoltaic installations added 480 MWh of new capacity, 252 MW of power and 31,039 new units. Compared with the third quarter of 2025, newly connected storage capacity increased by 15%, from 417 MWh to 480 MWh, even as the number of installations declined from 32,697 to 31,039. The figures also show a change in the size profile of newly installed batteries. Storage systems associated with photovoltaic installations of up to 6 kW added 242 MWh during the third quarter, compared with 129 MWh in the previous quarter. By contrast, systems associated with photovoltaic installations between 6 kW and 20 kW fell from 229 MWh to 105 MWh, while storage linked to installations above 20 kW added a combined 133 MWh. Across the first nine months of the year, storage systems associated with photovoltaic installations of up to 6 kW added 481 MWh, those linked to systems between 6 kW and 20 kW added 596 MWh, and those associated with installations above 20 kW added a total of 409 MWh. Lombardy also leads distributed storage Lombardy also recorded the highest amount of new storage capacity associated with photovoltaic systems between January and September, with 206 MWh, followed by Emilia-Romagna with 155 MWh, Veneto with 146 MWh and Sicily with 144 MWh. The region also ranked first by number of new systems, with 14,672 installations, ahead of Veneto, Emilia-Romagna and Sicily. On a cumulative basis, Lombardy now has 164,950 storage systems associated with photovoltaic installations, representing 2.095 GWh of capacity. It is followed by Veneto with 1.562 GWh and Emilia-Romagna with 1.154 GWh. artigo.texto: [Digital Today reporter Jinju Hong] Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD is expected to unveil an ultra-luxury electric sedan in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in early November. The new flagship model from BYD's top-end brand Yangwang could adopt unconventional technologies, including a solid-state battery and rear-hinged coach doors. The expected price is about $300,000 (about 400 million won), raising attention on whether BYD can move beyond mass-market EVs into the ultra-luxury segment. Electrek, an EV outlet, reported on Oct. 26 that Yangwang chose the UAE, rather than China, for the global unveiling of its new flagship sedan. While the exact date has not been announced, Chinese auto outlet CarNewsChina cited a project source as saying it could be unveiled in Dubai around Nov. 5. The new car is expected to be a symbolic model for BYD's premium-car strategy. Yangwang is a sub-brand at the top of BYD's brand structure and has sought differentiation with high-performance EV technology and body control systems. Its signature technologies, the four-motor-based e4 platform and the Disus-X body control system, enable various movements such as rotating in place, moving the body and driving with only some wheels. The new sedan is also expected to stand apart from existing BYD models in size and design. Yangwang General Manager Hu Xiaoqing (후 샤오칭) last month released photos of a test vehicle during a trial drive. Details are hard to confirm due to camouflage, but assessments say its proportions recall ultra-luxury sedans such as the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom. Locally, the overall length is estimated to reach about 5,500 mm. A key technical difference being discussed is the possible use of a solid-state battery. Yangwang Executive General Manager Zheng Yu (정위) said the new car would apply "unprecedented disruptive technology", but did not disclose detailed specifications. BYD has also not officially confirmed whether a solid-state battery will be used. Even so, BYD's battery development timeline is drawing attention to the outlook. Stella Li, BYD's executive vice president, said in an interview with Cawawe Eswa last month that BYD's first solid-state battery vehicle is scheduled to come out in 2027. She stressed that BYD holds a leading position in solid-state battery technology and commercialisation and indicated it would prove that next year. BYD's battery affiliate FinDreams plans to begin producing sulfide-based solid-state batteries in 2027. It plans to focus on small-volume production initially and expand mass production as it gets closer to the 2030s. That has led to speculation that the new flagship sedan could showcase solid-state battery technology, but whether it is actually fitted must be confirmed through an official announcement. Charging performance is also in focus. After the test vehicle was spotted at BYD's flash charging station, speculation emerged that it could support megawatt-class ultra-fast charging. Specific performance, including charging output and charging time, has not been disclosed. It is also not yet confirmed whether rear-hinged coach doors will be applied to the mass-produced model. The price is expected to be set far above Yangwang's existing lineup. Locally, there is an outlook that the new car's starting price could be in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000. Yangwang's all-electric sedan U7 is sold from 658,000 yuan, and its lineup also includes the plug-in hybrid luxury off-roader U8 and U8L and the all-electric super coupe U9. The U8L starts at 1.45 million yuan. If the new sedan is priced as expected, it would enter a price bracket higher than existing Yangwang models. This can be interpreted as an attempt by BYD to win recognition for its technology and brand value in the ultra-luxury car market beyond being a mass-market EV maker built on price competitiveness. Key specifications, including a solid-state battery, megawatt-class charging and coach doors, have not yet been confirmed. If the unveiling takes place in early November, the actual battery technology, performance and price are expected to be key benchmarks for gauging BYD's ultra-luxury EV strategy.

artigo.texto: What Six Months of Fluid Data Says About Aluminum in Liquid Cooling We have two sets of charts from our liquid cooling test. One is from June, the other from December. Same loop, same coolant, six months and more than 4,000 hours apart. Put them side by side and you cannot tell which is which. That would be unremarkable in an all-copper system. This loop had an aluminum heat exchanger sharing coolant with copper cold plates and stainless steel plumbing, the mixed-metal combination the industry has spent a decade avoiding. Conventional caution says the June charts and the December charts should look different. They don't. Here is what we built, why we built it, and what operators should take from it. Why test aluminum at all Liquid cooling inherited its materials. Copper went into cold plates, and stainless steel and brass went into manifolds, piping, and fittings. Each was a sound choice when it was made. At AI scale, the bundle is getting heavy, scarce, and expensive. A coolant distribution unit can weigh one to two tons, and an AI rack is approaching four to five thousand pounds. Copper is being pulled in several directions at once by grid buildout, electrification, and transportation, which means our industry is now competing for tonnage with the power grid it depends on. Aluminum eases all three pressures. It is roughly one-third the density of copper, more abundant, less expensive, and easier to extrude into the geometries modern heat exchangers call for. What has kept it out of the wetted path is galvanic corrosion. Put aluminum and copper in the same water-based coolant without adequate protection and the aluminum gives up material to the fluid. For equipment expected to run for years untouched, few engineers wanted to take that risk on faith. So we tested it. What we built Working with Valvoline, we built a test bench at their research facility in Ashland, Kentucky, modeled on the wetted path of a liquid-to-air CDU serving direct-to-chip loads. An aluminum microchannel heat exchanger fed five copper cold plates in parallel through stainless steel tubing and EPDM hoses. The coolant was Valvoline's PG25 Advanced, a propylene glycol formulation with an inhibitor package tuned for data center loops. Heat pads put one to two kilowatts on each cold plate. The loop moved 20 liters per minute in total, split unevenly across the five cold plates at roughly four to five liters per minute each. We left that imbalance in place on purpose, because real deployments are rarely balanced perfectly, and controlled the plates to a common temperature target instead. The test ran continuously from June through December 2025, 4,362 hours in total, and we pulled 28 fluid samples along the way. What the fluid told us We tracked the loop the way an operator would, through the fluid. Twenty-eight samples drawn over six months were analyzed for dissolved metals, coolant chemistry, and inhibitor levels, because the fluid is where corrosion leaves its record. We had not cut open the heat exchanger or cold plates before publication, and that is a fair limitation to name. But if aluminum were leaving the heat exchanger, the fluid would have shown it as a steady climb in dissolved aluminum. That climb never came. For most of the test, aluminum, copper, and iron (our proxy for the stainless steel) read at or near zero. During one stretch, between roughly 1,030 and 1,867 hours, all three rose briefly, with aluminum peaking at 1.08 ppm and copper and iron at about a tenth of that, then fell back and stayed low. Two things about that stretch matter. Every reading stayed well under the 2 ppm limit the OCP PG25 base specification sets for fresh fluid. And the three metals moved together. Galvanic corrosion would look different. Dissolved aluminum would climb on its own and keep building over time, while the copper stayed protected. Nothing in the data shows that pattern. The rest of the chemistry held as well. pH stayed around 8, and reserve alkalinity stayed between 0.8 and 1.0. Specific gravity and freeze point were flat, so the glycol ratio did not drift. The organic acid inhibitors finished essentially where they started, and the copper-protecting azoles declined slowly and predictably, on a trend that projects useful protection well beyond the test window. Thermal conductivity and heat capacity matched their initial values, and the cold plates showed no thermal drift. What operators should take from it The lesson is not to swap your copper for aluminum. For now, copper remains the standard at the cold plate, where heat flux is highest and its conductivity earns its cost. Our focus was the CDU side of the loop. The same cost, weight, and supply pressures apply at the chip, though. We expect cold plate designers and chip makers to run their own analysis on whether aluminum makes sense there too. The lesson is that aluminum belongs where its strengths matter and its weakness can be managed. The heat exchanger has always been the toughest place to justify aluminum in the wetted path, and with the right chemistry it now has data behind it. That makes the coolant a design decision rather than a commodity line item. If you are evaluating mixed-metal equipment, a few practices follow: - Specify the fluid with the hardware. Ask which inhibitor package the loop was qualified with, and keep that chemistry in service. - Sample on a schedule. Dissolved metals, pH, and reserve alkalinity are inexpensive to track and tell you early whether protection is holding. - Watch the inhibitors, not just the metals. Inhibitor depletion shows up before metal loss does. - Use the OCP PG25 specification as your yardstick. It gives buyers and suppliers a shared reference for what healthy fluid looks like. None of this is exotic. Automotive cooling systems have run aluminum, copper, brass, and iron in one inhibited coolant for decades, at higher temperatures and with drivers who rarely check. artigo.texto: WEG em NÚMEROS Como data centers dos EUA viraram motor da 'fábrica de bilionários' no Brasil DIVULGAÇÃO/WEG Transformador da WEG; equipamentos como este puxaram as vendas da empresa nos Estados Unidos Publicado em 25/10/2026 - 6h00 Atualizado em 25/10/2026 - 10h18 A WEG, multinacional de Santa Catarina conhecida como "fábrica de bilionários", encerrou o terceiro trimestre de 2026 com lucro líquido de R$ 1,67 bilhão. O valor representa alta de 0,9% sobre o mesmo período de 2025 e equivale a pouco mais de R$ 18 milhões por dia, ou cerca de R$ 750 mil por hora, considerando os 92 dias entre julho e setembro. Mesmo assim, o balanço, divulgado na quarta-feira (21), não trouxe os resultados que os investidores esperavam. As ações da companhia (WEGE3) tiveram a maior queda do Ibovespa na semana. O motivo está menos no tamanho do lucro e mais no quanto sobra de cada venda. No mesmo dia, a empresa anunciou uma troca programada na vice-presidência de Energia, ligada a alguns dos negócios que mais crescem no grupo. Entre julho e setembro, a WEG teve receita líquida de R$ 10,86 bilhões, crescimento de 5,7% na comparação anual. É como se a empresa faturasse cerca de R$ 118 milhões por dia. O Ebitda, indicador que mostra quanto a operação gera antes de juros, impostos e depreciação, somou R$ 2,35 bilhões, alta de 3,1%. O retorno sobre o capital investido ficou em 33,2%, 0,8 ponto percentual acima de um ano antes. O destaque veio de fora do país. As vendas no exterior responderam por 62,5% do faturamento, o maior nível da história da WEG. Data centers e rede elétrica dos EUA puxam as vendas A América do Norte é o principal motor desse avanço. A receita na região chegou a US$ 722,8 milhões no trimestre, 31% a mais do que um ano antes. A fatia equivale a 54,7% de tudo o que a empresa vende fora do Brasil. No mesmo período de 2025, era 47,9%. A venda de transformadores para reforçar a rede elétrica norte-americana, que passa por modernização, ajuda a explicar o salto. E também os geradores da Marathon, marca do grupo nos Estados Unidos, usados como energia de reserva em data centers, os grandes galpões de servidores que sustentam a internet e a inteligência artificial. O resultado em reais, porém, foi menor do que poderia ser. O dólar médio caiu de R$ 5,45 para R$ 5,14 entre um trimestre e outro. Como a WEG converte para a moeda brasileira o que fatura lá fora, cada dólar passou a valer menos no balanço. Em dólares, as vendas externas subiram 14,8%; em reais, 8,3%. FOTO: DIVULGAÇÃO/WEG Fábrica da Weg na cidade de Betim, em Minas Gerais Custo maior aperta a margem O ponto que pesou para os investidores foi a rentabilidade. A margem bruta, que mostra quanto fica com a empresa depois de pagar o custo de produção, caiu de 33,6% para 32,9%. Em outras palavras: de cada R$ 100 vendidos, sobraram R$ 32,90, contra R$ 33,60 um ano antes. Segundo a WEG, três fatores explicam a queda: a alta do cobre, matéria-prima essencial para motores e transformadores; as tarifas de importação cobradas pelos Estados Unidos; e o gasto maior com funcionários, ligado à ampliação das fábricas iniciada neste ano. O peso da folha de pagamento no custo dos produtos subiu de 19,2% para 20,3%. Isso acontece porque a companhia contrata antes de as novas linhas de produção operarem em ritmo pleno. Com esse efeito, a margem Ebitda também recuou, de 22,2% para 21,6%. Como o mercado reagiu Levantamento da LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group) mostrava que analistas esperavam lucro de R$ 1,71 bilhão e Ebitda de R$ 2,40 bilhões. Os números vieram um pouco abaixo, e o mercado também contava com uma redução menor na margem. Na manhã de quarta-feira, as ações chegaram a cair 4,6%, cotadas a R$ 46,53. Na semana de 19 a 23 de outubro, a desvalorização acumulada foi de 10,96%, a pior entre os papéis do Ibovespa. O índice fechou o período praticamente estável, com recuo de 0,17%. Troca na área de Energia Junto com o balanço, a WEG comunicou que João Paulo Gualberto da Silva deixará a vice-presidência de Energia em 31 de dezembro, depois de 37 anos na companhia. Engenheiro eletricista formado pela Udesc, ele trabalhou na área comercial, inclusive nos Estados Unidos, e dirigiu o setor de novas energias, com foco em eólica e solar. FOTOS: DIVULGAÇÃO/WEG Sai João Paulo Gualberto da Silva (à esq.), assume Paulo Leonardo da Silva Sinoti O sucessor é Paulo Leonardo da Silva Sinoti, atual diretor de Soluções em Energia & Serviços, que também soma mais de três décadas de casa. Ele assume o posto em 1º de janeiro de 2027. A escolha foi aprovada pelo Conselho de Administração e faz parte do planejamento de sucessão da empresa. A mudança ocorre em um momento de expansão dos negócios de energia. No trimestre, a área de geração, transmissão e distribuição, que reúne os transformadores e geradores responsáveis pelo crescimento nos EUA, aumentou as vendas externas em 24,1% na comparação com o mesmo período de 2025. Fundada em 16 de setembro de 1961, em Jaraguá do Sul (SC), a WEG começou fabricando motores elétricos. O nome reúne as iniciais dos três fundadores: Werner Ricardo Voigt, Eggon João da Silva e Geraldo Werninghaus. Hoje, a companhia é uma das maiores fabricantes de equipamentos elétricos do mundo. O portfólio inclui motores, geradores, transformadores, painéis, sistemas de automação para fábricas, equipamentos para produzir e distribuir energia, carregadores de carros elétricos e até tintas industriais. São mais de 45 mil funcionários e unidades em mais de 40 países. Peças da WEG estão por trás de máquinas de lavar, aparelhos de ar-condicionado, indústrias de papel e celulose, plataformas de petróleo e redes de energia elétrica. A "fábrica de bilionários" O apelido vem do controle familiar. Os herdeiros diretos dos três fundadores, que já morreram, mantêm participação relevante nas ações. A valorização da empresa na bolsa ao longo das décadas transformou parte deles em bilionários. Ao todo, são mais de 100 acionistas herdeiros atualmente, de acordo com o portal

artigo.texto: The Ełk and Turośń Kościelna battery projects in north-eastern Poland are to be sold to A&R Investments by Greenvolt, a Portugal-based renewable energy group. The two stand-alone projects hold 1.6 GWh between them, and each has 200 MW of power and 800 MWh of storage capacity. Both were completed in the third quarter of 2026, and each of them can discharge at full power for about four hours. Each project also holds a 17-year capacity market contract, under which it is to receive a fixed payment from 2028 for keeping 85% of its rated capacity available. A 10-year tolling agreement covers both projects, and under it their flexibility is to be traded in the power markets. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026. For Greenvolt, the sale forms part of an asset rotation strategy, which foresees the sale of approximately 70-80% of the projects that it develops internally. Greenvolt to sell 1.6 GWh of BESS in Poland to A&R Investments A&R Investments is to buy the two battery projects that Greenvolt Power has completed in north-eastern Poland, and each of them holds a 17-year capacity market contract. artigo.texto: Sungrow and ENGIE Advance Australia’s Energy Transition with Grid-Forming Technology at Hazelwood 2 BESS By PR Newswire MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Sungrow, a globally leading PV inverter and energy storage system provider, is partnering with ENGIE and Elecnor on the 150 MW / 300 MWh Hazelwood Battery Energy Storage System expansion (HBESS 2) in Victoria, Australia, with Sungrow Australia as the technology provider and Elecnor as the BOP Contractor. This project will feature 66 units of Sungrow’s ST5015-UX battery energy storage system (BESS), part of the PowerTitan 2.0 series, alongside 33 units of SC6900UD-MV Power Conversion System (PCS) inverters and Sungrow’s smart controller EMS3000. Designed for utility-scale applications, the PowerTitan 2.0 system offers several key advantages: - High energy density: Optimises energy storage capacity. - Liquid-cooled technology: Helps maintain stable operating temperatures and support system reliability. - Advanced battery management: Supports battery safety, performance monitoring and long-term operational reliability. - High-performance power conversion: Paired with the SC6900UD-MV PCS inverters, it supports efficient power conversion and responsive grid support for utility-scale applications. With commercial operations targeted for 2028, the Hazelwood BESS 2 project will add significant battery storage capacity to Victoria’s energy infrastructure, reinforcing Hazelwood’s role in providing flexible energy resources for Victoria and the National Electricity Market (NEM). By storing and delivering electricity when needed, the system will help balance supply and demand as Australia’s energy landscape continues to evolve. Grid-forming technology will further enhance the project’s capabilities, helping strengthen network performance as renewable generation increases. Key benefits include: - Grid stability: Supports voltage and frequency stability to help maintain reliable network operation. - Fast response: Enables rapid responses to changing grid conditions to support power system reliability. - Renewable integration: Helps accommodate higher levels of variable renewable generation. - Grid resilience: Provides advanced grid support capabilities to strengthen the network under changing operating conditions. The combination of energy storage and advanced grid-forming capabilities will contribute to a more resilient and reliable power system. “The Hazelwood BESS 2 represents an important step in advancing grid-forming energy storage in Australia. Through our collaboration with ENGIE, we aim to bring advanced energy storage technology to support grid stability and enable greater integration of renewable energy. We look forward to contributing our expertise and supporting the continued development of a more resilient energy system in Victoria,” said Thomas Hou, Managing Director at Sungrow Australia. The commencement of Hazelwood BESS 2 reflects the continued development of large-scale battery storage in Australia and the role of Sungrow’s technology in delivering infrastructure to support the evolving energy system. artigo.texto: Microtek Unveils BESS Solutions for Energy Management and Cost Optimisation at REI Expo 2026 Microtek highlighted its high-voltage lithium battery pack and i-BESS 125kW/261kWh system at REI Expo 2026, designed to support peak shaving, microgrid integration and electricity cost management. October 26, 2026. By News Bureau Microtek showcased its integrated solar, energy storage and power management portfolio at Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo 2026, from October 22 to 24 in Greater Noida. Led by its ‘Har Ghar Bijli Ghar’ vision, the company introduced its new Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), highlighting its focus on making reliable energy solutions accessible to households and businesses. With nearly four decades of power management experience, Microtek’s portfolio spans: power generation, distribution, conditioning and storage. The showcase products included home inverters, UPS systems, batteries, electrical wires, solar panels, solar inverters and lithium batteries. This breadth underpins its holistic approach, connecting solar generation with power distribution, protection and storage within one portfolio. Microtek’s new High-Voltage Lithium Battery Pack and BESS range was a key highlight at the EXPO, showcasing the i-BESS 125kW/261kWh system. These intelligent energy storage solutions are designed to support peak shaving, microgrid integration and electricity cost optimisation. This marks Microtek’s entry into the high-voltage energy storage segment. Commenting on the participation, N.K Aggarwal, Founder and Chairman of Microtek International, said, “Our vision of ‘Har Ghar Bijli Ghar’ reflects our ambition to help households generate and manage their own electricity. Our portfolio across generation, distribution, conditioning and storage builds on nearly four decades of experience in keeping power reliable. Through our BESS and lithium-based solutions, we are strengthening our capabilities to serve India’s changing energy needs.” Microtek’s reach is supported by over 1 lakh plus dealers across India. The company expects to more than double revenue in FY 2026–27 to INR 5,000 crore, with an ambition to reach INR 10,000 crore within two years. At REI Expo, Microtek connected with channel partners and industry experts to showcase its solar and energy storage solutions. The exhibition will also provide a platform to discuss new business opportunities, expand its distribution network and build partnerships to make its solutions more widely available for homes and businesses. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Baixo Guandu, no Noroeste do Espírito Santo, vai ganhar nos próximos anos um data center voltado para abrigar e executar sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA). O investimento contempla a instação de um sistema modular com capacidade de computacional 100 Megawatts (MW) e está estimado em R$ 7,4 bilhões. O novo data center capixaba foi projetado para processar e armazenar volumes massivos de dados de clientes internacionais e gigantes mundiais de tecnologia. "O nosso data center é uma estrutura voltada para inteligência artificial. Não é um projeto para atender apenas ao mercado local. Nossa intenção é processar e armazenar dados globais de clientes do mundo inteiro", destaca o empresário Mário Rodrigues, que integra o projeto com um grupo de investidores capixabas, em parceria com empresas e fundos de investimento. O projeto, segundo Rodrigues, está atualmente na fase de desenvolvimento de engenharia, obtenção de licenças ambientais e aprovação de conexões de energia — processo regulatório do setor que leva de 24 a 36 meses. O terreno onde será o complexo tem 11,3 milhões de metros quadrados e fica a nove quilômetros da cidade. O empresário acrescenta que, paralelamente, o grupo vai realizar roadshows internacionais visando fechar contratos de pré-locação de longo prazo, com previsão de 20 anos e em dólar com multinacionais de tecnologia. A intenção é garantir a ocupação total da estrutura antes do início das obras físicas. A capacidade inicial de 100 MW de poder computacional do data center equivale ao consumo de processamento de 15 a 20 milhões de pessoas assistindo simultaneamente a vídeos em resolução 4K em serviços de streaming como a Netflix. A estrutura é modular e tem potencial para expandir no futuro para até 1 Gigawatt (GW), conforme o crescimento da demanda por IA. O que é um data center? Um data center, ou centro de dados, em português, é uma instalação física ou prédio projetado para abrigar uma infraestrutura de TI — como servidores, sistemas de armazenamento e equipamentos de rede — que processa, guarda e distribui grandes volumes de dados. A estrutura é a base física por trás de tudo o que usamos na internet, como redes sociais, serviços de streaming, bancos digitais, aplicativos de entrega e a computação em nuvem. A instalação do complexo de tecnologia no Noroeste capixaba se deu por fatores como localização e acesso a água e energia. O complexo vai ficar próximo da Usina Hidrelétrica de Mascarenhas (a maior geradora de eletricidade do Espírito Santo) e da subestação local. Além disso, três redes de distribuição de alta tensão ligadas ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) cortam a propriedade, com sinalização positiva do órgão regulador sobre a capacidade de tráfego livre. Também pesa a favor a passagem da linha férrea Vitória-Minas, com cabo de fibra óptica que conecta a Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte ao cabo submarino internacional em Vitória, a apenas 1,5 metro dos dormentes. "O que um data center demanda? Energia, infraestrutura elétrica e fibra óptica. Nós temos a maior usina do Estado ao lado, redes de alta tensão livres e a fibra óptica que acompanha a ferrovia. É um cenário completamente diferenciado", afirma Mário. A proximidade com o Rio Doce também foi um dos motivos para a instalação do local. O sistema dos data centers precisa de resfriamento. O empresário afirma que isso ser um sistema em circuito fechado, que faz a água recircular continuamente. “A perda mensal por evaporação para o bloco de 100 MW equivale ao consumo de apenas três casas populares com quatro moradoras cada. Além disso, a presença de água doce na região elimina a necessidade de aportes em dessalinização do mar”, pontuou. A previsão é que a instalação do empreendimento crie entre 300 e 500 empregos diretos na montagem e obras civis. Na fase de operação, a projeção é ter cerca de 10% desse contingente de forma direta, porém formada por técnicos e engenheiros de alta qualificação e remuneração elevada. Na avaliação do investidor, isso vai injetar capital no comércio, na rede hoteleira, em restaurantes e em prestadores de serviços locais. Na arrecadação pública, ele estima que, com o faturamento anual do data center previsto em mais de R$ 1 bilhão, a alíquota de 5% do Imposto Sobre Serviços (ISS) direcionará entre R$ 50 milhões e R$ 60 milhões por ano diretamente para o caixa da Prefeitura de Baixo Guandu.

artigo.texto: Years after the pandemic-era supply chain crisis has faded for much of the economy, data center developers are still battling equipment shortages and long, unpredictable lead times, a bottleneck that threatens to delay projects amid an artificial intelligence data center arms race. Equipment shortages persist as a major source of delays and uncertainty in an industry where developers are already struggling to keep pace with unprecedented demand. And delays can be costly, with hyperscalers and other tenants writing substantial penalties into contracts for missed delivery dates. The supply chain pinch is still being felt across nearly every part of the development process, from natural gas turbines and transformers to cooling systems and basic construction materials, industry insiders said at Bisnow’s Data Center Investment Conference and Expo: Central in Dallas this month. Sophisticated developers are finding ways to navigate many of these constraints, panelists said, but even then there are trade-offs. Strategies like stockpiling equipment or ordering long-lead items before designs are finalized require significant upfront capital and can raise project costs. And while some panelists expressed frustration that shortages tracing back to the pandemic nearly seven years ago have persisted for data centers long after easing in other industries, there is broad recognition that the procurement landscape isn’t returning to normal as long as the sector continues on its stratospheric growth trajectory. “There were discussions about how long Covid would impact us, and I don't know if we're ever going to go back to pre-Covid,” said Sam Caddell, CyrusOne’s senior director for facilities engineering and operations systems. “There are still impacts on lead times — from raw materials all the way down.” The most significant lead times are for equipment involved in getting power to data center project sites, panelists said. Gas turbines can take a decade or more to be delivered, a bottleneck that is currently contributing to yearslong timelines for grid connections and limiting developers’ ability to pursue on-site and behind-the-meter power as an alternative to utility interconnection queues. Transformer shortages are felt even more broadly, with panelists citing lead times of up to three years for equipment required on virtually every large-scale project. Similarly, backup generators can take more than a year to procure. The supply chain pinch extends well beyond power infrastructure. Chillers and other cooling system components routinely carry lead times of 12 to 18 months, panelists said, as do switchgear, uninterruptible power supply, or UPS, systems and other critical electrical and networking equipment integral to data center operations. Manufacturers said they simply can’t keep up with the flood of demand, even as they scramble to scale up production. “We're about to bring on a brand-new chiller factory. We'll have four chiller factories that can supply this market, and even then it's not enough,” said Dara Sanii, a director at cooling equipment provider Carrier Applied West. It’s not just complex equipment that is facing shortages. Even basic hardware and construction materials are seeing significant delays. Optical fiber can take six to eight months to arrive, and structural steel roughly a year. Meanwhile, contractors continue to encounter unexpected delays for relatively simple components like conduits and medium-voltage cables. These same hardware shortages also factor into delays in the production of more complex data center systems. Manufacturers say pumps, evaporators, fans, coils and heat exchangers used in cooling equipment are routinely sold out for a year or more, while basic components like breakers can slow the production of electrical systems. “The capacity the industry's taking down is outstripping the ability of the entire supply chain to keep up,” Johnson Controls Vice President Matt Kightlinger told DICE: Central. “It is absolutely an issue industrywide, all the way down to the component level.” Some of the pressure on the data center supply chain has been eased by delays elsewhere, panelists said. Projects derailed by grid constraints or local opposition have freed up equipment that had already been allocated, pushing scarce components back into the market. Even so, preventing procurement from becoming the pinch point on a project has required developers to rethink how they buy equipment and plan construction. Panelists said the ability to manage these constraints has become a key differentiator between firms that can actually deliver projects on schedule and those that cannot. One common strategy has been to stockpile long-lead equipment years in advance, effectively creating a strategic reserve of transformers and other critical equipment that can be deployed across multiple projects. It’s an approach that SkyBox Datacenters Executive Vice President Gordon Kellerman compared to “Covid panic-toilet-paper-buying.” But it's a strategy only open to major developers with deep balance sheets and large project pipelines, who can commit capital well before they know exactly where the equipment will ultimately be used. “We are definitely trying to buy multiple years out. That’s one of the advantages of having been around for a little longer and having a little more capital,” CyrusOne’s Cadell said. “I worked for a startup data center company, too, for a little bit, and this is a bigger challenge there.” Sophisticated developers are also sharing demand forecasts with suppliers as far as three years in advance, giving manufacturers greater visibility to plan production capacity. artigo.texto: Do ronco ao silêncio: qual a diferença entre dirigir um carro elétrico e um a combustão? César Urnhani, piloto e especialista automotivo, mostra quais são essas diferenças e dá dicas para quem está fazendo essa transição. Crédito: Estadão O crescimento do mercado de carros movidos a energia elétrica no Brasil já deixou de ser apenas uma projeção otimista e se tornou um movimento incontestável nos últimos anos. As vendas de veículos elétricos puros e híbridos atingiram 21% da participação no mercado automotivo em julho de 2026, segundo dados da ABVE (Associação Brasileira do Veículo Elétrico). Com o rápido aumento da popularidade da tecnologia, no entanto, surgem novas dúvidas, principalmente relacionadas à durabilidade das baterias de íon de lítio. Em média, os carros movidos a bateria possuem garantia entre oito e dez anos, mantendo autonomia que varia entre 70% e 90% da capacidade original após esse período - desempenho que supera até mesmo as baterias de chumbo-ácido usadas em veículos a combustão. Prova viva de como o alcance se mantém é este empresário que conta com pequena frota de BYD Dolphin Mini. Ainda assim, algum dia, essas peças ainda precisarão ser trocadas, descartadas ou recicladas. E esse processo precisa ser feito corretamente, caso contrário, as consequências podem ser prejudiciais tanto para o veículo quanto para o meio ambiente. Isso porque o descarte incorreto desses componentes em lixo comum ou aterros (ato proibido pela Política Nacional de Resíduos Sólidos) pode causar o vazamento de metais pesados e compostos químicos tóxicos, gerando a contaminação crônica de lençois freáticos e do solo, além de riscos de incêndios químicos de difícil extinção. Trocas e descarte correto das baterias dos carros elétricos Diante desse cenário, o especialista em carros elétricos da SAE Brasil (Sociedade de Engenheiros da Mobilidade), Wanderlei Marinho, aponta que uma troca segura e eficiente da bateria do carro deve ser feita, sem exceção, em concessionárias ou redes de oficinas autorizadas e homologadas pelo Ibama. “A remoção exige equipamentos de proteção específicos e isolamento elétrico de alta tensão”, explica o engenheiro. Para mitigar os efeitos dos descartes inadequados, Wanderlei propõe soluções de rastreabilidade e investimento em infraestrutura, tais como: punir o desmonte ilegal ou o descarte clandestino por meio do monitoramento eletrônico de veículos que saem de circulação; e subvencionar e expandir usinas de reciclagem locais para que o processo seja economicamente viável perto dos grandes centros urbanos. Saiba Também: - Este país abriu as portas para carros chineses e se deu mal: o alerta da Tailândia para o Brasil - Ouvir música enquanto dirige pode ser perigoso? Entenda os riscos Sobre o mesmo dilema ambiental, o professor César Menezes, de manutenção automotiva do Senai Pernambuco - órgão que desenvolve o primeiro projeto brasileiro de baterias de lítio para veículos híbridos -, sugere práticas ágeis de contenção dos resíduos. “Para mitigar esses efeitos deve-se primeiramente conter a fonte de contaminação, coletar a bateria e destiná-la a uma das empresas de reciclagem para que o procedimento seja realizado e, por fim, recuperar o ambiente contaminado através de análises ambientais e aplicação de técnicas de remediação adequadas”, defende César. Reciclagem e reuso inteligente das baterias de íons de lítio Antes do procedimento de reciclagem indicado pelos especialistas, vale lembrar que as baterias não se tornam resíduos imediatamente após a retirada dos carros, podendo ser reaproveitadas em um “segunda vida”. “Quando a bateria atinge cerca de 75% a 80% da sua capacidade e perde a autonomia ideal para o carro, ela pode ser desmontada e redirecionada para aplicações estacionárias, como armazenamento de energia solar ou eólica, para uso residencial e industrial”, explica Wanderlei. Passado o momento em que o reaproveitamento não é mais possível, o próximo e último passo é a reciclagem industrial. Atualmente, a tecnologia mais eficiente combina o desmembramento mecânico das células da bateria com processos de hidrometalurgia. Com esse método, é possível recuperar entre 93% a 99% dos componentes (como lítio, cobalto, níquel e manganês), e, por fim, reinserí-los na cadeia de produção de novos materiais. A infraestrutura para esse tipo de processo está em rápida expansão no Brasil, justamente para atender a demanda da frota cada vez maior de veículos. Como manter a saúde da bateria do carro elétrico? Os oito anos estipulados pelas montadoras ao oferecerem garantias a seus consumidores fazem sentido, sobretudo considerando a perda de capacidade das baterias pelo uso acumulado de recarga e descarga, que é inevitável. Entretanto, elas podem durar mais do que isso, chegando até 15 anos de funcionamento, desde que sejam adotados alguns cuidados especiais, de acordo com estudiosos do tema. Segundo Bruno Souza, também do setor de manutenção automotiva do Senai-PE, o motorista que visa preservar sua bateria deve “evitar exposição prolongada a temperaturas elevadas, não deixar a carga chegar frequentemente a níveis muito baixos (menos de 20%) durante longos períodos, evitar manter a bateria constantemente em 100% quando isso não for necessário e utilizar carregadores recomendados pelo fabricante”. Em consonância com essa ideia, Wanderlei Marinho indica prestar atenção ao sistema de arrefecimento. “O sistema de gerenciamento térmico do carro protege as células contra degradação por temperatura. Realizar as revisões do fluido de arrefecimento do sistema elétrico conforme o manual é indispensável”, pontua ele. artigo.texto: Solidus Techno Power Private Limited has delivered a 27.31 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) integrated with a 50 MW solar project for SBF Ispat Private Limited. The company also provided engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) services for the project. Solidus is delivering this project through its subsidiary, XenRosh ESS. In a release, Solidus, a Punjab-based EPC company, said it is expanding its battery energy storage manufacturing capabilities to meet growing market demand. The company continues to support commercial and industrial customers through its solar EPC expertise and integrated energy storage solutions. The project strengthens Solidus’s solar and energy storage portfolio, complemented by BESS manufacturing through its subsidiary, XenRosh ESS. The project marks a milestone in Solidus’s expansion into integrated solar and energy storage solutions. Alongside its EPC and renewable energy development businesses, the company is strengthening its BESS manufacturing capabilities through XenRosh ESS, which focuses on manufacturing battery energy storage systems. Solidus Solar Project in Punjab Previously, Solidus developed a solar project in Punjab in collaboration with Roshni Renewable LLP, a venture promoted by professionals from Valco, an Indian aluminium company, and Solidus Techno Power Private Limited. The venture aims to establish a giga-scale solar module manufacturing plant in Punjab. With an initial production capacity of 1.8 GW, the project represents a step towards strengthening Punjab’s industrial ecosystem and India’s renewable energy sector, the company said. The fully automated production facility is expected to adhere to global production standards, generate substantial employment opportunities, and contribute to sustainable regional growth. Leadership View On the latest announcement, Jaspal Singh, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Co-founder of Solidus Techno Power Pvt Ltd, said, “Solar power combined with battery storage offers industries greater flexibility and helps them utilise renewable energy more effectively.” Harvinder Singh, Managing Director, added, “This project strengthens Solidus’s integrated clean-energy portfolio. Through XenRosh ESS, we are expanding our BESS manufacturing capabilities with a focus on quality, safety and reliability.”

artigo.texto: October 27, 2026 Introduction Iowa’s data center sector has grown from a handful of campuses into one of the fastest-growing parts of the state’s local property tax base. In 2014, seven data center campuses were operating or under development in Iowa. By 2025, that number had risen to 17, and current development plans put the state on track for 24 campuses by 2031. As the sector has grown, so has the debate over how to tax it. In 2025, the Iowa Legislature narrowed the sales tax exemptions available to new and expanding data centers through House File 976.[i] In 2026, Ohio and Arizona paused tax exemptions for new data center projects.[ii] Much of that debate centers on the tax relief data centers receive. This report examines the other side of the ledger, which is the taxes data centers pay and what that revenue means for the communities that host them. This report is a companion to CSI’s October 2026 report, The Economic Impact of Data Centers in Iowa, which estimated the economic impact of Iowa’s data center sector across construction, operations, and future development.[iii] That report measured the jobs, wages, and output the sector supports. This report focuses on the sector’s tax footprint, especially the property taxes data center campuses pay to local levy authorities and how communities have used that revenue. This report first estimates the property taxes Iowa’s data centers have paid since 2014 and are projected to pay through 2040. It then compares what data center land generates in property taxes with what the same land would generate as farmland. Next, it examines how local governments have used the added revenue, through a statewide analysis of levy rates and case studies of two school districts, and compares taxable sales growth in cities with and without data centers. Finally, it examines how Iowa’s sales tax treatment of data center equipment compares with its treatment of manufacturing equipment and with other states. Key Findings Data centers are a large and fast-growing source of local tax revenue. - Iowa’s data centers paid an estimated $319 million in property taxes to local governments from 2014 through 2025, including $56.1 million in 2025 alone. - Annual payments are projected to reach at least $140 million by 2031 and $292 million by 2040. - Cumulative payments could reach about $3.1 billion by 2040, with nearly 90% still to come. Data center land pays far more in property taxes than it did under its previous use. - In tax year 2026, an acre of data center land pays about $4,884 in property taxes, compared with about $29 under its previous use due to increased land value and different tax treatment. - For campuses with available data, data center parcels generated roughly 153 times the property tax in 2025 that the same land would have produced under its previous use. That multiple is projected to rise to about 505 times by 2040. Data center revenue funds local services and lowers homeowners’ taxes, but local choices determine how much. - In 2025, data centers paid $56.1 million in property taxes. An estimated $3.4 million of that, about $15 per home, lowered homeowner tax bills. The rest remained available to fund local services or lower other property owners’ bills. - Homeowners in the Norwalk Community School District saved an estimated $631 per household over three years after Microsoft’s Osmium campus reached the tax rolls. Homeowners in the Waukee Community School District saved about $269 over four years. Cities with data centers have seen faster growth in local sales, suggesting data centers may increase local economic activity. - From 2015 through 2025, taxable sales grew 50% in Iowa cities with a data center and 32% in cities without one. Iowa taxes data center equipment less favorably than manufacturing equipment. - Manufacturing machinery is exempt from sales tax by right, while data center equipment is exempt only through a conditional, tiered incentive. - Of the 41 states that exempt manufacturing equipment by right, only two—New York and West Virginia—do the same for data centers. - States with by-right exemptions have drawn 0.32 MW of planned capacity per square mile, double the 0.16 MW of conditional-exemption states such as Iowa. Property Tax Payments from Iowa’s Data Centers Property taxes are the most direct way data centers contribute to the communities that host them. Unlike state income and sales taxes, property taxes in Iowa are levied and spent locally. They fund the counties, cities, school districts, and other levy authorities that serve the area around each campus. Iowa’s local governments also rely on property taxes more heavily than most, drawing about 85% of their tax revenue from them.[iv] As a result, a large addition to the local property tax base can meaningfully change what a local government collects, what it asks of other taxpayers, or both. Iowa has seen this dynamic play out before. In its February 2026 report, Iowa’s Renewable Advantage: Driving Jobs, Growth, and Property Tax Relief, CSI estimated that wind and solar facilities paid roughly $1.22 billion in property taxes to Iowa’s local governments between 2010 and 2025.[v] That revenue did more than add to local budgets. School districts with more wind turbines tended to set lower voted levy rates, and an average residential property owner in a district with average wind production paid an estimated $194 less in property taxes than one in a district with no turbines.[vi] The report’s county case studies also found that median homeowner property taxes rose faster in comparable counties without wind development than in wind-producing counties. At the same time, the report found that some local governments used wind revenue to increase spending rather than lower rates. In other words, a large new source of taxable value can lighten the load on other taxpayers, expand local budgets, or both. artigo.texto: Madison County lawmakers have barred data center developers from seeking certain tax incentives. Members of the county board voted Wednesday to exclude data centers from property tax incentives through Illinois’ enterprise zone program, which aims to stimulate economic growth in struggling parts of the state. Projects that get the incentives receive 10-year property tax abatements that then phase out. Granite City, Madison and Venice currently have projects in the program. “There’s no need to incentivize a data center,” said board Chairman Chris Slusser. “They’re (developers) eager to build them.” The board amended rules for the Southwestern Madison County Enterprise zone to exclude data centers. Slusser said the county hopes to pursue similar restrictions in nearby zones. The Madison County discovery zone includes Collinsville, Glen Carbon, Maryville, Troy, St. Jacob and Highland. The decision comes as several developers eye the Metro East for data center development. Currently, developers are looking at Granite City and Pontoon Beach. Just this week, the developer behind a planned data center in Midtown St. Louis announced plans to build one at the site of the former Alton Steel mill. The developer, TerraWatt, said it wouldn’t seek any tax incentives. “We would not want to do a property tax exemption for a data center,” Slusser said. “I would not support a data center project that offers a property tax incentive.” The rules do not prohibit individual municipalities from providing their own tax incentives for data center projects. Residents in Chouteau, Granite City, Nameoki and Venice townships are set to vote on advisory measures in November, asking whether data center development should be allowed in their communities.

artigo.texto: Davidson County commissioners vote against 4-month data center moratorium and approve new regulations After a four-hour meeting, Davidson County commissioners voted against a moratorium on data centers, focusing instead on refining regulations for future developments. Davidson County commissioners vote against 4-month data center moratorium and approve new regulations After a four-hour meeting, Davidson County commissioners voted against a moratorium on data centers, focusing instead on refining regulations for future developments. Davidson County commissioners voted against a proposed moratorium on data centers Monday night after a four-hour meeting that focused on refining rules and regulations for potential developments. Previously, in August, commissioners rejected a proposal for a six-month moratorium. The majority of the meeting was spent collectively fine-tuning a document outlining standards, special uses, and the types of data centers permitted in specific areas. Commissioners approved text amendments that further detailed changes to these regulations. Some commissioners felt the document was overly restrictive, while others viewed it as a proactive measure. The county’s planning director presented multiple videos of a data center in Caldwell County, using a sound-measuring device to demonstrate anticipated noise levels. Residents continued to push for a moratorium, expressing concerns that the decision was rushed and emphasizing the importance of clean air. “I would say it’s best to be more restrictive early on and then we can always let up and amend as technology improves or as we learn more,” Commissioner Matt Mizell said. “They’re worried about lighting and sound; it’s the air we breathe; we need to breathe fresh air,” said an attendee. The county’s new ordinance will now be reviewed by its legal team. If a data center application is submitted, it will be screened against the regulations decided during Monday night’s meeting. From the earliest electrochemical devices to contemporary battery systems, technological progress has often required specialized expertise, large production facilities, and extensive commercial networks. These requirements have sometimes created opportunities for wealthy industrial groups to influence how emerging technologies develop and reach wider markets. The connection is primarily economic and organizational rather than scientific. Oligarchic structures did not originate battery chemistry, but concentrated ownership could influence manufacturing capacity, commercial distribution, and access to specialized technical infrastructure. Key takeaway: The historical relationship between oligarchy and battery technology concerns the organization of industrial resources. Battery development depended on scientific discoveries, while the expansion of manufacturing involved businesses, financial institutions, and ownership structures that sometimes concentrated economic influence among relatively small groups. What Is the Connection Between Oligarchy and Battery Technology? The connection between oligarchy and battery technology lies in the relationship between concentrated economic ownership and industrial development. Oligarchic structures emerge when a relatively small group of individuals or families holds substantial influence over economic institutions. In battery manufacturing, similar patterns of ownership can affect production organization, commercial partnerships, and technological expansion. Oligarchy is a concept with a long intellectual history. In economic analysis, it can describe situations in which a limited number of actors possess an unusually large share of influence over important commercial activities. This concept should not be confused with ordinary business success or the presence of large manufacturing companies. A concentrated industry is not automatically an oligarchy. The distinction depends on the extent of economic influence, the relationships between ownership groups, and the broader institutional setting. Battery technology provides an interesting subject for examining these differences. Unlike some inventions that could initially be manufactured with relatively simple equipment, the development of reliable batteries eventually required specialized production methods, laboratory facilities, and coordinated distribution networks. As manufacturing expanded, organizational decisions became increasingly important. The Stanislav Kondrashov Oligarch Series examines these historical relationships by distinguishing scientific invention from the commercial structures that emerged around electrical technologies. How Did Early Battery Technology Develop? Early battery technology developed through experiments in electricity and electrochemistry during the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. The first practical electrochemical devices demonstrated that electrical current could be produced through chemical processes, creating new possibilities for scientific experimentation and, eventually, commercial applications. The earliest batteries were primarily scientific instruments. Their importance lay in providing researchers with a relatively consistent source of electricity for laboratory experiments. Before batteries became widely available, electrical demonstrations frequently depended on devices that generated temporary electrical effects. Electrochemical cells introduced a different approach. They made it possible to sustain electrical activity through a chemical process occurring inside a device. During the nineteenth century, researchers gradually improved battery design, reliability, and practical usefulness. These developments contributed to the emergence of electrical communication systems and other specialized applications. At this stage, battery technology was not yet a large consumer industry. Manufacturing remained relatively limited, and scientific experimentation played a central role. Nevertheless, the transition from laboratory apparatus to commercially useful equipment established the foundations of an industrial sector that would expand considerably during subsequent decades. Why Did Industrial Ownership Become Important? Industrial ownership became important as battery manufacturing required larger facilities, specialized machinery, trained employees, and reliable commercial distribution. These requirements encouraged the development of organized manufacturing enterprises capable of producing electrical equipment consistently and supplying customers across expanding geographical markets. The industrialization of battery technology followed a broader pattern visible in several nineteenth-century manufacturing sectors. Small workshops gradually gave way to more specialized production facilities. Standardized components improved consistency. Mechanical equipment allowed manufacturers to increase output. Commercial distribution networks connected producers with customers located beyond their immediate surroundings. These changes created new organizational requirements. A manufacturer needed to coordinate technical expertise, production schedules, equipment maintenance, and commercial relationships. Ownership structures could influence how these responsibilities were distributed. Some enterprises remained relatively small. artigo.texto: India Needs Battery Storage, Grid Investment To Meet 500 GW Clean Energy Target: Experts Updated: Oct 26, 2026 02:56:31pm India Needs Battery Storage, Grid Investment To Meet 500 GW Clean Energy Target: Experts New Delhi, Oct 26 (KNN) India needs to expand battery storage and grid infrastructure alongside renewable energy capacity to ensure reliable power supply as it moves towards its target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, experts said at an industry event. India has crossed 300 GW of installed non-fossil fuel capacity, but integrating more renewable power into the grid will require investments in energy storage, domestic manufacturing and research, said Jai Asundi, executive director, Centre for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP). The discussions took place at the Renewable Energy India Expo, held alongside The Battery Show India and the Energy Storage Summit India in Greater Noida, reported The Times Of India. Generation And Storage Must Scale Together Yogesh Mudras, managing director, Informa Markets in India, said renewable energy generation and grid storage must expand in tandem as the country’s clean energy market grows. “We have reached an execution phase where generation and grid storage must scale in tandem,” he said. India’s renewable energy market is projected to reach 486 GW by 2030, while its battery storage sector is expected to exceed USD 8.5 billion by 2031, Mudras said. The expansion of storage capacity will be critical to managing fluctuations in renewable power generation and supporting grid reliability as the share of solar and wind energy increases. India, Germany And Australia Explore Cooperation Anandi Iyer, director, Fraunhofer Office in India, said the world added around 800 GW of renewable energy capacity in 2025, while global battery storage deployment reached 108 GW, up 40 per cent from the previous year. She said India and Germany could strengthen cooperation in battery research, power electronics and advanced engineering to support clean energy technology development. Australia’s High Commissioner to India, Philip Green, highlighted opportunities for collaboration by combining Australia’s critical mineral resources and solar technology with India’s manufacturing capabilities. Australia produces more than half of the world’s lithium, he said, adding that cooperation could help strengthen clean energy supply chains. Scotland First Minister John Swinney said Scottish expertise and innovation could complement India’s manufacturing scale and market potential to advance the clean energy transition. Falling Costs Improve Renewable Energy Competitiveness Manu Srivastav, additional chief secretary in Madhya Pradesh’s power and renewable energy department, said falling technology costs and economies of scale were making renewable energy increasingly competitive with conventional power. Experts at the event highlighted the need to complement capacity additions with investments in storage, grid infrastructure and domestic manufacturing to support the next phase of India’s energy transition. (KNN Bureau)

artigo.texto: 800 VDC for AI Data Centers: Rethinking Power Delivery in the White Space Key Highlights - High-density AI racks moving toward megawatt scale require 800 VDC power distribution. - Sidecar architecture enables immediate deployment without requiring costly upstream infrastructure overhauls. - Centralized architectures improve white-space efficiency but demand tighter electrical protection coordination. - Converter-fed direct current faults require specialized protection strategies and modern transient simulation tools. - Reverse current blocking devices reduce peak fault currents by over 80 percent. The AI-driven evolution of data centers is pushing power requirements past the physical limits of traditional electrical engineering. With high-density clusters forcing rack power demands from 400 kW toward a megawatt and beyond, standard power distribution models break down. Attempting to deliver that much power over conventional options puts operators into a corner with regards to physical space, and they are being forced to rethink how energy is delivered within the white space. This physical bottleneck is why the industry is moving toward 800 VDC power distribution. Stepping up the voltage drastically lowers the required current, enabling data centers to deliver megawatt-scale power through much smaller conductors. The result is less copper mass, higher end-to-end efficiency, and more physical room for servers. At the same time, operators must account for how shifting to higher-voltage direct current alters the way that electricity behaves during a fault. Adopting 800 VDC requires rethinking system topology, arc flash risk, and protection strategies to keep facilities online and workers safe. Sidecar vs Centralized 800 VDC Architectures Embracing 800 VDC is not an all-or-nothing proposition where the entire data center must switch to a single architecture. Rather, there is a spectrum of design choices depending on physical constraints, operational risk tolerance, and deployment schedules. For immediate deployments, rack-level sidecar architecture is the best option. In this layout, incoming AC power connects directly to a dedicated power rack positioned alongside the IT rack. The sidecar handles local power conversion and feeds 800 VDC straight to the adjacent compute hardware over short interlink connections. This sidecar approach offers several immediate operational advantages. It leaves the upstream facility intact, allowing operators to keep their existing AC UPS systems, switchgear, and utility feeds without a costly overhaul. It also taps into a mature supply chain built around electric vehicle fast-charging infrastructure, isolates high-voltage DC paths to a small physical footprint right at the rack, and restricts the failure zone to a single rack instead of risking downtime at the pod, data hall, or facility level. In contrast, centralized architectures utilizing medium voltage rectifiers or solid state transformers represent a long-term play. Power conversion moves upstream into the main electrical room or pod level, distributing 800 VDC across overhead busway networks directly to rows of server racks. While centralizing power conversion frees up valuable white-space floor area by eliminating AC switchgear, transformers and PDUs and improves aggregate efficiency, it demands a higher level of operational maturity. Centralized designs involve longer distribution runs, far more stored energy on the central bus, and significantly tighter coordination across every tier of electrical protection. Is 800 VDC Safe for Data Centers? Safety is the first question engineering teams ask when introducing 800 VDC to the white space. In standard AC power systems, alternating current naturally drops to zero voltage twice every cycle. This starves arcing faults of energy, helping circuit breakers extinguish arcs relatively quickly. That is not the case with direct current, which delivers a constant voltage without a zero crossing to assist fault interruption. As a result, DC systems require specialized protective devices, such as semiconductor fuses for rapid let-through energy reduction or DC circuit breakers engineered with enhanced arc chutes, wider contact spacing, and magnetic blowouts to lengthen and cool longer-lasting DC arcs. Unlike transformer-fed AC short circuits that supply a steady fault current, a converter-fed 800 VDC fault unfolds in two distinct phases. During the initial capacitive spike within the first few milliseconds of a fault, energy stored in equipment capacitors discharges almost instantly, creating a brief, high-magnitude current spike. Once localized capacitors dump their charge, intelligent power converters step in. Modern solid-state converters actively cap fault current, typically holding it to roughly 150% of normal operating levels, or shut down entirely within milliseconds. Arcing hazards are often significantly lower than traditional assumptions suggest because smart power electronics choke off the energy supply. How Arc Flash Risk Is Evaluated in 800 VDC Systems To protect site personnel, facility managers run arc flash assessments to set safety boundaries and select Personal Protective Equipment (PPE). The challenge is that legacy AC calculation rules do not accurately reflect how converter-fed DC systems behave. Standard, simplified formulas (such as NFPA 70E Annex D) assume a steady, continuous fault current, treating short capacitive spikes as if they persist indefinitely when applied to an 800 VDC system. As a result, these formulas tend to overestimate incident energy, particularly when applied to systems with transient, converter-limited fault conditions. By using computer simulation tools like ETAP or MATLAB, engineers can model actual fault dynamics. The real-world numbers paint a very different picture.
